desc: Optional, skippable refresher: Git, the shell, and the Go toolchain (go, modules, run/build/test).
text: Let me be transparent with you for exactly one sentence: this chapter is optional. If you've already got Go installed, you know what a terminal is, and you've typed go build at least once in your life — skip ahead. Chapter 1 is waiting, and it's where the real work begins. Still here? Good. That means one of two things: you're brand new to Go's toolchain, or you've been winging it and you want to understand what you've actually been running. Either way, you're in the right place. I'll cover the toolchain, modules, and the shell basics a Go developer actually needs — in the time it takes to drink a coffee. Fast, complete, and no wasted motion. That's how I do everything.

heading: The Toolchain
text: The Go toolchain is the single go binary that ships with every Go installation. It contains the compiler, linker, test runner, formatter, static analyzer, and module manager — invoked as subcommands (go build, go test, go vet, …). One install, everything included. Goes deeper in Building & Shipping Go Binaries. Let's start with the thing you run every single day: the go command. It's not a dozen separate tools — it's one binary that does everything. Here's the subset that matters right now. go run main.go compiles your program into a temp binary and immediately executes it. Perfect for quick iteration. Not for production deployment — the compiled artifact is thrown away. go build compiles your package into a binary on disk. For a main package, you get an executable named after the module (or the directory). This is what you ship. go test ./... finds every test.go file in every package under the current directory and runs them. The ./... pattern is the idiomatic "all packages." Learn it by heart. go vet ./... runs Go's built-in static analyzer. It catches real bugs the compiler misses — unreachable code, mismatched Printf format strings, a mutex copied by value. Always run it. go fm

heading: Go Modules
text: Before Go modules (pre-1.11), everyone put their code in $GOPATH/src/github.com/you/yourproject and dependency management was a collective nightmare. Modules ended that. Understanding the before-and-after will keep you from being confused by ancient Stack Overflow answers.

heading: GOPATH: the old world (2 minutes of history)
text: In the GOPATH era, all Go code on your machine lived under one directory tree — typically /go. Your project was at $GOPATH/src/github.com/yourorg/yourservice. Dependencies were fetched with go get and landed in $GOPATH/src alongside your own code. There was no versioning, no lockfile, and no isolation between projects. Two projects that needed different versions of the same library would fight each other. It was, and I say this with professional authority, a mess.

heading: Modules: the new world (Go 1.11+, required since 1.16)
text: A module is the unit of versioning and distribution in Go. It's a directory tree of Go source files with a go.mod file at the root. go.mod declares the module's own import path, the minimum Go version it needs, and its direct dependencies with their minimum versions. The module system replaced the old GOPATH arrangement in Go 1.11 and has been required since 1.16. A module is a directory tree of Go source code with a go.mod file at its root. The go.mod file declares: 1. The module's own import path (e.g. github.com/acme/payments) 2. The minimum Go version this module requires 3. Its direct dependencies with their minimum required versions You can put your module anywhere on disk. No GOPATH constraint. That single command creates a go.mod. Here's what it looks like for our healthcheck service: When you add a dependency (say, a request router): Go adds it to go.mod and pins the exact checksum in go.sum. The go.sum file is a cryptographic ledger — every module version you depend on has its expected SHA-256 hash. Tamper with a dependency and the build fails. This is the supply-chain security you didn't have with GOPATH. Your module's manifest. Declares the module path, minimum Go versi

heading: Cross-Compilation & Env
text: Here's where Go earns its production reputation. Building a Linux ARM64 binary from your macOS laptop takes one command: No cross-compiler toolchain. No Docker. No fuss. Go ships with support for every major OS/arch combination baked in, and it produces statically linked binaries that need nothing installed on the target machine. GOOS and GOARCH are environment variables that tell the Go compiler which OS and CPU architecture to target. Set them before go build and you get a binary for that platform — no cross-compiler, no container required. GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 builds for Linux on Apple Silicon/AWS Graviton. The full matrix of supported pairs is printed by go tool dist list. The two environment variables every Go developer should know: Target operating system. Common values: linux, darwin (macOS), windows, freebsd. Defaults to the machine you're building on. Target CPU architecture. Common values: amd64 (x86-64), arm64 (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton), 386, arm. Defaults to the machine you're building on. Where go install puts installed binaries. Defaults to $GOPATH/bin (typically /go/bin). Add this to your $PATH so installed tools are available. The old workspace root. Still use

heading: What go build Produces
text: A static binary contains everything it needs to run: your compiled code, all imported packages, and the Go runtime (scheduler, garbage collector, memory allocator). Unlike a Java .jar (needs a JVM) or a Node app (needs the node runtime plus node modules), a Go static binary runs on a bare machine with nothing else installed. It's why Go is the language of choice for CLIs and container images deployed FROM scratch. Let's make this concrete and then tie it back to the animated pipeline we already saw. When you run go build -o healthcheck . on the healthcheck package, you get a single, statically linked native binary . No install step. No runtime dependency on the server. No "but what version of the JVM do you have?" No node modules. Copy it to the target machine. Run it. Every Go binary contains a copy of the Go runtime — roughly 200–300 KB of compiled code that provides: The goroutine scheduler (GMP model): multiplexes potentially millions of goroutines onto a small, fixed-size pool of OS threads. We'll go very deep on this in Part 2's scheduler chapter. The garbage collector (tri-color concurrent mark-sweep): reclaims heap memory without stopping the world for meaningful durations.

heading: Reading the Docs
text: Here's a confession most tutorials are too proud to make: everybody drowns in pkg.go.dev at first. You look up one function, it returns a type you've never seen, you open that type, it has a field of another type, you open that — and twenty minutes later you have thirty tabs open and no idea what you were originally trying to do. Definitions of definitions of definitions. I'm going to fix that permanently, because reading docs well is the single highest-leverage skill that separates an engineer from someone who just copies Stack Overflow. The root error is simple: you're reading a reference like it's a book. pkg.go.dev is a lookup table, not a tutorial. You don't read it cover to cover. You go in for one thing, get it, and leave. pkg.go.dev is the official documentation site for every public Go package; godoc is the tooling that generates it. Crucially, the docs aren't written separately — they're extracted directly from the doc comments in the package's source code. The site for the standard library shows the exact same text you'd get from go doc in your terminal, for the Go version that package targets. A doc comment is the // comment placed immediately above an exported declarat

heading: The disease vs. the cure, drawn
The five rules
text: 1. Anchor on ONE task — never 'understand the package.' Not "learn net/http." Instead: "GET a URL, read the body." You read only the path that serves that task. A task is a destination; without one, every link looks equally worth clicking, and that's how you drown. 2. First sentence only, to triage. Every Go doc's opening sentence is a designed, standalone summary. Read it, decide is this my function? , and move on. You do not read the rest of a doc block unless you've committed to using that symbol. 3. Signature → Example → prose, in that order. For any function: read the signature (what goes in, what comes out — that's 80% of what you need), then the runnable Example on the page, and only fall back to the prose if you're still confused. Examples are faster than definitions because they're real, working code. 4. Black-box every type until it blocks you. A type you receive is a name plus what it represents — not a door you must open. http.Get hands you Response; you need .Body and maybe .StatusCode. You do not need to expand Response → Header → MIMEHeader. Treat io.Reader as "a thing I can Read() from." Open a type only when you are actually blocked without its internals. 5. Two-ho

heading: Black-boxing, proven
text: Rule 4 sounds like a shortcut you'll pay for later. It isn't — it's how Go is designed to be used. You program against a type's contract , not its guts. Watch one function consume three completely different concrete types it knows nothing about, purely because each satisfies the one-line contract of io.Reader: Four lines of doc-reading (strings.NewReader, bytes.NewBufferString, io.LimitReader, io.ReadAll), zero type-definitions opened, and it works. That's the whole game. The browser invites rabbit holes because everything is a hyperlink. The go doc command does not — it prints one symbol at a time , offline, for the exact Go version you have installed. There is nothing to click, so you can't fall in. Live in go doc and the drowning problem mostly disappears: the tool enforces the two-hop discipline for you. The reading rules aren't folklore — they exploit how Go documentation is generated . Docs are extracted from source. go doc and pkg.go.dev read the // comment sitting directly above each exported declaration. chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
desc: Packages, variables, the basic types, zero values, control flow, and functions — the bedrock of every Go program.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Everyone thinks they can write Go. They type func main, they print "hello world," they feel like a genius. Adorable. You're not going to be one of those people. By the end of this chapter you'll understand what every line actually does — the package machine, the type system, the zero value, the one loop to rule them all — because I refuse to be associated with anyone who guesses. Let's begin. You're lucky to have me.

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Packages and main
text: Let me set the scene, because we never learn syntax in a vacuum — that's how amateurs do it. You're building the checkout service for an online store. The very first thing it has to do is the most embarrassing thing to get wrong: add up the prices in a cart . We'll build toward that for the whole chapter. And we'll store money the only way a professional ever does — as a whole number of cents (1499, not 14.99). Floating-point money is a crime, and we'll prosecute it properly in Part 3. For now, just trust me: integers. Here is the smallest real Go program that compiles and runs: Three pieces, and every one of them is load-bearing. Let me break it down — one idea at a time. package main — every Go file belongs to a package. The package named main is special: it's the one Go turns into an executable program. No main package, no runnable binary. import "fmt" — you pull in other packages by importing them. fmt ("format") is the standard library's printing and formatting package. Go is famously strict here: import something you don't use and the compiler refuses to build . Not a warning. A hard error. Good. Sloppiness shouldn't compile. func main() — the entry point. When you run the pr

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Under the Hood: there is no virtual machine
text: When you run go build (all examples in this course use Go 1.26 , the current stable release as of early 2026), Go's compiler turns your source straight into native machine code , and the linker bundles it — plus the Go runtime itself (the scheduler, the garbage collector, the memory allocator) — into one self-contained executable . No interpreter. No JVM. No node modules. No shared-library scavenger hunt on the production box. That's why a Go service deploys as a single file you can scp to a server, or drop into a FROM scratch Docker image that's a few megabytes total. The "runtime" isn't a program you install — it's a library statically linked inside your binary . When the OS loads that binary, the runtime boots up first, then it calls your main. Hold onto this picture. When we reach the scheduler and the garbage collector later in Part 2, we're talking about code that's shipping inside every binary you build — not some external daemon.

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Variables and Types
text: Go is statically typed : every variable has a type that's fixed at compile time. But Go is also smart enough to figure most of them out, so you rarely have to nag it. There are several ways to make a variable. You should know all of them and reach for the shortest one that's clear: That last form, :=, is the one you'll use 90% of the time. The catch: := only works inside a function . At package level (outside any function) you must use var. A variable is a named slot that holds a value of a fixed type. The short form price := 1499 is a declare-and-assign : Go creates the variable, figures out its type from the right-hand side (int here), and fills it in — all in one line. The longer var price int = 1499 says the same thing with more ceremony. Use := inside functions (where you declare things); use var at package level or when you want the zero value with no initial assignment. This is where the amateur reveals themselves. They learned C, so they write loops and declarations like they're being charged by the keystroke in the wrong direction: Both compute the same cart total. One of them makes me wince. The right-hand version says exactly what it means — "for each price p, add it to

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Under the Hood: a string is a window, not a buffer
text: A Go string is a tiny, read-only two-word header: a pointer to some bytes, and a length. That's it. The bytes are immutable — once a string exists, you cannot reach in and change byte 3. Try s[0] = 'X' and the compiler stops you cold. Strings are often UTF-8 text, and string literals in source usually are, but a string can contain arbitrary bytes. This has a consequence beginners trip over constantly: len(s) returns the number of bytes , not characters. The string "café" is four characters but five bytes , because é is encoded as two bytes in UTF-8. If you want to count characters (runes), you range over the string or use utf8.RuneCountInString. Why does Go do it this way? Because making the byte length cheap and the string immutable means strings can be sliced and passed around cheaply. Speed and safety, paid for with one sharp edge you now know about.

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Zero Values
text: Now the feature that separates Go from the languages that haunt your nightmares. In Go, every type has a zero value — the value a variable gets when you declare it without assigning anything. Numbers get 0, strings get "", booleans get false, and pointer/slice/map types get nil. There is no "undefined" or "garbage" like in C. Why it matters: you can declare an accumulator with var total int and immediately start adding to it, because Go guarantees it starts at exactly 0. Well-designed Go types are built so their zero value is already useful — you declare and go. In Go, a variable declared without a value is never garbage and never undefined. It gets its type's zero value — a sensible, defined default. This is a deliberate, load-bearing design decision, and it shows up everywhere in idiomatic Go. int, float64, byte, and friends all start at 0. The empty string. Length 0. Never nil. Every freshly declared bool is false. Reference-like types start as nil — the typed "nothing." (We'll meet these properly next chapter.) Pointers — and the new builtin that creates them — belong to a later chapter. But here's a small Go 1.26 upgrade worth knowing exists: new now accepts an optional initia

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Control Flow
text: Go's control flow is aggressively minimal, and I mean that as the highest compliment. Fewer constructs, fewer ways to be wrong. if needs no parentheses, always needs curly braces, and can run a little init statement first — perfect for the error-handling pattern you'll write ten thousand times: for is the only loop in Go. There is no while. There is no do-while. There's just for, wearing different outfits: Let me animate the workhorse — the three-part loop summing our cart — so you can see the condition-check / body / increment rhythm instead of just trusting it. switch is Go's clean answer to a stack of if/else. No fall-through by default (a feature — you almost never want C's accidental fall-through), and cases can be any value, not just integers:

chTitle: Go Fundamentals: Syntax, Types & Control Flow
heading: Functions
text: A function packages logic behind a name. The signature is read left to right: name, parameters with their types, then the return type(s). prices []int is a parameter named prices of type "slice of int." The lone int after the parentheses is the return type. Simple. Now the part that makes people fall in love with Go: A function packages a reusable piece of logic behind a name. In Go the signature reads left to right: func name(param type) returnType. The standout feature is that Go functions can return more than one value — the convention is always (result, error). This is how Go handles errors: no exceptions, no thrown values, no hidden control flow. The caller receives both values and is forced to acknowledge the error right there. If you ignore it with , you're making a deliberate, visible choice — not accidentally swallowing a failure. Functions can return multiple values. This is how Go does errors — no exceptions, no hidden control flow. A function returns its result and an error, side by side, and you deal with the error right there: That if err != nil check is the heartbeat of every Go program ever written. It looks repetitive. desc: Structs and methods, interfaces defined by the consumer, idiomatic error handling, and slices & maps in depth.
text: Welcome back. You survived the fundamentals. Cute. Now we actually design things. Last chapter we pushed ints around and called it a cart. Today we build systems — real abstractions with behavior, contracts enforced by the compiler, error paths that don't lie to you, and collections that don't hide their cost. We'll model an Account, define a Ledger interface, and handle a NotFound error the right way. When you're done, the code you write will look like it was written by someone who's been doing this for years. Because it was taught by someone who has been. Me. You're welcome.

heading: Structs
text: Here's the scenario. You're building a banking backend. Your first task: represent a customer account. An account has an ID, an owner's name, and a balance. You could pass three loose values to every function — but that's the kind of chaos that makes incident reports at 3am. You need one thing that holds all three, travels together, and has behavior attached. That thing is a struct . A struct is a named collection of typed fields grouped into one value. You define it once with type Account struct ; the compiler fixes the memory layout. Pass a struct around and you get a copy of every field — that copy semantics story (when copying is right vs. when you need a pointer) goes deep in the next chapter.

heading: Fields and Composite Literals
text: A struct is a named collection of typed fields. You define it once; the compiler locks in the layout. This definition is non-runnable on its own — it's a type declaration. But creating and using one absolutely is: Two things worth burning into memory right now: Named field syntax (ID: "acct-001") is mandatory in production code. Positional Account works but breaks silently if someone reorders the fields later. %+v prints field names alongside values — indispensable for quick debugging.

heading: Zero-Value Structs
text: Here's the beautiful part. A struct's zero value is a struct where every field is its zero value. No garbage. No undefined memory. Just "", 0, false, and nil exactly where you'd expect them. A Balance of 0 is the right starting value for a new account. That's the Go proverb in action: make the zero value useful . When you design your own structs, ask yourself: "Does an all-zero instance of this type make sense?" If yes, you're done. If not, you probably need a constructor function — and that's fine too. Go has always had a built-in new(T) that allocates a zeroed T and returns T. Go 1.26 extends it to accept an initial value expression : new(expr) allocates a value of the same type as the expression, initialises it to that value, and returns a pointer to it. This is handy when a struct field is intentionally a pointer (to signal "optional / unset"): Before Go 1.26 you needed either &years (which can alias the local variable in subtle ways if you reuse years) or a helper like func intPtr(n int) int (34). new(expr) is cleaner. The version is Go 1.26 — on older toolchains, keep using &years or a helper.

heading: Embedding and Composition (Not Inheritance)
text: Go has no inheritance. This is intentional and wonderful. Instead of Account extends BaseEntity, Go uses embedding — you include one struct inside another, and its fields and methods are promoted directly. Embedding is composition , not inheritance. Account doesn't become an AuditInfo — it has one and borrows its fields. This distinction matters when we get to interfaces: an embedded type's methods are promoted too, which is how Go builds up behavior without a class hierarchy. Named-field syntax: Account . Always use named fields in production — positional breaks when fields are reordered. Every field starts at its zero value. Design types so the zero value is valid and useful — then you don't need a constructor. An unnamed field of a struct type. Its fields and methods are promoted to the outer struct. Composition, not inheritance — no vtable, no overhead. Never use a positional composite literal (Account ) in production code. When a new field is added to the struct, every positional site silently misassigns values and the compiler doesn't always catch it. --

heading: Methods
text: A struct with fields but no behavior is just data. Methods give it behavior — they're functions with an extra receiver argument that binds them to a type. A method is a function with a receiver — an extra first argument that binds the function to a specific type. func (a Account) Summary() string is a value receiver : Go passes a copy of Account and the method cannot mutate the original. func (a Account) Deposit(n int) error is a pointer receiver : Go passes the address, so writes go to the real struct. Rule of thumb: read-only behavior uses value receivers; state-mutating behavior uses pointer receivers. Pick one and stay consistent across all methods of the type.

heading: Value Receivers
text: A value receiver gets a copy of the struct. The method can read every field but cannot mutate the original.

heading: Pointer Receivers
text: A pointer receiver gets the address of the struct. Mutations through it persist to the original. This is how you implement any method that changes state. a.Balance we return an error instead of going negative. This is idiomatic — return the error, let the caller decide. Never silently allow an overdraft.", pose: "blocked", role: "guard", state: "warn", beat: "problem" }, ]} caption="Pointer receivers mutate; value receivers read. Pick one per type and never mix them."

heading: The Receiver Intuition
text: The rule is simple: if the method needs to mutate the struct, or if the struct is large enough that copying it is wasteful, use a pointer receiver . Otherwise, a value receiver is fine and communicates "this method is read-only." There's one more hard rule: be consistent within a type . If any method on a type uses a pointer receiver, use pointer receivers on all methods of that type. Mixing the two makes the method set hard to reason about and breaks interface satisfaction in subtle ways (the full story is in the Data Semantics & Data-Oriented Design chapter — I'm giving you the practical rule now and the deep mechanics next time). Gets a copy. Safe for read-only methods. Communicates 'I don't mutate this.' Small structs only. Gets the address. Required for mutation. Also correct for large structs where copying is expensive. Pick one and stick to it across all methods of a type. Mixed receivers on one type is a code smell that breaks interface satisfaction. Calling a pointer-receiver method on a non-addressable value (e.g. a map element returned directly) won't compile. The compiler can't take the address of a temporary. Use a variable. --

heading: Interfaces
text: This is the section that separates Go engineers who get it from the ones still writing Java in a Go-shaped box. Pay attention. An interface is a set of method signatures. In Go, satisfaction is implicit : any type that has the right methods satisfies the interface — no implements keyword, no declaration at the type site. Crucially, the consumer (the package that needs the behavior) defines the interface, not the producer (the package that provides the concrete type). This keeps packages decoupled and interfaces small. A Ledger interface defined in the payment service contains only the methods that service actually calls — the Postgres implementation satisfies it for free without importing or knowing about the interface.

heading: The Consumer Defines the Interface
text: In most languages, the producer declares the interface: class Account implements IAccount . The type author announces what contracts it satisfies. Go flips this on its head. The consumer defines the interface. If your PaymentProcessor package needs something that can post a debit, you write that interface in your package. Any type from anywhere — even packages you don't own — that has a PostDebit method with the right signature automatically satisfies it. No declaration. No implements keyword. No coupling between packages. This is called implicit interface satisfaction , and it is the single most powerful design mechanism in Go. Why does this matter? Because: 1. It decouples packages. The ledger package doesn't import account. You can swap in any type that satisfies the interface — a real Account, a test double, a mock, a different implementation entirely. 2. Small interfaces. Because you define the interface where you use it, you define only what you need. The Debitable interface above has one method. That's intentional. 3. Retroactive satisfaction. You can make a third-party type satisfy your interface without touching its source. If database/sql.Tx happens to have the methods yo

heading: Implicit Satisfaction in Practice
text: Let's build the Ledger scenario end to end:

heading: The Empty Interface and any
text: any is an alias for interface — an interface with zero methods. Because every type in Go has at least zero methods, every type satisfies any. It is the escape hatch for genuinely heterogeneous data: JSON decoders, log fields, generic containers in older code. The cost is that all static type information is thrown away — you must recover it at runtime with a type assertion (v.(int), which panics if wrong) or a type switch. Prefer a named interface whenever you can name the behavior you need. any is a last resort. interface — written as any since Go 1.18 — is an interface with zero methods. Every type in Go satisfies it, because every type has at least zero methods. You'll see it in JSON decoding, generic logging, and old stdlib APIs. any is a last resort for genuinely heterogeneous data. The moment you can express the behavior you need as a named interface, do it. any throws away all static type safety and forces you to reach for type assertions at runtime — which panic if you're wrong.

heading: The Nil-Interface Trap (Intro)
text: This one bites every Go engineer exactly once, and I'd rather you bite it here than in production at 11pm. An interface value is two words internally: a type pointer (which concrete type is stored) and a data pointer (where the value lives). A nil interface has both words as nil. But there's a trap: a non-nil interface can hold a nil pointer. The classic manifestation comes up with error returns: The fix is simple: functions that return an interface type (error, your own interfaces) must return a true interface nil — return nil — not a typed nil pointer. Never return a concrete typed nil and let it be assigned to an interface. Part 2 covers the full typed-nil-error trap with every variation; for now, know the rule and know why it exists. Under the hood, every non-empty interface value is exactly two machine words — let's call them itab and data. itab (the interface table pointer) — points to a structure that contains: A pointer to the type metadata of the concrete type (its size, alignment, GC shape, name) A pointer to the method table : the actual function pointers for every method the interface requires, pre-resolved at the time the value was assigned to the interface data — hold

heading: Errors
text: Go's error handling is not a flaw. It's a philosophy. The philosophy is: every error is visible, every error is deliberate, and no error hides in a stack frame nobody checked . If that sounds boring, good. Boring is what runs in production. error is a plain interface built into Go's standard library: type error interface . Any type with an Error() string method is an error. A nil error means "no error" — the entire if err != nil idiom works because of this. This means you can create rich, typed errors with extra fields (like an account ID and the shortfall in cents) and the caller can extract those fields with errors.As. The full error-handling story — wrapping, chains, typed errors at scale — is Part 2.

heading: The error Interface
text: error is just an interface in the standard library: That's it. Any type that has an Error() string method is an error. This means: You can create errors trivially (errors.New, fmt.Errorf) You can create rich typed errors with extra fields The nil of an error interface value means "no error" — the entire error-handling pattern hinges on this

text: You saw this pattern in Go Fundamentals but let's make it explicit. Every time a function can fail, it returns (T, error). Every time you call that function, you check the error immediately and completely . No deferring, no ignoring, no . The wrapping with %w is important and we'll cover it in a moment. First, the cardinal sin: Discarding an error with is not laziness — it's sabotage. You are guaranteeing that the next engineer to be paged at 3am won't know why the books don't balance. Don't be that person.

heading: Sentinel Errors and errors.Is
text: Sometimes the caller needs to distinguish between types of errors. "Account not found" should be handled differently than "insufficient funds." Sentinel errors are package-level error values you compare against: The critical part: use errors.Is , not ==. errors.Is unwraps a chain of wrapped errors (from %w) to check if the sentinel appears anywhere in the chain. A plain == only checks the outermost error and misses wrapped sentinels.

heading: Slices & Maps
text: Last chapter you used []int and map[string]int without looking under the hood. That ends now. These aren't magic — they're data structures with specific costs and specific gotchas, and knowing their internals is the difference between writing fast, correct Go and writing slow, surprising Go. A slice is a three-word header: a pointer to an underlying array, a length (how many elements are visible), and a capacity (how many the array can hold before a reallocation). Copying a slice copies the header — both copies share the same backing array until one of them appends past capacity and triggers a fresh allocation. This shared-array aliasing is the source of a whole class of subtle bugs. The full escape-analysis and allocation story is Part 2 Performance Engineering.

heading: The Slice Header: Pointer, Length, Cap
text: A slice is three words : a pointer to the underlying array, a length, and a capacity.

text: append adds elements to a slice. When there's room in the underlying array (len This is the aliasing gotcha: two slice headers sharing the same underlying array can write on each other's data. The defensive pattern is the full slice expression s[low:high:max] to set capacity deliberately, or a copy when you need a genuinely independent slice. A slice value is three machine words: a pointer to the backing array, a length (int), and a capacity (int). heading: Maps: Swiss Tables and Unspecified Iteration
text: A map is Go's built-in hash table: map[KeyType]ValueType. Under the hood, as of Go 1.24, the standard runtime uses a Swiss Table-style implementation with groups of eight key-value slots and control bytes for fast probing. Two things that trip beginners: (1) accessing a missing key returns the zero value silently — always use the comma-ok idiom to distinguish "key absent" from "key present with zero value"; and (2) maps are not safe for concurrent access — a concurrent write races with any other access, and the runtime often terminates the program when it detects map misuse. Concurrent map patterns are covered in the Concurrency chapter. A map in Go is a hash table. As of Go 1.24's standard runtime, it is backed by a Swiss Table-style structure: groups of eight slots plus a control word, probed by hash fragments rather than by linked-list chaining. Watch keys get routed — the hash decides the bucket, collisions share it, and that routing is why iteration order is a lie: Run it twice and you should not expect the same order. The language spec leaves map iteration order unspecified, and the standard runtime deliberately varies it so programs that accidentally depend on order fail ear

heading: The Comma-Ok Idiom
text: Accessing a map key that doesn't exist returns the zero value for the value type — not a panic, not an error. That means balances["acct-999"] returns 0 silently. Internally, it uses: Slots : storage locations for key-value pairs. Groups : eight slots plus a control word. Control bytes : metadata that says whether a slot is empty/deleted/used and stores hash bits for fast rejection. Tables/directories : runtime structures that select and grow storage as the map changes. A per-map hash seed used by the runtime's probing and iteration behavior. How a lookup works: hash the key, use hash bits to choose the table/group probe path, compare the group's control bytes first, then compare full keys only for plausible matches. desc: Value vs pointer semantics and what copying really does; struct field ordering, alignment and padding; and designing data around how it's accessed, not just modeled.
text: Listen up, sport. This is the chapter where the amateurs fall behind and never catch up. Everyone learns to write Go code. Fewer learn what that code does to memory. Even fewer understand that the shape of your data — not the cleverness of your algorithms — is what separates a service humming along at 50,000 requests per second from one collapsing under the garbage collector's boot. Value semantics. Pointer semantics. Struct alignment. Data-oriented design. This is the mental model the rest of this course leans on. Get it right here and everything from goroutines to the GC will click into place. Get it wrong and you'll spend the rest of your career mystified by bugs that are, I assure you, completely your fault. You're extraordinarily lucky I'm the one explaining this. Let's make you dangerous.

heading: Value vs Pointer Semantics
text: Here's the scenario. You're on the payments team. You've got a Transaction type that your handlers read, validate, and pass around for processing. A new engineer touches it. Suddenly, a transaction that should have been declined gets approved. The logs say the validation ran. The validation says it rejected it. And yet: approved. Money went somewhere it shouldn't. That's a value/pointer semantics bug. I've seen it a dozen times. It always comes from someone who doesn't truly understand what happens when Go copies a value or follows a pointer. Today, that's not you.

heading: The Copy: what value semantics actually means
text: A variable holds the value itself , not a reference to it. Assignment and function calls copy every byte. Mutations to the copy are invisible to the original. Why it matters: small, immutable types are safe to share freely — the caller can never be surprised by a callee that modifies its own copy. In Go, assignment copies. Full stop. When you write b := a, Go copies every byte of a into b. They share nothing. Mutating b cannot affect a. This is value semantics — the name says it: you're working with the value , not with a reference to the original. Every field gets duplicated. The two variables occupy different addresses in memory. This is safe, predictable, and exactly what you want — unless you intended for both variables to observe the same mutation.

heading: The Pointer: what pointer semantics actually means
text: A variable holds an address pointing at a value elsewhere in memory. Assignment copies the address, not the data, so both sides share the same underlying value. Mutations through a pointer are visible to every holder of that address. Why it matters: required when a type is large (copying is expensive), has a managed lifecycle, or must be mutated by multiple parts of the program — but it introduces shared mutable state, which demands discipline. A pointer holds an address — where in memory a value lives. When you assign a pointer, you copy the address, not the value. Both variables now point at the same underlying data . Mutating through one is visible through the other. Now watch both side-by-side as an animation. This is the exact moment the payments bug above was born — a developer passed by value when they meant to mutate. The pointer version takes the same caller, the same struct — but passes an address instead of a copy. Watch the mutation survive the return this time:

heading: When to use value semantics vs pointer semantics
text: The receiver is the implicit first argument of a method — (t Transaction) is a value receiver (method gets a copy; mutations are lost), (t Transaction) is a pointer receiver (method operates on the original; mutations persist). Why it matters: the method set of a type changes depending on which kind you use, affecting which interfaces the type satisfies. Inconsistency between methods on the same type is a reliable source of subtle bugs. This is the decision you make once per type , and then you commit to it. Mixing both on one type is the source of the bug at the top of the section. Here's the rule of thumb: The type is small (fits in a few words), immutable or safely copyable, and has no identity beyond its data. Think: int, time.Time, a Point , a Money . Copying is cheap and correct. The type is large (copying is expensive), has a lifecycle you manage explicitly (open/close, acquire/release), must be shared and mutated by multiple parts of the program, or wraps OS resources. Think: http.Request, sql.DB, os.File. If a method mutates the receiver, it must use a pointer receiver (t Transaction). If all methods on a type use pointer receivers, never call a method on a non-addressable

heading: Struct Layout & Alignment
text: Now the part that trips up even experienced engineers. Your Transaction struct doesn't just hold your fields — it lays them out in memory according to rigid rules, and those rules can silently make your struct larger than you think. Alignment is the requirement that a value of size N start at a memory address divisible by N — e.g., an int64 must sit at a multiple-of-8 address. Padding is the invisible zero-bytes the compiler inserts between struct fields to satisfy alignment. The compiler never reorders your fields; it pads between them as declared. Why it matters: poor field ordering can silently inflate a struct's size by 40–60%, increasing memory use, GC pressure, and cache misses — with no warning from the compiler.

heading: What alignment is and why the hardware demands it
text: Modern CPUs read memory in word-sized chunks (typically 8 bytes on 64-bit systems). For performance and correctness, hardware often requires that a value of size N be stored at a memory address that's a multiple of N. This requirement is called alignment . An int64 (8 bytes) must start at an address divisible by 8. An int32 (4 bytes) must start at an address divisible by 4. A bool (1 byte) can sit anywhere. When the Go compiler lays out a struct, it honors these alignment requirements by inserting invisible padding bytes between fields. The size of your struct on disk, in memory, or over the wire may be larger than you expect. Let's prove it with unsafe.Sizeof: Run it. Watch WastefulEvent print 40 bytes and EfficientEvent print 24. That's a 40% size difference from nothing but field ordering — no logic changed, no data changed, just layout. Now let's watch the byte-by-byte story unfold so you can see why the padding appears: Now reorder the exact same five fields — biggest first — and watch the padding collapse:

heading: The padding rule you can apply immediately
text: The practical heuristic: order your struct fields largest to smallest. Group all your int64/float64/pointer fields first, then int32/uint32, then int16/uint16, then bool/int8/byte. This isn't always perfect but it eliminates the catastrophic cases. If you want the compiler to catch bad ordering automatically, golangci-lint ships fieldalignment — a linter that flags structs where reordering would shrink them. Add it to your CI. You can also run the analyzer directly: The Go spec defers alignment requirements to the target architecture, but in practice on amd64 (and arm64): bool, int8, uint8, byte: size 1, alignment 1 int16, uint16: size 2, alignment 2 int32, uint32, float32, rune: size 4, alignment 4 int64, uint64, float64, complex64, pointer, uintptr: size 8, alignment 8 int, uint: same as the native word size (8 bytes on 64-bit) A struct's alignment is the maximum alignment of any of its fields. A struct's total size is padded up to a multiple of its own alignment. Arrays have the same alignment as their element type. Interface values are two words (type pointer + data pointer or value). Why doesn't the compiler reorder fields automatically, the way some C compilers do with -fpack

heading: Data-Oriented Design
text: Here's where the philosophy kicks in. Most engineers model data the way they'd model it in a UML diagram: every entity is a struct, every entity has a pointer to the next one, and the whole system is a beautiful web of references. The hardware hates this. And the garbage collector hates it even more. Data-oriented design means shaping data structures around how they are accessed , not just how they are modeled. The two layouts are: Array of Structs (AoS) — []Transaction, each element holds all fields together; and Struct of Arrays (SoA) — parallel slices per field ([]int64 for amounts, []bool for flags). Why it matters: when a hot loop touches only a subset of fields (e.g., just Amount across 1M records), SoA loads only the needed field into cache — 8 amounts per 64-byte cache line vs. 2 full structs. Wrong layout = 10–50× slower without touching the algorithm.

heading: The scenario: scanning a million transactions
text: You're building a fraud detection pipeline. Every night, you scan a month's worth of transactions — a million records — looking for anomalies. The hot loop reads the Amount and Currency fields of every transaction and computes aggregate statistics. Profile this naively and you'll find your program spending most of its time not computing but waiting for memory . The problem is cache misses. A modern CPU L1 cache line is commonly 64 bytes. When the CPU loads data, it loads an entire cache line at once. If your data is laid out contiguously — each element right next to the previous one — each cache line load gives you multiple useful elements to process. If your data is pointer-chained — every element is a separate heap allocation scattered across memory — each element is a potential cache miss, and the CPU can stall for tens to hundreds of nanoseconds depending on platform, locality, and memory pressure. This is the Array of Structs (AoS) vs. Struct of Arrays (SoA) design choice, and it can determine whether a hot loop is merely fast or orders of magnitude slower despite using the same algorithm.

heading: Concrete vs pointer-chained data
text: The other dimension of data-oriented design: prefer []Transaction over [] Transaction when you own the lifecycle and don't need stable addresses. This isn't about micro-optimization. A fraud detection pipeline scanning 1M records can be 10–50× faster with contiguous layout vs. pointer-chained layout, purely because cache utilization goes from 33% to near 100% for the hot field. The algorithm is identical. The data layout is everything.

heading: When NOT to use SoA / contiguous layout
text: Data-oriented design isn't "always use SoA." It's "design data around how it's accessed." If you always fetch a complete transaction record — ID, Amount, Currency, Approved, all together — then []Transaction (AoS) is correct, because each cache line brings you everything you need for one record. SoA wins when your hot path touches only a subset of fields across many records. []int64 for amounts, []bool for approval flags. Your scan touches 100% of what it loads. []Transaction — load one struct, use all its fields. One allocation, one cache-line neighborhood. Use [] T when T is large and mutated independently, when stable addresses are required (concurrent goroutines holding references), or when T has a non-value lifecycle (implements io.Closer, etc.). Premature SoA is as harmful as premature optimization. Splitting a struct into parallel slices makes insertion/deletion harder, breaks at-a-glance clarity, and is wrong if your access pattern is whole-record. Profile first; reach for SoA when the profiler shows hot-field scans eating time.

heading: The full mechanical-sympathy story is in Part 2
text: This section gave you the first, usable taste of why data layout matters. The complete story — CPU cache hierarchies, cache-line size, false sharing between goroutines, branch prediction, and using pprof + go tool trace to measure all of it — lives in Part 2, Chapter 8: Performance Engineering . That's where we'll take a running service, profile it, watch the flame graphs, and apply everything you just learned here to real hot paths. Consider this chapter the vocabulary ; Part 2 is the practice . Escape analysis is the compiler pass that decides whether a value lives on the stack (cheap: a pointer bump, no GC) or the heap (allocated by the runtime, tracked and collected by the GC). A value "escapes" to the heap when it must outlive the function that created it — returned by address, stored in a heap struct, passed to a goroutine closure, or boxed into an any. Why it matters: taking a pointer when you didn't need to can silently push a value to the heap, adding GC pressure and destroying cache locality. Use go build -gcflags="-m" ./... to see every escape decision. Every goroutine starts with a small stack (about 2 KB in current Go implementations) that grows dynamically. Local vari

desc: Goroutines, channels, select, sync primitives, and the core concurrency patterns — with the scheduler underneath.
text: Listen up, sport. This is the chapter. The one that separates the Go programmers from the Go engineers . Anyone can spin up a goroutine. Precious few understand what happens when they do, why their program deadlocks at 3am, or why the race detector lit up like a Christmas tree in production. I have personally written concurrent Go that made distributed systems engineers weep — from admiration . You're going to learn it correctly, from the scheduler underneath to the patterns on top, because I refuse to send you into the world writing goroutine leaks and calling it "async." We're fanning out price lookups for a checkout service. Twelve vendors, one response deadline, one goroutine per vendor. By the end of this chapter, you'll build exactly that — correctly — and understand every moving part. Let's go.

heading: Goroutines
text: Here's the scene: a customer hits "Buy Now." Your checkout service needs prices from twelve vendor APIs — sequentially, that's 12 × 80ms = 960ms. Your SLA is 200ms. Sequential is a death sentence. You need concurrency. Go's answer is the goroutine : a lightweight, cooperatively-and-preemptively scheduled function that runs concurrently with everything else. You launch one with the go keyword, and the Go runtime handles the rest. A goroutine is a function running concurrently with the rest of your program, managed by the Go runtime rather than the OS. It starts with a 2 KB growable stack (versus 1–8 MB for an OS thread), so you can run hundreds of thousands of them. You create one with go f() — that's the entire syntax. Why it matters: goroutines are what make Go's concurrency model practical at scale; without them, concurrent I/O would require the same number of expensive OS threads as concurrent tasks. That's the problem. Now watch what concurrency looks like: All three calls are now in flight at the same instant. Because they overlap instead of queueing, the work finishes together rather than one after another:

heading: The go keyword
text: The only syntax you need is go in front of a function call: The call happens in a new goroutine. The calling goroutine — main in this case — continues immediately . There is no blocking, no thread ID to track, no handle returned. If you need the result, you'll use a channel (next section) or a sync.WaitGroup (sync section). If main() returns, every goroutine in the program dies instantly , even ones that haven't finished their work. That's why naive go examples sleep at the end — to keep main alive. In real code, you use a sync.WaitGroup or a done channel to wait properly.

heading: Concurrency vs. parallelism
text: These two words are not synonyms, and mixing them up is the kind of sloppiness I find personally offensive. Concurrency is the structure of your program — multiple things in progress at once, possibly taking turns on a single CPU. You can have concurrency on one core. Parallelism is simultaneous physical execution — multiple things running at the exact same clock tick on multiple CPU cores. Go's goroutines are concurrent by design. Whether they run in parallel depends on GOMAXPROCS — the maximum number of logical processors executing Go code at once. As of Go 1.25, the default is container-aware: it considers logical CPUs, CPU affinity, and Linux cgroup CPU quota. On a 4-core machine with no tighter quota, up to 4 goroutines run in true parallel. The rest take turns. As of Go 1.25, the runtime reads Linux cgroup CPU quotas and sets GOMAXPROCS accordingly — so a container with a 2-CPU limit gets 2 Ps without any library tricks. The full details and container deployment guidance are in Part 2 · Chapter 5 (The Go Scheduler in Depth) .

heading: Goroutines vs. OS threads
text: Why not just use OS threads directly? Because goroutines are dramatically cheaper: An OS thread starts with a 1–8 MB fixed stack. A goroutine starts with a small growable stack (about 2 KB in current Go implementations) that expands and contracts as needed. You can run hundreds of thousands of goroutines where threads would exhaust memory. OS thread context switches go through the kernel. Goroutine switches are coordinated in user space by the Go runtime scheduler, so the overhead is much lower and stays practical at very high concurrency. Spawning an OS thread needs a large stack reservation and kernel work. Spawning a goroutine starts with a small growable stack and runtime bookkeeping, so you can create large numbers of goroutines where threads would run out of memory first. Controls how many logical processors execute Go code simultaneously. Default: container-aware since Go 1.25. Setting it to 1 makes your concurrent program single-threaded — useful for debugging races. When a goroutine blocks on a network or disk call, the Go runtime parks it and gives its OS thread to another runnable goroutine. The blocked goroutine costs almost nothing while waiting. A goroutine that block

heading: Channels
text: Goroutines run concurrently. But how do they talk to each other, and how does a goroutine hand off a result without a data race? Channels — Go's typed communication pipes. Send a value in, receive it out. The channel handles synchronization for you. A data race happens when two goroutines access the same memory location concurrently and at least one of the accesses is a write — with no synchronization between them. The result is erroneous: you might read a stale or inconsistent value, or crash if the race corrupts a multiword runtime data structure. In Meridian's ledger service, a data race on an account balance could silently corrupt a transfer. Go ships a built-in race detector (go run -race) that catches these at runtime. A channel is a typed conduit for passing values between goroutines safely. Sending on a channel ( ch The Go proverb: "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating." Back to our checkout scenario: we need to collect prices from goroutines running in parallel. A channel is how each goroutine sends its result back to the collector.

heading: Unbuffered vs. buffered channels
text: A buffered channel decouples sender and receiver. The sender can drop up to cap(ch) values and keep going — no waiting — as long as the buffer isn't full. The receiver can drain those values even if the sender is long gone. Watch the mechanism itself — the buffer filling, draining, and the exact moment a send blocks : The buffer now holds all three prices and the senders are gone. main() drains them on the same results channel:

heading: Channel direction
text: Channels can be restricted to send-only or receive-only in a function signature. This is not a safety theater — it lets the compiler catch you sending where you should only receive, and vice versa. Use it on every function that owns one side of a channel: A bidirectional chan int can be passed anywhere a directional channel is expected — the restriction is applied at the usage site.

heading: Closing a channel and ranging over it
text: When a sender is done sending, it closes the channel. Receivers can detect this: The idiomatic pattern is range over a channel — it loops until the channel is closed and empty: Only the sender should close a channel. If you close a channel from multiple goroutines, or close it twice, you get a runtime panic. The rule: the goroutine that creates and sends on a channel is the one that closes it. The receiver never closes; it just detects the close via the second return value or a range loop ending.

heading: Nil channels
text: A nil channel (a chan int that was never initialized with make) blocks forever on both send and receive. This sounds useless, but it's a deliberate tool in select (next section) — you can disable a case by setting its channel to nil. A deadlock is a state where every goroutine in a program is blocked waiting for something that will never happen — so nothing can ever run again. Go's runtime detects the simplest case (all goroutines sleeping) and panics with all goroutines are asleep — deadlock!. A nil channel receive, two goroutines each waiting for the other to send first, or a sync.Mutex locked twice by the same goroutine are all classic deadlock triggers. Why it matters: a deadlock in a Meridian payment handler means the service hangs silently — no crash, no response, just a frozen process until your health check kills it. When you call make(chan int, 5), the runtime allocates an hchan struct on the heap. The key fields (simplified from runtime/chan.go): When a goroutine sends on a full channel (or an unbuffered channel with no receiver ready), the runtime: 1. Locks the hchan. 2. Creates a sudog (a goroutine/value pair) and enqueues it on sendq. 3. Parks the goroutine (marks it n

heading: select
text: You have N vendor goroutines, each sending on its own channel. You want a result as soon as one arrives, then move on. That's exactly what select does: it waits on multiple channel operations and runs one ready case. If several cases are ready at the same time, Go chooses among them pseudo-randomly. select is Go's multi-way channel switch. It blocks until one of its case channel operations is ready, then executes that case. If multiple cases are ready simultaneously, Go picks one at random (not the first written). A default case makes select non-blocking — it fires immediately if no channel is ready. Why it matters: select is how you implement timeouts, cancellation, and racing multiple concurrent results without spinning — it's the only way to wait on more than one channel at once.

heading: The default case — non-blocking channel ops
text: Add a default case and the select never blocks — if no channel is ready right now, it takes default immediately: This is the idiom for checking a channel without blocking — a non-blocking read/write.

heading: Timeout pattern with time.After
text: time.After(d) returns a time.After creates a new timer every call, not a goroutine. Since Go 1.23, unreferenced timers can be garbage-collected before they fire, so this is no longer the old "timer leak" trap. In a loop that calls it thousands of times per second, though, you're still allocating thousands of timers. In hot paths, reuse a time.Timer with Reset() — or better, use context.WithTimeout . We'll see context in full in Part 1 · Chapter 6 .

heading: Draining done channels
text: The canonical way to signal "stop now" across goroutines is a done channel — a chan struct you close when work is finished: Closing a channel broadcasts to all receivers simultaneously — every goroutine blocked on The done channel pattern you just learned is exactly what context.Context wraps into a proper API — cancellation, deadlines, and timeout in one. You should use context.Context in real production code instead of a raw done channel. It gets its own full chapter in Part 1 · Chapter 6 .

heading: sync Primitives
text: Channels are for communication between goroutines . When you just need to protect a shared value from concurrent reads and writes, reach for sync — it's simpler and faster. Back to our checkout: after collecting all vendor prices, we want to accumulate them into a summary struct from multiple goroutines. That struct needs a lock.

heading: sync.Mutex and sync.RWMutex
text: A sync.Mutex is a binary lock: held or not held. Only one goroutine can hold it at a time. Everyone else blocks until it's released. A sync.Mutex (mutual exclusion lock) is a binary lock: exactly one goroutine holds it at a time. Call mu.Lock() to acquire — any other goroutine that tries will block until you call mu.Unlock(). Always pair with defer mu.Unlock() so you can't forget to release it. A sync.RWMutex extends this to allow many concurrent readers but only one writer. Why it matters: when goroutines share a struct (like Meridian's account balance), a mutex turns a data race into a guarantee — only one goroutine mutates the value at a time. When goroutine 1 unlocks, the parked goroutines wake one at a time — the same lock simply changes hands down the line: sync.RWMutex is a reader-writer lock: multiple goroutines can hold the read lock simultaneously, but a writer needs exclusive access: Use RWMutex when reads heavily outnumber writes — a price cache, a config snapshot. If writes are frequent, a plain Mutex is often faster (less bookkeeping).

heading: sync.WaitGroup
text: A WaitGroup lets a goroutine wait for a collection of goroutines to finish. A sync.WaitGroup is a counter that tracks running goroutines. You increment it before spawning a goroutine (or use wg.Go in Go 1.25+, which does this automatically), the goroutine decrements it when done (wg.Done()), and the caller blocks on wg.Wait() until the counter reaches zero. Why it matters: without a WaitGroup (or a channel), main() exits and kills every goroutine before they finish — a silent data loss. The WaitGroup is the idiomatic "wait for all of them" tool when you don't need results (use a channel when you do). Go 1.25 added wg.Go(func()) — a single call that does wg.Add(1), spawns the goroutine, and wires up wg.Done() automatically. This is now the idiomatic way to launch tracked goroutines: If you're reading pre-1.25 code, you'll see the manual three-step pattern: Critical rule for both forms: wg.Add or wg.Go must be called before the goroutine starts running , never inside the goroutine. If the goroutine starts and calls wg.Done() before wg.Add(1) lands, you underflow and panic. wg.Go eliminates that footgun by design.

heading: sync.Once
text: sync.Once runs a function exactly once , even if called from thousands of goroutines simultaneously. The canonical use is lazy initialization of a shared resource: Use a mutex when you're protecting a shared value (a counter, a map, a struct). Use a channel when you're communicating between goroutines (passing results, signaling events, coordinating flow). Both prevent races; channels are richer but heavier. ⚠ Never copy a Mutex, WaitGroup, or Once after first use. They contain internal state. Pass them by pointer or embed them in a struct that's always used via a pointer. If you see func foo(mu sync.Mutex) — that's a copy, and the lock is now broken.

heading: Core Patterns
text: You have the primitives. Now the patterns — the idiomatic compositions that show up in every production Go service. We'll cover two here; the full catalog (fan-in/fan-out, pipelines, errgroup, singleflight, semaphores, heartbeats) lives in Part 2 · Chapter 5 (Concurrency Patterns) .

heading: Worker pool
text: You have a queue of jobs (e.g. price lookups for 500 products in a cart). You don't want 500 goroutines at once — that swamps the vendor APIs and exhausts memory. A worker pool caps concurrency: N workers drain a shared job channel. Each worker loops back to range jobs for the next SKU. The pool keeps churning through the remaining six jobs until the closed channel is drained:

heading: Generator / pipeline (intro)
text: A generator is a goroutine that produces a stream of values on demand, exposing them as a Each stage is a goroutine that reads from its input channel and writes to its output channel. Data flows through, one value at a time. Stages can be composed freely, run at their own pace, and shut down cleanly by closing the channel. The full pipeline and fan-in/fan-out catalog — including cancellation, error propagation with errgroup, and bounded parallelism — lives in Part 2 · Chapter 5. ⚠ Goroutine leak — the classic case: you launch a goroutine that sends on a channel. The receiver returns early (timeout, error, select picked a different case). The sender is now blocked on a channel nobody reads, forever. Fix: use a buffered channel so sends never block, OR add a done channel to your select so the sender can exit when signaled. ⚠ Loop variable capture (pre-Go 1.22): in a loop like for , v := range vendors , all goroutines captured the same v — the last iteration's value. Fix in older code: pass v as a parameter (go func(v string) (v)). In Go 1.22+, loop variables are per-iteration so this bug is gone — but you'll encounter pre-1.22 code in the wild. Know it. Go 1.26 adds an experimental g

heading: Exercises
text: You've watched the goroutines dance. Now make them dance for you . I want to see idiomatic code, not C++ with channel syntax. Let's go. Write a program that launches three goroutines. Each goroutine prints a greeting with its ID (1, 2, 3). Use a sync.WaitGroup to wait for all three before main returns. wg.Go (Go 1.25) handles wg.Add(1) and defer wg.Done() automatically — one call, no footguns. We capture id := i before the closure to pin each loop iteration's value. Write a fanOutPrices(vendors []string) []int function that launches one goroutine per vendor (each sleeps 20ms and returns 999), collects results into a buffered channel, and returns a slice of all prices. Demonstrate it runs in 20ms total, not N×20ms. The buffered channel (cap = len(vendors)) ensures goroutines never block on send. The closer goroutine waits for all workers before closing, enabling the range to terminate. Build a SafeCounter struct with an Inc() method and a Value() int method, protected by a sync.Mutex. Launch 1000 goroutines each calling Inc() once, then print the final count. Run it with go test -race (or confirm the count is always 1000). Without the mutex, the race detector (go run -race main.go)

heading: The Lab
text: Listen very carefully. I designed this test myself. It has exactly two bugs — a goroutine leak and a data race — and I am personally curious whether you can find them both. The race detector is your weapon. The flag is your reward. Don't embarrass me. This program fans out to four vendor goroutines and has two bugs that will bite you in production. Find them, fix them, and run the verifier. The observable invariants don't lie, and neither do I. You've earned the concurrency chapter. Let's lock in what you own: A goroutine is a lightweight concurrent function started with go. It begins with a small growable stack and is vastly cheaper than an OS thread. The Go runtime's GMP scheduler multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto a handful of OS threads via work-stealing. Channels are typed communication pipes between goroutines. Unbuffered channels are rendezvous points (both sides block until they meet). Buffered channels decouple sender and receiver up to the buffer capacity. close(ch) signals no more sends; range ch loops until closed. Only the sender closes. Receiving from a closed-and-empty channel returns the zero value with ok=false. select multiplexes channel operations — it wait

desc: Type parameters, constraints and type sets, inference and its limits, and how the compiler implements generics (GC-shape stenciling + dictionaries).
text: Let me tell you something. For years, the Go community argued about generics. People wrote blog posts. They filed issues. They begged . And I waited — patiently, like a professional — because I wasn't going to put my name on something half-baked. Go 1.18 landed generics in March 2022. Done correctly. Typed correctly. Implemented with an efficiency story nobody talks about because most people don't go deep enough to understand it. You're going to be different. You're going to know not just the syntax but how the compiler turns one generic function into machine code, why GC-shape stenciling exists, and when — precisely when — generics are the right tool versus an interface. By the end of this chapter, you'll write generic code that would make me nod. That's the highest compliment I give. Let's go. You're lucky to have me. --

heading: Reading the Syntax
text: Here's the scenario that makes generics feel necessary instead of academic. You're building a payments platform. You have []Transaction, []Account, and []AuditEntry — all slices of different types — and you keep writing the same Map, Filter, and Reduce functions for each. Three times. With copy-paste drift. When a bug appears in one, you hunt the other two. Before generics, your options were: copy-paste (criminal), an interface (loses type information), or reflection (slow and unreadable). After generics, you write the function once and the compiler enforces type-safety at every call site. A type parameter is a compile-time placeholder for a concrete type, written in square brackets after a function or type name — e.g. [T any]. The caller fills it in (either explicitly or by inference) and the compiler generates type-safe code for that specific type. Without type parameters you need one copy of the function per type; with them, you write it once. Instantiation is the act of supplying a concrete type for a type parameter, producing a specific version of the generic function or type. It can be explicit (Minint) or inferred (Min(a, b) when a and b are int). Instantiation is a compile-

heading: Type parameters: the square-bracket annotation
text: A type parameter is a placeholder type, announced in square brackets right after the function name, that the caller fills in with a real type. Read it left to right: func Min — a function named Min [T interface ] — "I accept a type parameter T that must satisfy this constraint" (a, b T) — two parameters, both of type T T — the return type, same T the caller supplies Instantiation is when you provide the concrete type. It can be explicit or inferred: Let me animate what the compiler sees at each call site, so you understand that each instantiation is a distinct type-check:
