desc: The red → green → refactor loop; writing the test first and letting it drive the design; growing a Meridian transfer validator test-by-test; table-driven TDD, test doubles via interfaces, the testing pyramid, and the honest cases where TDD helps versus where it gets in the way.
text: Here's the thing, sport. The previous chapter taught you how to write tests. This chapter teaches you something far more dangerous: how to let tests write your code . That distinction — test after versus test first — is the difference between a safety net and a steering wheel. TDD is not a religion. I'm going to teach you the discipline and I'm going to tell you exactly when it gets in your way — because I only deal in truth. By the end, you'll have grown a real Meridian transfer validator rule-by-rule, you'll know what "red → green → refactor" actually feels like in Go, and you'll have an honest map of when TDD earns its keep and when it doesn't. Let's go. --

heading: The Red-Green-Refactor Loop
text: The loop itself, one full revolution on a real rule: Before a single line of code, let me show you the situation . You're an engineer at Meridian. A transfer request lands: amount, source account, destination account. Before you wire up database calls, HTTP handlers, or any of that, you need a function that says yes or no — a validator . Right now it doesn't exist. How do you build it? The TDD answer: write a failing test first. Watch it fail (red). Write the minimum code to make it pass (green). Clean it up while it stays green (refactor). Repeat for every rule, one at a time.

heading: The three steps, explained
text: The loop has exactly three steps, and every one of them is deliberate: 1 — Red: write a failing test first. Before you write a single line of production code, write a test that describes the behavior you want. Run it. It must fail — if it passes before you write anything, either the behavior already exists (good to know) or the test is wrong (fix it before proceeding). A test that cannot fail is worthless: it tells you nothing. The red step forces you to think about the interface first. What does this function take? What does it return? What is the caller's experience? You become your own first user before the code exists, and that changes what you build. 2 — Green: write the minimum code to make it pass. Not the "best" code. The minimum code. If a hardcoded return value makes the test green, write that — then immediately write the next test to force you out of the lie. The discipline of minimum code keeps you from over-engineering before you know what the next requirement actually is. Solve what the test asks for. Nothing more. 3 — Refactor: clean up while the tests stay green. Once green, you have a safety net. Rename a confusing variable. Extract a helper. Eliminate duplication.

heading: Tests Drive Design
text: Here's what nobody tells you when they pitch TDD as a "testing practice": it's actually a design practice . The red step is not just about catching bugs. It's about forcing you to use your own API before it exists. On the job: You're adding the Meridian transfer validator. Without TDD, you might write a ValidateTransfer function with five parameters, a config struct, and a context — because "that's how production code usually looks." Then the test is awkward to set up, and you don't notice until your second user (another engineer) tries to call it. With TDD: you write the test first. You type the call site. Immediately, AmountCents int64, FromID string, ToID string, CurrencyCode string starts to feel like too much. You reorganize into a TransferRequest struct before the function exists. The test tells you what ergonomic looks like.

heading: TDD nudges you toward better design
text: Three patterns that emerge naturally when you write tests first: Small functions with clear inputs and outputs. If your function is hard to test — lots of setup, lots of globals — it's hard to test because it's doing too much . TDD surfaces that immediately. You split it because you're tired of writing test setup. Interface-shaped dependencies. If Validate needs to check a balance, and you write the test first, you can't call a real database. So you define an interface — BalanceStore — and pass a fake. The interface is naturally minimal: only what the validator needs, nothing more. This is the consumer interface pattern from Go idioms. TDD builds it automatically. Injectable, global-free code. "No globals — inject deps" is a Go proverb. TDD enforces it. A function that reads a global config is painful to test (you mutate globals between tests — a race waiting to happen). TDD makes you pass config as a parameter because you have to. Go's interface system is implicit : a type satisfies an interface by having the right methods — no declaration required. This is central to why TDD feels natural in Go. When you write a test first and need a fake database, you define the interface in the

heading: Grow It Rule by Rule
text: Time to build something real. We're growing the Meridian transfer validator from nothing, one rule at a time. Each cycle: write the failing test, watch it fail for the right reason, write minimum code to pass, refactor. Five rules total: 1. Amount must be positive (cents, never zero or negative) 2. Balance must be sufficient (source account has enough) 3. Accounts must differ (source ≠ destination) 4. Currencies must match (no cross-currency transfers at this layer) 5. Amount must be a whole number of cents (never fractional — integer-only, defended at the type level) We'll run through all five cycles. The tests are shown as test.go (non-runnable in the playground — Codapi runs go run, not go test); the validator itself ships as a runnable playground at the end so you can see it exercised. --

heading: Cycle 1 — Amount must be positive
text: The test (write this first): Run: go test ./... → compile error. Validate and TransferRequest don't exist. RED. Minimum code to pass (green): Run: go test ./... → PASS. GREEN. Refactor: Nothing to clean yet — the code is already minimal. Move on. --

heading: Cycle 2 — Balance must be sufficient
text: The test (add to the table — or a new func): Run: FAIL — Validate ignores the store. RED. Minimum code: Run: PASS. GREEN. Refactor: pull the balance check into a named helper checkBalance — tests still pass. --

heading: Cycle 3 — Accounts must differ
text: Run: FAIL (nil, want error). RED. Minimum code: add if r.From == r.To before the balance check. Run: PASS. GREEN. Refactor: no structural change needed. --

heading: Cycle 4 — Currencies must match
text: Run: FAIL (nil for empty currency). RED. Minimum code: if r.Currency == "" . Run: PASS. GREEN. --

heading: Cycle 5 — Integer cents, never fractional
text: This rule is defended at the type level : Amount is int64. You cannot represent $4.999 or 0.001. But we add an explicit test to document the contract and lock it in — and we use int64 in the struct to make the intent undeniable. Run: PASS immediately. This test is green before we add code — which is correct : int64 already prevents fractional cents at the type level. The test documents the contract. We keep it. Amount int64 in TransferRequest is not a style preference. Floating-point money is how you get $14.9999999999998 silently crossing a ledger boundary. The type system is your first line of defense: int64 for cents means the compiler refuses a float64. Your validator never sees a fraction. State this in a comment on the struct field — future engineers will thank you or, more likely, you'll thank yourself at 2 a.m. Now the complete, runnable validator — exercised via a main that replays all five rules and prints PASS/FAIL: --

heading: Table-Driven TDD and Test Doubles
text: Once you have a few cycles under your belt, two techniques compound your velocity: growing the table instead of writing new test functions, and faking dependencies with hand-written structs instead of a mock framework.

heading: Growing the table
text: In TDD, the test table starts with one row per cycle and grows as you discover new rules. You don't write the full table upfront — you don't know all the cases yet. You add a row, watch it fail, make it pass, refactor, add another row. The table is now the documentation of the validator's behavior. Every rule is a row. New rules become new rows — and you TDD each one by adding the row (watch it fail), then writing the minimum code.

heading: Test doubles via interfaces — no framework needed
text: The fakeStore you saw above is a test double — a stand-in for the real BalanceStore (Postgres in production). Hand-written. No mockgen, no testify/mock. Here's the pattern in full: You can also make the fake configurable — return a preset error to test the "balance lookup fails" path: Now testing the "DB is down" path is one line: store := &fakeStore . Hand-written fakes are the right default for small interfaces like BalanceStore. Reach for a framework (gomock, testify/mock) when: (1) the interface has eight methods and you only care about two, (2) you need to assert exact call sequences across many tests, or (3) the interface is from a third-party library and a realistic fake would be hundreds of lines. Start with fakes. Add a framework when fakes hurt , not before. --

heading: The Testing Pyramid — Honest Take
text: Fast, isolated, deterministic. One function, controlled inputs, fakes for deps. Milliseconds per test. Run on every file save. Your primary feedback loop. The validator tests you just wrote are all unit tests. Slower — real deps in containers. Verify your SQL queries, Redis pipelines, Kafka offset handling against the actual system. Run in CI on every PR, gated behind a build tag so they don't slow your local loop. Slowest. Drive the full Meridian stack — real services, real network, real database. Catch integration mismatches that survive unit and integration tests. Run pre-deploy, not per commit. Keep this layer thin. If 80% of your tests are E2E, they will be slow, flaky, and point you at the wrong layer when they fail. A failing unit test names the function. A failing E2E test names a symptom. Build the pyramid right: wide unit base, selective integration middle, narrow E2E top.

heading: When TDD genuinely helps
text: TDD shines brightest for code with clear rules, pure logic, and minimal external state . The Meridian validator is the canonical example: five rules, no ambiguity, no UI, no network. Every new rule starts as a test. You can't build the wrong thing because the test specifies exactly what "right" means before you start. More categories where TDD earns its keep: Money math. Every arithmetic function that touches cents: fee calculations, split transfers, coupon application, rounding rules. The rules are exact; the tests are exact; the feedback is instant. Parsers and serializers. A function that turns a string into a structured request has a crisp contract. Fuzz it and TDD it — they compose naturally. State machines. Transfer statuses (pending → processing → settled → failed) are just rules. TDD builds the transition table while keeping illegal states caught immediately. Pure algorithms. Sorting, batching, aggregation. No deps to fake; tests run in microseconds.

heading: When TDD gets in the way
text: TDD is a discipline, not a commandment. The engineers who apply it dogmatically to everything produce slow feedback loops and fragile test suites. Here's the honest map: Exploratory / prototype code. You don't know the right shape yet. Writing tests for an API you haven't designed slows exploration. Spike first — write throwaway code without tests — then TDD the parts that survive into production. UI and visual code. Testing whether a button looks right via TDD is theater. Test the logic behind the button (event handlers, state transitions, data formatting) with unit tests; use manual or screenshot tests for the visual layer. Integration glue. Code whose only job is wiring two libraries together — a Postgres driver to your repository layer — is often better tested with a real integration test than a sea of fakes. TDD with fakes for glue code tests the glue's test, not the glue's behavior. Pure throwaway scripts. A one-shot data migration, a CLI tool you'll run once, CI helper scripts. Test the logic inside them if it's reusable; don't TDD the scaffolding. Start with TDD for the layer you're building today, not your entire codebase. Pick the next function you need to write — if it h

desc: Build a CLI that exercises everything so far — flags, I/O, errors, concurrency — shipped with a real, runnable test suite.
text: You've absorbed eight chapters of Go. Syntax, structs, interfaces, error wrapping, goroutines, channels, testing. Impressive. For a student. Now it's time to stop learning about building things and actually build one — something that runs, something that handles real data, something that ships with a test suite that I am personally comfortable putting my name next to. Which is a higher bar than you realize. We're going to build txstat: a concurrent transaction-file analyzer. Feed it newline-delimited records, get per-account totals, minimums, maximums, and counts back. It will parse, aggregate concurrently with a worker pool, and print a report — or emit JSON if you ask nicely. The whole thing ships with table-driven tests, a fuzz test for the money parser, and a -race-clean concurrency test. By the end of this chapter, the compiler won't be the only thing that can vouch for your code. All code targets Go 1.26. Let's go.

heading: Scaffold
text: Every production CLI has the same skeleton problem: how do you wire flags, I/O, and program structure before you've written any real logic? Do it wrong and you're trapped — a global os.Stdin call buried inside your parser makes testing a nightmare. Do it right and every piece is independently testable. Here's the scenario. A fintech startup processes millions of transactions per day. Each is written as one JSON line to a log file: The ops team needs daily summaries — per account, total debits/credits, min/max amounts. They need it fast, they need it scriptable, and right now they have a Python script that takes four minutes on a large file. You're going to replace it with a Go binary that takes seconds, reads from a file or stdin, and is testable without touching the filesystem.

heading: Module and layout
text: Three packages. Each one does exactly one thing. parse reads records; aggregate computes stats; report formats output. main.go wires them together with flags and I/O. A CLI (command-line interface) is a program you invoke from the shell by name, optionally followed by flags — named options like -workers 4 or -json. Go's standard flag package reads those flags from os.Args and stores the parsed values in typed pointers you dereference after flag.Parse(). Why it matters: a well-designed flag surface is the difference between a tool that's trivially testable (pass any reader, any writer) and one that's hard-wired to os.Stdin and impossible to test without spawning a subprocess.

heading: Flags first
text: When you call flag.Parse(), Go's flag package reads os.Args[1:] — everything after the binary name. Each element is either a flag (-workers 4 or -workers=4) or a positional argument. How flag values are stored. flag.Int("workers", 4, "…") allocates an int, registers it by name in the default FlagSet, and returns a pointer to that int. When Parse() sees -workers 8, it writes 8 through that pointer. You dereference it after Parse() returns with workers. This is why you must call flag.Parse() before using any flag value — the pointer's target is still the default until then. FlagSet is the real type. flag.Parse() is just a method call on the package-level flag.CommandLine — a flag.FlagSet pre-initialized with the binary name. In tests you create your own FlagSet so you can parse flags without touching os.Args and without exiting the test process when a required flag is missing (the default ExitOnError would call os.Exit(2) — fatal for a test). Use flag.NewFlagSet("test", flag.ContinueOnError) in tests. os.Args is a plain slice. os.Args[0] is the executable path; os.Args[1:] is everything the shell passed. On Linux the kernel fills the argv array; the Go runtime copies it into the slic

heading: Parse
text: stdin is the default source of bytes a program reads from (the terminal, or a pipe from another command). stdout is where it writes results. In Go, both are os.File values (os.Stdin, os.Stdout) that implement io.Reader and io.Writer — meaning any function that accepts those interfaces works equally well with a file, a pipe, or a test's strings.NewReader. bufio wraps an io.Reader with a buffer and a line scanner: instead of issuing one read syscall per byte, it reads a large chunk, then hands your code one line at a time. Without buffering, reading a 50 GB file line-by-line would drown the kernel in syscalls. Why it matters: accepting io.Reader instead of os.File is the single change that makes every I/O function in this project independently testable without touching the filesystem. The parser lives in its own package so it's testable without running the full program. Its job: read an io.Reader line by line, parse each JSON record, and emit a channel of results. Errors go on a separate channel so the caller can decide whether a bad line is fatal.

heading: The cents rule
text: Notice AmountCents int64 — not float64. This isn't a style choice. It's correctness. Financial systems that use float arithmetic have a long, storied history of inventing or destroying fractions of cents at scale. An int64 holding cents can represent every amount up to about $92 trillion without losing a single cent. A float64 can't reliably represent 0.1. We enforce this at the type level in the parser so the rest of the program never has to think about it. Some payment APIs send "amount": "14.99" — a decimal string to avoid the float problem on the wire. If your input uses that format, parse it as a string and convert: multiply by 100 and round, or use strconv.ParseFloat then math.Round. Never store the float; convert to int64 cents immediately in the parser. The fuzz test below will make sure your conversion is correct under adversarial input.

heading: Concurrency
text: A worker pool is a fixed set of goroutines that all read from the same shared channel. You control concurrency by controlling the pool size, not by spawning one goroutine per record (which would launch millions and exhaust memory). Each worker loops: receive a record, process it, loop back. When the channel closes, workers exit. Why it matters: unbounded goroutine spawning crashes under large workloads; a bounded pool gives you parallel throughput with predictable resource usage. The pattern goes deep in Concurrency Patterns (Part 2). Now the reason ops is going to love this tool. A 50 GB transaction file has millions of records. Parsing them sequentially is fine — the bottleneck is disk I/O, not CPU. But aggregating them — computing per-account stats — can be done in parallel if we shard work by account. We'll use a classic bounded worker pool: a fixed number of goroutines draining a shared jobs channel. Once the channel is empty and closed, each worker ships its private map to the result channel and the merge pass folds them into one: The naive approach to a concurrent aggregator is one sync.Mutex-protected global map. Workers lock, update, unlock. This works , but under a high r

heading: Graceful cancellation on SIGINT
text: The signal.NotifyContext call in main.go wires up SIGINT (Ctrl-C) to the context. When the signal fires, ctx.Done() closes. Both the parser's goroutine and every worker goroutine check ctx.Done() in their select loops. They ship what they have and exit cleanly — no abandoned goroutines, no half-written output. signal.NotifyContext(ctx, sig...) is a thin wrapper introduced in Go 1.16. It creates a child context and registers a channel with the OS signal machinery via signal.Notify. When one of the listed signals arrives, the runtime's signal handler (a dedicated goroutine that sits on a sigqueue) writes to the registered channel. The wrapper reads that channel and calls the context's cancel function — which closes ctx.Done(). All goroutines blocking on ctx.Done() in a select statement are unblocked immediately. The defer stop() call is important: it tells the runtime to stop forwarding those signals to this context's channel, releasing the channel and preventing a goroutine leak inside the signal package itself. Miss it and the signal package holds a reference to your channel forever. On Linux, signals arrive as POSIX signals delivered to the process. Go's runtime catches them in a

heading: Output
text: Two output formats: a human-readable table for the terminal, and JSON for piping into other tools. Both write to an io.Writer — the real binary passes os.Stdout, the tests pass a bytes.Buffer.

heading: Tests
text: This is the part that separates the people who say they write Go from the people who actually write Go. We're going to write four kinds of tests, all in the same project, and they're all going to pass with -race. I've accepted nothing less from myself for years. Now it's your turn.

heading: Race test for concurrent aggregation
text: TestRunRace above relies on the race detector and a large-enough record count to expose any latent races. As of Go 1.25, the new testing/synctest package lets you run goroutines inside a fake clock where time advances only when all goroutines are blocked — making concurrency tests deterministic without time.Sleep or large iteration counts. If you find yourself writing timing-sensitive tests for the worker pool or the streaming parser, synctest.Test(t, ...) is worth reaching for. The Testing chapter (Part 1, Chapter 8) covers testing/synctest in depth. A golden file is a file on disk holding the known-correct output of a function — the "gold standard" the output must match. The test calls the function, captures its output into a buffer, then diffs the buffer against the file. If the output changes unexpectedly, the test fails. To update intentionally, run with an environment variable (e.g. UPDATE GOLDEN=1) and the test overwrites the file. Why it matters: for formatting-heavy output like a tabular report, manually asserting every field is brittle and verbose. The golden file captures the whole output in one shot and makes any regression immediately visible as a diff.

desc: Building real CLIs in Go: the stdlib flag package in depth, Cobra for subcommands and persistent flags (the kubectl/gh pattern), urfave/cli as the alternative, Viper config integration, interactive prompts and TUIs with Bubble Tea, and generating shell completions.
text: Here's a little fact that should make you feel things: kubectl, docker, gh, terraform, hugo, helm — the CLI tools that run most of the world's infrastructure — are all Go. Not Rust. Not Python. Not C. Go. You just finished building txstat with the stdlib flag package. That was a proud day. For a beginner. Now you're going to learn how teams build tools that scale from one subcommand to hundreds, ship shell completions, read config files, and give operators an interactive terminal UI when the situation demands it. By the end, you'll understand why the biggest CLIs in the world are Go programs — and you'll be able to build one yourself. Lucky you, having me to show you how. -- --

heading: The stdlib flag package, in depth
text: You used flag.Int, flag.String, and flag.Bool in the project chapter. That's the surface. Let's go to depth, because the stdlib flag package has sharp capabilities that most engineers never discover — and knowing its limits is exactly what tells you when to reach for a framework. Go's flag package, in stdlib since day one, parses command-line arguments from os.Args. You register typed pointers (flag.String, flag.Int, flag.Bool, flag.Duration, flag.Var) before calling flag.Parse(). After parsing, dereference the pointers to read values. The underlying engine is a flag.FlagSet — a named registry of flags; flag.Parse() just calls the package-level flag.CommandLine FlagSet. Understanding FlagSet directly is what lets you build per-subcommand parsers and testable flag logic without touching os.Args in tests. Why it matters: for a single-command tool, flag is perfect and zero-dependency. Its limit is that it has no concept of nested subcommands — implementing those by hand with multiple FlagSet instances is exactly what frameworks like Cobra formalize.

heading: Every flag type you actually need
text: flag ships typed constructors for the values you use day-to-day. Each returns a pointer to the parsed value: flag.Duration is underused and excellent — it parses Go duration strings (5s, 2m30s, 100ms) straight to time.Duration. No manual parsing needed.

heading: Custom flag.Value: a cents amount flag
text: The real power move: implement flag.Value to teach the flag package a new type. Any type that satisfies the two-method interface gets first-class treatment as a flag — printed in usage, set by the parser, validated at parse time. flag.Value is the interface flag uses for custom flag types. Implement two methods: String() string (the default/current value, used in -help output) and Set(s string) error (called by the parser with the raw string from os.Args). Return a non-nil error from Set to reject the value — the parser prints usage and exits. Why it matters: it lets you parse rich types (amounts in cents, lists of strings, log levels) directly into your own types rather than accepting a raw string and converting later. Validation moves from your business logic into the flag registration, so bad CLI input fails fast with a clear message. Register it with flag.Var: Here's the whole thing runnable so you can watch it parse:

heading: FlagSet for manual subcommand dispatch
text: Before Cobra existed, teams built subcommand CLIs by hand using flag.FlagSet — one per subcommand. It's more ceremony than a framework, but zero dependencies and it runs anywhere:

heading: Positional args and flag.Args()
text: After flag.Parse(), everything that wasn't consumed as a flag or its value ends up in flag.Args() — a []string of positional arguments. This is how you make a tool that accepts both --json and a list of account IDs: Go's flag package stops at the first non-flag argument. So meridian accounts list acct 001 --json will not parse --json — acct 001 terminates flag parsing. The convention is meridian accounts list --json acct 001. Cobra handles this more flexibly with cobra.Command.TraverseChildren.

heading: The limits of flag — what motivates a framework
text: The stdlib flag package is honest about what it is: a simple, flat, single-level parser. It gives you: Named flags with types and defaults A usage string auto-generated from flag registrations Custom flag types via flag.Value Positional args via flag.Args() What it does not give you: Nested subcommands (e.g., meridian accounts list vs. meridian accounts create) Persistent flags that automatically propagate to all subcommands Auto-generated help trees that show subcommands and their own flags Required-flag enforcement built in Shell completion generation For a tool with two or three subcommands, hand-rolling with FlagSet is completely reasonable — less code, no dependencies. Once you have four or more subcommands, especially nested ones, a framework pays for itself in the first afternoon. On the job: The kubectl team wrote their own subcommand library before Cobra existed, then migrated. You don't have to repeat that arc. Use flag for focused single-command tools; reach for Cobra when you need a subcommand hierarchy. --

heading: Cobra — the de-facto CLI framework
text: What Cobra actually is — a tree of commands, walked left to right from your argv: needs go get github.com/spf13/cobra — snippets in this section are not runnable in the playground. Cobra (github.com/spf13/cobra) is the CLI framework behind kubectl, gh, docker, hugo, helm, and hundreds of other production Go tools. It wraps Go's flag.FlagSet in a tree of cobra.Command structs — each command declares its own flags, help text, argument validators, and a RunE function. Cobra auto-generates help/usage output, propagates persistent flags down the command tree, and can generate shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell. Why it matters: Cobra doesn't add magic — it formalizes exactly the boilerplate you'd write by hand with flag.FlagSet, so you can focus on command logic instead of dispatch machinery.

heading: The command tree
text: A Cobra CLI is a tree of cobra.Command values. The root command becomes your binary name; sub-commands hang off it; sub-sub-commands hang off those.

heading: Sub-commands: accounts list and transfer create
text: Each cobra.Command gets a Use string (the sub-command name plus argument placeholders), a Short (one-line help), and either Run (no error return) or RunE (returns error — prefer this): Now meridian accounts list --limit 50 works and meridian accounts --help lists the list sub-command automatically. Cobra generates all of that. A subcommand is a named dispatch point inside a CLI that scopes its own set of flags and logic. In meridian accounts list, accounts is a sub-command grouping account-related operations, and list is the leaf sub-command that runs. Subcommands let a single binary grow to dozens of operations without collapsing into a flat flag namespace where --transfer and --verify-ledger live side by side and confuse everyone including the author.

heading: Local vs. persistent flags
text: This is the distinction that separates people who understand Cobra from people who copy-paste it. A local flag (added with cmd.Flags()) is visible only on that exact command — it appears in that command's --help and nowhere else. A persistent flag (added with cmd.PersistentFlags()) is inherited by every sub-command in the subtree rooted at that command. The canonical use: put auth tokens, --config, and --output-format on the root command as persistent flags so every sub-command gets them automatically. Put --limit or --amount as local flags on the specific commands that need them.

heading: PersistentPreRun: cross-cutting setup
text: Here's a pattern every production Cobra CLI uses: PersistentPreRun runs before the RunE of every command in the subtree. This is where you put auth loading, config file reading, and telemetry initialization — once, not repeated in every command:

heading: The full meridian transfer create example
text: Running meridian transfer create --from acct 001 --to acct 002 --amount 50.00 prints: Running with a missing required flag: Cobra generates that error and usage block. You wrote zero formatting code. Every cobra.Command holds two flag.FlagSet values: one for local flags and one for persistent flags. When Cobra resolves a command path (e.g., transfer create), it merges the persistent FlagSets from every ancestor into a combined FlagSet before calling the target command's flag parser. This is why --token registered on the root command is visible to transfer create — Cobra's merge step adds it to the target command's flag parsing context. cmd.Flags() returns the merged FlagSet (local + inherited persistent). cmd.LocalFlags() returns only the flags registered directly on this command. This matters when you're generating help text or shell completions programmatically. Required flags (MarkFlagRequired) are enforced by checking the merged FlagSet after parsing but before calling PersistentPreRun or RunE. Cobra checks whether each required flag's Changed field is true (set to true by the FlagSet when a value is parsed). An unset required flag returns an error that Cobra wraps into a usage

heading: urfave/cli — the lighter alternative
text: needs go get github.com/urfave/cli/v2 — snippets in this section are not runnable in the playground. urfave/cli (github.com/urfave/cli/v2) is the other major Go CLI framework. Where Cobra leans into a tree of structs with init() wiring, urfave/cli uses a declarative cli.App with cli.Command slices and action functions. It's lighter (no code-generation companion, smaller API surface), has built-in shell completion, and makes simple apps feel slightly less ceremonial. It's the framework behind a number of popular dev tools and is particularly popular for smaller microservice operator CLIs. The same meridian transfer create in urfave/cli:

heading: Cobra vs. urfave/cli: the honest comparison
text: Neither is wrong. Pick based on your team's constraints: You need a large subcommand tree with inherited persistent flags, generated shell completions, and man pages. Your tool resembles kubectl or gh in scope. Your team is already familiar with Cobra. Most Go CLI tools in the ecosystem use Cobra, so contributors onboard faster. Your tool has a modest number of commands. You want slightly less ceremony and prefer the declarative cli.App struct over the init()-based wiring Cobra uses. You appreciate built-in EnvVars support per flag (urfave/cli bakes in env-var fallback). Good for microservice operator CLIs that don't need code generation. Neither framework is a dependency you should add carelessly. For a tool with one command and three flags, flag from stdlib is still the right answer — zero dependencies, ships in the Go toolchain, and requires nothing. Add a framework when the subcommand tree earns it. --

heading: Config integration & the precedence story
text: A mature CLI reads configuration from multiple sources. The operator should be able to set --token on the command line, fall back to MERIDIAN TOKEN in the environment, fall back to /.config/meridian/config.yaml, and ultimately fall back to a compiled-in default. This layering has a name. env file default)" Config precedence is the priority order in which a CLI resolves a configuration value when it's available from multiple sources. The convention, codified by the 12-factor app and enforced by every serious CLI, is: flags beat environment variables beat config files beat compiled-in defaults . Each layer overrides the one below. Why it matters: operators in a container deployment can set env vars without touching the binary; they can override with explicit flags in CI without modifying environment setup. Getting the precedence wrong means an env var silently overrides a flag the operator just typed — a confusing, maddening experience.

heading: Wiring Viper with Cobra
text: Viper (github.com/spf13/viper) is the companion to Cobra for config file reading. It knows about YAML, TOML, JSON, and .env files, and it provides the glue to implement the precedence story correctly.

heading: Doing it without Viper
text: For smaller tools you don't need Viper. Implement precedence by hand in PersistentPreRun — it's about ten lines: On the job: The cross-reference here is intentional. Viper and the full configuration story — vault integration, secret rotation, validate-at-startup patterns — live in the Configuration & Secrets Management chapter (Part 2). What matters right now is understanding where config resolution lives in a CLI: in PersistentPreRun, before any RunE runs. A CLI that reads a config file should validate it immediately, at startup, before running any command. If the config is malformed or a required value is missing, print a clear error and exit with a non-zero code. Do not let a bad config surface as a cryptic API error three commands deep. The PersistentPreRun hook is the right place — it runs before any command's logic, and its error return propagates cleanly. --

heading: Interactive prompts & TUIs
text: Sometimes a CLI needs to talk back to the operator — confirm before an irreversible action, show a progress spinner during a long API call, or surface a dashboard of live account states. This is where interactive prompts and terminal UIs come in.

heading: Confirmation prompts and interactive forms
text: For simple confirmations (Y/n) and structured forms, two libraries are popular in the Go ecosystem: charmbracelet/huh — a declarative form builder (text inputs, selects, multi-selects, confirms). Newer, excellent DX. AlecAivazis/survey/v2 — battle-tested, prompt-by-prompt, wide adoption. A confirmation before an irreversible transfer:

heading: Spinners and progress
text: Long API calls should not leave the operator staring at a blank terminal. A spinner signals "I'm working, not hung": For deterministic progress (file ingestion, batch operations), a progress bar with a known total is clearer than a spinner.

heading: Full TUIs with Bubble Tea
text: When the CLI needs to display live-updating information — a streaming feed of recent transfers, a dashboard of account balances, a transaction ledger that updates in real time — you need a full terminal UI. This is what Bubble Tea is built for. A TUI (terminal user interface) is a full-screen interactive program that runs inside a terminal emulator, handling keyboard input and rendering frames of output — think htop, k9s, or the interactive Git UI lazygit. Bubble Tea (github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) is the Go library for building TUIs. It implements the Elm architecture : your application is a Model (all state), an Update function (pure: takes a Model and a Msg, returns a new Model and a command to run), and a View function (pure: takes a Model, returns a string to render). The runtime loops: receive a Msg (keypress, timer, API response), call Update, render with View. Why it matters: the pure functional model makes TUIs testable — you can test Update by asserting on the returned Model without a real terminal. Bubble Tea is used for gh, the Charm toolchain, and dozens of developer tools. Here is the smallest complete Bubble Tea Model for a live Meridian account dashboard: Bubbl

heading: Shell completions & shipping
text: The difference between a good CLI and a great one is often nothing more than whether pressing Tab works. Shell completion is the behavior where pressing Tab after partially typing a command or flag causes the shell to complete it or list options. For meridian tran to complete to meridian transfer, and meridian transfer create --fr to expand to --from, the shell needs a completion script — a file of shell functions that the shell sources at startup. Cobra generates these scripts automatically for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell. Why it matters: without completions, operators type full flag names from memory and make typos. With completions, the CLI is self-documenting and pleasant to use. It's a one-function call in Cobra and zero effort for users who install via Homebrew or a package manager.

heading: Cobra auto-generates completions
text: The operator runs meridian completion zsh /.zsh/completions/ meridian once. After that, meridian shows all subcommands; meridian transfer create -- shows --from, --to, --amount.

heading: Dynamic completions
text: For flags whose valid values come from an API (e.g., --from should complete with real account IDs), Cobra lets you register a completion function per flag: Now meridian transfer create --from acct queries the API and returns matching account IDs. This is the pattern kubectl uses for kubectl get pods completing with real pod names from the cluster.

heading: Man pages
text: Cobra also generates man pages (cmd.GenManTree(dir)), which Homebrew and Linux package managers install automatically. One call, zero manual formatting.

heading: Shipping — GoReleaser and the Building & Shipping chapter
text: Cross-compilation, GoReleaser, signing, and the mechanics of distributing a Go binary are covered in depth in the Building & Shipping Go Binaries chapter (Part 1). The short version for CLIs: This cross-compiles for linux/amd64, linux/arm64, darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, and windows/amd64; creates a GitHub release with checksums; and generates Homebrew formula and Scoop manifest. The completion scripts can be embedded via go:embed and extracted by meridian completion --install. On the job: The gh CLI ships via Homebrew, the official GitHub CLI installer, and Scoop on Windows. Installation automatically hooks in the completion scripts. When you build meridian for Meridian's ops team, the same approach means your colleagues never have to hand-type --from acct . They Tab-complete it from a live list. --

desc: Idiomatic Go patterns — functional options, accept-interfaces/return-structs, worker pools, fan-in/out, middleware via closures — and where the GoF patterns do and don't fit.
text: Let me tell you something the Gang of Four textbook won't. Those patterns were written for Java. Java needs seventeen classes and an abstract factory to open a file. Go is not Java, and I am not your Java professor. Go has its own patterns — smaller, sharper, and a thousand times harder to get wrong. By the end of this chapter you will understand functional options, the accept-interfaces/return-structs discipline, dependency injection without a framework, worker pools, fan-in/fan-out, middleware chains, and exactly which classic GoF patterns survive the translation into Go — and which ones should have their passports revoked. You are, as always, extraordinarily lucky to be here.

heading: Functional Options
text: A functional option is a function with the signature func( Config) that mutates a private configuration struct. Instead of a constructor that takes fifteen arguments, you define one constructor plus a set of With functions — each returning an option. Callers compose exactly what they need; the rest stays at its safe default. Why it matters: telescoping constructors (NewClientWithTimeoutAndRetries) explode combinatorially and cannot be composed at runtime. Functional options scale to any number of knobs with zero breaking changes to existing call sites. Picture this: you are building an HTTP client for your payment gateway. You need timeouts, retry counts, a base URL, optional tracing, maybe a custom transport. The naive approach is a struct with fifteen fields and a constructor that takes fifteen arguments. The slightly-less-naive-but-still-wrong approach is fifteen separate NewClientWith constructors. Both are embarrassing. Let me show you the right way.

heading: The telescoping constructor problem
text: The functional options pattern replaces a proliferating family of constructors with a single constructor that accepts a variadic list of Option functions, each of which mutates a private config struct. Here is the full, runnable implementation: Each WithTimeout(d) call allocates a new function value on the heap — a closure . The closure captures the variable d (in this case, the time.Duration argument) by reference at the moment WithTimeout returns. When the constructor loops over opts and calls o(cfg), the closure's captured d is read and written into cfg.timeout. The compiler performs escape analysis to decide whether the closed-over variable lives on the stack or must be heap-allocated. A closure that outlives the function that created it (as our Option values do — they're passed to the constructor) causes its captures to escape to the heap. This is one or two small allocations per option, which is entirely acceptable; the composability and testability you get in return are worth far more. The func( config) signature is the entire abstraction. No interface, no reflection, no registry — just a first-class function type. Go's type system makes this as lightweight as it gets.

heading: Accept Interfaces Return Structs
text: Accept interfaces in function parameters — your function asks for the narrowest behavior it needs (e.g. io.Reader), so callers can pass any type that satisfies it. Return structs (concrete types) from constructors — so callers get the full API without artificial restriction. Why it matters: accepting a concrete sql.DB couples your function to one implementation forever and blocks testing. Returning an interface hides methods the concrete type has, forcing callers into type assertions they should never need. This is the single most-quoted Go design proverb, and the most consistently misunderstood. Let me fix that right now. The rule has two halves: 1. Accept interfaces — your function parameters should be interface types where possible, so callers can pass anything that satisfies the contract. This is where you consume behavior. 2. Return structs (or concrete types) — your function's return type should be the concrete thing it actually creates, so callers get the full API without artificial restriction. Here is the anti-pattern that violates both: The reason returning an interface is harmful: it hides the return type. If you return io.ReadCloser but the concrete type also implements

heading: Dependency Injection
text: Dependency injection means passing a service's collaborators in from the outside — as constructor arguments — instead of reaching for package-level globals or calling New () internally. In Go the idiomatic form is: define a minimal interface next to the consumer, accept that interface in the constructor, and inject real or fake implementations at the call site. Why it matters: global deps are invisible (you can't see what a function depends on), untestable (no substitute without a real DB/network), and cause race conditions in parallel tests. Injected interfaces make every dependency explicit, swappable, and mockable with a five-line fake. Dependency injection sounds like a framework. In Go it is not. It is just: pass the thing as a parameter instead of reaching for a global . The real-world scenario: your OrderService needs a database, a payment gateway client, and a mailer. The wrong way is to call package-level globals from inside the service methods. The right way is to put those dependencies in the struct and inject them at construction time. Here is the testable pattern in full: An interface value in Go is exactly two machine words : a pointer to the type descriptor (also cal

heading: Worker Pools
text: A worker pool is a fixed set of N goroutines that all read from one shared job channel, bounding how much memory and CPU you use regardless of how many jobs arrive. Fan-out is distributing one stream of work to multiple goroutines in parallel. Fan-in is merging the results from multiple parallel goroutines back into one output channel. Why it matters: spawning one goroutine per job works fine at 100 jobs; at 50,000 it exhausts memory. Processing jobs sequentially misses the overnight window. A pool gives you the throughput without the blowup. Your payment batch processor needs to reconcile 50,000 transactions overnight. Spawning 50,000 goroutines would exhaust memory. Doing them one-by-one would miss the window. You need bounded parallelism : a fixed-size pool of worker goroutines, each pulling from a shared job queue. Before Go 1.25, launching a pooled goroutine required three lines: wg.Add(1), then go func() (). The boilerplate was easy to get wrong — forget the Add and Wait returns early; forget the defer Done and the pool never shuts down. As of Go 1.25, wg.Go(func() ) does both in one call: it increments the counter and starts the goroutine. The examples in this chapter use th

heading: Fan-In and Fan-Out
text: Fan-out splits one stream of work across multiple goroutines. Fan-in merges multiple streams back into one. Together they are the pipeline architecture for every high-throughput Go service. Real scenario: your fraud-detection pipeline ingests a stream of payment events, fans them out to three parallel analyzers (velocity check, geo-anomaly check, device fingerprint check), and fans their verdicts back into one decision stream. 50000 — FLAGGED." }, , ]} caption="One source channel splits across three checker goroutines that run in parallel — each lane processes its share of events independently." / Every checker has finished its slice of the work. Now fanIn merges the three independent lanes back into one stream the caller can range over:

heading: Middleware via Closures
text: The onion, walked: a request passes IN through every layer, the response passes back OUT through the same layers in reverse: A middleware is a function with the signature func(http.Handler) http.Handler. It takes the next handler, returns a new handler that does something before or after calling the original. This is the decorator pattern : each middleware wraps the previous one, forming a chain. In Go, closures make it effortless — the returned handler captures next in its environment and calls it when the request arrives. Why it matters: logging, auth, rate limiting, and tracing are cross-cutting concerns — they need to run on every request. Without middleware you copy that logic into every handler. With a chain, each concern lives in one place, is independently testable, and can be added or removed without touching handlers. Every HTTP service needs cross-cutting concerns applied to every handler: logging, auth checks, rate limiting, request tracing. Doing this inside each handler is a crime. The Go way: middleware as a function that wraps a handler function . The type is func(http.Handler) http.Handler. That's it. A middleware takes a handler, returns a new handler that does so

heading: GoF Patterns in Go
text: Let me be direct: most of the Gang of Four patterns exist to solve problems that Go's language features simply do not have. Go has first-class functions, implicit interface satisfaction, and composition over inheritance. Several GoF patterns collapse into nothing.

heading: Singleton — and why you almost certainly don't need one
text: The Java Singleton's entire job is to ensure a class is instantiated exactly once. In Go, package-level variables are already initialized exactly once by the runtime. sync.Once handles the lazy case. A package-level singleton is globally mutable shared state. Tests cannot run in parallel without races. You cannot inject a fake. The moment you want two different databases in a test, you're stuck. Prefer injection : create the dependency once in main, inject it everywhere it's needed. Reserve sync.Once for genuinely expensive one-time initialization (a connection pool, a compiled regex) where construction cost is real.

heading: Factory — just a constructor function
text: In Java, a Factory is a class whose job is to create other classes. In Go, that's just a function. NewPaymentClient(...), NewOrderService(...) — you've been writing factories this entire chapter. If you need a family of factories keyed by a string (e.g., "stripe" → Stripe client, "paypal" → PayPal client), a map of constructor functions is idiomatic:

heading: Strategy — just an interface (or a function)
text: The Strategy pattern says: define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each, make them interchangeable. In Go, a one-method interface is the strategy pattern. You've already seen this: ChargeGateway is a strategy. OrderStore is a strategy. If the strategy has exactly one method, consider making it a function type instead:

heading: Observer — channels
text: The Observer pattern: when an event happens, notify all subscribers. In Go, that's a channel. Interested goroutines range over the channel; when you're done, close it. No Subscribe/Unsubscribe machinery required. For multi-subscriber fan-out (each subscriber gets every event), a sync.Map of channels or a dedicated broker type works. But the idiomatic Go first instinct is always: can I just use a channel?

heading: Adapter — a wrapper struct or a function
text: When you need a type to satisfy an interface it wasn't designed for, write a thin wrapper struct (or a function type conversion, like http.HandlerFunc). This is the Adapter pattern, and in Go it costs almost nothing:

heading: Command — a func, or a struct with one method
text: The Command pattern packages "a thing to do" as an object so you can queue it, log it, retry it, or undo it. The GoF version is an interface with an Execute() method plus a concrete command class per action. In Go, a command is usually just a func() error — a first-class value you can put on a channel, store in a slice, or replay from a write-ahead log. Why it matters: a payment processor that retries failed charges, replays a backlog after an outage, or supports undo needs to treat each action as data, not as a hard-coded call site. A func() error is a command. You only reach for a struct when the command also needs to carry metadata — an idempotency key, a name for logging, an Undo counterpart. Here a Meridian transfer queue stores commands and replays them: The GoF Command interface with one ConcreteCommand class per action is pure ceremony here — a closure captures the receiver and arguments for free. Reach for a struct only when you need Undo() alongside Execute().

heading: State — a method field, not a class hierarchy
text: The State pattern lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes — a payment that behaves differently while pending, authorized, captured, or refunded. The GoF version gives each state its own class implementing a shared State interface, and the context delegates to the current state object. In Go, a small state machine is usually clearer as a typed constant plus a transition table (a map), or a single field holding a behavior func. Why it matters: a transaction's allowed transitions are the business rules — encoding them as data makes the illegal moves obvious and testable. A map from (state, event) to the next state captures the whole machine in one readable block — no class per state: A State interface with four state classes would scatter the transition rules across four files. The transition map keeps every legal and illegal move on one screen — that is the spec.

heading: Template Method — a func field, not inheritance
text: The Template Method pattern fixes the skeleton of an algorithm and lets subclasses fill in specific steps. The GoF version uses an abstract base class with final template method and abstract hook methods. Go has no inheritance, so you compose: a function holds the invariant steps and calls hook functions (or a small interface) for the variable ones. Why it matters: every payment rail (ACH, card, wire) runs the same pipeline — validate, reserve, settle, notify — but settles differently. The shared skeleton lives once; only the rail-specific step varies. The skeleton calls injected hooks; each rail supplies just its settle step: No abstract base class, no protected overrides — the skeleton is a plain function and the variable step is a parameter. When several steps vary together, group them into a small interface instead of passing five funcs. Package-level var (eager) or sync.Once (lazy). Prefer injection over globals. A function (or map of functions). NewXxx() is already a factory. A one-method interface, or a function type if it's a single operation. A channel. Subscribers range over it; close it when done. A wrapper struct with the right method names. Or a function type conversio

heading: The rest of the catalog, the Go way
text: The classic Design Patterns book lists twenty-three. We've covered the ones that matter daily; the remaining structural and behavioral patterns deflate into Go idioms just as hard. Here's the whole rest of the catalog, each collapsed to the Go thing it really is — so when an interviewer or an old Java colleague names one, you can translate on the spot: A tree where leaves and branches share one interface — so a caller treats a single account and a group of accounts the same. In Go: one interface (Balancer ), a leaf type and a slice-holding branch type that both implement it. No abstract base. (Runnable example below.) One simplified type in front of several messy subsystems. In Go this is just a struct with a few methods that orchestrate the internals — type PaymentService struct with a Charge() that calls all three. You already write these; the GoF just gave it a name. A stand-in with the same interface as the real thing, adding caching, lazy-loading, access control, or remoting. In Go: a wrapper struct that satisfies the same interface and forwards (or short-circuits) to the wrapped value. A caching client is a proxy; an RPC client stub is a proxy. A request walks a chain until o

heading: Error Wrapping
text: One more pattern that is distinctly Go: wrapping errors to add context without losing the original . This is not a GoF pattern — it is a Go-specific discipline. The problem: your service's PlaceOrder returns an error. The caller wants to log it with enough context to debug it. But they also want to test for specific error types (e.g., "is this a card decline vs. a DB error?"). This chapter gives you the wrapping pattern. Error handling at scale in Part 2 goes much deeper: error trees, sentinel vs. typed errors, the typed-nil-error trap, and designing errors across package boundaries for a distributed service.

heading: Builder & Fluent APIs
text: A builder is a mutable object that accumulates state across method calls and produces a finished value with a final Build(). A fluent API is the style that makes it read like a sentence: every step returns the receiver, so calls chain. The GoF Builder needs a director plus a builder class hierarchy; in Go it's one struct whose methods return q. Why it matters: functional options are one-shot — every option sees the same config and they can't react to each other. When construction is staged (each step depends on prior state), conditional (add a clause only sometimes), or accumulative (build a list across a loop), a builder is clearer than juggling a slice of options. You learned functional options first because they're the right default. But options have a ceiling: they all run against one config in one pass, blind to each other. The moment you need to branch on what's been built so far — add a WHERE only if a filter exists, append a join inside a loop — a mutable builder reads better. The classic Go builder defers all errors to Build(), so the chain stays clean — no error check after every call (the same trick bufio.Scanner uses with Err()): Two mechanics make this work. heading: Advanced Functional Options
text: Two refinements of the options pattern. A self-referential option has the signature func( T) Option — applying it returns the option that undoes it , so callers can set a value temporarily and restore the old one (Rob Pike's original design). An interface option replaces func( config) with an Option interface whose concrete types each apply themselves — so options become named types that appear in godoc, can carry their own String(), and can be inspected or logged. Why it matters: the func form is perfect for write-and-forget config; the self-referential and interface forms add undo and introspection when you need them. The plain func( config) option you already know is the 90% case. Here are the two upgrades for the other 10%.

heading: Self-referential options: set, then restore
text: Rob Pike's original options design returned the previous value as a new option, so any temporary change is trivially reversible — crank verbose logging for one request, then put it back:

heading: Options as an interface: named, inspectable, documented
text: When you want options to show up in godoc with real names, carry a String() for logging, or be stored and compared, make Option an interface instead of a bare func. Each option becomes a small named type: The generic MustT T collapses a (value, error) pair to just the value by panicking on error. It's the right tool for things that are programmer errors if they fail — var schema = Must(Compile(...)) at package scope, where a bad pattern means the binary should never have shipped. The stdlib does this with regexp.MustCompile and template.Must. Never use it on a request path or for I/O that can fail at runtime: a panic there kills the goroutine and, unrecovered, the process. Must is for startup invariants, not error handling.

heading: Type-Safe Idioms
text: Three idioms that push bugs from runtime to compile time. Newtype IDs (type AccountID string) give distinct domain types so the compiler rejects mixing an AccountID with a CustomerID. Bit-flag enums ( 1

heading: Newtype IDs: make the compiler catch swapped arguments
text: A function taking (from, to string) happily accepts a customer ID where an account ID belongs. Define distinct named types and that bug stops compiling:

heading: Bit-flag enums: a set of booleans in one integer
Sealed sum types: a closed set of variants
text: Go has no enum of structs, but an interface with an unexported method is a sealed type: only the declaring package can satisfy it, so the set of implementations is closed and known. A type switch over it is provably exhaustive — and the exhaustive linter will fail your build if you forget a case: Event declares one method, isEvent(), and it's lowercase — unexported. To satisfy Event, a type must have an isEvent() method, but a type in another package literally cannot write one: it can't name the unexported method from outside the declaring package. So the only Event implementations that can ever exist are the ones in this file. The set is closed. That closure is what makes the type switch trustworthy. With an open interface, some other package could add a variant tomorrow and your switch would silently fall through to default. With a sealed one, the compiler-plus-exhaustive-linter combination guarantees every case is handled — Go's nearest equivalent to the sum types (enum/sealed) of Rust and Swift. The default: panic is a belt-and-suspenders guard for the unreachable case.

heading: Lazy Init & Generic Helpers
text: Lazy initialization defers expensive setup until first use, done exactly once even under concurrency. Go 1.21 added sync.OnceValue, sync.OnceFunc and sync.OnceValues — they wrap a function and memoize its result, replacing the older sync.Once + package-var dance. A generic decorator wraps a function in another function of the same signature , adding behavior (caching, retries, timing) the caller can't see. Why it matters: these are the modern, boilerplate-free forms of two patterns you already met — the lazy Singleton and the wrapper — now that generics and the Once helpers exist.

heading: sync.OnceValue: the modern lazy singleton
text: Earlier you saw the lazy singleton with sync.Once plus a package-level variable. Go 1.21's sync.OnceValue collapses that into one line — the function runs at most once, its result is cached, and it's safe under concurrent first-callers: Three helpers, picked by what your init returns: sync.OnceFunc(f) wraps a func() that returns nothing (run once for its side effect); sync.OnceValue(f) wraps a func() T and caches the one value; sync.OnceValues(f) wraps a func() (T, error) (or any two results). All three are goroutine-safe and run the wrapped function exactly once. Prefer them over a hand-rolled sync.Once + guard variable — fewer moving parts, nothing to forget.

heading: Generic decorators: wrap a function, keep its shape
text: The middleware pattern wrapped http.Handler. Generics let you wrap any function while preserving its exact signature. Here Memoize turns a pure func(K) V into a caching version — the caller can't tell the difference:

heading: Generic containers: a real Set, finally
text: The map[T]struct set idiom (from the DSA appendix) becomes a reusable, type-safe Set[T] with generics — struct keys cost zero bytes, so it's as cheap as the raw map:

heading: More Behavioral Patterns
text: Three more behavioral idioms. The Null Object is a do-nothing implementation of an interface you return instead of nil, so callers never nil-check. Pub/Sub (the Observer pattern done right) is a broker that fans one event out to many subscriber channels. A custom iterator is a func(yield func(V) bool) — Go 1.23's range-over-func — that the for/range statement can drive, with iter.Pull to step it by hand. Why it matters: Null Object kills nil-guard clutter, a generic broker is the clean Observer, and range-over-func lets your own types be ranged over like slices and maps.

heading: Null Object: a do-nothing default instead of nil
text: If metrics might be unconfigured, the wrong fix is if s.metrics != nil scattered everywhere. The right one is a no-op implementation that's always safe to call:

heading: Pub/Sub: the Observer pattern, done right
text: The GoF section noted "Observer is a channel." Scaled up to many subscribers, that's a broker : subscribers each get their own channel; publish fans out to all of them, non-blocking so one slow consumer can't stall the rest. Generics make it work for any event type:

heading: Custom iterators: make your type range-able
text: Go 1.23's range-over-func lets you write a function the for/range loop can consume. Return an iter.Seq[V] — a func(yield func(V) bool) — call yield per element, and stop the instant it returns false (that's how the consumer's break reaches you). iter.Pull flips a push iterator into one you advance by hand: A push iterator is func(yield func(V) bool). For each value you produce, you call yield(v). yield returns true to mean "keep going" and false to mean "the consumer is done" — which happens when the for/range body hits a break, return, or panic. You must check that return and stop immediately. Forget the if !yield(v) and the consumer's break can't take effect; worse, calling yield again after it returned false makes the runtime panic. iter.Pull(seq) drives the push iterator in the background (the current implementation parks it on a goroutine, resumed on demand) and hands you next() and stop(). Each next() resumes the iterator until the next yield, returning (value, true); when the sequence ends you get (zero, false). Always defer stop() — it tells the background iterator to shut down and run its deferred cleanup (closing a file, say) even if you quit early. Pull is exactly what y

text: A last sharp trick: a method value (acct.Deposit) is a method already bound to its receiver — a func(int64) you can pass as a callback. A method expression (( Account).Deposit) leaves the receiver unbound, becoming a func( Account, int64) you supply the receiver to at call time: A mutable struct whose methods return q. Defer errors to Build(). Use over options for staged/conditional construction. func( T) Option — applying it returns the option that undoes it. Temporary set-and-restore for free.
