desc: Routing, middleware and handlers; advanced JSON (custom marshalers, RawMessage, omitempty, safe decoding); streaming with json.Encoder and NDJSON; and real-time with server-sent events and WebSockets.
text: Listen up, sport. You've got the database humming, the queries are parameterized, and the schema is clean. Now you need to expose all of that to the world — and the world is unforgiving, malicious, and will send you garbage JSON at 3 a.m. In this chapter I'm going to show you exactly how Go's HTTP server works, from the moment a TCP connection lands all the way to the moment you flush the last byte of a WebSocket frame. Routing, middleware, advanced JSON, streaming so your memory stays flat even as your dataset grows, server-sent events, and full-duplex WebSockets. Our running scenario is Meridian's payments API : the POST /transfers endpoint, a streaming account-statement export, and a live transfer-event feed for the operations dashboard. By the end you'll know every layer of the stack, and you'll know how the dangerous one operates. You're welcome. --

heading: Handlers, Routing & Middleware
text: The scenario: Meridian's payments service needs a REST API — account lookups, POST /transfers, and a live statement stream. Let's stand it up correctly — no guessing, no cowboy wiring — starting from the one interface that governs everything in net/http. On the job: Every production Go HTTP service you'll encounter is built on exactly this interface. Get the wiring wrong and you end up with a global mux, no method matching, and zero middleware — and you discover that at code review, not at 3 a.m.

heading: The http.Handler interface
text: A handler is any value that knows how to respond to an HTTP request. In Go, the http.Handler interface has one method — ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, Request) — and everything in net/http speaks it: a function, a struct, a middleware chain, the mux itself. You need it because every incoming request needs something that takes the request, does the work, and writes the response — and the single interface lets all these shapes be composed and wrapped uniformly. Every HTTP handler in Go satisfies a single interface: That's it. One method. ResponseWriter is where you write the response; Request carries the incoming request. Anything that has ServeHTTP(ResponseWriter, Request) is a valid HTTP handler — a struct, a closure, a middleware chain — all the same interface. http.HandlerFunc is a function type that satisfies Handler: So you can write a plain function and adapt it with http.HandlerFunc(myFunc). In practice, http.HandleFunc does this for you on the default mux. We'll use our own mux below, which is the correct production approach.

heading: ServeMux and Go 1.22+ routing
text: A ServeMux is a request multiplexer — a table that maps URL patterns to handlers. When a request arrives, the mux finds the longest matching pattern and calls that handler's ServeHTTP. You need one because a real API has tens of routes, and wiring them by hand into a single ServeHTTP is a maintenance disaster. Go 1.22's ServeMux also matches on HTTP method (GET /api/accounts/ ) and extracts named wildcards via r.PathValue. http.ServeMux is Go's built-in router. Before Go 1.22, it was minimal: exact paths and trailing-slash prefix matches. Go 1.22 gave it a major upgrade — method + path patterns, named wildcards, and precedence rules . Go 1.26 changes one existing behavior: ServeMux's automatic subtree-root redirects now use 307 Temporary Redirect instead of 301. The redirect applies when you register a subtree pattern with a trailing slash (or ... wildcard) and a client requests the subtree root without the slash. For example, registering /assets/ redirects /assets to /assets/ unless /assets is registered separately. Before Go 1.22, ServeMux had no method matching and no named wildcards — you needed a third-party router like chi or gorilla/mux. Go 1.22 closed the gap for most use-c

heading: Middleware — func(http.Handler) http.Handler
text: Middleware is a function that wraps a handler, runs code before and/or after it, and returns a new handler. The canonical Go signature is func(http.Handler) http.Handler. You need it because cross-cutting concerns — authentication, logging, rate limiting, request IDs — belong outside your business logic, applied uniformly at the routing layer. Middleware composes like Russian dolls: stack them with a chain helper, and they execute in order on every matching request. Middleware is a function that wraps a handler, runs code before and/or after it, and returns the wrapped handler. The canonical signature is func(http.Handler) http.Handler.

heading: Graceful shutdown
text: A production HTTP server must drain in-flight requests before dying. Server.Shutdown does it: The 15-second timeout means: give in-flight requests up to 15 seconds to finish, then hard-close anything that's still open. Wire it to os.Interrupt (Ctrl-C) and Kubernetes SIGTERM so rolling deploys drain cleanly. When a new TCP connection is accepted, net/http spawns one goroutine to own it for its lifetime — the conn.serve goroutine. That goroutine reads requests off the connection in a loop, calls your handler's ServeHTTP synchronously, and writes the response. For HTTP/1.1, the goroutine handles one request at a time (pipelining is the exception). For HTTP/2, net/http runs a multiplexing layer so multiple streams share one connection; each stream gets its own goroutine calling your handler. ResponseWriter is backed by a bufio.Writer — writes are buffered until the handler returns or you call Flush(). The first call to Write or WriteHeader freezes the response status; calling WriteHeader after Write is a no-op (and logs a warning). This is why you must set headers before writing the body. The Shutdown method calls Close on the underlying net.Listener (stops accepting new connections),

heading: Advanced JSON
text: Meridian's API speaks JSON. But the naive json.Marshal / json.Unmarshal approach will get you into trouble the moment a field is optional, a payload is polymorphic, or a client sends hostile input. Let's go deeper. On the job: The POST /transfers handler is hit by both internal services and third-party integrations. Every one of them is a potential attacker or a misconfigured client. Safe JSON decoding is not optional — it is the first gate.

heading: Custom MarshalJSON and UnmarshalJSON
text: Implement json.Marshaler and json.Unmarshaler on your types for full control:

heading: json.RawMessage for deferred and polymorphic decoding
text: Sometimes you don't know the shape of a field until you've read another field. json.RawMessage lets you defer decoding — capture the raw JSON bytes first, then decode into the right type once you know what it is.

heading: omitempty gotchas and struct embedding
text: omitempty skips a field when it holds the zero value — but the zero value depends on the type: omitempty omits 0, false, and "". This is usually what you want. Use a pointer field ( string, int64) when you need to distinguish zero from absent. omitempty does NOT omit a non-pointer struct even if all its fields are zero. Use MyStruct if you need true omission. A time.Time zero value (0001-01-01) is NOT omitted by omitempty because time.Time is a struct, not a primitive. Use time.Time or implement MarshalJSON to emit null for the zero value. Struct embedding flattens fields into the parent's JSON, but can produce surprises with custom marshalers:

heading: Decoding untrusted input safely
text: A client sending you JSON is a client you cannot trust. Three rules for every handler that decodes a request body: Rule 1: limit the body size. Without a size limit, a client sends a 1 GB body and your server allocates 1 GB of memory. Use http.MaxBytesReader on the request body before decoding. Rule 2: reject unknown fields. By default, json.Decoder silently ignores JSON keys it doesn't recognize. A typo in a field name sends the data into a black hole. Use d.DisallowUnknownFields() to return an error instead. Rule 3: decode once, into a strict shape. Never decode into map[string]interface . Decode into a typed struct with exactly the fields you expect. Go 1.25 added net/http.CrossOriginProtection — a middleware that blocks cross-origin requests that aren't legitimately CORS-preflight'd. It rejects POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests that carry a Content-Type and originate from a different origin without a matching preflight, catching a class of CSRF attacks that SameSite=Lax cookies alone don't prevent. Wrap your state-mutating routes with it: This is separate from CORS headers (which you still set for legitimate cross-origin callers). Auth & API Design (Part 1, Chapter 17) cove

heading: Streaming & NDJSON
text: A streaming response writes data to the client incrementally as it is produced, rather than buffering the full payload in memory first. NDJSON (Newline-Delimited JSON) is the wire format: one complete JSON object per line, separated by \n, with no enclosing array. You need it whenever the result set is unbounded or large — Meridian's statement export, a reconciliation dump, a live event feed — because allocating 400 MB per request to build a single JSON array is a month-end outage waiting to happen. Here's the scenario: Meridian's account-statement endpoint needs to stream up to 100,000 transfers for a monthly report. Naively, you fetch all rows from the database, marshal them into a JSON array, and write the whole thing at once. Your server allocates hundreds of megabytes per request, and the client waits for the entire response before it can show a single row. That's a crime against memory and a crime against UX. The fix is streaming : write rows to the client as they come out of the database. json.Encoder lets you marshal one object at a time. NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON) is the format — one JSON object per line, no enclosing array. On the job: Statement export endpoints are

heading: Streaming with json.Encoder and NDJSON
text: The moment you call w.Write(...) or w.WriteHeader(...), the HTTP headers are frozen and sent. If an error occurs mid-stream, you cannot change the 200 status to 500 — the client has already seen the 200. Log the error and close the connection. This is why you must handle any setup errors (like the DB query failing) before starting to write rows. http.ResponseWriter in net/http is backed by a bufio.Writer (typically 4 KB). Writes go into the buffer and are flushed to the network automatically when the buffer fills or the handler returns. For streaming you need to flush manually: w.(http.Flusher).Flush() calls through to bufio.Writer.Flush() which calls the underlying TCP Write syscall. Go 1.8+ guarantees that the concrete ResponseWriter implements http.Flusher for HTTP/1.1. For HTTP/2 it also flushes the frame to the network. The type assertion flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher) is the safe way — some testing ResponseWriter implementations (like httptest.Recorder) implement Flusher but don't actually push bytes anywhere, which is fine for tests. Prefer http.ResponseController (Go 1.20+): Rather than type-asserting to http.Flusher directly, wrap the ResponseWriter in an http.ResponseCon

heading: Server-Sent Events
text: Server-sent events are a browser-native protocol for one-way, server-to-client streaming over a plain HTTP connection. The server sets Content-Type: text/event-stream and keeps the connection open, writing text frames (id:, event:, data:, blank line) as events happen. The client's EventSource API reconnects automatically using the last id: it saw. You need SSE when the server pushes data the client only reads — live dashboards, notifications, audit feeds — and you want the simplicity of HTTP (works through proxies and CDNs) without the complexity of WebSockets. Server-sent events (SSE) give you a one-way live stream from server to client. Think: Meridian's operations dashboard showing live transfer events without the client polling every second — new POST /transfers completions appear the moment they're processed. The client opens one HTTP connection and keeps reading; the server pushes updates as they happen. SSE uses plain HTTP with Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each event is a few lines of text terminated by a blank line. The browser (or any SSE client) reconnects automatically if the connection drops, using the last id: it received. On the job: SSE is the right tool for Meri

heading: WebSockets
text: A WebSocket is a full-duplex, persistent connection between client and server. After an HTTP upgrade handshake, both ends can send frames at any time over a single TCP connection — no request/response cycle, no polling. You need it when the client and server both send in real time: Meridian's trading desk dealers send filter updates back to the server while the server pushes rate ticks to them. SSE only goes one way; WebSockets go both. Full-duplex. Bidirectional. One persistent connection, both ends sending whenever they want. For Meridian's trading desk — where dealers send filter updates (which currency pairs to watch) and the server pushes matching rate ticks in real time — this is your tool. WebSockets start as an HTTP request and upgrade to the WebSocket protocol. After the upgrade, the connection bypasses the normal HTTP request/response cycle entirely. On the job: WebSocket connections linger for hours. A server that doesn't enforce write deadlines will accumulate goroutines blocked on a single slow client. In a payments system, that slow client can be a mobile app on a flaky cellular connection — and it will block your goroutine until the TCP stack times out, which can tak

heading: The HTTP Upgrade handshake
text: The HTTP upgrade handshake is how a plain HTTP connection becomes a WebSocket. The client sends GET /ws with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, and a Sec-WebSocket-Key header. The server validates the key and responds 101 Switching Protocols — after which HTTP is over. The TCP connection is hijacked from net/http and handed directly to the WebSocket layer; frames (not HTTP packets) now flow in both directions. You need to understand this because after the 101, net/http's WriteTimeout no longer applies — the connection is outside its control, and you must enforce deadlines yourself. After the 101, HTTP is over. The TCP connection is hijacked from net/http and handed to the WebSocket layer. Frames (not HTTP packets) flow in both directions.

heading: Using coder/websocket
text: The coder/websocket package is context-aware, doesn't require goroutines for lifecycle management, and handles the upgrade cleanly. We'll use it here. (gorilla/websocket is the older alternative — battle-tested but not context-aware.) The handlers above work perfectly under httptest for unit tests (shown in the exercises below). The playground sandbox terminates long-lived connections — label SSE and WebSocket code clearly in your tests and run them locally or in a containerized environment.

heading: Read/write goroutine model and ping/pong
text: WebSocket connections need keepalives: ping frames from the server, pong frames from the client. coder/websocket handles ping/pong automatically when you use its built-in CloseRead mechanism or set a read deadline. Always set a write deadline before writing to prevent a slow client from blocking your goroutine forever:

heading: When to choose SSE vs WebSockets vs polling
text: Simple. Client asks every N seconds. Works everywhere. Best for low-frequency, low-latency-requirement data (daily reports). Wastes bandwidth at high frequency. Server pushes one-way over HTTP. Works through proxies and CDNs. Best for live dashboards, notifications, audit feeds where the client only watches. Auto-reconnect built in. Full duplex. Client and server both send freely. Best for interactive real-time features: trading, collaborative editing, chat, multi-player. Proxy-hostile (needs upgrade support). WebSockets are overkill for dashboards that only receive data. SSE is simpler, proxy-friendly, and reconnects automatically. Reach for WebSockets only when the client genuinely needs to send messages back to the server in real time. When websocket.Accept (or gorilla/websocket's Upgrader.Upgrade) is called, it uses http.Hijacker — an interface that net/http's concrete ResponseWriter implements. Hijack() returns the raw net.Conn and a bufio.ReadWriter, removing the connection from net/http's management entirely. From that moment on, net/http forgets about that connection: no more buffering, no more request/response framing, no timeout from WriteTimeout. The WebSocket library ow

heading: Server Hardening
text: You've built the handler. You've wired the middleware. Now you're going to skip the part that every junior engineer skips — and that every security postmortem traces back. The default http.Server has no timeouts . None. A client that sends one byte per minute will hold a goroutine and a TCP connection open indefinitely. A thousand of them will stop your server from accepting legitimate traffic. This attack has a name: Slowloris. And it works on unprotected Go servers out of the box. On the job: You won't spot this in local dev or in a load test with well-behaved clients. It shows up in a production incident when someone opens 10,000 slow connections and your server stops accepting real traffic. Operations pages you. The postmortem says "no timeouts configured." Senior engineers set these reflexively.

heading: The timeout knobs
text: http.Server exposes five timeout fields. None of them have a default: Field What it covers Recommended starting value --- --- --- ReadHeaderTimeout Time to receive the complete request headers 5 s — set this first, always ReadTimeout Time to receive headers + full request body 10–30 s depending on expected payloads WriteTimeout Time to write the full response 30–60 s; for streaming/SSE, set to 0 and control per-write with context.WithTimeout IdleTimeout How long a keep-alive connection may sit idle between requests 60–120 s (body cap) http.MaxBytesReader on the request body 1 MiB for API handlers; 0 for streaming ReadHeaderTimeout is the cheap, must-set Slowloris mitigation: Go reads headers in a tight loop from the TCP buffer, so this timeout fires before any user-land handler code runs. It costs almost nothing but closes the attack surface. ReadTimeout covers the entire read phase including the body. For handlers that stream large uploads, set ReadTimeout to 0 and use http.MaxBytesReader to cap individual request bodies instead. WriteTimeout covers the write phase. Set it to 0 for SSE and WebSocket handlers — those connections intentionally live beyond a normal write window, and

heading: Capping request bodies with http.MaxBytesReader
text: Even with ReadTimeout set, an attacker can send a 2 GB request body inside the timeout window if your upstream connection is fast. http.MaxBytesReader wraps the body's Read method and returns an error the moment the byte count exceeds your limit: For multipart uploads (file ingestion, NACHA batch files), do not load the entire multipart into memory. Use r.ParseMultipartForm(maxMemory) — it spills to a temp file on disk when the in-memory threshold is exceeded — and validate each part's size before reading: A client that omits Content-Length and streams slowly can still OOM a server that reads multipart naively. Cap every part before reading.

heading: Secure response headers as middleware
text: Timeouts and body caps protect the server . The next layer protects the client — specifically, the browser that renders responses from Meridian's API and its admin console. A handful of response headers tell the browser to refuse a list of attacks it would otherwise happily perform on your users' behalf. They cost nothing to set and they belong in one middleware applied to every route — not sprinkled per-handler where someone will forget half of them. Secure response headers are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to enforce a security policy on the content you return — which scripts may run (Content-Security-Policy), whether to second-guess your declared content type (X-Content-Type-Options), how much referrer information to leak (Referrer-Policy), and who may embed your pages in a frame (X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors). You need them because the browser's defaults are permissive for backwards compatibility, and a single missing header is the difference between an XSS payload that fizzles and one that drains an account. The four that matter most for a JSON/admin surface like Meridian's: Forbids MIME sniffing — the browser guessing a response's type by peeking at

heading: Hardened server: before and after
text: If you set WriteTimeout to 30 s on a server that also handles SSE or WebSocket connections, those handlers will be forcibly closed after 30 seconds — regardless of whether they're still actively pushing data. The fix: use a single http.Server for short-lived API routes with a WriteTimeout, and a separate http.Server on a different port (or route prefix) for streaming/WebSocket routes with WriteTimeout: 0. The streaming handlers control their own write deadlines per-message via context.WithTimeout. Timeouts in http.Server are implemented via net.Conn.SetDeadline on the underlying TCP connection. When ReadHeaderTimeout is set, the conn.serve goroutine calls SetReadDeadline before entering the header-read loop, then resets it to zero (or applies ReadTimeout) after headers are read. When WriteTimeout is set, it calls SetWriteDeadline before calling ServeHTTP. Because these are set on the net.Conn directly, they fire at the OS level — blocked Read and Write calls return net.Error with Timeout() == true. This is why a WriteTimeout fires even if your handler is in a json.Encode call — the underlying Write syscall times out. For WebSocket connections, Hijack() hands you the raw net.Conn, a

text: Right. Exercises were your warmup, sport. This is my test. I designed it myself, and I'm personally invested in your failure rate. Don't disappoint me. The buffered version is a memory time bomb. The safe-decode version is the door you close before the attacker walks through. Make both changes. When all four checks print PASS and the final line reads ALL CHECKS PASS, the flag is yours. No partial credit. -- You now own the full HTTP server stack — and the hardening layer that seniors set without being asked: http.Handler / HandlerFunc — the one interface; every handler, middleware, and mux satisfies it. Go 1.22's ServeMux adds method + path patterns and r.PathValue wildcards. Go 1.26 changes automatic subtree-root slash redirects from 301 to 307. desc: Password hashing, sessions vs tokens, JWTs and their footguns, OAuth2/OIDC, passkeys (WebAuthn) and MFA; plus REST conventions, versioning, pagination, idempotency and OpenAPI.
text: Listen up, because I'm only going to say this once: the most catastrophic breaches in history weren't caused by clever zero-days or nation-state APTs. They were caused by engineers who stored passwords in plain text, signed JWTs with the secret "secret", and built APIs so inconsistent that their own clients gave up trying to parse the errors. You are not going to be one of those people. Not on my watch. This chapter is two disciplines in one. The Auth half covers password hashing done right, sessions versus stateless tokens, the full JWT machinery and every footgun bolted onto it, OAuth2/OIDC so you stop treating "Login with Google" as magic, and passkeys & MFA — the factors that hold when the password itself has already leaked. The API Design half covers REST conventions, status codes that actually mean something, versioning, pagination, idempotency, error shapes, and generating an OpenAPI contract from Go. We'll secure and design Meridian's ledger API — specifically the POST /transfers endpoint and the checkout auth flow — all the way through this chapter. This chapter is long because it has to be. Auth done halfway is worse than auth not done at all. --

heading: Password Hashing
text: Here's the scene: you're building authentication for Meridian's ledger API. A user registers with an email and a password. How do you store it? On the job: Meridian's checkout endpoint processes real transfers. If a credential database leaks and passwords aren't properly hashed, every account is compromised — and the regulatory fallout is worse than the breach itself. The catastrophically wrong answer — the one that has destroyed companies — is to store the password as-is, or to hash it with MD5 or SHA-256. Both approaches look like they're "doing something secure." Neither is. Let me break down why, one step at a time. A password hash is a one-way transformation of a plaintext password into a fixed-size digest. The point is that verification requires only re-running the same transformation — you never store the plaintext. What makes bcrypt and argon2id different from general-purpose hashes (MD5, SHA-256) is that they are deliberately slow and memory-hard : tunable work factors make brute-force economically infeasible even after a database leak. Get this wrong and a single breach exposes every user's password.

heading: Why fast hashes are a crime
text: MD5, SHA-256, SHA-512 — these are general-purpose hashes. They're designed to be fast . A modern GPU can compute 10 billion SHA-256 hashes per second. If your database leaks (and someday it will), an attacker can brute-force every 8-character password in minutes using pre-computed rainbow tables or GPU cracking rigs. What you need is a hash that's deliberately slow and memory-hard — one where computing it costs real CPU and RAM, so brute-forcing 100 million candidates becomes economically infeasible. The battle-tested standard. Built-in cost factor (work factor) — you dial the CPU cost. Each hash is unique because bcrypt embeds a random 22-character salt. Rounds-based: at cost 12, one hash takes 250ms on a modern CPU. Attacker on a GPU? Slowed to thousands per second, not billions. The 2015 Password Hashing Competition winner. Two variants: argon2i (side-channel resistant) and argon2id (recommended — best of both). Three tuning knobs: time, memory, and parallelism. Memory-hard: requires RAM, not just CPU, which cripples GPU/ASIC cracking rigs. The modern recommendation for new systems. Memory-hard, pre-dates argon2. Used by some older systems. Decent but argon2id is preferred for n

heading: bcrypt in Go
text: Go's golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt package makes this straightforward. Here's a complete, correct implementation: bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword runs in constant time — it doesn't short-circuit the moment it finds a mismatch. This prevents timing attacks , where an attacker measures tiny differences in response time to deduce how much of the hash matched. Never do a plain bytes.Equal or == comparison for secrets. For non-bcrypt secrets (API keys, HMAC tags) use crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare. When bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword(password, cost) runs, it: 1. Generates 16 random bytes from crypto/rand — this is the salt. The salt is unique per password, so two users with the same password get completely different hashes. bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword does not accept a caller-provided randomness source; the salt comes from Go's cryptographically secure random source. 2. Runs the Eksblowfish key schedule 2^cost times — at cost 12 that's 4,096 rounds of an expensive key setup. This is the "deliberately slow" part. The key schedule runs in time proportional to 2^cost, and you can tune that as hardware improves. 3. Encrypts the 24-byte magic string "OrpheanBeholderScryDoubt" 64 times using the r

text: For new systems, reach for argon2id. The API is slightly more manual because you manage the salt yourself: --

heading: Email Verification
text: You hashed the password. Beautiful. But you have no idea whether ada@example.com actually belongs to the human who just signed up — or whether they fat-fingered it, or typed someone else's address to harvest Meridian receipts. Account creation is only half done until the email is proven . This is the section that course you were eyeing spends an hour on, and it's the first time we actually send mail in Go. A transactional email is a one-to-one message triggered by a user action — verify-your-address, password reset, a payment receipt — as opposed to bulk marketing mail. It must be reliable and fast: a verification email that arrives ten minutes late loses the signup. Why it matters: at Meridian, the verification, receipt, and settlement-notice emails are part of the product's correctness, not decoration. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is the protocol mail servers speak to hand messages to each other. Your app connects to an SMTP server (your provider's, or your own relay), authenticates, and submits the message; the server takes over delivery. Go ships net/smtp in the standard library — minimal but enough to send. Why it matters: you rarely run your own mail server; you submi

heading: Minting the token — it's a bearer secret
text: The token in the verification link is a bearer credential : whoever holds it can verify the account. So it gets the same respect as a password — generated from a CSPRNG, stored hashed, expiring, single-use. 1. CSPRNG only. crypto/rand, never math/rand. A predictable token is a free account takeover. 2. Store the hash, not the token. A leaked database (or log line) of raw tokens is a leaked set of working verify-links. Store SHA-256(token); email the token. 3. Expire it. 24 hours is typical. An eternal token is an eternal liability. 4. Single-use. Consume it inside the same transaction that flips verified = true. Replaying a used link does nothing. 5. Constant-time compare the digest (crypto/subtle) so response timing can't be used to confirm a guess.

heading: Actually sending it — net/smtp
text: Here is the real mailer. It does not run in the playground above because it dials a network — the sandbox has none — but this is the production shape: net/smtp is frozen and deliberately minimal — SendMail does plain auth + STARTTLS on port 587, and that's about it. For implicit TLS (port 465) you dial the TLS connection yourself with tls.Dial and wrap it in smtp.NewClient. In real services most teams skip SMTP entirely and call the provider's HTTP API (SES/SendGrid/Postmark SDKs) for delivery receipts, bounce webhooks, and templating. The protocol knowledge here is what those SDKs wrap. The 201 Created in the timeline returns before SMTP. Sending mail is a slow, flaky, third-party network call; if you await it inside the signup handler, your signup latency and error rate become your mail provider's latency and error rate. Enqueue the send as a background job and return immediately. Retries, backoff, and dead-lettering for that job are exactly what we build in Background Jobs, Scheduling & Async Work (Part 2) — the verification email is the textbook async job. On the job: the single most common verification bug isn't crypto — it's the enumeration leak. If POST /users answers "email

heading: Sessions vs Tokens
text: After a Meridian user proves their identity at login, you need to remember it across requests. Two schools of thought: sessions (stateful, server-remembers) and tokens (stateless, client-carries). On the job: Meridian runs multiple API replicas behind a load balancer. Choosing session vs token is not just a design preference — it decides whether you need a shared session store, and what "logout" means under a race condition. A session is a server-side record keyed by a random ID sent to the client in a cookie. The server is the source of truth — revoke the record, revoke access instantly. A token (typically a JWT) is a self-contained signed credential the client carries; the server verifies the signature without a database lookup. Sessions win on revocability; tokens win on statelessness across replicas. The choice shapes your logout story and your infrastructure.

heading: Sessions: the server remembers you
text: In a session-based system: 1. User logs in → server creates a session record in a database or Redis, keyed by a random session ID. 2. Server sends the session ID to the client — typically in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie. 3. On every subsequent request, the browser sends the cookie; the server looks up the session ID in the store. 4. Logout: delete the session record. The cookie is instantly worthless. Advantages of sessions: instant revocation (logout is a DB delete), simple to reason about, no cryptographic complexity at the application layer. Disadvantages: requires shared state. If you run 10 API replicas, they all need access to the same session store (Redis, Postgres). Adds latency per request for the lookup. Horizontal scaling adds complexity.

heading: Tokens: the client carries the proof
text: In a token-based system, the server mints a signed token and sends it to the client. The token itself encodes the user's identity and permissions, signed with the server's key. To authenticate, the server just verifies the signature — no database lookup required. JWTs (JSON Web Tokens) are the most common format. They're the topic of the next section, and they come with enough footguns that they deserve their own treatment. localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on your page — including injected XSS payloads. If you must use JWTs, store them in HttpOnly cookies (same as sessions). The "localStorage for JWTs" pattern is one of the most widely spread security antipatterns in web development. It's wrong. Every time. --

heading: JWTs
text: JWT stands for JSON Web Token . It's a compact, URL-safe, self-contained token format that encodes claims — who you are, what you can do, when this expires — and proves they haven't been tampered with via a cryptographic signature. On the job: Meridian's POST /transfers endpoint is protected by a JWT middleware. If the signing key is weak or the algorithm isn't pinned, an attacker can forge admin tokens, authorize fraudulent transfers, and drain accounts before anyone notices. This section is security-sensitive — read it twice. A JWT is three base64url-encoded JSON objects joined by dots: a header (algorithm + token type), a payload (claims: who you are, when this expires, what roles you have), and a signature that proves the first two haven't been tampered with. The payload is encoded, not encrypted — never put secrets there. The signature only proves integrity; it does not hide the claims. An attacker who captures a JWT can read all the claims; they cannot forge a valid one without the signing key.

heading: Structure: header.payload.signature
text: A JWT is three base64url-encoded JSON objects joined by dots: Header (base64url-decoded): Payload (base64url-decoded): Signature : HMAC-SHA256(base64url(header) + "." + base64url(payload), secret key) The payload is not encrypted — it's just encoded. Anyone who intercepts the token can decode the header and payload. The signature only proves the payload hasn't been tampered with . Never put a password, credit card number, or PII in a JWT payload unless you're also encrypting it (JWE, a separate spec). , or via cookie."}, ]} caption="The server is stateless: it re-derives trust from the signature alone, not from a session store." /

heading: Implementing JWT in Go
text: The standard library doesn't have JWT support — you'll use github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5. Here's a complete, correct implementation:

heading: The JWT footguns
text: There are three footguns that have caused real production security incidents. Know them cold. The most notorious JWT vulnerability. The spec (RFC 7519) allows an algorithm of "none" — meaning the signature is empty and skipped entirely. A naive verifier that trusts the alg field from the token header itself will accept any unsigned token as valid. An attacker crafts in the header, forges any claims they want, and sends an empty signature. Always validate the algorithm yourself in the key function — never accept what the token claims. HS256 is symmetric: you sign and verify with the same secret. If the secret is short, predictable, or taken from a wordlist, an attacker who captures one valid token can brute-force the secret offline (they just need to find a key where HMAC(header.payload, key) == signature). Use at minimum 32 bytes of crypto/rand entropy. Or switch to RS256/ES256 (asymmetric) — then even a compromised public key can't sign tokens. Never skip ExpiresAt (exp claim). A JWT without an expiry is valid forever — a leaked token is permanent compromise. Short-lived access tokens (15min–1h) + refresh tokens (longer-lived, stored server-side and revocable) is the right pattern

heading: Access tokens vs refresh tokens
text: Short-lived access tokens + long-lived refresh tokens is the production pattern. Here's the flow: Access token: signed JWT, 15 minutes to 1 hour, sent on every API request. Stateless — server verifies the signature, no DB needed. When it expires, the client needs a new one. Refresh token: opaque random string (or a JWT), stored server-side in a table, long-lived (7–30 days). Client uses it to silently get a new access token without re-entering credentials. Because it's stored server-side, you can revoke it instantly by deleting the row — this is your "logout" and "revoke all sessions" lever. --

heading: Authorization and RBAC
text: Everything up to here answered who are you — the password check, the session, the verified JWT signature. That's authentication . It is not the same question as what are you allowed to do — and conflating the two is how a read-only auditor ends up able to move money. On the job: Meridian has two kinds of internal users on the same API. An admin can create transfers; a compliance auditor can only read them. They authenticate identically — same login, same JWT machinery. The difference is purely authorization. If POST /transfers only checks "is this a valid token?" and not "does this user hold transactions:write?", the auditor's perfectly-valid token authorizes a transfer it should never be allowed to make. That's a 403 that should have happened and didn't. Authentication establishes who the caller is (valid credentials → a known user). Authorization decides what that authenticated caller may do (this user holds the permission this endpoint requires). They are sequential and distinct: authentication produces a 401 when it fails ("not logged in"); authorization produces a 403 when it fails ("logged in, but not allowed"). Get them backwards and you either leak access or leak the existe

heading: Roles vs permissions
text: The naive approach stuffs a single role string into the JWT ("role": "admin") and scatters if role == "admin" checks through the handlers. It works until you have a third role, or a permission that two roles share, or an "admin who can't delete" — then the if ladder rots. The model that scales is permission-based : define fine-grained permission codes that name a capability, not a person. A permission is a fine-grained capability code like transactions:read or transactions:write. Users are granted a set of permissions (usually via roles — an admin role bundles transactions:read + transactions:write; an auditor role bundles only transactions:read). Each endpoint declares the one permission it requires, and a middleware checks the caller's set for it. Why it matters: capabilities compose and evolve without rewriting handlers — adding a new role is a data change, not a code change, and every endpoint's requirement is stated in exactly one place. For Meridian we'll use two codes — transactions:read and transactions:write — and align endpoints to them: requires transactions:read — admin and auditor both have it. requires transactions:write — admin only. requires transactions:write — adm

heading: The requirePermission middleware
text: Model the permission set as a slice with a membership check, then write one middleware that guards a handler with a required code. Authorization runs after authentication has already put a user on the request — it checks the set and returns 403 Forbidden if the code is missing. The middleware is the only place the rule lives. Wire it onto each route with the permission that route demands: In a real service requirePermission wraps your authentication middleware (which puts the user on the context) — so the full chain is authenticate → look up permissions → check the required code → handler . Each layer answers exactly one question. Grant a user the minimum permission set their job requires, and nothing more — the same principle as minimal OAuth2 scopes in the next section. Meridian's auditor gets transactions:read because reading is their entire job; they never get transactions:write "just in case." When an account is compromised, the blast radius is exactly the permissions that account held. A read-only token that leaks cannot move money. Design the permission codes narrow and assign them stingily. --

heading: OAuth2 and OIDC
text: OAuth2 is an authorization framework. OIDC (OpenID Connect) is an authentication layer built on top of it. When you add "Login with Google" to Meridian's checkout, you're implementing the OAuth2 authorization-code flow with OIDC claims. On the job: If you skip the state CSRF parameter, an attacker can trick a Meridian user into linking their bank account to the attacker's Meridian session — a classic account-takeover vector. This isn't theoretical; it's been exploited in production fintech apps. The most important concept to internalize: in OAuth2, there are three actors: 1. Resource Owner — the user. 2. Client — your application, asking for access on behalf of the user. 3. Authorization Server / Provider — Google, GitHub, your own OAuth server. This is who the user actually logs into, and who issues tokens. Your Go service can be a client (you're consuming someone else's OAuth, e.g. "Login with GitHub"), or a provider (you're building the OAuth server that other services authenticate against). Most backends are clients. OAuth2 is an authorization framework: it lets a user grant your app limited access to their account on another service without giving you their password. In the au

heading: The Authorization-Code Flow
text: The whole dance, hop by hop — note which legs run through the browser and which run server-to-server: The state parameter is load-bearing — it prevents CSRF attacks where an attacker tricks a user into authenticating with the attacker's account. Generate it with crypto/rand, store it in the session before the redirect, and verify it on callback.

heading: Scopes: asking for the minimum
text: Scopes define what access you're requesting. read:user is not user:email is not repo. Request the minimum scope your app actually needs — this is the principle of least privilege applied to OAuth2. Users see the scope list on the consent screen; asking for repo:write when you only need to read a username will (correctly) alarm them.

heading: Access tokens vs refresh tokens (OAuth2 side)
text: In OAuth2, access tokens are short-lived (minutes to hours) and used to call the protected API. Refresh tokens are longer-lived, stored on your server, and used to get new access tokens when the old ones expire — without requiring the user to log in again. The provider can revoke a refresh token (e.g. the user revokes your app's access), which immediately cuts off future token refreshes. OAuth2 is authorization-only — it proves a user granted you access, but tells you nothing about who they are . OIDC adds an id token — a JWT signed by the provider — that contains claims like sub (stable user ID), email, name, and email verified. The sub claim is the stable identifier you store locally to represent that user. Don't use email as the primary key — it can change. --

heading: Passkeys and MFA
text: Monday, 03:40. Meridian's login endpoint is suddenly handling forty thousand attempts an hour — and 0.8% of them succeed . Not because anything you built is broken: those are correct email-and-password pairs, harvested from some other company's breach and replayed by bots, because humans reuse passwords. This is credential stuffing , and it's the most humbling attack in the book: your bcrypt verification, your sessions, your JWTs all behave exactly as designed — and you lose anyway. The password is a secret your user already gave to a hundred other websites. You never controlled it. On the job: for a fintech, the second factor isn't optional hardening. The EU's PSD2 Strong Customer Authentication rules require two independent factors for payment actions, SOC 2 auditors ask where MFA is enforced, and your fraud team will tell you account takeover is the top loss vector. Meridian ships MFA, or Meridian doesn't operate in Europe. MFA requires proof from two or more different categories of factor: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (phone, hardware key), something you are (fingerprint, face). The category rule is the whole game: a password plus a security question i

heading: TOTP: the offline second factor
text: The six-digit code from Google Authenticator is a TOTP — a time-based one-time password. The design is twenty years old and a small masterpiece of constraint engineering. HOTP (RFC 4226, 2005) generated codes from a shared secret and a counter , but counters drift out of sync. TOTP (RFC 6238, 2011) made one substitution: the counter is the current Unix time divided by 30. Now both sides can compute the same code with no communication at all — the phone needs no network, no SMS, no battery beyond the clock. That's why it works in airplane mode, and why it became the default second factor for a decade. The full mechanism, end to end: 1. Enrollment. The server generates a 20-byte random secret (crypto/rand, nothing less) and shows it once as a QR code encoding an otpauth://totp/Meridian:dana@example.com?secret=BASE32...&issuer=Meridian URI. The phone stores the secret. From this moment, server and phone share a symmetric key. 2. Code generation. Both sides compute HMAC-SHA1(secret, floor(unixTime/30)), then dynamically truncate : the low nibble of the final HMAC byte picks an offset, 31 bits are read from there, and the result mod 10⁶ becomes the six digits. 3. Verification. The serve

heading: Where TOTP dies
text: Now the uncomfortable part. A pixel-perfect phishing page at meridian-payments.app proxies your real login in real time: the victim types their password and their fresh TOTP code into the wrong website, the attacker's script replays both against the real meridian.app within the 30-second window, and the session is gone. TOTP proved possession — to whoever asked . The human is the origin check, and humans fail origin checks at 3am. The other second factors fare no better. SMS is strictly worse: SIM-swap attacks and SS7 interception led NIST SP 800-63B to restrict it back in 2017 — in a fintech context, treat SMS codes as a legacy liability. Push approvals ("Tap to approve this login") die to MFA fatigue : bomb the victim's phone with prompts at 2am until they tap Approve to make it stop — that's how Uber's internal network fell in 2022. Number-matching patches it, but the pattern stands: every factor a human can relay, a human can be tricked into relaying.

heading: Passkeys: making phishing structurally impossible
text: The fix is to take the human out of the trust path entirely. The lineage: hardware U2F keys (Yubico and Google, 2014) proved that challenge-response with per-site keys kills phishing; FIDO2/WebAuthn (a W3C standard, 2019) built that ceremony into every browser; passkeys (2022 onward) made the same WebAuthn credential discoverable and synced through iCloud Keychain / Google Password Manager, so ordinary humans get hardware-key security without ever seeing a USB stick. As of 2026, every mainstream browser and OS ships it. A passkey is an asymmetric keypair minted by the user's device for exactly one website. The private key lives in the platform authenticator (Secure Enclave, TPM, or a synced keychain) and never leaves; the server stores only the public key. Login is challenge-response: the server sends fresh random bytes, the device signs them after a biometric/PIN unlock, the server verifies with the stored public key. There is no shared secret to steal, stuff, or phish. Two ceremonies, both brokered by the browser's navigator.credentials API: Registration. The server sends a random challenge plus its rpID (meridian.app). The authenticator mints a keypair scoped to that rpID , seal

heading: Step-up authentication
text: MFA isn't a login-time binary; it's a freshness property. The session (or JWT claims — you built both earlier in this chapter) records how the user authenticated and when . Reading a balance can ride a day-old session; moving $25,000 should demand strong auth from the last few minutes: This composes exactly like the requirePermission middleware from the RBAC section — authorization asked may you ; step-up asks is it really, recently you . Phishable, SIM-swappable, SS7-interceptable. NIST has restricted them since 2017. In a fintech, an SMS-only second factor is a finding, not a feature. Offline, cheap, standardized — and relayable in real time by a proxy phishing page. Encrypt the secret at rest (it must be recoverable); hash the recovery codes (they are passwords); rate-limit verification. One tap at 2am under prompt-bombing and the account is gone — MFA fatigue took down Uber in 2022. Number-matching helps; the human relay problem remains. Per-origin keypairs; the browser signs the true origin into the ceremony. Phishing fails structurally, breaches leak only public keys, and one biometric gesture covers two factor categories. Account recovery is the new perimeter. An email-only

heading: REST Design
text: Now we pivot. Auth secures the API; the next four sections are about designing it. We'll use Meridian's ledger API as the running example throughout. On the job: Inconsistent REST design isn't just aesthetically bad — it breaks client SDKs, breaks auto-generated OpenAPI docs, and makes every outage harder to diagnose because nobody agrees on what a 200 with an error body means.

heading: Resources and URLs
text: REST is about resources, not actions. The URL names a thing ; the HTTP method describes what to do with it. Rules: Nouns, plural: /accounts, /transactions, /users — not /getAccount or /accountList. Nesting for ownership: /accounts/123/transfers — transfers that belong to account 123. Don't go deeper than two levels of nesting. /accounts/123/transfers/456/line-items — that's too deep; consider /transfers/456/line-items instead. IDs in the path, not the body: DELETE /accounts/123, not POST /accounts/delete with .

heading: Status codes that actually mean something
text: The general success. GET, PUT success. Body contains the resource. POST that created something. Include a Location header pointing to the new resource. Success with no body. DELETE, or a PATCH that returns nothing. The client sent malformed input — invalid JSON, missing required field, wrong type. Include a body explaining what was wrong. The client is not authenticated (no token, or token is invalid/expired). "401" means "not logged in." The client is authenticated but not authorized. "403" means "logged in but not allowed." Resource doesn't exist — or you're hiding it (returning 404 instead of 403 to not leak existence). The request can't be completed due to a state conflict — duplicate key, optimistic lock failure, idempotency key collision. Syntactically valid but semantically wrong — amount is negative, account is closed, insufficient funds. Never return 200 with an error in the body. with HTTP 200 is an abomination. It breaks every HTTP-aware middleware, breaks monitoring, breaks retry logic, and makes me profoundly sad. Use the right status code. The response body elaborates; it does not override.

heading: API versioning strategies
text: You will change your API. The question is how to manage that change without breaking existing clients. Three strategies: /v1/accounts, /v2/accounts. Most common, most explicit. Clients know exactly what they're talking to. The downside: it duplicates routes, and people sometimes forget to update the version prefix. New to most Go teams — start here. Accept: application/vnd.ledger.v2+json or API-Version: 2026-01-01. Keeps URLs clean. Harder to test in a browser. Stripe uses date-based header versioning — it's elegant but complex to route in middleware. /accounts?v=2. Easy to add, easy to miss. Caching is harder because the version is part of the query string. Generally the weakest option, but you'll see it in legacy systems. For most Go services, URL path versioning is the right default . It's obvious, it's easy to route in net/http, and it's impossible to miss: Keep /v1 alive while clients migrate. Deprecate it loudly (a Deprecation response header, documentation, email). Delete it on a published schedule, not quietly. Pagination breaks a large list into pages so you don't return 100,000 transfers in one response. heading: Sorting: the SQL-injection footgun in ORDER BY
text: List endpoints invite a ?sort= parameter (?sort=amount, ?sort=-created at for descending). It looks harmless, and it is the single most common way an otherwise-parameterized API gets a SQL injection. The reason is a hard SQL limitation: you cannot use a placeholder parameter for a column name or for ASC/DESC . Placeholders ($1, ?) only bind values . So the tempting move is to interpolate the client's string straight into the query — and now ?sort=amount; DROP TABLE transfers -- is your problem. A sort safelist is the fixed set of column names (and directions) your endpoint permits a client to sort by. Because ORDER BY can't be parameterized, you must validate the client's sort value against this allowlist and reject anything not on it — never interpolate the raw string into the SQL. Why it matters: the safelist is the boundary between "the client picks a sort order" and "the client writes arbitrary SQL." It's also good UX — an unknown sort key gets a clean 422, not a 500. The pattern: keep an explicit safelist, confirm the requested value is a member, then map it to a trusted column + direction you control. Anything not on the list is a 422 Unprocessable Entity, never a query. Do n

heading: Idempotency and Errors
text: An idempotency key is a client-generated UUID the client includes in every state-mutating request (Idempotency-Key: ). The server stores the result of the first execution keyed by that UUID; if the same key arrives again (a retry after a timeout), the server replays the cached result without re-executing. This turns a non-idempotent operation — POST /transfers — into one that can be safely retried. Without it, a network timeout followed by a retry creates two transfers: money moves twice. In a ledger system, that's not a bug — it's fraud.

heading: Idempotency keys for writes
text: A network timeout is not a failure — it's an unknown. The request may or may not have reached the server. If your client retries a POST /transfers after a timeout and it had already succeeded, you've just double-charged someone. In a ledger system, this is catastrophic. The solution: idempotency keys . The client generates a unique key (typically a UUID v4) for each logical operation and sends it in a header (Idempotency-Key: ). The server: 1. Checks if it's seen this key before (in Redis or Postgres). 2. If yes: return the cached response from the first execution. 3. If no: execute the operation, store the result keyed by the idempotency key, return the result. In Meridian's double-entry ledger (covered fully in Part 3, "Double-Entry Ledgers"), idempotency keys are critical infrastructure, not a nice-to-have. A payment retry without idempotency creates a second debit/credit pair — the books no longer balance and someone's money is wrong. Wire idempotency keys into every state-mutating operation from day one. Retrofitting it later is miserable.

heading: CSRF protection for API routes (Go 1.25+)
text: JSON APIs that accept Authorization headers are generally safe from classic form-based CSRF, but browser-based clients that rely on session cookies are not. Go 1.25 introduced net/http.CrossOriginProtection, which validates the Sec-Fetch-Site, Origin, and Referer Fetch metadata headers to reject cross-origin requests automatically. On the job: Meridian's checkout endpoint accepts cookie-authenticated sessions in addition to Bearer tokens. Without CSRF protection, a malicious page can trigger POST /transfers from a logged-in user's browser with zero JavaScript — the browser sends the cookie automatically. net/http.CrossOriginProtection is a defense layer — it rejects requests that look cross-origin based on Fetch metadata headers. It is not the same as setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin (that's CORS, which is about what browsers are allowed to read). Use both: CORS to control what clients can read, CrossOriginProtection to reject mutations that shouldn't be coming from other origins at all.

heading: Why CSRF happens, and the two classic defenses
text: The Fetch-metadata approach above is the modern, low-effort layer. But you should understand why CSRF is possible at all, because it explains both the older defenses and exactly which clients need them. CSRF is an attack that abuses ambient credentials : a browser attaches a site's session cookie to every request to that site, including requests triggered by a different , malicious site. So a logged-in Meridian user who visits evil.example can have their browser silently fire POST /transfers to Meridian — cookie attached, request authenticated — with no JavaScript and no token theft. Why it matters: anything authenticated by an automatically-sent cookie is exposed; anything authenticated by an explicit Authorization: Bearer header is not , because the browser does not attach that header cross-site. That last point is the key triage: a pure token-in-header API is largely immune to classic CSRF (the attacker's page can't set your Authorization header). CSRF is a problem specifically for cookie/session-based auth, where the credential travels automatically. Two defenses, usually layered: Defense 1 — the SameSite cookie attribute. This is the cheapest and most effective single control.

heading: OpenAPI/Swagger: your API contract
text: OpenAPI is a machine-readable specification for your REST API — the types, endpoints, parameters, request/response schemas, and authentication requirements. It's the contract between your service and every client that consumes it. On the job: Meridian's partner banks integrate against the ledger API. Without a published OpenAPI spec, every integration is reverse-engineered from curl examples in a Slack thread. With a spec, partners generate typed SDKs in their language of choice. The spec also feeds contract tests — the moment a Go struct change breaks the spec, CI catches it before production. In Go, you have two approaches: 1. Spec-first: write the openapi.yaml manually, then generate server stubs and client SDKs from it. Tools: oapi-codegen, openapi-generator. 2. Code-first (generate from Go): annotate your handlers and types, then generate the spec. Tools: swaggo/swag, go-swagger. For most teams, spec-first with oapi-codegen produces cleaner results — the spec is the single source of truth and you always have it. heading: GraphQL: what it solves and what it costs
text: GraphQL is not a replacement for REST; it's a solution to a specific set of problems REST has. What GraphQL solves: Overfetching: REST endpoints return fixed shapes. If the mobile client only needs id and name from a GET /accounts/ that returns 30 fields, it wastes bandwidth. GraphQL lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need. Underfetching (N+1 in the client): displaying a list of accounts with each account's last transfer requires N+1 REST calls. A GraphQL query fetches both in one round trip. Schema introspection: the schema is self-documenting and tooling (GraphiQL, code generators) can interrogate it. What GraphQL costs: Complexity. Resolvers, dataloaders to kill N+1 on the server side, a query parser, depth limiting to prevent DoS from deeply nested queries, cost analysis. That's real infrastructure. Caching. HTTP caching (CDN, ETag, Cache-Control) works beautifully with REST's GET semantics. GraphQL's POST-based queries mostly bypass it. Rate limiting. A REST endpoint has a predictable cost. A GraphQL query's cost is variable — a single query can trigger dozens of resolver chains. When REST wins: internal services talking machine-to-machine, APIs with stable and well-

desc: Serving files with http.FileServer/ServeContent, range requests and caching headers; embedding assets with go:embed and io/fs into one binary; and CDNs — edge caching, fingerprinted and signed URLs.
text: Let me paint you a picture. The Meridian dashboard you just built has a login screen, a React bundle, a logo, and two dozen SQL migration files. Right now they live on a file system somewhere — which means they can drift out of sync, get deleted, or sit on a server you forgot to provision. Embarrassing. By the end of this chapter you'll serve files like a professional — range requests, conditional GETs, 304s, embedded binaries, and a CDN in front of the whole operation. One binary. One command. No apologies. You're lucky to have me for this one.

heading: Serving Files
text: Here's the scene: the Meridian dashboard ships a static bundle — index.html, app.9f3a1.js, a logo, and a PDF regulatory-disclosure document. Users hit your Go service and expect those files to come back fast, with the right content types, and with support for resumable downloads (because that disclosure PDF is 40 MB and connections drop). Go's net/http package does most of this for free. Let's peel it apart one layer at a time.

heading: http.FileServer — the one-liner that does everything
text: http.FileServer is Go's built-in handler for serving a directory tree. Give it an http.FileSystem and you get listings, content-type sniffing, Last-Modified headers, conditional-GET (304) support through modification times, and byte-range requests (206) — all free. http.ServeContent is its lower-level cousin: you hand it any io.ReadSeeker (a bytes.Reader, an open file, a generated report) and it runs the same range and conditional-request machinery on your data. If you want ETag-based validation, set the ETag header yourself before calling it. Both are critical because hand-rolling file serving almost always means missing 304 or range support — breaking resumable downloads and wasting bandwidth. On the job: You reach for http.FileServer when a service needs to serve a directory of static assets — dashboard bundles, migration SQL files, report PDFs. Get the wiring wrong and every URL either 404s or leaks files it shouldn't. http.FileServer takes an http.FileSystem and returns an http.Handler. Point it at a directory and you get: directory listings, content-type sniffing, Last-Modified headers, conditional GET support (If-Modified-Since, plus ETag preconditions if you set an ETag hea

heading: http.ServeContent and http.ServeFile — surgical control
text: When you need to serve a single file — or a []byte you already have in memory — reach for http.ServeContent or http.ServeFile. They give you the same range-request and conditional-request machinery as http.FileServer, but you pick the source. On the job: http.ServeContent is the right tool when you're serving generated output — a freshly built account statement PDF, a CSV export of Meridian's ledger — that you already have as bytes or an open file handle. The magic of ServeContent is the io.ReadSeeker — the seeker is what makes range requests work. A range request asks for a slice of the file (bytes=0-1023), and Go needs to Seek to the right offset before reading. If your source can't seek, range requests silently fall back to full-file responses.

heading: Range requests and 206 Partial Content
text: A range request is an HTTP GET with a Range: bytes=N-M header asking for a specific byte slice of the file, not the whole thing. The server responds 206 Partial Content with only that slice. Why it matters: large downloads (a 40 MB regulatory PDF) can resume after a dropped connection — the client just sends a new range request starting where it left off. Video players use the same mechanism to scrub without downloading the entire file. Without range support, every dropped connection restarts the download from byte zero. When a browser or download manager sends Range: bytes=0-1023, the server should respond with 206 Partial Content and only that slice. This is how large file downloads resume after a dropped connection, and how video players scrub without downloading the whole file. http.FileServer and http.ServeContent handle this automatically. Let's watch a range request unfold. http.ServeContent automatically emits Accept-Ranges: bytes in every response, advertising that range requests are welcome. Without this header, browsers won't attempt to resume a download — they'll start over. You get it for free; just don't override it.

heading: Content-Type detection
text: http.ServeFile and http.ServeContent detect the Content-Type from the file extension using mime.TypeByExtension. If the extension is unknown, they sniff the first 512 bytes with http.DetectContentType. You should always trust this over setting it yourself — a misconfigured Content-Type on a PDF served as text/html is a stored-XSS vector (covered in Part 2, "Application Security Baseline"). Full directory-serving handler. Takes http.FileSystem. Listings, caching, range requests — all automatic. Best for static asset trees. Single file from the OS filesystem. Same caching and range machinery. Use when you know the path at request time. Most flexible — any io.ReadSeeker. Use for in-memory data, generated reports, or files you opened yourself. Wraps the OS filesystem as http.FileSystem. The standard argument to http.FileServer. Removes a URL prefix before it reaches the file server, so /assets/app.js maps to ./static/app.js not ./static/assets/app.js. Never serve user-supplied paths directly with os.Open. An input like ../../etc/passwd is a path-traversal attack. http.FileServer normalizes paths with path.Clean before opening — that's one reason you use it instead of rolling your own.

heading: Caching Headers
text: Serving a file is one thing. Serving it efficiently — so the browser doesn't download the same 400 KB JS bundle on every page load — is the discipline that separates a professional from a hobbyist. The three headers that matter: Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified. They work together to answer two questions: "how long can you cache this?" and "has it changed since you last asked?" Three headers that work as a team. Cache-Control is a directive telling browsers and CDN proxies how long they may keep a cached copy (max-age=31536000 = one year; no-cache = revalidate every time; no-store = keep nothing). ETag is a server-chosen token that identifies a specific version of a response; Last-Modified is the timestamp validator. On a repeat request the browser sends If-None-Match: or If-Modified-Since: ; if the content hasn't changed the server replies 304 Not Modified — headers only, no body. The browser uses its cached copy and saves all the bandwidth. Miss this on the Meridian dashboard and every page load re-downloads the full 400 KB JS bundle, even when nothing changed.

heading: Cache-Control — tell proxies and browsers what to do
text: Cache-Control is a directive, not a timestamp. The most important values for a static-asset server: public — any cache (proxy, CDN, browser) may store this. max-age=31536000 — cache for one year (in seconds). Use this for fingerprinted assets like app.9f3a1.js. immutable — the content will never change for this URL. Skip revalidation entirely (supported by modern browsers and CDNs). For HTML pages and API responses that must always be fresh: no-cache doesn't mean "don't cache" — it means "cache it, but always revalidate before using the cached copy." Use no-store if you genuinely want nothing stored (e.g. a bank statement download for a logged-in user).

heading: ETag and Last-Modified — the revalidation pair
text: http.FileServer sets Last-Modified automatically. It does not invent a content ETag for you; if your caching policy relies on If-None-Match, set the ETag header yourself before serving the content: Last-Modified: — a timestamp. ETag: " " — an optional validator you choose, commonly a content hash or build fingerprint. On the next request, the browser sends these back: If-Modified-Since: — "only send the body if it changed after this time." If-None-Match: " " — "only send the body if the ETag is different." If nothing changed, the server responds with 304 Not Modified — headers only, no body. The browser uses its cached copy. On a dashboard loaded 50 times a day, this turns 400 KB of JS into zero bytes transferred, 49 times. Let's watch a conditional GET flow — the 200 path and the 304 path side by side.

heading: Setting Cache-Control in your own handler
text: http.FileServer does not set your production cache policy. For production you'll want to set Cache-Control yourself — especially for fingerprinted assets that can be cached forever. http.FileServer calls Stat on every request to get the file's ModTime and size, then delegates to http.ServeContent. The standard handler uses the modification time for Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since checks. It does not construct an ETag from size and modtime. If you need ETag precision, compute a content hash or use a build fingerprint and set w.Header().Set("ETag", value) before calling http.ServeContent. ServeContent will honor ETag precondition headers when the response already has an ETag. The conditional checks themselves live in net/http/fs.go: ETag checks use the ETag header you supplied, and modification-time checks use the modtime passed to ServeContent. The file body is not sent for a 304 cache hit. Go version note (Go 1.26 baseline): the immutable Cache-Control directive is not set by the stdlib — you add it in your own middleware as shown above. --

heading: go:embed & io/fs
text: Here's where the magic happens, sport. I'm going to show you how to ship the Meridian dashboard — HTML, JS, CSS, fonts, and all your SQL migration files — inside a single self-contained binary . No deployment steps to copy static assets. No "where did the templates go?" production incident at 2 a.m. One binary. One ./server. Done. //go:embed is a compiler directive (Go 1.16+) that bakes files or directories into the binary at link time. You declare a variable of type string, []byte, or embed.FS immediately below the directive and the linker stuffs the file bytes into it. embed.FS is a read-only in-memory filesystem that implements fs.FS — the same interface used by os.DirFS, ZIP readers, and test fixtures, so your code doesn't know or care whether it's talking to disk or a binary blob. Why it matters: it eliminates the entire class of deployment failure where static assets (the dashboard JS bundle, SQL migrations, HTML templates) were left off the server. One binary, one deploy, nothing missing.

heading: The //go:embed directive
text: On the job: //go:embed eliminates an entire class of deployment failures — the "static assets didn't get copied to the server" incident. At Meridian, this is the difference between a dashboard that works on first deploy and one that 404s on the logo. //go:embed is a compiler directive (Go 1.16+) that tells the linker to bake files or directories directly into the binary. It must appear immediately above a variable declaration of type string, []byte, or embed.FS. A few rules the compiler enforces: The path is always relative to the package directory . You cannot escape upward (../). You can use glob patterns: //go:embed static/ .html templates/ / .tmpl. The embed.FS is read-only — it's baked into the binary at compile time. Directories named or . and files named or . are excluded by default. Use all: prefix to include hidden files: //go:embed all:static.

heading: embed.FS and the io/fs.FS abstraction
text: embed.FS implements fs.FS — the interface from io/fs (Go 1.16) that abstracts a read-only filesystem. Its definition is beautifully minimal: This means the same code can work with a real OS filesystem, an embedded filesystem, a ZIP archive, or a test fixture — anything that implements fs.FS. That's the power: your handlers don't need to know whether they're talking to disk or to a binary blob.

If you embedded static/, requests for /index.html will look for static/index.html in the FS. Use fs.Sub to strip the prefix:

heading: CDNs
text: On the job: A CDN is the difference between a Meridian dashboard that loads in 5 ms for a Singapore-based operator and one that takes 600 ms. You will configure this on your first production deploy; get the cache headers wrong and you'll be explaining to users why they're still seeing last month's UI. You've got a Go binary serving static assets beautifully. Now imagine 50,000 Meridian users in Singapore, São Paulo, and Stockholm all hitting your single US-East origin server. The JS bundle is 400 KB. The round-trip latency to North America from Singapore alone is 200 ms. Multiply that by every asset on every page load and you have a slow, expensive product. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) solves this by caching your assets at dozens of edge nodes around the world. A user in Singapore gets the file from an edge node in Singapore — not from your origin server. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a global network of edge nodes (caches) placed close to users — Singapore, São Paulo, Stockholm. When a user requests a file, it comes from the nearest edge, not your origin server. The edge stores a copy based on the Cache-Control header your origin sets. A cache miss means the edge doesn't

heading: How a CDN edge cache works
text: The CDN sits between users and your origin server (the Meridian Go binary). On the first request for an asset, the edge node doesn't have it — that's a cache miss . It fetches the file from origin, caches it, and serves it to the user. Every subsequent request for the same asset from anywhere near that edge node is a cache hit — origin is never touched. The CDN decides how long to cache a response based on the Cache-Control header your Go server sets. max-age=31536000 means "cache for a year." no-cache means "revalidate with origin every time." Setting these correctly is the difference between a CDN that helps you and one that just adds latency. A fingerprinted URL embeds a hash of the file's contents in the filename: app.js → app.9f3a1.js. The hash is derived by the build pipeline and changes whenever the file changes, which means the URL changes too. The CDN has never seen the new URL, so it fetches fresh from origin automatically — no invalidation API call needed. The old URL stays cached harmlessly until its TTL expires. Why it matters: without fingerprinting, deploying a new JS bundle leaves CDN edge nodes around the world serving the old one for hours or days — breaking users

heading: Cache invalidation — the hardest problem
text: The classic engineering joke: "There are only two hard things in CS — cache invalidation and naming things." CDN cache invalidation is the real-world manifestation of this. If you deploy a new JS bundle with the same URL (/static/app.js), the CDN edge nodes around the world are still serving the old one — until their max-age TTL expires. That could be days. Your users get a broken mix of old JS and new HTML. The solution is fingerprinted (content-hashed) URLs . Your build pipeline hashes the file contents and embeds that hash in the filename: Now the URL is the version. A new deploy produces a new hash, a new URL — the CDN has never seen it, so it fetches fresh from origin. The old URL remains cached (harmlessly) until it expires. Zero invalidation calls needed. Your Go server (or embedded binary) serves the hashed filenames. Your HTML references the hashed filenames. The CDN caches them forever with max-age=31536000, immutable.

heading: Signed URLs for private files
text: On the job: Meridian's quarterly account statements are per-user PDFs that must never be cached at a shared CDN edge. A signed URL lets you serve them via the same CDN infrastructure while keeping access time-limited and user-specific. Misconfigure this — allow Cache-Control: public — and you've handed one user's statement to the next person to hit that edge node. Fingerprinted URLs work for public assets. But the Meridian dashboard also serves private quarterly statements — PDFs that only the account holder should access. You can't cache these at the CDN edge with a public URL. The solution is a signed URL : a URL with a cryptographic signature (usually an HMAC) and an expiry timestamp embedded as query parameters. The CDN or your origin server validates the signature before serving the file. Expired or tampered URLs return 403 Forbidden. Content-hash in the filename means the URL changes whenever the file changes. CDN caches forever, no invalidation calls. The standard for public static assets. HMAC + expiry in the query string. Origin (or CDN) validates the signature. Used for private files where per-user access control matters. Tells the CDN not to cache this response — it's us

text: No skimming, sport. These are hands-on. The compiler is unimpressed by reading comprehension. Use httptest.NewRecorder to demonstrate that http.StripPrefix is wired correctly by printing the path the inner handler sees. Without http.StripPrefix, the inner handler (and the real http.FileServer) would look for ./public/files/report.pdf — one extra path segment that makes every lookup fail.
