heading: The Lab
text: Enough theory. I set this test personally, and I want to be very clear: I find sloppiness in cache headers personally offensive. Now show me what you've got. Meridian's CDN bill is growing because the middleware is defeating browser and CDN caching. Two bugs, four checks, one flag. Fix the middleware, make the conditional-GET handler honour the ETag, and collect it. http.FileServer serves an entire directory tree with caching, range requests, and content-type detection built in. http.StripPrefix maps URL paths to filesystem paths. http.ServeContent is the flexible alternative — it takes any io.ReadSeeker and handles 206 Partial Content plus conditional requests. It honors ETag preconditions if you set the ETag header yourself. Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable + fingerprinted URLs is the CDN-friendly pattern for public static assets. Cache-Control: private, no-store is for sensitive authenticated content. 304 Not Modified means a validator such as Last-Modified or an app-provided ETag matched — the body is omitted and the browser uses its cached copy. //go:embed bakes files and directories into the binary at link time. embed.FS implements fs.FS, giving you fs.ReadF

desc: Why caching exists, Redis as the workhorse, cache-aside/read-through/write-through strategies, and the hard part: invalidation, stampedes and singleflight.
text: Here's the thing, sport: every great system I've ever built — and I've built them all — has a secret weapon. It's not a fancy algorithm. It's not some clever data structure. It's knowing when to not go to the database. That's caching. Serving a pre-computed answer from fast memory instead of running the same query for the ten-thousandth time. Done right, it's the difference between a snappy product and a database that weeps at 9 a.m. Done wrong, it's a system that confidently serves lies. I've seen both. One of them makes me proud. The other makes me… twitch . We're going to do it right. Redis as the engine. go-redis as the driver. And singleflight as the mechanism that stops a stampede dead in its tracks. By the end, you'll cache with precision — and you'll know the one thing you absolutely, categorically must never cache at Meridian (hint: it's the account balance). You're fortunate I'm the one teaching this.

heading: Why Caching
text: Let me set the scene. It's 9:03 a.m. on a Monday. Meridian's platform just opened trading hours and every single user simultaneously hits the account dashboard — the same user profile rows from the accounts table, the same JOIN against plan details, the same ORDER BY. Your database has answered that question 40,000 times today and every answer was identical . Every query scanned the same pages off disk. Every connection was held for the same 18 milliseconds. The database is panting like a dog in July. That is the problem caching solves: don't do expensive work you already did . On the job: This exact scenario — the 9 a.m. trading-hour surge where a popular read path expires just as load spikes — is when you get paged. Getting caching wrong means DB connection exhaustion under predictable load. Getting it right means the DB barely notices. A cache is a fast, temporary store that holds a copy of data so you can serve repeat reads without re-running the original expensive operation. When a request arrives, you check the cache first (a hit — return instantly) and only fall back to the database on a miss . The cache is always secondary — the database is the source of truth. A cache can

heading: The cost you're actually paying
text: Before you cache everything in sight, understand what you're signing up for. A cache introduces a second system that must be kept consistent with the first. Every cached piece of data is a potential lie — a promise that this is still true. Your job is to manage that promise honestly. The trade-off: freshness vs. speed vs. load . You are permanently choosing somewhere on that triangle. Pure freshness (no cache) costs speed and load. Pure speed (long TTL, no invalidation) costs freshness. Good caching is knowing where on that triangle each piece of data actually belongs — and being honest about it. Only cache data that is either (a) expensive to compute and stable for a known window, or (b) read many times between writes. If data changes on every read or after every write, a cache adds complexity without benefit. If data must always reflect the authoritative value (like a money balance — we'll cover this), a cache is a trap.

heading: Caching Layers
text: Caching isn't one thing. There are multiple layers where you can intercept a request and serve a pre-computed answer — each with different trade-offs in latency, consistency, scope, and complexity. Data stored directly in your Go process's heap — a sync.Map, a plain map protected by a sync.RWMutex, or a library like patrickmn/go-cache or dgraph-io/ristretto. Fastest possible: a memory read. Scope is one process — every replica has its own copy. Works brilliantly for small, infrequently changing, read-heavy data like config, feature flags, or a small product list. A dedicated caching service — Redis or Memcached — shared across all replicas. Millisecond latency over the network instead of nanoseconds in-process, but consistent across every instance and far larger capacity than one process's heap. This is the workhorse tier for most backend services. HTTP-layer caching at a CDN edge node for public, cacheable responses. Covered in depth in the previous chapter (File Servers & CDNs). Relevant here because caching strategy at the CDN layer (Cache-Control headers, cache busting via versioned URLs, purge APIs) is the same discipline applied at the edge rather than inside your service. In

heading: Tying back to the CDN chapter
text: In the previous chapter (File Servers & CDNs) we set Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600 on static assets and used versioned URLs to bust the CDN cache when assets changed. That is caching strategy — just applied at the HTTP layer. The same principles apply here: TTLs express how long you trust the data, versioned keys / fingerprinted URLs bust the cache explicitly, and stale-while-revalidate is the HTTP equivalent of serving from cache while refreshing in the background. Keep that mental model — it's the same problem.

heading: Redis as the Workhorse
text: Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory data structure store. It's not a database in the ACID sense — it's a fast, specialized tool for holding data that you can afford to reconstruct if it disappears. In production, you will use it for caching, session storage, rate-limiting counters, pub/sub, job queues (Asynq, later in the course), and distributed locks. Redis is a single-threaded event loop written in C. All command processing is serial — no locking, no concurrency inside the server. This sounds like a liability but is a superpower: no mutex contention, no deadlocks, predictable latency. The single thread reads commands from a non-blocking socket, executes them against the in-memory hash table, and writes responses. I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue) lets one thread manage thousands of client connections simultaneously. Data lives in a hash table keyed by string. The value can be one of several internal encodings — plain string, integer, list, hash, sorted set, hyperloglog, stream, and more — but from the client's perspective they're all keyed by a string key. Redis selects a compact encoding (e.g. listpack for small hashes and sorted sets) that the server transparently p

heading: Core data types
text: You need to know six types cold. Everything else is a specialization. The universal type. Stores bytes — JSON, plain text, integers, binary blobs. Commands: GET, SET, INCR, APPEND. A SET key value EX 60 sets a string with a 60-second TTL. The workhorse for caching serialized Go structs. A map within a key — HSET user:42 name Alice age 30. Useful when you want to store and update individual fields of a struct without serializing and deserializing the whole thing. Commands: HGET, HSET, HMGET, HDEL. An ordered sequence of strings, push/pop from either end. Natural job queue: LPUSH queue job, BRPOP queue 0 (blocking pop). Commands: LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, LRANGE. Unordered collection of unique strings. Useful for tracking membership — active sessions, unique visitors. Commands: SADD, SISMEMBER, SMEMBERS, SINTERSTORE. Like a Set but every member has a score (float). Sorted by score. Perfect for leaderboards, rate-limiting windows, delayed jobs. Commands: ZADD, ZRANGE, ZRANGEBYSCORE. Append-only log with consumer groups — Redis's answer to Kafka for lightweight message passing. Beyond caching scope; mentioned for completeness. Commands: XADD, XREAD, XREADGROUP.

heading: Driving Redis from Go with go-redis
text: The canonical Go client is github.com/redis/go-redis/v9. It wraps every Redis command as a typed Go method, handles connection pooling, and supports pipelining and pub/sub natively. go-redis needs a real Redis server at localhost:6379. The playground snippet below replaces Redis with a minimal in-process mock so you can run it in the sandbox and see the pattern. Real Redis code is identical in shape — the swap is just the dependency.

heading: Pipelining: batching commands to cut round-trips
text: Every Redis command is a round-trip: send, wait, receive. If you need to set 100 keys, 100 round-trips at 0.5ms each is 50ms. A pipeline batches commands into one write and one read, cutting that to 0.5ms total. The above snippet requires a running Redis instance. The runnable example below demonstrates the same batching pattern with an in-memory stand-in so you can observe the structure without infrastructure.

heading: An in-process cache demo (fully runnable in the sandbox)
text: Here's a self-contained example you can actually run: a naive in-process cache with TTL eviction, demonstrating the GET/SET/miss pattern without any external dependency. On the job: Redis's single-threaded model means one slow Lua script or a KEYS scan blocks every other client. In production, Meridian's on-call engineers have been paged because a KEYS call on a large keyspace froze the Redis instance for seconds. Use SCAN for iteration; never KEYS in production.

heading: Eviction policies
text: When Redis hits its maxmemory limit, it evicts keys. Your policy choice determines which keys get sacrificed. Evict the least-recently-used key across all keys. The standard choice for a pure caching tier where all keys are fair game. Evict the least-frequently-used key. Better for workloads with long-lived hot keys — LFU keeps your truly popular keys warmer than LRU does. Same as above but only among keys that have a TTL set. Useful when Redis serves double duty — caching (TTL set) and persistent storage (no TTL). Protects the persistent keys. Evict the key closest to expiry. Cheapest to compute; crude choice. Return an error on write when full. Appropriate for Redis used as a queue or primary store — never for a cache, because it will take your service down when full. Choosing noeviction for a caching Redis is one of the most common configuration mistakes I see. It turns a temporary slowdown (cache miss) into a hard outage (error on every SET). Use allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a caching Redis. Your cache is disposable . Let it evict.

heading: Cache Strategies
text: There are four patterns for keeping a cache and a database in sync. Each has a different read path, write path, and consistency profile. Know all four. Pick based on your workload.

heading: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
text: The application code owns the cache. On a read: check the cache first; on a miss, go to the database, populate the cache, return the result. On a write: write to the database, then invalidate (or update) the cache. This is the most common pattern and the one you'll use 80% of the time. At Meridian, the account profile read path (GET /accounts/ /profile) uses cache-aside: profile data is read on every dashboard load but updated rarely, so caching it for 5 minutes cuts database load dramatically. On the job: Cache-aside is correct for read-heavy, infrequently-written data. If your write rate approaches your read rate, you're adding cache churn with little benefit. Measure before you cache. Let's animate a cache-aside read for both a HIT and a MISS — these are the two paths you need to memorize.

heading: Read-through
text: Similar to cache-aside, but the cache layer handles the DB fallback — not the application. Your application only ever talks to the cache; on a miss, the cache fetches from the DB itself. Libraries like ristretto with a Loader func implement this pattern. In Go, the distinction is mostly architectural: cache-aside logic lives in your service code (explicit), read-through logic lives in the cache client (implicit). Read-through is cleaner when many code paths need the same entity — you can't forget the fallback because the cache handles it.

heading: Write-through
text: On every write, the application writes to both the cache and the database synchronously — the cache is always up to date. Reads are always cache hits (no cold misses). The trade-off: every write is slower (two writes instead of one), and you bear the cost of caching data that may only be read once. Write-through is the right choice when read latency is more critical than write latency, and when you can afford to keep every written value in cache.

heading: Write-behind (write-back)
text: The application writes to the cache immediately and returns. The cache asynchronously flushes writes to the database in the background. This gives the lowest write latency but the highest risk: if the cache crashes before flushing, you lose writes. Only appropriate for data where some loss is acceptable. For financial data: never. Cache-aside: app manages the miss. Read-through: cache manages the miss. Both give the same hit/miss behavior; the difference is where the fallback logic lives. Cache-aside is more explicit and debuggable. Read-through reduces duplicated fallback code. Write-through: synchronous, safe, slower writes, always warm cache. Write-behind: asynchronous, fast writes, risk of data loss. Use write-through for anything that matters. Write-behind only for ephemeral counters or data where durability is not required. Write-behind with financial data is not engineering — it's recklessness. If the cache crashes between the write and the DB flush, the money write is simply gone. The database is the source of truth for money. Always write there synchronously. The cache gets updated after — or just gets invalidated. We'll repeat this in the fintech section.

heading: Invalidation — The Hard Part
text: Phil Karlton's famous quip: there are only two hard problems in computer science — cache invalidation and naming things. He was right. Invalidation is where good caching discipline ends and subtle production bugs begin.

heading: TTL: time-based expiry
text: The simplest strategy: every cache entry has a time-to-live. When it expires, the next read is a miss and the value is refreshed from the database. You accept that cached data may be up to TTL seconds stale. Choosing a TTL is a business decision disguised as a technical one: Product catalog that changes a few times a day → TTL of 5–15 minutes is fine. Exchange rate that changes every second → TTL of 1–5 seconds, or skip caching entirely. User session → TTL that matches your session expiry. Account balance → no TTL will make this safe; don't cache the authoritative balance (more soon).

heading: Explicit invalidation (cache busting)
text: When data changes, actively delete or update the cache key. This gives you immediate consistency rather than waiting for TTL expiry. Naively: delete the cache key, then update the database. Problem: between delete and DB update, a concurrent reader misses the cache, reads the old value from the database (update not yet committed), and re-populates the cache with stale data. The key is now fresh again with the old value. The safer order for cache-aside: write to the DB first, then invalidate the cache . On the next read, the miss fetches the already-committed new value. This is a narrower race window but not zero — for truly strict consistency, you need distributed transactions or a queue, which is Part 3 territory.

heading: Versioned keys
text: Instead of invalidating, you change the key. The old key simply ages out via TTL; the new key starts fresh. Useful for bulk invalidation — change a version prefix and every old key becomes unreachable.

heading: Failure mode 1: cache stampede (thundering herd)
text: On the job: A stampede is not a theoretical concern — it is the most common caching failure in production. It happens every time a heavily-read key expires under load. At Meridian, the 9 a.m. trading-hour surge is the predictable trigger: every connected client loads the same account dashboard, the same profile TTL expires, and 500 goroutines all slam the database simultaneously. Here is the scenario in full. It's 9:00 a.m. Meridian's account dashboard TTL expires. At that exact moment, 500 concurrent requests all miss the cache simultaneously. All 500 goroutines see a miss. All 500 go to the database. All 500 fire the same SELECT against the accounts table. The database goes from idle to 500 parallel queries in milliseconds. It falls over. Your service falls over. This is a cache stampede — also called a thundering herd. It's not hypothetical; it happens any time a popular key expires under load. The fix is singleflight. Go 1.25 added wg.Go(func()) to sync.WaitGroup. It calls wg.Add(1), launches the function in a new goroutine, and calls wg.Done() when the function returns. This replaces the three-line wg.Add(1) / go func() () idiom you'll see in older code. All WaitGroup examples

heading: The singleflight fix
text: golang.org/x/sync/singleflight collapses duplicate concurrent calls into one. If 500 goroutines all call group.Do("account:dashboard", fetchFromDB) simultaneously, exactly one goroutine executes fetchFromDB. The other 499 block and wait. When the one goroutine returns, all 500 receive the same result. One DB query. Zero stampede. Now watch the two timelines side by side — before and after singleflight. singleflight.Group maintains a map[string] call protected by a sync.Mutex. A call is a struct holding the in-flight request's WaitGroup, the result value, and the error. This is a conceptual model — treat it as such; the exact implementation is in golang.org/x/sync/singleflight and may evolve. When you call group.Do(key, fn): 1. Lock the mutex. 2. Look up the key in the map. 3. If a call exists (an in-flight request for this key): increment its WaitGroup counter, unlock the mutex, and call c.wg.Wait() — you block. 4. If no call exists: create a new call, add it to the map, unlock the mutex, and run fn() in the current goroutine. The function is not spawned in a new goroutine — it runs inline. 5. When fn() returns, store the result in c.val and c.err, remove the key from the map (whil

heading: Failure mode 2: cache penetration
text: A user requests product:99999 — a product that doesn't exist. Cache miss, DB miss, nothing to cache. If an attacker hammers your service with thousands of non-existent IDs, every request punches through to the database. Your cache provides zero protection. The fix: cache negative results too. Store a sentinel value (e.g., " NOT FOUND ") with a short TTL for missing keys.

heading: Failure mode 3: hot keys
text: A single Redis key receives an outsized share of all traffic — for example, the home page product list, or a viral item in a flash sale. Redis is fast but not infinitely so. A single key can become a bottleneck if enough goroutines hammer it simultaneously. Mitigations: Local read-through : cache the hot key in-process (L1) with a very short TTL (1–5 seconds). Absorbs most of the Redis traffic. Key replication : write the value to N keys (product:list:shard:0 … :N-1) and read from a random shard. Spreads the read load. Read replicas : Redis Cluster or sentinel with read replicas can distribute reads. Every TTL is a commitment to a maximum staleness window. max-age=300 means you accept data up to 5 minutes old. That's fine for a product catalog. It is not fine for an account balance, an order status the user is waiting on, or a risk limit. Before you set a TTL, write down the business consequence of serving a 5-minute-old value. If the answer is "none, users won't notice," cache it. If the answer is "a user could over-spend their limit," do not cache the authoritative value — or cache a read-only derived form with explicit staleness guarantees documented in your service contract.

heading: Caching in Fintech
text: Here is where everything gets serious. I need you to hear this clearly. On the job: The worst production incident I have seen from caching in fintech was not a stampede — it was a payment authorization that read a cached balance. A user had a zero balance; the cached value said otherwise. The payment went through. The reversal took three days and two engineering escalations to untangle. Don't be that engineer. Never cache an authoritative account balance. Not with a 1-second TTL. Not with explicit invalidation. Not with singleflight. The ledger balance is the source of truth. It is the thing every financial decision depends on. If your service reads a stale balance — even for 100 milliseconds — a user could authorize a payment they cannot cover, or be blocked from a payment they can make. That is a financial error. In regulated environments, it is an audit finding. At Meridian: you may cache the account profile (name, plan tier, notification prefs) for 5 minutes — it is read-heavy and financially inert. You must never cache accounts.balance cents as the input to a payment authorization. The profile is safe to cache. The balance is not. The authoritative balance lives in the databas

heading: What you CAN cache safely in fintech
text: Just because you can't cache the balance doesn't mean you cache nothing. There's plenty of derived, read-only, or bounded-staleness data that's safe and valuable to cache. Product names, descriptions, fee schedules, supported currencies. These change infrequently (a few times per day at most). Cache with a 5–15 minute TTL. Explicit invalidation on admin writes. Exchange rates change constantly, but for display purposes (showing the user what their GBP is worth in USD) you can serve a rate that's up to 30–60 seconds stale, as long as transactions always use a freshly fetched rate at execution time. Cache the display rate; never cache the execution rate. Name, address, notification settings. These are read on every page load and change rarely. Cache with a 1–5 minute TTL, invalidate on profile update. Safe: this data doesn't affect financial correctness. Configured limits like daily transfer caps may be safe to cache for a few seconds as read-mostly config — but invalidate immediately on limit changes, and always re-read before the final authorization decision. Treat with care. Never cache a derived balance that becomes the input to a financial decision. "Cache the balance for displa

heading: The right architecture: cache at the read model, not the write model
text: In a CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) architecture (covered in depth in Part 3's Event-Driven Architecture & Kafka chapter), you have a strict write model (the ledger) and a read model (derived views). The cache belongs on the read model . The write path (posting a transaction, authorizing a payment) always goes straight to the database. The read path (rendering the Meridian dashboard, showing recent transfers, displaying the "available balance" estimate for UI purposes) can be aggressively cached. --

heading: Exercises
text: Stop nodding. Start building. These aren't optional. Extend the Cache struct from this chapter to add a Delete(key string) method and a Len() int method that only counts non-expired keys. Write a main that sets three keys, deletes one, sleeps past the TTL of another, and verifies Len() returns 1. Delete explicitly invalidates a key. Len scans and counts only live entries. In production, a background goroutine or periodic scan would remove expired entries from the map to free memory — this implementation lazily leaves stale entries until they're explicitly read or the Len scan discards them. Write a generic function GetOrSetT any (T, error)) (T, error) that implements the cache-aside pattern: check the cache first (unmarshal JSON), on a miss call fetch, marshal the result, cache it, and return. Use encoding/json. Then write a main that calls it twice for the same key and verifies the second call doesn't re-execute fetch. Generics ([T any]) let one function handle any JSON-serializable type without per-type boilerplate. The second call goes straight to the cache; fetch is never called again. This is the idiomatic Go pattern for a cache-aside read layer. Using the ProductStore from th

heading: The Lab
text: Enough warm-up. You've seen the stampede — now you're going to stop one. I designed this personally. I've set the verifier to fire fifty goroutines at your service simultaneously, all with a cold cache, and it's going to count how many times the database gets hit. If the answer isn't exactly one, you haven't solved it. If the answer is one, you get the flag. Don't embarrass me. The stampede is real. The ProductStore above is Meridian's dashboard service at 9 a.m. Fix the injected clock so TTL expiry is testable, then add call deduplication so 50 concurrent misses fire exactly one DB call. The DO-NOT-EDIT main will tell you exactly which check fails first. You've earned this: Why caching : latency, load shedding, protecting the database. A cache is a shield. The database is what you're protecting. Caching layers : in-process (fastest, per-process), distributed/Redis (milliseconds, shared), CDN (HTTP-layer, same discipline). Pick the layer based on your consistency requirement. Redis : event-loop command execution, low-latency simple operations, six core types. go-redis/v9 is the idiomatic Go driver. Set TTLs. Use allkeys-lru for a pure cache. Pipeline batch writes. Strategies : cach

desc: Tie together HTTP + SQL + auth with deliberate API design and a caching layer into a real backend service, fully tested.
text: You've been patient. You've sat through HTTP, SQL, auth, API design, concurrency, and caching. All the pieces are on the board. Now we're going to play the game. This chapter is where you build Gator — a real backend service that fetches RSS feeds concurrently, stores posts in Postgres, gates everything behind auth, and serves a paginated personal feed with a Redis caching layer. Not a toy. Not a stripped-down demo. A service you could deploy right now. Gator is a backend service that lets users subscribe to RSS/Atom feeds and read a unified personal post feed. Under the hood a background worker continuously fetches every registered feed, deduplicates posts by URL, and stores them in Postgres. Users authenticate with an API key; the HTTP layer serves their personal feed, paginated and cached. The domain is simple so the architecture is the lesson : HTTP + SQL + auth + concurrency + caching, all wired together correctly. Six stages. Fully tested — table-driven handlers, httptest mock feed servers, -race on the scraper and cache, golden-file API response tests. I designed this project personally, and I have very strong opinions about the final result. A note on the scenario: Gator is

heading: Schema and Layout
text: Before a single HTTP handler is written, we need a firm foundation: the database schema, the project layout, and the data-access layer. This is the architectural skeleton — get it wrong here and every layer above wobbles.

heading: The scenario
text: Gator lets users register accounts, subscribe to RSS/Atom feeds, and read a personalized post feed. Under the hood a background worker continuously scrapes every registered feed concurrently. The architecture has three concerns that must stay separate: storage (Postgres), transport (HTTP), and background work (the scraper). Our project layout will make those boundaries explicit.

heading: Project layout
text: This is the clean/hexagonal layout from Software Design & Architecture. internal/ prevents other modules from importing our guts. The database package is generated code — do not edit it by hand. Business logic never touches database/sql directly; it only sees the database.Queries type. Transport never touches the scraper. Each layer only knows about the one below it.

heading: Database schema
text: Three tables. Let's look at all three, then wire the migrations. The url UNIQUE constraint on posts is load-bearing: it's the deduplication guard. The scraper can INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and idempotently re-scrape a feed. No duplicates. No application-layer set operations. Rather than writing Go boilerplate by hand, we use sqlc to generate type-safe Go code from annotated SQL files. You write the query once, in SQL, with a -- name: annotation; sqlc generate produces a Go function with the exact correct parameter and return types. The generated database.Queries type wraps a sql.DB and exposes these as real typed methods — GetAccountByAPIKey(ctx, apiKey string) (Account, error). The compiler rejects mismatched types at build time, not at 3 a.m. when a prod query returns the wrong shape. sqlc is not magic: it parses your schema and queries statically. It does not protect against runtime misuse of context or connection-pool exhaustion. Those are your job. SetMaxOpenConns, SetMaxIdleConns, and SetConnMaxLifetime on the sql.DB must be set — from config, not hard-coded. Covered in SQL & Databases in Go. Go 1.26 baseline; sqlc 1.27+.

heading: Wiring the dependency graph
text: The main.go wires everything together using dependency injection — no globals, no init() side-effects, no package-level singletons. Here is the skeleton: --

heading: Auth Middleware
text: Every route in Gator is scoped to an authenticated user. We use API-key auth here — simple, stateless, suitable for a developer-facing aggregator. The pattern is exactly what the Auth & API Design chapter (Part 1, Chapter 17) covered; let's see it applied concretely. Auth middleware is an http.Handler wrapper that runs before your business handler on every request. It extracts a credential from the request (here: Authorization: ApiKey ), validates it against the database, and either stores the resolved identity on the request context (allowing the request through) or returns 401 Unauthorized immediately. Every protected route is wrapped in it — the default is closed, and you explicitly opt in to public access. Without it, any route you forget to protect is publicly reachable. On the job: In production, skipping auth middleware on a single route is one of the most common security incidents — someone forgets to wrap a new handler, and a privileged endpoint is publicly reachable. The authed wrapper function in NewRouter makes the default closed: every new handler must explicitly opt in to protection or explicitly opt out.

heading: Storing a user on the request context
text: The middleware extracts the ApiKey header, loads the account from the DB, and stores it on the request context. Handlers retrieve it with a typed key — never a raw string. Using a raw string as a context key — ctx.Value("account") — is a time bomb. Any package that happens to use the same string collides silently. The unexported contextKey struct type is only addressable from inside internal/auth, so collisions are physically impossible. --

heading: HTTP API
text: With auth in place, we can build the five endpoints that define Gator's public surface. Each endpoint follows the REST conventions and error shapes from HTTP Servers: JSON, Streaming & WebSockets — consistent, versioned, cursor-paginated.

heading: Cursor-paginated posts endpoint
text: Cursor pagination returns the next page by anchoring to the last item seen — here, the published at timestamp of the last post on the previous page — rather than counting rows with OFFSET. The client passes ?before= and the query returns posts published before that point. Why it matters: OFFSET n skips n rows at query time; if new posts arrive between page 1 and page 2, OFFSET 20 silently skips posts the user never saw. A timestamp cursor is stable under concurrent inserts. It also uses an index efficiently, where large offsets force a full index scan. The posts feed is the hot read path. We use cursor pagination — a before timestamp cursor — not offset pagination. Why? A user scrolling their feed while new posts arrive will get gaps and duplicates with offset pagination; a cursor doesn't move. On the job: The switch from offset to cursor pagination is one of the most impactful backend changes you can make for any feed or timeline product. Offset pagination is fine for admin dashboards with small, static datasets; it breaks visibly for any live, insert-heavy feed. --

heading: Concurrent Feed Fetcher
text: The concurrent feed scraper is a background goroutine that drives periodic feed fetching. A time.Ticker fires on a configurable interval (e.g. every minute); on each tick, scrapeAll queries every registered feed URL from the database and dispatches each one to a bounded worker pool — a buffered channel acting as a counting semaphore that limits how many feeds are fetched simultaneously. Each worker goroutine makes one outbound HTTP GET, parses the RSS/Atom XML, and upserts new posts with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING. When the service receives SIGTERM, context cancellation propagates into every in-flight HTTP request and a sync.WaitGroup ensures all workers finish before the process exits. Without the concurrency ceiling, a service with thousands of feeds would exhaust file descriptors and outbound connection slots. The scraper is the heart of Gator. It must: 1. Fetch all registered feeds on a regular interval 2. Run multiple fetches concurrently — not one at a time 3. Respect a concurrency ceiling so we don't hammer every feed server simultaneously 4. Tear down cleanly when the service stops This is the worker pool pattern from the Concurrency chapter (Part 1, Chapter 4), wired to a time

heading: Caching Layer
text: The scraper calls c.InvalidatePostsForFeed(ctx, feedID) after every successful scrape. The handler calls c.GetLatestPosts and c.SetLatestPosts. Here's the cache package that backs those calls. Cache-aside means the application code — not the cache itself — decides when to read from and write to the cache. On a read: check the cache first; on a miss, fetch from the database, store the result in the cache, then return it. On a write (new posts scraped): explicitly delete the relevant cache entries so the next read repopulates with fresh data. The TTL is a backstop — staleness is bounded even if explicit invalidation is missed. Cache-aside is correct for derived, reconstructable data (latest posts); it is wrong for authoritative data (account existence, permissions, monetary balances) where staleness equals incorrectness. The strategy is cache-aside (lazy) : we populate the cache only after a cache miss, and we invalidate on writes. We never cache anything authoritative — auth lookups are always live, balances (if this were a fintech service) would always be live. Only the derived, reconstructable hot read — the latest posts page — is cached. On the job: The most common caching mistak

heading: Testing Suite
text: Here's where the professional separates from the hobbyist: the test suite is not an afterthought. It is a first-class deliverable. Let me walk you through every layer of testing Gator deserves. On the job: A concurrent service without a -race test is a service with unknown correctness. The race detector has caught real production bugs — double-incremented counters, corrupted maps, subscriber sets with missing entries — that code review missed entirely. Run go test -race ./... in CI. No exceptions. Go 1.25 added testing/synctest, a package for testing concurrent code deterministically by controlling a fake clock and goroutine scheduling. It is particularly useful for testing ticker-driven loops (like Scraper.Start) without wall-clock delays. For this project the -race + httptest.Server approach is sufficient; testing/synctest becomes essential when you need to test time-dependent behavior (backoff, rate limiting, TTL expiry) without time.Sleep in tests. See the Time, Clocks & Timers chapter (Part 2, Chapter 4) for the full treatment.

heading: Race-detector test on the concurrent scraper and cache
text: The most important test in the suite — run go test -race ./... and this must be silent: The Go race detector (available since Go 1.1) instruments every memory access at compile time using ThreadSanitizer (TSan) . When two goroutines access the same memory address concurrently — and at least one write is involved — TSan logs the access locations, goroutine stacks, and the specific variable. The cost: programs compiled with -race run roughly 2–20x slower and use 5–10x more memory. That is why you don't ship -race binaries; you run them in CI. go test -race ./... is non-negotiable for any concurrent service. A race that TSan catches in a test is a bug that would corrupt data silently in production. The scraper specifically needs -race testing because it writes to database.Post rows from N goroutines while the cache is being read and invalidated. Without the semaphore and the correct use of sync.WaitGroup, these accesses overlap. TSan catches exactly this class of bug — don't let it surprise you at 3 a.m. Go 1.26 baseline (race detector available since Go 1.1; overhead figures are stable across recent releases). --

desc: When to split a monolith, service boundaries, inter-service communication, and the operational cost microservices really carry.
text: Let me tell you something the conference-circuit crowd will never admit: most teams that reach for microservices aren't ready for what comes with them. They see Netflix. They don't see the hundred-person platform engineering team keeping it running. You just finished building a real backend — HTTP server, SQL, auth, a caching layer, the whole thing. That's not nothing. That's a monolith , and right now? It's probably the right architecture for you. By the end of this chapter you'll know exactly when that stops being true, how to split a service correctly when the day does come, what inter-service communication actually costs, and why "just microservice it" is one of the most expensive sentences in software. You'll also have the vocabulary and the muscle memory to do it well when the time is right. Lucky you — you've got me.

heading: Monolith vs Microservices
text: Here's the scene: you and two engineers have been building Meridian , a payments and ledger backend. One binary. One Postgres. One deploy. It handles user accounts, payment processing, and email notifications. Traffic is growing; the team wants to move fast without stepping on each other. Someone says the magic word: microservices . Before you do anything, understand what you're actually choosing between. A monolith is a single deployable binary — all domains (accounts, payments, notifications) compiled and deployed together. Service calls are function calls: zero network, zero serialization, compiler-checked types. A microservices architecture splits those domains into separate binaries that communicate over a network. That network hop changes the failure model, the latency, and the operational complexity. Neither is inherently better — the question is whether the benefits of independence justify the cost of distribution for your team right now . For most teams, it doesn't, yet.

heading: The modular monolith — the architecture nobody talks about
text: A monolith is a single deployable unit. That doesn't mean spaghetti. A well-structured monolith is divided into clean packages with enforced dependency directions — it just happens to compile into one binary and run as one process. Inside one process, calling across packages is a function call . Nanoseconds. No network. No serialization. No partial failure. The compiler checks your types at every boundary. Rollback is one git revert and a redeploy. This is what you built in the Blog Aggregator project (Part 1). And it is good . Microservices split those packages into separate binaries that communicate over a network. That network hop changes everything — and we'll be very precise about what changes and why.

heading: Conway's Law: your architecture mirrors your org chart
text: In 1967, Mel Conway observed that organizations build systems that mirror their communication structures. If you have one team, you'll build one system. If you have three teams, the system will naturally cleave into three pieces — because the teams can't coordinate closely enough to do otherwise. This is a description , not a prescription. Don't split into microservices to "enable team autonomy" if you don't actually have multiple autonomous teams. You'll pay the operational cost of microservices while your two engineers are still Slacking each other about shared DB schemas.

heading: When a split is actually justified
text: You should consider splitting when at least two of these are true: One domain has dramatically different resource needs than others (CPU-bound notification rendering vs. I/O-bound payments ledger) and you're paying for it. At Meridian, notification fan-out during settlement windows is the canonical example. Multiple independent teams exist, and deploy coupling is measurably slowing them down — not hypothetically, measurably . A failure in one domain must not cascade to another, and the current monolith structure makes isolation impossible without architectural change. One service genuinely needs a different runtime, language, or data store — not because it's fashionable, but because the domain demands it. Regulations (PCI-DSS, HIPAA) require specific subsystems to be isolated with auditable network controls between them. Microservices do not make bad code good. A tangled monolith becomes a tangled distributed system — now with network timeouts. Fix the design first; then, only if you must, split it.

heading: Service Boundaries
text: Suppose the pain is real and a split is warranted. Where do you cut? This is the most consequential technical decision in a microservices architecture, and it's the one most often rushed. A bad cut produces a distributed monolith — the worst of both worlds.

heading: Bounded contexts and domain-driven design
text: A bounded context is a subsystem where one domain model is internally consistent and authoritative. Inside the context, the model is coherent; outside it, the same concept (e.g. "account") may have a different shape. A service boundary is where you draw the cut: the bounded context becomes a separate deployable. Cut in the wrong place and two services become inseparable — you own a distributed monolith. Cut correctly and each service can be deployed, scaled, and failed independently. The concept comes from Domain-Driven Design (DDD); you don't need to read the whole book to apply the lens. The right lens is domain-driven design (DDD) and specifically bounded contexts . A bounded context is a subsystem where a particular domain model is internally consistent and owns its own language. For Meridian, the natural bounded contexts are: Accounts — user identities, balances, account state. The concept of an "account" here is a financial entity with a ledger balance; it is not the same as a "user profile" in a CMS. Payments/Ledger — double-entry bookkeeping, transfers, posting journal entries. (SQL & Databases in Go covers the SQL layer that underpins this; Part 3 goes deep on ledger desig

heading: The distributed monolith anti-pattern
text: You have a distributed monolith when services are split into separate deployables but remain tightly coupled: A distributed monolith is what you get when you split a codebase into separate services but fail to separate their coupling . The services share a database, call each other synchronously across the board, or require coordinated deploys — so you have all the operational complexity of microservices with none of the independence. It is strictly worse than either a well-designed monolith or a well-designed microservices architecture. The tell: if you can't deploy service A without coordinating with service B, your boundary is wrong. Two services read and write the same tables. A schema change in one instantly breaks the other. You have all the coupling of a monolith with none of the simplicity. Service A calls B calls C calls D — synchronously. A is now blocked on D's latency and D's availability. Any single failure cascades to all callers. A business operation requires 10 sequential HTTP calls across services to complete. You haven't decomposed the domain — you've shredded a function across a network. A shared database between services is not a microservices architecture. It i

heading: Data ownership — one service, one schema
text: Each service owns its data store. Full stop. Other services don't get direct database access — they get an API. When Meridian's Payments service needs to check an account balance before posting a transfer, it calls AccountsService.GetBalance via the API. When the Payments service posts a Transfer, it emits a TransferPosted event that Notifications subscribes to. Nobody reaches across the schema boundary. This has a real cost: you lose ACID transactions that span service boundaries . A Transfer that debits Account A and credits Account B — both owned by Meridian's Payments service — is fine. A transfer that requires updating both Payments and triggering a real-time Notifications delivery atomically is not — you need the saga pattern for that (Part 3: Transactions, Consistency and Sagas). On the job: The urge to "just join the tables" across service boundaries is real, especially under deadline pressure. It always feels like a small shortcut. It always costs you later when one team renames a column.

heading: Inter-Service Communication
text: The defining failure mode of synchronous chains — one slow link, felt at the front door: Services need to talk. How they talk shapes every other property of the system — latency, availability, coupling, and failure modes. Synchronous communication (HTTP, gRPC) means the caller blocks until the callee responds — simple to reason about, but it ties the caller's availability directly to the callee's. If the callee is slow or down, the caller is affected. Asynchronous communication (message queues, events) means the caller publishes a message and returns immediately; the callee processes it later. This decouples availability — the caller keeps working even if the callee is down — but introduces eventual consistency: the caller can't immediately know the outcome. Right tool for the job: use sync for queries where the caller needs the answer before proceeding; use async for work that can happen later (notifications, audit logs, downstream projections).

heading: Synchronous vs. asynchronous
text: The fundamental choice is whether the caller waits for an answer (synchronous) or fires and moves on (asynchronous). The caller blocks until the callee responds. Simple to reason about, easier to debug. Right for queries where you need the answer before proceeding. REST over HTTP and gRPC are the standard choices. The caller publishes a message and returns immediately. The callee processes it later (maybe much later). Right for workflows that don't need an immediate answer — notifications, audit logs, downstream projections. Kafka, NATS, RabbitMQ. Deep treatment in Part 3.

heading: REST over HTTP — the pragmatic default
text: For most synchronous inter-service calls, plain HTTP/JSON (the same net/http you already know) is the right starting point. It's debuggable with curl, it's observable with standard tooling, and it adds zero new dependencies. On the job: In Meridian's Payments service, every call to Accounts before posting a Transfer is a synchronous inter-service call. Getting the timeout and error handling wrong here means a slow Accounts pod takes Payments down with it. Here is a minimal AccountsClient in Meridian's Payments service — a thin HTTP wrapper that calls the Accounts service to validate an account before accepting a transfer: A few things to notice. context.Context is the first argument — this isn't ceremony, it's how the caller's deadline and cancellation propagate into the HTTP request. We use http.NewRequestWithContext (not http.NewRequest) so the context is wired to the transport. And we give http.Client an explicit Timeout — never trust a downstream service to respond in finite time. Let's make this runnable with httptest so you can see it working without a real server:

heading: gRPC — when you need the next level
text: HTTP/JSON is fine for most inter-service calls. When you need strong typing across service boundaries, streaming, or significantly better throughput , gRPC is the answer: schema-first with Protocol Buffers, efficient binary wire format, generated clients in any language, and built-in deadline propagation. gRPC gets full treatment in Part 2, Chapter 17: gRPC and Service-to-Service Communication (slug: grpc-service-communication). For now, the mental model: where HTTP/JSON lets you call across services without a shared schema, gRPC defines the contract in a .proto file and generates client/server code from it — the compiler catches API mismatches before they reach production. For Meridian's internal transfer RPC, gRPC is the right long-term answer; for getting started, HTTP/JSON is fine. In production you run multiple replicas of each service for availability and throughput. A load balancer or reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy, HAProxy, or a cloud LB) sits in front of those replicas and distributes traffic across them. It also handles TLS termination, health checking (dropping unhealthy replicas from rotation), and connection pooling. This is a deep topic — it gets full treatment in Deploy

heading: Service discovery basics
text: Service discovery is how a service finds the network address of another service at runtime. In development, you hardcode localhost:8081. In production, services run as multiple replicas with dynamic IPs that change on every deploy and restart — so you can't hardcode them. The two common approaches: DNS-based (each service gets a stable DNS name backed by a load balancer, e.g. accounts.meridian.svc.cluster.local in Kubernetes) and registry-based (services register themselves at startup with a registry like Consul or etcd; clients query the registry). Kubernetes handles this automatically via its internal DNS. Without service discovery, a single replica restart breaks every caller that had its IP hardcoded. When Payments needs to find Accounts, it needs to know the Accounts service's address. In local development that's localhost:8081. In production it's more complex: services are deployed with dynamic IPs, auto-scaled, and restarted constantly. Service discovery is the mechanism by which services find each other. The two common approaches: DNS-based — each service gets a DNS name (e.g., accounts.meridian.svc.cluster.local in Kubernetes). The DNS entry points at the load balancer. Si

heading: The request journey with a load balancer
text: An in-process function call in Go is essentially free: push arguments onto the stack, jump to the function, pop the return value. Time: nanoseconds. Failure modes: panics, which you control. A network call across service boundaries is a different animal entirely. Here's what actually happens and what it costs: 1. Serialization and deserialization. The Go struct must be encoded to JSON (or protobuf) at the sender and decoded back to a struct at the receiver. For a simple AccountInfo, this is microseconds. For a large payload or a hot path, it compounds. 2. TCP overhead. A connection must be established (or reused from a pool), data split into packets, packets transmitted, acknowledgments received. Even on localhost, a minimal HTTP round-trip takes tens of microseconds. Over a datacenter network, 0.5–2ms is typical. Across availability zones, expect 1–5ms. 3. OS context switches. The kernel is involved for every send and receive. Goroutines block on I/O and yield their OS thread (the scheduler parks them and gives the thread to another goroutine — Concurrency: Goroutines, Channels & Select covers this), then get rescheduled when the response arrives. 4. New failure modes. A function

heading: The Operational Cost
text: Here's where I stop being charming and start being honest with you. Microservices are genuinely powerful — at the right scale, with the right team, for the right reasons. They are also genuinely expensive to operate, and most of that cost is invisible until you're in it.

heading: Distributed tracing — debugging across process boundaries
text: In a monolith, a slow request shows up in one stack trace. In a multi-service system, that request touched five services, each with its own logs, its own trace, and its own wall clock. Without distributed tracing , you can't reconstruct what happened. The standard today is OpenTelemetry — an instrumentation SDK you add to each service to emit spans (units of work with a start time, end time, and metadata). Spans are linked by a trace ID propagated in request headers (traceparent). The trace aggregator (Jaeger, Tempo, or your cloud provider's equivalent) stitches spans from multiple services into a single flame graph. A trace for the transfer request above would show: time spent in the gateway → time spent in Payments before calling Accounts → time spent inside Accounts → time spent back in Payments posting the ledger entry → time spent in the response path. When Accounts is slow, it lights up in the trace immediately. This is covered in depth in Part 2, Chapter 10: Observability: Telemetry and Acting On It . What you need to know now: plan for it from the first service split, not after you can't debug anything. On the job: The first time you debug a multi-service issue without dist

heading: Partial failure — the hardest problem
text: In a monolith, a call either returns a result or panics — you always know the outcome. In a distributed system, a third outcome exists: partial failure . The request left the caller, traveled the network, may have been processed by the callee, but the response was lost (network blip, pod restart, timeout). The caller doesn't know whether the operation happened. If it retries, did it double-charge? Partial failure is the single hardest problem in distributed systems, and it's why idempotency keys are mandatory for any mutating operation in financial systems — they let you safely retry without executing twice. In a monolith, a call either succeeds or it doesn't. In a distributed system, a call can partially succeed — the request reached the target, the target processed it, but the response was lost. You don't know if it ran. If you retry, did you double-charge? This is why idempotency keys are not optional in financial systems, and why every mutating inter-service call that matters needs one. Deep treatment in Part 3, Chapter 4: Idempotency and Exactly-Once Semantics . The pattern: include a unique Idempotency-Key header on every write (every POST /transfers Meridian processes); the

heading: Partial failure cascading vs. containment
text: The fix is not complicated, but it requires discipline: 1. Every outbound call has an explicit timeout. Not the http.DefaultClient with no timeout — a http.Client with a Timeout set. 2. Non-critical calls are async where possible. Notifications don't need to block the transfer response. Enqueue them; deliver them separately. 3. Circuit breakers open after sustained failure, returning a fast error instead of queuing blocked goroutines (Part 2, Chapter 11: Reliability Patterns).

heading: Eventual consistency — your data will be stale sometimes
text: In a monolith with one database, a read after a write sees the write. In a distributed system where data is owned by separate services and communicated via events, a read by one service may not yet reflect a write that happened in another. This is eventual consistency — the system will converge on the correct state, but not necessarily immediately. Some things to embrace: Model state transitions explicitly (e.g., a Meridian Transfer moves through pending → settled → failed) rather than treating everything as immediately consistent. Don't query Payments for data that should have been pushed from Accounts via an event — you might be reading stale state. Reconciliation jobs (a background worker that periodically validates that state is consistent across Meridian's services) are a necessary safety net, not an admission of defeat. On the job: The first time a customer support ticket says "the payment shows posted but the notification never arrived," you will wish you had a reconciliation job running. Add it before you need it.

heading: Deployment and versioning complexity
text: With a monolith, "deploy" means one artifact, one version. With microservices, you have N services in production simultaneously, and during a rolling deploy, you have two versions of one service running at the same time alongside fixed versions of all other services. This means: API changes must be backward compatible until you're certain all callers have upgraded. Never remove a field from a response payload before all consumers have stopped reading it. Schema migrations must be expand-contract — add the new column, backfill it, switch all callers, then drop the old. Same pattern as SQL & Databases in Go, now applied to service APIs. Service versioning (e.g., /v1/accounts vs. /v2/accounts) gives you a clean migration path, but you pay for maintaining two versions until the old one is retired.

heading: The honest summary
text: Independent deployability, independent scalability, fault isolation, genuine team autonomy, the ability to use the right technology for each domain. Distributed tracing, partial failure modes, network latency on every inter-service call, eventual consistency to reason about, deployment versioning discipline, an operational platform (Kubernetes, service mesh, observability stack) to run it all. You come out ahead when the benefits (autonomy, scale, isolation) outweigh the costs. For most teams, that means multiple autonomous teams, proven product-market fit, and genuine independent scaling needs. The most common microservices mistake: splitting prematurely, then discovering the services are too tightly coupled to deploy independently anyway — the distributed monolith. The second most common: no distributed tracing, so debugging takes ten times as long as it did in the monolith. --

Use a 2-second timeout on the http.Client. Use http.NewRequestWithContext so the context also applies. The http.Client.Timeout bounds the entire request (including dial + TLS + read body). http.NewRequestWithContext wires the caller's cancellation signal to the transport so an upstream context cancellation also aborts the request mid-flight. If the call fails for any reason (including a timeout), return the fallback and a nil error — log the error with slog. If the call succeeds, return t

text: Alright, sport. Time to prove you've actually absorbed what this chapter said about partial failure. I designed this one myself, and I'm very interested in whether you pass. Meridian's slow Accounts server is going to hang for 10 full seconds. Your job is to make sure Payments doesn't share that fate. Add the timeout, return the 503. You now know more about microservices than most people who claim to "do microservices" — because you know when not to. That restraint? That's the mark of a real engineer. It's no me , obviously, but it's something. Onward: Docker and containerization next — getting what you just built into a box that runs the same everywhere.

desc: Images, layers and the build cache, multi-stage builds down to scratch/distroless, and docker compose for local multi-service development.
text: Let me be very clear about something. Shipping a Go service without a container is like showing up to a black-tie event in sweatpants — technically present, but deeply embarrassing. Docker isn't ops magic; it's engineering . And because Go compiles to a single static binary with the runtime baked in, you have an unfair advantage every other language envies. We are going to exploit that advantage mercilessly. By the end of this chapter you will understand what a container actually is at the Linux kernel level, how image layers and the build cache work (and how to exploit both), how to produce a Go binary in a scratch image that's smaller than your average podcast MP3, and how to wire your entire local dev environment together with a single docker compose up. The containerization fundamentals live here. The next chapter — Building & Shipping Go Binaries — goes deep on cross-compilation, CGO ENABLED=0, and the static-binary trap behind scratch images. After that, production rollout — CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes, rolling deployments — is Deployment & Infra: CI/CD + Kubernetes. I'll link you forward when we get there. You're working on Meridian's ledger service from the last several cha

heading: What a Container Actually Is
text: Here is the thing that 80% of engineers get wrong, because they were taught it wrong: a container is not a virtual machine. A virtual machine emulates hardware and runs an entire guest OS. A container is just a regular Linux process — the same kind as the one running your shell — that the kernel has been told to isolate and constrain . A container is an ordinary Linux process (or process tree) that the kernel has been told to isolate with namespaces (each container gets its own view of the PID table, network stack, filesystem, etc.) and constrain with cgroups (hard limits on CPU, memory, and I/O). No hypervisor, no guest OS — the container shares the host kernel directly. That is why containers start in milliseconds and add negligible runtime overhead compared to a virtual machine. That isolation comes from two Linux kernel features working together.

heading: Namespaces: the illusion of a private world
text: A namespace is a kernel-level wrapper that gives a process (or group of processes) its own private view of a resource that would otherwise be global. Docker uses six of them: The container process sees itself as PID 1 and can't see host processes. Your Go service thinks it owns the machine. A private network stack: its own interfaces, routing table, and port space. Port 8080 inside the container is not host port 8080 until you publish it. A private filesystem tree. The container's / is not the host's / — it's a layered union filesystem (more on this shortly). A private hostname. Your container can call itself ledger-service without the host knowing or caring. Isolated System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues — processes in different containers can't signal each other accidentally. Map container UIDs to host UIDs. Run as root inside the container, mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host. Namespaces create isolation, not security boundaries. A poorly configured container running as root can still escape to the host through kernel exploits or volume misuse. Never run production containers as root if you can avoid it — use a non-root USER in your Dockerfile.

heading: cgroups: the resource accountant
text: Control groups (cgroups) are the kernel's mechanism for limiting and accounting for resource usage by a group of processes. Namespaces say "this process has its own view of things." cgroups say "this process is only allowed to use X% of CPU and Y MB of memory." When Docker says --memory=256m --cpus=0.5, it's writing limits into a cgroup hierarchy in /sys/fs/cgroup. The kernel's scheduler and OOM killer read those limits. When a container blows past its memory budget, the OOM killer terminates it — the same mechanism that kills any runaway Linux process. On the job: When Meridian's ledger service gets OOM-killed in production, the first question is always "what cgroup limit did we set?" — not "is there a memory leak?" Set both a request and a limit in your deploy config, and monitor container restarts as a first-class signal. This is the entire secret. A container is a process tree under namespaces (for isolation) and cgroups (for resource limits), running against a union-mount filesystem. No hypervisor. No hardware emulation. Kernel overhead is negligible; startup is measured in milliseconds, not seconds.

heading: Images vs. containers
text: An image is a read-only, content-addressed snapshot of a filesystem plus metadata (entrypoint, env vars, exposed ports). It's the artifact you build and push to a registry. It does not run. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image: Docker adds a thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers and starts the process inside a fresh set of namespaces. Many containers can share one image simultaneously — zero duplication of the image bytes. The terms get conflated. Here is the exact distinction: An image is a read-only, layered snapshot of a filesystem plus metadata (the entrypoint command, environment variables, exposed ports). It's an artifact you build, tag, and push to a registry. It doesn't run. A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image. Docker adds a thin, writable container layer on top of the read-only image layers when it starts a container. Writes inside a running container land in that ephemeral top layer — when the container is removed, those writes are gone. Multiple containers can run from the same image simultaneously, each with its own writable layer, all sharing the same underlying read-only layers. Zero redundancy; excelle

heading: Images, Layers & the Build Cache
text: The cache rule in one animation — one changed line, and everything BELOW it rebuilds: Every Dockerfile instruction produces one layer — an immutable, content-addressed snapshot of the filesystem delta from the previous instruction. Docker caches each layer keyed on the instruction text plus the state of the filesystem at that point. When you rebuild, Docker replays cached layers until it hits a change, then rebuilds from that point down. Getting the layer order right is the single biggest lever on incremental build speed: a poorly ordered Dockerfile re-downloads all your Go modules on every source change; a correctly ordered one serves them from cache and rebuilds in seconds. Every instruction in a Dockerfile produces exactly one layer — an immutable, content-addressed snapshot of the filesystem delta from the instruction before it. Layers are the unit of caching. Get the order wrong and you bust the cache on every build. Get it right and incremental rebuilds take seconds.

heading: The anatomy of a Dockerfile
text: Here is a naive Dockerfile for the Meridian ledger service — the kind a developer writes at 11pm when they just want it to work: This builds. It runs. And it rebuilds from scratch on every single code change, downloading all your modules every time. For a service with 50 dependencies, that's painful. The fix is instruction ordering. Docker's layer cache is keyed on the instruction itself plus the state of the filesystem at that point . The moment a COPY instruction finds that the files being copied have changed, that layer and every layer below it is invalidated. The trick is to copy only what each step needs , starting with the most stable things. The invariant: copy things that change slowly before things that change fast. Dependency manifests change maybe once a week. Source code changes every hour. Putting COPY go.mod go.sum + go mod download before COPY . . means the entire module download step is served from the local layer cache on every incremental rebuild. On the job: Every extra second of CI build time compounds across dozens of engineers pushing dozens of times a day. At Meridian's team size, a 45-second rebuild vs. an 8-second one is the difference between a fast feedba

heading: Build arguments and cache invalidation
text: One footgun: if you use ARG to inject a build-time value (say, a version string), and the ARG instruction appears before a RUN go build, that ARG is part of the layer key — changing the version string will bust the cache for everything below it. Place ARG instructions as late as possible, after expensive cached steps. Docker BuildKit (enabled by default since Docker 23) adds parallel stage execution, inline cache hints, SSH agent forwarding, and secrets that don't land in image layers. Always build with DOCKER BUILDKIT=1 (or use docker buildx build) and add syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 as the first line of your Dockerfile to unlock the full feature set.

heading: Multi-Stage Builds
text: A multi-stage build uses multiple FROM instructions in a single Dockerfile. Each stage is an independent filesystem. You compile in a heavy builder stage (full Go toolchain, source, module cache), then COPY --from=builder only the compiled binary into a tiny final stage. Docker discards the intermediate stages entirely — they never enter the final image. The result: a production image that contains exactly what the binary needs to run , not what it took to build . Here is where Go's static binary becomes your superpower. The builder stage needs the full Go toolchain — compiler, linker, stdlib sources, module cache. The final container running in production needs none of that . It needs exactly one thing: the compiled binary. Multi-stage builds solve this with multiple FROM instructions in a single Dockerfile. Each stage is independent. You compile in a fat build stage, then COPY --from=builder just the binary into a tiny final stage that ships to production.

heading: From fat to scratch
text: On the job: At Meridian, the difference between a 12MB scratch image and an 800MB fat image is the difference between a 3-second rolling deploy and a 3-minute one. Slow image pulls mean longer rollouts, more overlap between old and new instances, and more pressure on the container registry. Keep images small. Let's look at the full multi-stage Dockerfile for the Meridian ledger service: That final image contains exactly two files: the CA bundle and the binary. Nothing else. No shell. No package manager. No curl an attacker could use. No old OpenSSL. No Python interpreter left by a careless base image maintainer. FROM scratch is Docker's special empty base image — literally nothing: no shell, no libc, no package manager, no attack surface. It works for a Go binary built with CGO ENABLED=0 because that binary links nothing at runtime. Distroless images (gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12) are a middle ground: a stripped-down Debian with timezone data and CA certificates, but still no shell. 2–3MB larger than scratch; easier to debug; required when your binary links against C libraries via CGO.

heading: scratch vs. distroless
text: scratch is the purest option — nothing. But nothing means no shell for debugging . If your service panics at 3am, you can't docker exec in and poke around. Google's distroless images (gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12) are a middle ground: they add CA certificates, timezone data, and /etc/passwd — but no libc (that lives in distroless/base), no shell, and no package manager. They're 2–3MB larger than scratch but easier to operate. (For a CGO binary that needs glibc, use distroless/base-debian12.) For a pure Go binary with CGO ENABLED=0, scratch is the right default. For a binary that links against C libraries (CGO), use distroless/base-debian12 which includes glibc.

heading: Why CGOENABLED=0 matters — the short version
text: When you set CGO ENABLED=0, the Go linker produces a fully static binary — no calls to the dynamic linker (ld.so), no dlopen, no shared library dependencies whatsoever. The Go runtime, standard library, and all imported packages are compiled into the binary at link time. That's why the binary works in a scratch image with no libc present. This is possible because Go's standard library reimplements most OS interfaces in pure Go (the network stack, DNS resolver, crypto). The CGO ENABLED=1 default exists for packages that wrap C libraries (like database drivers using libpq, or packages using OpenSSL). For a service that uses pure Go drivers and the stdlib, CGO ENABLED=0 is always the right choice for containers. The mechanics of static vs. dynamic linking, the ELF PT INTERP flag, ldd output, cross-compilation gotchas with CGO, and the -ldflags="-s -w" strip flags are all covered in depth in the next chapter — Building & Shipping Go Binaries (/part-1/building-shipping-binaries). This chapter gives you enough to write a correct Dockerfile; the next one explains exactly why it works. This is a conceptual model — a simplification of the actual linker and loader behaviour. When CGO ENABLED

heading: Docker Compose
text: Containers in isolation are useful. Containers talking to each other are where the real work happens. The ledger service needs PostgreSQL for its double-entry ledger and Redis for its distributed rate limiter (from Part 2). Running three separate docker run commands with the right flags, networks, and volume mounts, in the right order, by hand, every time — is not engineering. It's suffering. Docker Compose is a declarative YAML format for defining and running multi-container applications on a single host. You describe every service (its image or build context), the environment variables it needs, how the services depend on each other, what ports to expose, and which named volumes to mount — then docker compose up wires it all together and starts the stack. Service names become DNS hostnames on the private Compose network, so the ledger service reaches Postgres at postgres:5432 without any IP configuration. This is your local dev environment — not production (production is Kubernetes, covered in Deployment & Infra: CI/CD + Kubernetes ). Docker Compose is a declarative format for defining and running multi-container applications. One docker-compose.yml file describes the entire loca

heading: The ledger service compose file
text: Let's walk through the key concepts, one by one.

heading: Networks: container DNS for free
text: By default, Compose creates a private Docker network for every docker-compose.yml and attaches all services to it. On that network, service names are DNS hostnames . The ledger service connects to Postgres at postgres:5432 — not localhost:5432 (that's the host machine) and not an IP address (those change). The Docker daemon runs an embedded DNS resolver that resolves postgres to the container's internal IP. This is why the DB URL is postgres://ledger:secret@postgres:5432/ledger — postgres is the service name, which is the DNS name on the Compose network.

heading: dependson with healthchecks
text: On the job: Without a real healthcheck, Meridian's ledger service races against Postgres on every docker compose up in dev, fails to connect, and crashes — then the engineer adds sleep 5 to their startup script, and six months later that sleep is in production. Don't do this. depends on alone only waits for the container to start . It does not wait for the service inside to be ready . Starting a Postgres container takes a few seconds for the database to initialize; if the ledger service connects immediately, it gets a connection refused and crashes. The condition: service healthy form waits until the healthcheck passes before starting the dependent service. The healthcheck for Postgres runs pg isready — the official Postgres "is the server accepting connections?" probe. For Redis, redis-cli ping returns PONG when the server is ready. This is the correct pattern. Never use sleep 5 as a substitute for a real healthcheck.

heading: Volumes: data that survives restarts
text: Named volumes (pg data, redis data) are managed by Docker and persist across docker compose down / docker compose up cycles. They mount into the container at the paths where each service stores its data. Without named volumes, every docker compose down would wipe your local Postgres data. With them, the data survives service restarts and even container image upgrades. When Docker Compose creates a network, it spawns an embedded DNS server at a fixed address (typically 127.0.0.11) and injects that address into each container's /etc/resolv.conf as the nameserver. When your Go process calls net.LookupHost("postgres"), the Go resolver reads /etc/resolv.conf, finds 127.0.0.11, and sends a DNS query to the Docker daemon's resolver. The Docker daemon maintains a mapping of service name → container IP, updated as containers start and stop. If you scale a service (docker compose up --scale worker=3), round-robin DNS returns all three IPs. This is a primitive form of client-side load balancing — production services use a proper load balancer (see Deployment & Infra: CI/CD + Kubernetes), but for local dev it's perfectly sufficient.
