desc: Delve (breakpoints, stepping, goroutine switching, remote/headless), reading panics and stack traces, full goroutine dumps and the deadlock detector, and production debugging with GODEBUG, net/http/pprof and core dumps.
text: Let me tell you something about broken software, sport. Every engineer on Earth has written it. The great ones — the truly great ones — know how to find it. Fast. Surgically. Without guessing. You just finished the concurrency chapter. You know the patterns. You know the memory model. And now your payments service is deadlocking under load at 2 a.m. and you have a goroutine leaking somewhere and the on-call alert has been firing for eleven minutes. What do you do? You reach for the right tool. Not fmt.Println. Not prayer. The right tool . By the end of this chapter you'll command Delve — Go's real debugger — read a panic stack trace in under ten seconds, dump every goroutine in a live process, and instrument a production service for debugging without redeploying. The runtime has been screaming at you this whole time. You just didn't know the language. You're about to learn it. Lucky you.

heading: Delve — the Go Debugger
text: Here is the scenario we are living inside for this entire chapter. Meridian Payments — a Go service that handles fund transfers between accounts — has two bugs in production. One: the /transfer handler deadlocks under concurrent load, locking the entire service. Two: a goroutine leaks from the /webhook handler; every inbound webhook spawns a goroutine that never exits. The service OOMs in about four hours under normal traffic. You have been paged. I'm watching. Let's go. On the job: Lock-order inversions surface under load — two concurrent transfers between the same account pair hit each other's mutexes and hang the service. A deadlock that takes four hours to reproduce in testing kills you in ten minutes in production.

heading: Installing and running Delve
text: Delve is Go's purpose-built debugger. Not GDB. Not LLDB bolted on. Delve understands goroutines, the Go scheduler, DWARF debug info generated by the Go toolchain, and interfaces. Install it once: Three entry points — know all three: dlv debug compiles your program with full debug info (disabling optimizations that would confuse the debugger) and drops you at a prompt. You have not started the program yet — it is loaded and waiting.

heading: Breakpoints
text: A breakpoint tells Delve to stop execution the moment the program reaches a particular line, function, or condition. When it stops, the world freezes and you can inspect everything. Three forms: line , function , conditional . The conditional form is gold — instead of stopping on every call to Transfer, it stops only when a specific account is involved. For a high-traffic service this is the difference between useful and useless.

heading: Stepping through execution
text: Once Delve stops at a breakpoint, you step through the code one unit at a time: Let me animate stepping through the Transfer function so you can see what each command actually does.

heading: Inspecting variables and the call stack
text: Stopped at a breakpoint, you have full visibility into the running program: locals shows every local variable in the current frame. print evaluates any expression. stack shows the full call chain from here to main. frame N jumps you into any frame in the stack so you can inspect that frame's locals too. This is how you see not just where the program is, but how it got there .

heading: Switching between goroutines
text: This is Delve's superpower over any general-purpose debugger. Go programs have potentially thousands of goroutines. Delve can show them all and let you jump between them. Goroutines 18 and 19 are both blocked trying to acquire the same mutex. Goroutine 1 holds it and is inside debit(). We can now see exactly which goroutines are contending and on which lock. This is not guesswork — this is evidence.

heading: Debugging a single failing test
text: When a test is failing and the failure isn't obvious from the output, dlv test is the first thing I reach for. Not printf. Delve. You have the full debugger — breakpoints, stepping, variable inspection — inside the test harness. The test's goroutines show up in goroutines. The mutex state is inspectable. Whatever the test is doing wrong, you can watch it happen one instruction at a time.

heading: Attaching to a running process
text: When you need to debug a process that's already running (a staging server, a long-running worker), dlv attach is the tool: Important: attaching stops the process during the debug session. In production this means downtime. Use a replica, or prefer the production-safe techniques in Section 3. Attach is the right tool for staging, pre-production, or a process you can safely pause.

heading: Headless/remote debugging inside a container
text: In a container or over SSH, you can't run the TUI interactively. Run Delve in headless mode as a server and connect from your local machine: The connection protocol is JSON over TCP. Your local dlv connect (or VS Code) speaks to the remote Delve server that's running the actual binary. You get the full interactive debugger — breakpoints, goroutine switching, the works — through the tunnel. Delve's API gives full control over the target process — read memory, set variables, execute arbitrary code. Bind it to 127.0.0.1 or an internal interface and tunnel through SSH. Never --listen=0.0.0.0:2345 on a publicly reachable host. When you type break handler.go:47, Delve does something elegant and ruthless. Step 1: look up the address. The Go toolchain embeds DWARF (Debugging With Arbitrary Record Formats) debug info in every binary unless you strip it. DWARF is a table that maps source file + line number to machine-code addresses. Delve parses this table to find the address of the instruction that corresponds to line 47. Step 2: replace one byte. On x86-64, Delve reads the original byte at that address, saves it, and writes 0xCC — the INT3 instruction (software interrupt 3). One byte. That

heading: Reading the Runtime's Signals
text: The Go runtime is always watching. It knows when goroutines deadlock. It knows the full call stack of every goroutine at any moment. It can dump all of that to stderr on demand. You just need to know how to ask — and how to read what comes back.

heading: Reading a panic and its stack trace
text: On the job: A panic in production kills the request goroutine and prints a stack trace to your log aggregator. If you can't read it in ten seconds, you're flying blind while the alert fires. Here is a program that panics. Let's make it on purpose, because understanding the output is a skill you need before you're reading it at 3 a.m. Run that and you see something like this: Here is how to read it — top to bottom, three beats. Beat 1 — the goroutine header: goroutine 1 [running] tells you which goroutine panicked and its state. For a panic, the state is running. For blocked goroutines (which we'll see soon) the state will be chan receive, sync.Mutex, select, etc. Beat 2 — the top frame is where it panicked: main.processTransfer at line 7 is the innermost frame — the exact function and line that called panic(...). This is the scene of the crime. Beat 3 — read downward for the call chain: each frame below tells you who called the frame above. handleRequest called processTransfer. main called handleRequest. Reading top to bottom, you reconstruct: main → handleRequest → processTransfer → panic. That's your full call chain. The bug is at the top; the trigger is in main.

heading: The deliberate deadlock the runtime detects
text: The shape you're hunting in every goroutine dump — a wait CYCLE: The Go runtime has a built-in deadlock detector. It's not optional and it's not configurable — it fires whenever all goroutines are blocked with no path forward. Here is what it looks like: The runtime prints: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock! is the runtime's cry for help. Every goroutine is blocked, none can wake any other, and execution will never proceed. The trace below it shows where each goroutine is stuck. In this case goroutine 1 is blocked at sync.runtime SemacquireMutex — deep in the mutex implementation — called from our double mu.Lock() at line 10. The runtime deadlock detector is conservative by design. If two goroutines deadlock but a third is still running (a background ticker, a separate HTTP handler), the detector stays silent. Those "hidden goroutines" mask the deadlock. You need the goroutine dump (next section) to find it in that case.

heading: Dumping every goroutine — SIGQUIT and GOTRACEBACK
text: On the job: When the service is hung and alerts are firing, a SIGQUIT dump gives you the complete goroutine state in under a second — without attaching a debugger or restarting the process. The most powerful single action in your production debugging toolkit: send SIGQUIT to your Go process and it will dump the full stack of every goroutine to stderr, then exit. On macOS and Linux, SIGQUIT is the default trigger. The Go runtime catches it before the OS can kill the process and emits the dump. You can also control the verbosity with the GOTRACEBACK environment variable: Here is what a two-goroutine deadlock looks like in a full dump: Both goroutines stuck at chan receive, line 34 of main.go. Line 34 is where transferFunds reads from a response channel that nothing will ever send to. Two goroutines, both waiting, neither can proceed. Deadlock.

heading: Hunting goroutine leaks
text: On the job: A leaking webhook handler starts invisible and kills the process in hours — the goroutine count climbs monotonically, memory grows, and by the time the OOM kills you it's too late to attach a debugger. Catch it with pprof while it's still small. A goroutine leak is subtler than a deadlock. The process keeps running; goroutines just accumulate. Over time, memory grows, CPU may spike, and eventually you OOM or the scheduler bogs down. The signature: Goroutine count climbs monotonically over time (visible in net/http/pprof — covered in Section 3) A goroutine dump shows many goroutines all stuck at the same line — often waiting on a channel that nothing ever closes The most common cause in HTTP handlers: a goroutine launched inside the handler but not tied to the request's context. When the client disconnects, ctx.Done() fires and the handler returns — but the leaked goroutine has no reference to the context and keeps running.

heading: Debugging in Production
text: You cannot attach Delve to a production process that serves real traffic. You cannot stop the world for an interactive debug session. But you are not helpless — the runtime has eyes everywhere, and you can wire them up before an incident happens.

heading: GODEBUG knobs
text: On the job: GC pressure and scheduler saturation show up in GODEBUG traces before they show up in latency metrics. Set gctrace=1 in staging whenever memory usage looks wrong — it tells you if GC is the culprit before you spend an hour profiling. GODEBUG is an environment variable that unlocks runtime telemetry without recompiling. Set it when starting the process: gctrace=1 prints a line for every GC cycle to stderr: Parse it for GC frequency and pause times. If GC is running every 200ms, your heap is under pressure. If pause times exceed a few milliseconds, investigate. schedtrace=1000 dumps scheduler state every 1000ms: how many goroutines are runnable, how many threads are spinning, how many Ps are idle. If runqueue grows over time, goroutines are piling up faster than the scheduler can dispatch them. These knobs are read at startup. They cannot be changed while the process runs. Set them in your process supervisor or container spec so they're available when you need them.

heading: net/http/pprof — profiling endpoints over HTTP
text: On the job: If pprof isn't wired up before an incident, it isn't available during one. Add it to every service at launch — you'll need the goroutine and heap profiles the moment something goes wrong at 2 a.m. Every Go HTTP service should import net/http/pprof on its admin listener. It adds a suite of debug endpoints you can query live — without restarting the process . The registered endpoints: The goroutine endpoint is the live equivalent of SIGQUIT: debug=2 gives you the full, human-readable dump of every goroutine's stack — the same format as a SIGQUIT dump, pulled over HTTP while the process keeps serving traffic. To see goroutine count over time — the leak detector — fetch the goroutine profile and watch the number: For deeper analysis, pull the profile into go tool pprof: As of Go 1.26, go tool pprof's web command opens a flame graph by default instead of the old call-graph SVG. The flame graph makes hot paths and accumulation patterns immediately visible — tall columns are long stacks, wide columns are frequently sampled code. The old graph is still available via (pprof) callgrind or the -http flag's dropdown. Goroutine leak hunting with the goroutineleak profile (Go 1.26 ex

heading: expvar — live variable inspection
text: expvar is the stdlib's simple key-value store for runtime state. Import it alongside net/http/pprof and expose any counters or gauges you care about: They're served at /debug/vars as JSON: memstats is always present and gives you live heap stats — HeapAlloc, HeapInuse, NumGC — without a full profile.

heading: Core dumps — GOTRACEBACK=crash
text: On the job: Fatal crashes in containerized services vanish without a trace unless you've set GOTRACEBACK=crash in your pod spec. Add it now — you won't be able to add it after the crash you need it for. For post-mortem debugging of a crash that you can't reproduce interactively: On a fatal error, the runtime prints the full goroutine dump and generates a core file. You can then analyze it with Delve: You have full variable inspection, stack frames, and goroutine switching — but you're in the past. The program has already died; you're examining its corpse. This is invaluable for crashes in production that you can't reproduce on demand.

heading: Print debugging — and when it actually beats a debugger
text: Here's the thing, sport. Print debugging isn't beneath you. It has a place. fmt.Println and slog (Go 1.21+) are the right tool when: The bug is in concurrent code where attaching a debugger would serialize the goroutines and change the timing, potentially making the race disappear (Heisenbug) You're debugging a system where you can't attach Delve — a remote process, a container with no terminal, a test that must run in CI The reproduction is intermittent and you need the state of many variables over thousands of calls, not a single paused moment slog with structured fields is the production version: Structured log fields are searchable in any log aggregator. A fmt.Println with string concatenation is not. For production: always slog. For a local scratch investigation: fmt.Println until you know where to look, then clean it up. The honest hierarchy: use Delve for complex control-flow bugs and goroutine state questions. Use goroutine dumps and pprof for concurrent and production bugs. Use print/slog when a debugger would change the behavior or when you need a stream of observations across many executions. When panic fires — or when SIGQUIT arrives, or when the deadlock detector trigg

desc: pprof, benchmarking, escape analysis, cutting allocations, sync.Pool, GC tuning; mechanical sympathy (caches, cache lines, false sharing); the execution tracer (runtime/trace, go tool trace); and profile-guided optimization (default.pgo) — feeding production profiles back into the compiler.
text: Listen up, sport. Every amateur I've ever fired — and there have been many — shared the same disease: they optimized by feel . They read a blog post, swapped a []string for a []byte, and announced they'd made things faster. Adorable. What they actually did was waste two days changing the wrong thing. Here's the truth only someone of my caliber can deliver: performance engineering is a measurement discipline first, last, and always. You profile. You read the numbers. You then fix what the numbers are pointing at — nothing else, nothing more. I once cut Meridian's ledger-report endpoint from 340ms to 11ms by fixing four lines the profiler found. Not forty. Four. Because I measured. By the end of this chapter you'll wield Go's full performance toolkit: pprof, benchmarks, escape analysis, sync.Pool, GC tuning, mechanical sympathy, the execution tracer, and PGO — feeding production profiles back into the compiler itself. You'll profile a real slow endpoint, identify the waste, and eliminate it surgically. And when you're done, maybe you'll be worth keeping around.

heading: pprof
text: Let me set the scene: it's a Monday morning and your on-call page fires. Meridian's ledger-report endpoint — the one that aggregates transaction history per account — is timing out at the 99th percentile. Your CEO is watching the dashboard. You have twenty minutes. The amateur opens their editor and starts guessing. You open a profiler. On the job: You hit the profiler the moment a latency SLO breach or an unexplained throughput drop lands in your inbox. Skipping it and editing code by instinct means fixing the wrong thing — and the page fires again next week.

heading: What pprof gives you
text: pprof is Go's built-in profiling framework. It collects four kinds of profiles, and you need to know all four because they point at different problems: Where is the CPU spending its time? Samples the current goroutine's call stack every 10ms (by default). Points you to hot functions. The first profile to reach for when things are slow . What is live on the heap? Also called the allocation profile — shows inuse objects and cumulative allocation sites. Points you to memory hogs and GC pressure. Where are goroutines blocking on synchronization (channels, mutexes, select)? Essential for diagnosing contention. Disabled by default — you must call runtime.SetBlockProfileRate. Which mutexes are being contested? Finer-grained than block for sync.Mutex/sync.RWMutex contention. Also disabled by default — call runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction. The goroutine profile (/debug/pprof/goroutine) shows a stack trace for every live goroutine. It's not a performance profile — it's a leak detector. If you see 50,000 goroutines where you expect 20, you have a leak, not a speed problem.

heading: Three ways to collect a profile
text: 1. In a test or benchmark (the easiest) This is the cleanest path: go test drives the workload, dumps the profiles, and you inspect them offline. We'll use this form for most of the chapter. 2. In a long-running server with net/http/pprof Drop one import and the endpoints appear on your HTTP mux, ready to sample whenever you need them — no restart required: Then from a terminal: This connects, collects 30 seconds of CPU samples, and drops you into an interactive REPL. net/http/pprof must be gated behind auth or bound only to a private interface. It lets anyone see your call stack, your heap layout, and your goroutine count — that is, everything an attacker needs. Expose it on a separate internal port (e.g. :6060) or protect it with http.BasicAuth. 3. Programmatically with runtime/pprof For precise control — profile only the hot section of a request, not the entire server lifetime:

heading: Reading a profile: top, list, web
text: Once you have a .out file, go tool pprof is your Swiss Army knife: The two most important columns in top output: flat — CPU time spent inside this function, not in its callees. A high flat means this function is the problem. cum (cumulative) — time spent in this function plus everything it calls . A high cum with low flat means the function is just a pass-through into something deeper.

heading: Reading a flame graph
text: go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.out opens a web UI with a flame graph — the most information-dense view in profiling. As of Go 1.26, the flame graph is the default view when you open the pprof web UI (previously it opened a call-graph). The CPU profiler works via SIGPROF signals . When you call pprof.StartCPUProfile, the runtime installs a signal handler and asks the OS to deliver SIGPROF at 100 Hz (every 10ms). When the signal fires, the runtime captures the current goroutine's call stack — a snapshot of the program counter chain from the leaf frame up to the root. These stack snapshots are counted and accumulated in a data structure. StopCPUProfile flushes it to the writer in pprof binary format. Because the profiler is sample-based , it introduces statistical error: a function that takes 8ms but runs rarely might never be sampled. The practical effect is that functions faster than 1ms are invisible at 100 Hz — they never live long enough to be caught. For those you need microbenchmarks , not CPU profiles. The heap profiler is different: it instruments mallocgc directly, recording a stack sample every N bytes allocated (default: once per 512 KB, controlled by runtime.MemProfileRate

heading: Benchmarking
text: Profiling tells you where the fire is. Benchmarks tell you whether your fix actually put it out — and by how much. They're your before/after measurement instrument. On the job: Always write a benchmark before you optimize and run it again after. Without a before/after number you cannot know whether your change helped, hurt, or did nothing. Gut feel is not evidence.

heading: testing.B and the benchmark loop
text: A Go benchmark is a test function named BenchmarkXxx that accepts testing.B. The framework auto-tunes the iteration count so the total measured time is statistically meaningful. Go 1.24+: prefer b.Loop() over for range b.N. Go 1.24 introduced testing.B.Loop(), which avoids the footgun of forgetting b.ResetTimer() in common patterns. Go 1.26 removed the inlining barrier inside b.Loop bodies, so it is suitable for micro-benchmarks. When you write for b.Loop(), the framework handles timer resets around the loop automatically. Use it for new benchmarks: If you're on an older toolchain or need compatibility, the classic form still works: Run it: Let's read that output: Number of iterations b.N ran. The framework chose this so the total run time is about 1 second — enough for a stable measurement. Time per operation — what you're optimizing. This is wall-clock time divided by b.N. Bytes allocated from the heap per operation. Enabled by -benchmem or b.ReportAllocs(). Your target for this chapter. Number of distinct heap allocation calls per operation. High counts drive GC pressure even if total bytes are small. GOMAXPROCS at time of run. Always include this in comparisons so you know the

heading: b.ReportAllocs() — make the allocations visible
text: Call b.ReportAllocs() at the top of any benchmark to force allocation reporting without needing -benchmem on the command line. Make it a habit: allocation regressions are invisible otherwise.

heading: The optimize-away pitfall — always use a sink
text: The Go compiler is smart enough to eliminate a computation whose result is never used. A benchmark that computes a value and throws it away may be benchmarking nothing . The fix: assign results to a package-level variable ("the sink"): The sink pattern is idiomatic and costs nothing at runtime — the compiler can't optimize across package boundaries.

heading: benchstat — reading before/after with confidence
text: A single benchmark run has noise. benchstat aggregates multiple runs and computes statistical significance: Output: The ± is the variance, p=0.000 means the improvement is statistically significant, and -85.51% is real. That's what a measurement-driven optimization looks like. = 1 second." }, , , ]} caption="The framework auto-tunes the iteration count so measurement noise is small relative to the signal. heading: Escape Analysis & Allocations
text: Here's the thing that separates a senior Go engineer from someone who just writes Go: knowing where your memory lives . On the job: Allocation pressure is the most common source of GC CPU overhead in Go services. Every extra allocation in a hot path means more GC work, more STW pause risk, and more latency tail. Fix the allocation count before reaching for GOGC tuning.

heading: Stack vs. heap — the two places your data can be
text: Every value in a Go program lives on the stack or the heap : Stack : memory owned by a single goroutine. Allocation is extremely cheap, often just a pointer bump. Freed automatically when the function returns. Goroutine stacks start small (about 2 KB in current Go implementations) and grow dynamically up to runtime limits. This is a simplified model; the runtime's actual stack management is more nuanced. Heap : shared memory managed by the GC. Allocation goes through mallocgc, which is lockless via per-P memory caches (mcache/mcentral) but still heavier than a stack bump. Freed asynchronously by the garbage collector — which costs CPU. Stack allocation is orders of magnitude cheaper than heap allocation. The goal of escape analysis is to keep as many values on the stack as possible. Here's an escape happening — one returned pointer turning a free stack slot into GC workload:

heading: go build -gcflags=-m — reading escape analysis output
text: Pass -gcflags=-m (or -gcflags="-m -m" for more detail) to see the compiler's escape decisions: "moved to heap" — the compiler decided this value must outlive its stack frame, so it heap-allocates it. "does not escape" — stays on the stack. This is what you want. "escapes to heap" — same as "moved to heap" but for explicit allocations.

heading: Why values escape
text: Values escape to the heap when the compiler cannot prove they're safe to free when the function returns. Common triggers: If you return &thing, thing must outlive the function — it escapes. Return the value instead when you can. Assigning a concrete value to an interface can force a heap allocation when the compiler cannot keep the boxed value on the stack. The smaller the value, the more this hurts proportionally. A goroutine closure that captures a variable forces that variable to the heap so both the goroutine and the enclosing function can see it. Large local values are more likely to be moved to the heap when the compiler decides stack allocation is not a good fit. Keep large reusable buffers behind pointers or in sync.Pool. Passing a value to fmt.Println or any function that takes any (interface) will escape that value to the heap. In a hot inner loop, this is death by a thousand allocations. Use slog with typed fields, not fmt.Printf, in production hot paths.

heading: Reducing allocations: slice and map preallocation
text: The most common source of unnecessary heap pressure is growing containers from nothing . Every time append outgrows a slice's backing array, it allocates a new one and copies the old contents. The fix is trivially cheap: tell Go the size upfront. Same rule for maps — if you know the approximate size, pass it to make:

heading: sync.Pool — reusing expensive scratch buffers
text: sync.Pool is a per-goroutine (actually per-P) cache of reusable objects. It's the right tool when you're allocating and discarding the same types of short-lived objects in a hot path — think byte buffers, encoder objects, or temporary slices. This is a simplified model of the pool internals; the actual implementation has additional complexity around victim caches and lock-free fast paths. sync.Pool maintains one local pool per P (logical processor in the GMP model — covered in depth in the "The Go Scheduler (GMP), In Depth" chapter). A Get call first checks the local P's pool: no mutex needed, zero contention. Only if the local pool is empty does it fall through to the global shared pool (which does need a lock) and then calls New. This design means that in a server handling many concurrent requests, each goroutine typically gets a buffer from its own P's pool without ever contending with others — O(1) effectively lock-free in the common case. The sharp edge: the GC drains the pool, but a victim cache lets an object survive one extra cycle. Since Go 1.13, each GC moves the pool's live items into a "victim" cache and discards the previous victim cache — so an unused object is droppe

heading: GC Tuning
text: Now let's talk about the engine running underneath everything: Go's garbage collector. On the job: GC tuning is a last resort, not a first instinct. First cut allocations (previous section). Only reach for GOGC/GOMEMLIMIT when profiling confirms GC CPU is a meaningful fraction of your service's budget.

heading: Tri-color mark-sweep — the 90-second version
text: Go's GC uses a concurrent tri-color mark-sweep algorithm. You don't need to memorize the algorithm — you need to understand the two costs it imposes, because that's what you're tuning: 1. CPU cost : the GC runs concurrently with your goroutines, using CPU cycles for marking and scanning. 2. Stop-the-world (STW) pauses : short STW phases still exist around a GC cycle. Go is designed to keep these pauses small, but the exact numbers are workload-dependent. Measure them with gctrace, runtime/metrics, pprof, or the execution tracer. Here is the algorithm itself, run over a real object graph — Meridian request objects, some reachable from the roots, some garbage: Go 1.26: Green Tea GC is the default. Go 1.26 ships Green Tea as the default collector. The release notes describe it as improving marking and scanning performance for small objects through better locality and CPU scalability, with benchmark-dependent reductions in GC overhead. It activates automatically; no configuration change is needed. If you're comparing benchmark numbers across Go versions, note that GC behavior changed in 1.26 and that alone can shift latency p99 figures.

heading: GOGC — the headroom knob
text: GOGC controls when the GC triggers. Its value is a percentage : the next GC fires when the heap has grown by GOGC% since the last collection. Default: GOGC=100 — GC fires when live heap doubles. GOGC=200 — GC fires when live heap triples (less frequent, more memory used). GOGC=off — GC disabled (dangerous; only for benchmarks or batch jobs with bounded memory). The math: if your live heap after last GC is 100 MB, and GOGC=100, the next GC fires at 200 MB. Setting GOGC=200 lets it grow to 300 MB before the collector fires — less CPU spent on GC, but more RSS used.

heading: GOMEMLIMIT — the soft memory limit (Go 1.19+)
text: GOGC is a relative knob. In a container or a Kubernetes pod where you have a hard memory limit, you want the GC to chase an absolute memory target. That's GOMEMLIMIT — a soft limit: the runtime works hard to keep the heap under it (collecting more aggressively as you approach), but the docs are explicit that it "makes no guarantees that it will maintain this memory limit under all circumstances." It is a strong backpressure signal, not a wall: With GOMEMLIMIT set, the GC will aggressively collect to stay under the limit, even if GOGC says it's not time yet. Think of it as: "GOGC controls the comfortable operating zone; GOMEMLIMIT prevents OOM kills." In practice: set GOMEMLIMIT to 90% of your container's memory limit, so the OOM killer doesn't fire before the GC gets a chance to clean up. GC fires at 2× live heap. Good for most services. Start here. Reduce GC frequency for throughput-sensitive services that have RAM headroom. Trades memory for CPU. Soft memory limit for containers — the GC chases it hard but it's not a guaranteed wall. Set to 90% of pod memory limit. Greatly reduces OOM kills. Disables GC. Only for batch programs with fixed inputs or microbenchmarks. Never in a lon

heading: Mechanical Sympathy
text: This is where it gets beautiful. You've cut allocations. You've tuned the GC. Now we go one level deeper — to the hardware your Go binary runs on. On the job: False sharing is a common culprit in concurrent Go services where throughput fails to scale with GOMAXPROCS. The race detector stays silent — it's not a data race — but the hardware contention is just as real. Profile throughput under different GOMAXPROCS values; if adding cores helps less than expected, false sharing is a prime suspect.

heading: CPU caches and cache lines
text: Your CPU has multiple levels of cache (L1, L2, L3). L1 is tiny ( 32 KB) and fast ( 1 ns). DRAM is large and slow ( 100 ns, a 100× difference). The CPU fetches data from RAM in cache lines — fixed 64-byte chunks on every modern x86 and ARM64 processor. When the CPU reads one byte, it loads the entire 64-byte line into cache. This has two profound consequences: 1. Contiguous data is fast. If your data is laid out as a flat slice of structs, the CPU prefetches the next cache line speculatively — you get near-zero memory latency after the first access. If your data is a slice of pointers to structs, each access dereferences the pointer to an arbitrary location in RAM — a cache miss every time. This is why the "Data Semantics & Data-Oriented Design" chapter matters so much: it pays off right here. 2. False sharing is a goroutine performance trap. If two goroutines running on separate CPU cores both read and write variables that live in the same 64-byte cache line , they fight over that cache line. Core A writes → invalidates Core B's copy → Core B reloads from L2/L3 → latency spike. The variable writes don't overlap, so there's no data race — the race detector stays silent. But the cach

heading: Data layout for the hardware
text: The payoff of the "Data Semantics & Data-Oriented Design" chapter is right here. If you designed your structs with access patterns in mind — keeping hot fields together, using flat []T slices instead of [] T — the hardware prefetcher can predict your access pattern and pre-load cache lines before you need them. A practical rule: if you iterate over a slice of structs touching only some fields, consider splitting the struct into two slices (one per field group). This is the "structure of arrays" (SoA) layout, and it's dramatically better for cache utilization in data-heavy loops like Meridian's ledger aggregation. Cache misses from false sharing won't show up in CPU profiles as obviously as CPU-burning functions — they manifest as increased latency and decreased throughput. The best way to detect them is to compare throughput with and without GOMAXPROCS=1: if single-threaded performance is much better proportionally than GOMAXPROCS=8, you likely have sharing issues. The execution tracer (next section) shows the scheduling overhead that false sharing causes. --

heading: The Execution Tracer
text: pprof tells you what is slow. The execution tracer tells you why by recording a precise event log of everything the runtime does — goroutine scheduling, GC pauses, syscalls, network I/O — over time. On the job: Reach for the execution tracer when pprof shows healthy CPU utilization but your latency p99 is still high. Scheduling stalls, GC interference, and goroutine pile-ups are invisible to the CPU profiler but obvious in a trace.

heading: runtime/trace — collecting a trace
text: Or from a benchmark: go tool trace and runtime/trace are the Go runtime execution tracer — a low-level tool for watching the Go runtime itself. It is completely separate from distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin), which tracks requests across service boundaries. We cover distributed tracing in the "Observability: Telemetry & Acting On It" chapter. These are different tools for different problems.

heading: What go tool trace shows you
text: The browser UI at localhost:PORT has several views: Every goroutine's lifetime: when it was created, how long it ran, when it was scheduled off the CPU, what it was waiting for. The critical view for goroutine leaks and scheduler stalls. GC events on a timeline: STW start/end, concurrent mark phases, sweep phases. Lets you see whether GC pauses are contributing to latency spikes. Each logical processor's goroutine scheduling. Are your P's busy? If a P sits idle while goroutines are runnable, you have a scheduling stall — likely a blocking syscall or channel wait without a worker to pick it up. Where goroutines blocked on I/O. Essential for finding whether a DB call or external API is the real bottleneck behind a slow endpoint.

heading: Micro vs. macro framing
text: Before we close, the framing that makes you an actual performance engineer and not just someone who knows the tools: Microbenchmarks (testing.B) measure a single function in isolation. They're excellent for validating that a specific change — preallocation, using sync.Pool, removing an allocation — actually helped. They're terrible for measuring end-to-end latency, because they don't include the actual workload mix, concurrency, or memory pressure of production. Macro profiling (pprof on a real server, execution traces from integration tests) tells you what actually matters in the full system. A function that's 50% of CPU time in a microbenchmark might be 2% of wall time in production because it's dwarfed by database I/O. The workflow is: macro profile first to find the hotspot → microbenchmark to measure the fix → macro profile again to confirm the win carried through . The event names below are illustrative; the actual event schema is internal to the runtime and changes across versions. Treat this as a conceptual map. The execution tracer works by having the runtime emit structured events into an in-memory ring buffer at every significant transition: Goroutine lifecycle: start, s

heading: Profile-Guided Optimization
text: Everything in this chapter so far runs one loop: you measure, you read the profile, you change the code. Profile-guided optimization — PGO — closes a second loop most engineers never touch: the profile goes back into go build, and the compiler changes its decisions. Same source, faster binary. The machine does the work. That's how I like my machines. On the job: PGO is the cheapest real win in Go performance. The Go team measured 2–7% CPU reduction on representative benchmarks when it shipped in Go 1.21, and the devirtualization work in 1.22 pushed some dispatch-heavy workloads past 10%. The price is one committed file and a refresh habit. If your service already exposes net/http/pprof — and after the first section of this chapter, it does — you are one curl away from the input. PGO feeds a CPU profile from a real run back into the compiler, which uses the sample weights to optimize the paths your program actually takes — more aggressive inlining of hot functions, and devirtualization of hot interface calls. go build activates it automatically when a pprof file named default.pgo sits in the main package's directory. Stable since Go 1.21.

heading: Why the compiler guesses without you
text: The compiler's static heuristics are tuned for the average of all Go programs, because at compile time that's all it can know. The inliner has a fixed cost budget per call site — small functions inline, anything past the budget stays a call. Interface method calls go through the itable indirection (the two-word interface header from the Idiomatic Go chapter) unless the compiler can statically prove the concrete type. Sane defaults — but your ledger service is not average. Production says most of its CPU lives in a handful of functions under POST /transfers: decode, validate, balance check. The compiler has no idea. The profile is how you tell it. The history explains the design. Classic PGO — GCC, MSVC, LLVM — demanded an instrumented build : compile a special counting binary, run a synthetic benchmark against it, rebuild using the recorded counts. Two builds, plus a benchmark that has to stay representative of production forever. In practice the benchmark rotted, the second build annoyed everyone, and teams quietly turned the whole thing off. Google's AutoFDO work flipped the model: sample the production binary you already run with an ordinary profiler, and accept slightly fuzzier

heading: Feeding the compiler
text: pgo=off builds without it; -pgo=path/to/profile.pprof overrides the default. The filename convention is deliberate: the profile is a build input , so it belongs in version control, goes through code review, and is recorded in the binary's build metadata — the same provenance discipline as the -ldflags build stamping from the Building & Shipping chapter.

heading: What actually changes: the hot interface call
text: Here's the optimization PGO unlocks that you cannot cleanly write by hand — not without wrecking your interface-based design. Watch the call site: Statically, the compiler usually can't prove which concrete type hides behind Validator at that call site — the value crosses a function boundary and could be anything. So it emits indirect dispatch. Cheap, but it blocks inlining , and inlining is the gateway optimization: once a body is inlined, escape analysis, bounds-check elimination, and constant propagation all get to see through it. With a profile showing one type dominating the site, the compiler emits a guarded devirtualization : The fast path is one type-descriptor comparison, then a direct — now inlinable — call. The slow path still handles the other 0.2% correctly. Your interfaces stay clean; the binary gets concrete-call speed where it counts. This is the "PGO-guided devirtualization" the Idiomatic Go chapter promised when it showed you the itable. desc: slog, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry tracing and correlation IDs — then the consumption side: SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, symptom-based alerting, dashboards, and the on-call/incident-response loop.
text: Let me be direct with you, sport. Most engineers learn to emit telemetry and then stop. They add a log.Println, pat themselves on the back, and go back to writing code that will silently destroy someone's Tuesday at 3 a.m. That's not engineering — that's interior decoration. Observability is a discipline in two acts: emitting signal that means something, and acting on it when something goes wrong. This chapter covers both. By the end, you'll have a ledger service that logs structured JSON with correlation IDs, exports Prometheus metrics for RED/USE method dashboards, and emits OpenTelemetry traces that let you follow a request across three services. Then — the part every other course skips — you'll define what healthy means as a number, build an SLO, understand error budgets, and wire up alerting that pages on the symptom a user feels, not some noisy internal cause. We instrument, we define healthy, we get paged when it isn't. That's the whole game.

heading: Structured logging with slog
text: Here's the scenario. Your ledger service processes fund transfers. A transfer fails at 02:47 UTC and you get paged. You crack open the logs and see: Splendid. Which transfer? Which account? Which user? Which service instance? You have nothing . This is what printf logging looks like in production, and it's the engineering equivalent of leaving a crime scene note that says "something happened." Structured logging is the fix. Instead of a free-form string, you emit a machine-readable record — key/value pairs alongside the message, written as JSON. Every downstream system — log aggregators, alerting rules, dashboards — can filter, group, and index those fields instantly. A log record that carries named fields (key/value attributes) alongside the message, serialised as JSON or another machine-readable format. Without it, a log line is a string only a human can parse; with it, every aggregator, alert rule, and dashboard can filter on level, transfer id, error, or any other field in milliseconds. log/slog (added in Go 1.21) is the standard-library implementation — your default for any Go service from here on. Go 1.21 shipped log/slog as the official structured logging package. It is your

heading: The three-line mental model
text: 1. A Logger emits records. 2. A Handler formats and routes them (JSON to stdout, text to stderr, both, whatever). 3. Every record carries a level , a message , and zero or more attributes (the key/value pairs). Run it and notice the output: each line is a valid JSON object with time, level, msg, and every extra attribute you passed. Copy it into jq and you can filter select(.level == "ERROR") in milliseconds. Do that with a printf string.

heading: Levels
text: slog has four built-in levels, lowest to highest: Debug, Info, Warn, Error. Your handler's minimum level gates what actually gets written. In production you almost always set Info as the floor — Debug is noise at scale.

heading: With — context fields that stick
text: Decorating every log call with "service", "ledger" would be maddening. With creates a child logger that permanently carries extra attributes. Inject it once at startup; every call inherits the fields: The child logger does not copy the parent's attributes on every call — it holds a slice of attr groups and the JSON handler renders them left-to-right. The slog.LogValuer interface, part of log/slog since Go 1.21, lets you defer expensive attribute resolution until the record is actually written. Structured logs are more dangerous than printf logs for one reason: they make it trivially easy to accidentally log a struct that contains a password, a card number, or a social security number. Implement slog.LogValuer on any type that holds sensitive data and return a redacted representation. Define a redact helper and use it at the logging boundary — never patch it after the fact. This connects directly to the Application Security chapter; a log line in an aggregator is just another attack surface.

heading: Text vs. JSON handler
text: NewTextHandler produces key=value pairs — friendlier for humans reading a local terminal, wrong for a production aggregator that ingests JSON. Use text in development, JSON in production. A twelve-factor config flag (LOG FORMAT=json text) makes this switchable at deploy time: slog.Attr values use a Value type that stores the most common kinds (Int64, String, Bool, Float64, Time, Duration) inline as a discriminated union — a kind byte plus a 64-bit slot — with no heap allocation. Only Any (which boxes an arbitrary interface ) allocates. The Record itself preallocates five attr slots inline (a [5]Attr array in the struct); the sixth and beyond spill to a heap slice. In practice, most log calls carry fewer than five attributes and touch zero heap. This is why slog is faster than zap on the hot path for low-attribute records as of Go 1.21. Check go doc log/slog.Value for the internals — the design is a masterclass in the data-oriented principles from Data Semantics & Data-Oriented Design (Part 1). --

heading: Metrics with Prometheus
text: Logs tell you what happened on individual requests. Metrics tell you how the system is doing in aggregate — requests per second, error rate, 99th-percentile latency — across every request for the past hour. You cannot derive those from logs efficiently. You need metrics. Prometheus is the de facto metrics standard for Go services. It works on a pull model: your service exposes a /metrics HTTP endpoint; a Prometheus server scrapes it on a schedule; dashboards and alerting rules query the scraped time-series data.

heading: The three types you actually use
text: A metric is a numeric measurement sampled over time — the aggregate view of what's happening across all requests, not any single one. Three shapes cover almost everything: a counter counts events (total transfers, total errors) and only goes up; a gauge records a current value that can rise or fall (active connections, queue depth); a histogram buckets observations by magnitude so you can derive percentiles (p99 latency). If structured logs are your microscope, metrics are your thermometer — cheap to read at any scale, instant to query. Monotonically increasing. Only goes up. Use for: total requests, total errors, total bytes sent. Never use a counter for a value that can decrease. A value that goes up and down. Use for: active connections, queue depth, goroutine count, memory in use. The current value is what matters. Records observations in configurable buckets and computes percentiles. Use for latency, request sizes. This is the type that powers your p99 SLO. Expensive but essential. High-cardinality labels will destroy your Prometheus. A label with one value per user ID, order ID, or URL path will create millions of time series and OOM your server. Labels must have a bounded, l

heading: RED and USE — what to measure
text: Two mental models tell you which metrics matter: RED (for request-driven services): R ate (requests/sec), E rror rate (errors/sec or error %), D uration (latency percentiles). These are what users experience. Wire all three for every meaningful operation. USE (for resources — CPU, memory, disk, goroutine pool): U tilization (how busy is it?), S aturation (how much backlog is queuing?), E rrors (hard failures). Use this lens on your infrastructure. A prometheus.Histogram with the default 11 buckets (DefBuckets) stores 11 atomic uint64 counters plus a sum and count — one counter per upper boundary. When you call Observe(v), the library walks the bucket boundaries and atomically increments every counter whose boundary is = v. The median and percentile queries in PromQL (histogram quantile) reconstruct an approximation using linear interpolation between buckets. This means your bucket boundaries determine accuracy — if all your transfers take 50–100ms but your buckets jump from 0.025s to 0.1s, the p99 estimate is coarse. Choose buckets that match your actual latency distribution. prometheus.LinearBuckets and prometheus.ExponentialBuckets help. The Prometheus Go client increments the bu

heading: expvar: zero-dependency metrics
text: Before you reach for a third-party client, know that the standard library already ships a metrics endpoint. The expvar package publishes application variables — plus a free dump of runtime.MemStats, the goroutine count, and your command line — as JSON on /debug/vars. Zero dependencies, three lines of wiring. For a small internal ledger tool, or for "is this thing even alive and how much memory is it eating," that's often all the visibility you need. expvar is the standard library's built-in metrics exporter. Calling expvar.NewInt("name") registers a concurrency-safe counter; expvar.Publish("name", expvar.Func(fn)) wires a live function (re-evaluated on every read) into the output. Mounting expvar.Handler() on GET /debug/vars serves every registered variable — alongside memstats and cmdline, which it exposes for free — as a single JSON object. No client library, no scrape config, no allocation on the hot path beyond an atomic add. So when do you pick which? expvar is built-in, instant, and perfect for quick visibility on a small service or a debugging session. Prometheus is still the production standard — it gives you the pull model with a real time-series database behind it, dimens

heading: Distributed Tracing with OpenTelemetry
text: What a trace actually is — one request, one trace ID, a span born at every hop: Logs and metrics answer "what happened" and "how much." Tracing answers "what path did this request take, and where did the time go?" In a system with three or more services, a single user action touches multiple processes — and when the latency on one request spikes, you need to know which span on which service is to blame.

heading: Vocabulary: spans, traces, and context propagation
text: A distributed trace is the end-to-end record of one request as it crosses multiple services. It is made of spans — each span is one unit of work (an HTTP handler, a DB query, a gRPC call) with a start time, end time, status, and attributes. Every span shares a trace ID (a 128-bit value that identifies the whole request) and carries its own span ID plus the span ID of its parent, forming a call tree. When latency spikes, the trace waterfall shows you exactly which span on which service is slow — information that logs and metrics alone cannot give you. A trace is the end-to-end story of one request, from the user's HTTP call to the final database write. A span is one unit of work within that trace — an HTTP handler, a database query, a gRPC call. Each span has a start time, end time, status, and arbitrary attributes. Every span carries a trace ID (identifies the whole trace) and a span ID (identifies this specific span). A child span records its parent's span ID, forming a tree. Context propagation is how the trace IDs travel across service boundaries — embedded in HTTP headers (the W3C traceparent standard) so a downstream service can attach its spans to the same trace. Go's context

heading: A traced request crossing three services
text: Here's the real scenario: a client calls the API gateway , which calls the ledger service , which calls the accounts service . All three emit spans to the same trace.

heading: Correlation IDs: tying logs + traces + metrics together
text: A correlation ID (also called a request ID or trace ID) is a single identifier threaded through every log line, trace span, and metric label for one request. Without it, a log error and its trace are two unrelated needles in a haystack. With it, grep correlation id=abc123 instantly surfaces every log line, the trace waterfall, and the exact metric observations for that request — even across three services. In practice, the OpenTelemetry trace ID is your correlation ID when OTel is wired; without OTel, a UUID injected in the outermost middleware and carried through context.Context does the same job. A correlation ID (also called a request ID or trace ID in many systems) is the key that lets you join a log line to the trace to the metric observation for the same request. In practice, the OTel trace ID is your correlation ID — you inject it into every log record at the handler level. Here's the idiomatic pattern for wiring them together in a single HTTP server: If you're not ready for full OTel, generate a UUID in your outermost middleware, store it in the request context with a typed key (never a plain string), and thread it into every slog.With call. That single ID lets you grep eve

heading: The Consumption Side
text: You've emitted the signal. Now what? This is the section most observability courses quietly omit, which is extraordinary because it's the half that actually keeps users happy.

heading: SLIs — what to measure
text: An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a metric that measures something a user actually notices — request success rate, latency percentile, error rate. An SLO (Service Level Objective) is the numeric target you commit to for an SLI: "99.9% of transfers succeed, measured over a 28-day window." The SLO is the contract — between your team and your users, and between reliability work and feature work. Without an SLO you cannot answer "is this broken?" — you can only answer "is this different?" The difference matters enormously at 3 a.m. An SLI (Service Level Indicator) is a quantitative measure of service quality. Not every metric is an SLI — an SLI specifically measures something a user notices . The canonical SLI set for a request-driven API: Availability : fraction of requests that succeeded (HTTP 2xx / total requests). Latency : fraction of requests faster than a threshold (e.g. p99 < 200ms). Error rate : fraction of requests that returned a server error (5xx). Throughput : requests processed per second. An SLI is not CPU utilization. A user does not experience CPU utilization. A user experiences a slow or failed request. Design your SLIs around the user's experience, not the machine'

heading: SLOs — the target
text: An SLO (Service Level Objective) puts a number on your SLI: "99.9% of requests succeed" or "99% of requests respond in under 200ms, measured over a 30-day rolling window." This is a commitment — to your users, your on-call team, and your business. For the ledger service: SLO: 99.9% of POST /transfers respond in < 500ms, measured over a 28-day window. That single sentence is worth more than a hundred dashboards without one, because now everyone agrees on what "broken" means.

heading: Error budgets — what burning one means
text: An error budget is the inverse of your SLO target — the fraction of requests that are allowed to fail or be slow. A 99.9% availability SLO means a 0.1% error budget: over 28 days of 10 million requests, that's 10,000 failures permitted. The budget is a shared resource owned jointly by product and engineering. While budget remains, shipping new features is allowed — risk is acceptable. When the budget hits zero, all hands pivot to reliability. This is not a cultural norm; it is a mechanical forcing function. It prevents "it's probably fine" from becoming "we're down on Friday." An error budget is the flip side of an SLO. If your SLO is 99.9% success, your error budget is 0.1% — the fraction of requests that are allowed to fail . Over a 28-day window of 10 million requests, your budget is 10,000 failing requests. Once you've spent your error budget, you stop shipping new features and focus entirely on reliability. This is not optional — it is the mechanism that prevents the engineering team from treating "always on" as someone else's problem. A burn-rate alert fires when your service is consuming its error budget faster than it can afford to . A burn rate of 1x means you'll exhaust t

heading: Alerting on symptoms, not causes
text: The single biggest source of alert fatigue is alerting on causes — internal metrics that may or may not matter to a user. CPU at 80%? The service might be perfectly fast. Disk iops elevated? Who cares if latency is fine? Page on what users feel. Investigate causes from there. The table: Alert type Example Problem --- --- --- Symptom (correct) p99 latency 500ms for 5 min Users are experiencing it right now Symptom (correct) Error rate 1% for 5 min Users are getting errors right now Cause (noisy) CPU 80% May not affect users at all Cause (noisy) DB connections 50 Not a user-visible metric The burn-rate model from the timeline above is the gold standard — it converts a slow SLO degradation (a problem that's real but not yet catastrophic) into a page that fires early with the right urgency.

heading: Dashboards that answer "is it broken and why"
text: A good dashboard has three layers: 1. The answer layer (top): Is the service healthy? The RED metrics — one number each — with a traffic-light color. Anyone can read it in five seconds. 2. The where layer (middle): Which component is degraded? Latency breakdown by endpoint. Error rate by error type. These narrow the blast radius. 3. The why layer (bottom): Linked traces for slow/errored requests. The slog JSON stream filtered to errors. This is where you go once you know where . A dashboard that shows 40 graphs and no traffic lights is not observability — it's data hoarding. If you can't answer "is it broken?" in under 10 seconds without knowing where to look, the dashboard has failed.

heading: The on-call / incident-response loop
text: Incidents follow a predictable arc. Running it well is a learnable skill. 1. Triage — Is this real? Is it user-impacting? What is the blast radius? Check the SLO dashboard first — it gives you the scope immediately. Declare an incident early rather than late. 2. Mitigation — Make the pain stop. This is not the time to find the root cause. Roll back the deploy. Scale up the replicas. Toggle the feature flag. Restore service; investigate afterward. 3. Root cause analysis + blameless postmortem — After service is restored, write a postmortem. The "blameless" part is not optional — if you blame a person, you learn nothing about the system that allowed the failure. A good postmortem has: timeline, impact, what went well, what went wrong, and concrete action items with owners and due dates. The action items are the feedback loop that makes the system more resilient over time. Every incident is a free lesson the system paid for. A blameless postmortem converts that payment into a documented weakness and a concrete fix. Teams that skip postmortems replay the same incidents. Teams that write good ones raise their SLO floor systematically. The ledger service we've been instrumenting all chap
