desc: What actually happens on disk when a database stores your data — explained from zero: the append-only log and the index trade-off, log-structured (LSM) engines with memtables, SSTables, compaction and Bloom filters, B-trees with pages, splits and the write-ahead log, how to choose between them (write amplification, sequential vs random writes), and why analytics uses column storage — all grounded in Meridian's ledger.
text: You've kept copies (replication) and split the data (sharding). Now we go down one more level — inside a single shard — to the thing that actually puts bytes on disk and finds them again: the storage engine . You will never write one from scratch. But you choose one every time you pick Postgres over Cassandra, or turn on a RocksDB backend, or wonder why your write-heavy table is slow — and those choices are unguessable until you know what the engine is doing under the hood. I'll teach this from absolute zero — no assumed knowledge of disks, trees, or indexes. We'll build the world's simplest database in a few lines, watch it fall over, and fix it twice, two completely different ways: the log-structured (LSM) way that powers Cassandra and RocksDB, and the B-tree way that powers Postgres and MySQL. By the end you'll know exactly why Meridian's transaction firehose loves one engine and its balance lookups love the other, what "write amplification" is and why it wears out your SSD, and why the finance dashboard stores the same data sideways. Let's go.

heading: The Index Trade-off
text: A database does exactly two things: you give it data, it stores it; you ask for data, it gives it back. Here's the entire thing, as simple as it can possibly be — an append-only log : Two ideas in those few lines carry the whole chapter: A log here is not application log output — it's an append-only sequence of records on disk . Writes only ever go on the end ; existing bytes are never modified. Why it matters: appending is the single fastest write a disk can do (no seeking, no rewriting), so almost every storage engine has a log at its core. The cost: old versions pile up, and finding a key means knowing where it is. An index is an extra structure derived from your data that makes reads faster — like the in-memory hash map above (key → byte offset). Why it matters: without an index, finding a key means scanning the whole file, O(n) — double the data, double the wait. With one, it's a direct jump. But every index must be updated on every write , so indexes speed up reads and slow down writes . That trade-off — pay on writes to save on reads — is the central tension of all storage engines, and why databases don't index every column by default. Our append-log-plus-hash-index is fast,

heading: LSM-Trees
text: The first fix keeps the append-only spirit but makes the on-disk files sorted . A sorted file of key-value pairs is called an SSTable , and the engine built around them is the LSM-tree (Log-Structured Merge-tree) — the heart of Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB, HBase, and Bigtable. An SSTable (Sorted String Table) is an on-disk file of key-value pairs sorted by key , with each key appearing once. A memtable is an in-memory sorted structure (a balanced tree or skip list) that buffers recent writes. Why it matters: sorting unlocks cheap range scans and lets two files be merged with a memory-light mergesort. Writes go to the fast memtable; when it's full, it's flushed to disk as a new immutable SSTable. You get log-speed writes and sorted files. Here is the write path. Notice every write is durable before it's acknowledged, via a separate write-ahead log: Reads are trickier: a key might be in the memtable, or the newest SSTable, or an older one. You check newest to oldest and stop at the first hit (newer overrides older). Deletes are just another write — a special tombstone marker. And to avoid touching every SSTable for keys that aren't there, each SSTable carries a Bloom filter (its own

heading: B-Trees
text: The other family throws out the log entirely. Instead of immutable sorted files, a B-tree divides the disk into fixed-size pages (typically 4–16 KiB) and updates them in place . It's the most widespread index structure on earth — every major relational database (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle) uses one. A B-tree stores sorted key-value pairs in fixed-size pages arranged as a balanced tree. One page is the root ; it holds keys and references to child pages, each child covering a key range, down to leaf pages holding the actual values. (Databases almost always use the B+tree variant: only the leaf pages hold values, internal pages hold keys purely for navigation, and the leaves are linked for fast range scans. We say "B-tree" loosely here; the on-disk reality is a B+tree.) The branching factor (references per page, often several hundred) keeps the tree shallow — three or four levels can address hundreds of terabytes. Why it matters: a lookup reads just one page per level (≈3–4 disk reads), giving fast, predictable read performance — the B-tree's headline strength. A lookup walks the tree from the root, following the one child whose range contains your key: A B-tree's basic write

heading: LSM vs B-Tree
text: Now the decision you'll actually make. The one-line rule: LSM-trees are better for writes, B-trees are better (and more predictable) for reads. Here's why , in the four dimensions that matter. LSM flushes whole segments — big sequential writes. B-trees overwrite scattered pages — small random writes. Disks (even SSDs) do sequential far faster, so LSMs sustain higher write throughput on the same hardware. One logical write becomes several physical writes: LSM (WAL + flush + each compaction), B-tree (WAL + the full page, even for a few changed bytes). Lower amplification = more app writes per unit of disk bandwidth, and less SSD wear. LSMs usually win here. B-tree: one page per level, 3–4 reads, predictable . LSM: may check several SSTables (Bloom filters help), so reads are less predictable and range queries must merge segments. B-trees generally read faster. LSM compresses SSTables well and rewrites them, so less fragmentation — but compaction competes with live traffic and can cause latency spikes under heavy writes. B-trees fragment over time (Postgres needs VACUUM). Write amplification is the ratio of bytes actually written to disk versus the bytes the application asked to write

heading: Bloom Filters
text: An LSM read may have to check many SSTables — and most of them won't contain your key. Reading each one to discover that is wasteful. A Bloom filter is a tiny, fast, probabilistic gate that says "definitely not here" or "maybe here," letting you skip most SSTables without touching them. A Bloom filter is a bit array plus a few hash functions that answers "is this key in this set?" with no false negatives (a "no" is always correct) but occasional false positives (a "maybe" might be wrong). To add a key, hash it to several bit positions and set them to 1; to test a key, check those bits — if any is 0, it's definitely absent. Why it matters: a few bits per key (≈10 bits → 1% false positives) lets an LSM skip SSTables that can't contain the key, turning many disk reads into one cheap in-memory check. The whole thing is just bit-setting and bitwise checks — watch it run: The magic is the asymmetry: a "no" is guaranteed , so it's always safe to skip. A "yes" might be a coincidence (other keys set those same bits), so you then do the real lookup — and on a false positive you've only wasted a little work. heading: Row vs Column
text: One last twist, and it's about layout . Everything so far stored a whole record together — fine for "fetch account 7." But Meridian's finance dashboard asks different questions: "sum the amount of every settled transaction this quarter." That scans millions of rows but needs one column . Storing rows together makes you read everything to get a little. Row-oriented storage keeps all of a row's fields next to each other (great for "give me this whole record" — OLTP). Column-oriented (columnar) storage keeps all values of one column together across rows (great for "aggregate this one field over millions of rows" — OLAP/analytics). Why it matters: an analytics query touching 3 of 100 columns reads only those 3 columns off disk in a column store, instead of dragging every full row through memory. Columnar storage also compresses far better, because a single column's values repeat. It's why warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, DuckDB, Parquet) are columnar. The bytes-read difference is stark — one aggregate query, same data, two layouts: Don't think "row store good, column store bad" or vice versa. It's the OLTP/OLAP split you met at the start of Part 2, made physical. Meridian's operational

heading: Exercises
text: Build the engine internals. Each is a real storage-engine mechanism in miniature. Implement set(key, val) and get(key) over an append-only log []string plus an index map[string]int. Updating a key appends a new value and repoints the index. Why does get stay fast even though old values are never erased? get is fast because the index always points at the latest position for a key, so a lookup is a single hash-map hit plus one indexed read — O(1). The stale old values still sitting in the log are never visited; they only cost disk space , not read time. Reclaiming that space is exactly what compaction does. desc: Everything that goes wrong once data lives on more than one machine — explained from zero: partial failure and why it's nondeterministic, unreliable networks (a timeout tells you almost nothing), unreliable clocks (time-of-day vs monotonic, NTP drift, why timestamps lie), process pauses that freeze a node mid-function, fencing tokens to stop zombie leaders corrupting data, and why a node must trust a majority quorum over its own judgment — grounded in Meridian paying a bank over a flaky network.
text: Everything you've built across this track — replicas, shards, storage engines — quietly assumed the machines mostly behave . They don't. Once your data lives on more than one computer connected by a network, you inherit a whole zoo of failures that simply cannot happen on a single machine: a request that vanishes without a trace, a clock that lies to your face, a process that freezes for thirty seconds in the middle of a function and wakes up thinking no time passed. This is the chapter where we turn the pessimism up to maximum and look the danger dead in the eye. I'll teach it from absolute zero — no assumed knowledge of networks, clocks, or operating systems. By the end you'll understand why, when Meridian asks a bank "did that payment go through?" and gets silence, the honest answer is "we cannot know," and why that single fact reshapes how you build payment systems. You'll see how two servers can both believe they're the leader and corrupt the ledger, and the beautiful little counter — the fencing token — that stops them. The good news at the end: from these unreliable parts, we can build reliable systems. But first you have to respect what's actually going wrong. Let's go.

heading: Partial Failure
text: On a single machine, software is mostly deterministic: it works or it crashes. A hardware fault usually takes the whole machine down — a kernel panic, a blue screen — because computers are deliberately designed to fail completely rather than return wrong answers. One machine is either fully working or fully dead. Comforting. The moment you add a network, that comfort is gone. A partial failure is when some parts of a distributed system are broken while others work perfectly — and crucially, it's nondeterministic : the same operation across the network may succeed, fail, or hang, unpredictably, from one moment to the next. Why it matters: you can no longer reason "it works or it doesn't." You might issue a request and never find out whether it succeeded . That uncertainty — not raw failure — is what makes distributed systems hard, and it's the root of nearly every bug in this chapter. The tempting path is to code the happy path and treat faults as rare edge cases. In a large enough system, that's fatal — "one in a million" happens every day when you have millions of operations. The professional reframe: assume the network will drop, delay, and reorder your messages; assume nodes wil

heading: Unreliable Networks
text: Meridian pays a partner bank $10,000 over the network. The call times out. Four completely different realities produce that identical timeout: The networks Meridian runs on — the internet, datacenter Ethernet — are asynchronous packet networks . One node sends a packet to another; the network promises nothing about whether or when it arrives. Send a request expecting a reply, and a depressing number of things can go wrong, all of which look the same to you. You might think TCP — with its retransmission, ordering, and checksums — makes the network reliable. It doesn't, for your purposes. TCP retransmits lost packets, but if the cable is unplugged it can't plug it back in; after a timeout it gives up and errors. And a TCP acknowledgement only means the remote kernel received the bytes — the application may have crashed before handling them. If you want to know a request succeeded, you need a positive response from the application itself , not from the transport. TCP solves "big messages over packets," not "did my operation happen." The only tool you have is a timeout — wait a while, then give up. But a timeout is a guess, and choosing its length is a genuine dilemma with no correct a

heading: Unreliable Clocks
text: Surely the clock is dependable? It is not. Each machine has its own quartz oscillator that drifts (runs fast or slow with temperature), nudged back toward reality by NTP (the Network Time Protocol) — which is itself only as accurate as the flaky network it syncs over. And there are two different clocks , for two different jobs, that beginners constantly confuse: A time-of-day (wall) clock returns calendar time (e.g. "2026-06-05 14:03:21 UTC"). It's synced by NTP and can jump backward (when NTP corrects drift) or skip (leap seconds, DST). A monotonic clock only ever moves forward at a steady rate; its absolute value is meaningless (nanoseconds since boot) but the difference between two readings is a trustworthy elapsed duration. Why it matters: use the wall clock for " when did this happen" (timestamps, expiry dates) and the monotonic clock for " how long did this take" (timeouts, response times). Measuring a duration with the wall clock is a classic bug — an NTP correction mid-measurement can make time appear to run backward. This connects straight back to the replication chapter. Remember last-writer-wins resolving conflicts by keeping the higher timestamp? Now watch what unreliab

heading: Process Pauses
text: Here's the failure that breaks the most "obviously correct" code. A running process can be frozen — mid-function, between any two lines — for an arbitrary length of time, without noticing . While it's frozen, the rest of the world moves on and may declare it dead. Causes are everywhere: a garbage-collection stop-the-world pause, a VM suspended for live migration, the OS swapping a page in from disk, the scheduler context-switching it out, even a stray SIGSTOP. Why is that catastrophic? Consider a leader that holds a lease (a lock with a timeout) so only it may write Meridian's settlement file: The deep lesson: the single-machine tools you know — mutexes, atomic counters — assume threads share memory and a common clock. None of that holds across machines. A distributed node must assume it can be paused at any instant and that the world will have moved on when it wakes. So you can't prevent zombies; you have to make sure they can't do damage. Which brings us to the fix.

heading: Fencing Tokens
text: A node that's been paused or partitioned but still thinks it holds the lease is a zombie . You can't always shut a zombie down in time (its delayed write might already be in flight). Instead you fence it: make the storage itself reject anything from a stale leaseholder. A fencing token is a number the lock/lease service returns with every grant, and it increases every time a lease is handed out. Every write to the protected resource must include the writer's token, and the storage service remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any write with a lower one . Why it matters: when a zombie wakes up and writes with its old token, the storage has already seen a higher token from the new leaseholder — so the zombie's write is refused, automatically, with no need to detect the zombie or trust any clock. (Same idea as Raft's term number , Paxos's ballot , Kafka's epoch .) Watch it reject a zombie: The elegance: the storage service needs no idea who is a zombie and no working clock. It just enforces "tokens only go up." A leaseholder writes immediately on acquiring the lease, and from that moment every older holder is permanently fenced. (If your storage supports an atomic compar

heading: Truth & Quorums
text: Step back to the disorienting core: a node can know nothing for certain about other nodes — only guess from messages it does or doesn't receive. And it can't even fully trust itself (it might be a paused zombie). So distributed systems stop relying on any single node's judgment and instead take a vote . A majority quorum is a decision that requires agreement from more than half the nodes. Why it matters: there can only ever be one majority at a time, so two conflicting decisions can't both win — that's what makes it safe . And it removes dependence on any single node: a majority can declare a node dead and that node must step down , even if it feels perfectly alive (it might be a zombie). With 3 nodes you tolerate 1 failure; with 5, you tolerate 2. This voting is the seed of consensus — the entire next chapter. Everything here assumes nodes are unreliable but honest — they may be slow, paused, or stale, but if they answer, they're telling the truth as they know it. A node that lies — sends arbitrary or malicious messages, casts contradictory votes — is a Byzantine fault , and tolerating it (the Byzantine Generals Problem ) is far more expensive. You need it for aerospace (radiation

heading: Exercises
text: Each exercise is a real defense against a real distributed-systems failure. Write knownOutcome(gotResponse bool) string returning what you actually know about whether a remote operation succeeded. For gotResponse == false, list the indistinguishable cases. Why does this push you toward idempotent operations? A positive application response is the only thing that confirms success. A timeout collapses three very different realities — never sent, never processed, or fully processed with a lost reply — into one indistinguishable signal. Because you can't tell "did nothing" from "did everything," the only safe design is to make the operation idempotent : safe to retry, because if it already happened, doing it "again" is a no-op. That's why payment APIs use idempotency keys. desc: How unreliable machines agree on a single truth — explained from zero: linearizability (the illusion of one always-fresh copy) and why it's a recency guarantee, when you actually need it (leader election, uniqueness, no double-spend), the cost (the CAP trade-off, CP vs AP), logical clocks (Lamport, hybrid) for causal ordering, and consensus itself — agreeing on one value, total order broadcast, Raft, and the majority that makes it safe — grounded in keeping Meridian's ledger correct.
text: Last chapter we turned the pessimism to maximum: networks vanish messages, clocks lie, processes freeze, and a node can't trust its own judgment. This chapter is the payoff — how you build something correct on top of all that chaos. How a pile of unreliable, paranoid machines can be made to agree on a single, fault-tolerant truth: who the leader is, what the balance is, which write came first. I'll teach it from absolute zero — no assumed knowledge of consistency models, clocks, or consensus algorithms. We'll start with the strongest promise a distributed system can make — linearizability , "behave as if there's just one always-up-to-date copy" — see exactly when Meridian needs it (and the surprising price it charges, every single read). Then we'll meet logical clocks that order events without trusting quartz, and finally consensus itself: the one hard problem that locks, leaders, uniqueness, and atomic commit all secretly reduce to — and which Raft and etcd solve with nothing more exotic than a majority vote. This is the summit of the distributed-data track. From chaos, order. Let's go.

heading: Linearizability
text: Replication gives you many copies, which means the copies can disagree (the stale read above). The strongest cure is a guarantee that makes all those copies look like one . Linearizability (also "strong" or "atomic" consistency) makes a replicated system behave as if there were a single copy of the data and every operation on it were instantaneous . Concretely it's a recency guarantee : the moment a write completes, every subsequent read — on any client, any replica — must return that value (or a newer one), never an older one. Why it matters: with linearizability the application stops worrying about replicas, lag, and conflicts entirely; it can pretend there's one perfect database. That simplicity is powerful — and, as we'll see, expensive. The precise rule is about ordering in real time : once any read has observed the new value, every later read must observe it too. There's an imaginary instant where the value atomically flips, and nothing may read "backward" across it: 0 (before flip)", note: "A reads early, before the flip. Returning the old 0 is fine — the write hadn't taken effect yet." }, , ]} caption="That last constraint is the whole game: once anyone sees the new value,

heading: When You Need It
text: Linearizability is expensive, so you spend it deliberately — only where stale reads cause real harm. There are a few places that genuinely require it, and Meridian hits all of them. A single-leader system must have exactly one leader (no split-brain). Electing one via a lease requires linearizability — two nodes must never both "win." This is the fencing/zombie problem from last chapter, and it's why coordination services exist. A unique username, one account per email, a balance that never goes negative , no double-booked seat — each needs a single up-to-date value all nodes agree on, checked atomically (like a compare-and-set). Without linearizability, two concurrent requests both "succeed." Two paths carry related info (a file write + a "process it" queue message). If the storage isn't linearizable, the message can outrun the data, and the consumer reads a stale or missing file. Recency closes the race. The "no negative balance" case is the one that should make a fintech engineer sit up: it's exactly an atomic compare-and-set on a single agreed value. Two withdrawals racing on the last ₦5,000 must not both see ₦5,000 and both succeed — that invents money. Only a linearizable che

heading: The Cost (CAP)
text: Here's the price. Suppose the network partitions — replicas split into two groups that can't reach each other (last chapter's netsplit). What does a linearizable system do? During a network partition , a replicated system must choose: stay linearizable by refusing requests on replicas that can't reach the leader/majority (it becomes unavailable there — " CP "), or stay available by letting every replica serve independently (giving up linearizability — " AP "). Why it matters: you can't have perfect consistency and availability when the network is split — that's the kernel of the (much-abused) CAP theorem . Note partitions aren't something you choose ; they happen. You only choose what to do when one does. And linearizable systems pay a latency tax all the time , not just during faults. Partitions aren't optional — the only way to "avoid" them is to have a single mac

heading: Logical Clocks
text: We need to order events across machines — "did the account go private before or after the photo upload?" Last chapter killed the obvious idea: wall-clock timestamps lie (drift, skew, jumps), so a causally-later event can get an earlier timestamp. The fix is a clock made of counting , not quartz. A logical clock is an algorithm that counts events rather than measuring time. A Lamport timestamp is a pair (counter, nodeID): each node increments its counter on every event, and whenever it sees a higher counter from another node, it jumps its own up to match before continuing. Why it matters: this guarantees that if event A happened-before B (A influenced B), then A's timestamp is less than B's — a total order consistent with causality , with no reliance on synchronized hardware clocks. Ties (same counter) break by nodeID, so every timestamp is unique. Watch causality survive without any real clock — Bryce's reply must out-number the message it answers: Lamport clocks give a total order but not linearizability — they order events that already happened, but can't guarantee a value is currently up to date. They also can't tell concurrency apart from ordering (for that you need vector cloc

heading: Consensus
text: Now the summit. Look back at the hard problems: electing one leader, a fault-tolerant atomic CAS, a fault-tolerant ID counter, agreeing to commit a multi-shard transaction. They look different. They are the same problem . Consensus is getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value , with four properties: agreement (no two nodes decide differently), integrity (no node changes its decision), validity (the decided value was actually proposed), and termination (every non-crashed node eventually decides). Why it matters: the first three are safety (always hold, even in a total outage); termination is liveness and requires a majority of nodes alive. Get consensus and you get leader election, locks, uniqueness, atomic commit, and a replicated log — all of them — because they're provably equivalent . The most useful packaging of consensus is a shared, append-only log — also called total order broadcast : every node sees the same entries in the same order. That single primitive gives you state machine replication (apply the same writes in the same order → identical replicas), which is how leader-based replication, event sourcing, and serializable transactions are all built. And the equiv

heading: Coordination in Practice
text: You will almost never implement Raft yourself. Instead you'll use a coordination service — ZooKeeper or etcd — a small, linearizable, consensus-backed store built for exactly the high-stakes, low-volume metadata that must never disagree. Two hard-won rules. First, never implement consensus yourself — it is infamous for looking correct and silently corrupting data on the unlucky fault ordering. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, or a database that embeds Raft (CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB). Second, consensus is expensive, so keep it small : don't run every write through Raft. Put only the metadata that must agree — who's the leader, the shard→node map, distributed locks, config — in the coordination service, and let it hand out leases and fencing tokens to the fast path. Meridian runs its high-volume ledger writes on a single-leader Postgres, and uses etcd only to elect that leader and guard the lease. Agreement where you must; speed everywhere else.

desc: Integer minor units vs decimal libraries, currency types, rounding modes and where they're legally defined, and multi-currency handling.
text: Listen up, sport. We're in Part 3 now — Fintech. The stakes are real money. Real accounts. Real regulators who will not accept "well, it was a floating-point rounding error" as an excuse. I've watched engineers make this mistake exactly once. The second time doesn't happen, because there is no second time. Here's the rule. Write it on your monitor. Tattoo it somewhere tasteful. Money is never a float. Not float32. Not float64. Not ever. By the end of this chapter you'll know why in the bones, you'll have the right types to replace it, and you'll be able to split a payment across three payees without losing a single cent. I'll be watching.

heading: Why Floats Are a Crime
text: Let me set the scene before we touch a single type. Meridian processes ten million transactions a day. A float64 fee calculation silently eats fractions of a cent on each one. Three months later the finance team finds a $47,000 discrepancy in the monthly reconciliation. No fraud — just math. That is not a hypothetical. That is Tuesday. On the job: Every time you see money stored as float64 in a production codebase, a reconciliation job downstream is producing wrong numbers. The error is invisible until the books don't close. IEEE-754 is the international standard for binary floating-point arithmetic — the spec your CPU's FPU implements when you write float64. It represents numbers as sign × mantissa × 2^exponent. Because the exponent is a power of 2 , the only fractions representable exactly are those of the form N / 2^k — halves, quarters, eighths. Decimal fractions like 0.1 (= 1/10) have no exact binary representation and are silently rounded to the nearest 52-bit value. For scientific computation this rounding is fine and expected. For money, where every cent must be exact, it is a defect at the hardware level. The fix is not to avoid IEEE-754 — it's to stop using it for money a

heading: The Binary Representation Problem
text: Here is the crime, rendered plain: Run it. Watch the output. That extra 0.00000000000000004 is not a display glitch — it's the actual value stored in memory. Now multiply that error across millions of transactions and compound it through fee calculations, interest accruals, and FX conversions. Your books will never reconcile. float64 is a 64-bit value split into three fields: 1 sign bit , 11 exponent bits , 52 mantissa (significand) bits . The value is (-1)^sign × 1.mantissa × 2^(exponent-1023). The exponent and mantissa are both binary — powers of 2. So the only fractions a float64 can represent exactly are those expressible as N / 2^k for some integers N and k: halves, quarters, eighths, and so on. 0.1 in decimal is 1/10. To express 1/10 in binary you need to divide by 10, but 10 = 2 × 5, and 5 has no power-of-two factorization . So 1/10 becomes a repeating binary fraction — like 1/3 in decimal. The CPU truncates it to 52 mantissa bits and rounds. What you get is: That's the actual value your variable holds when you write x := 0.1. It's close — but for financial math, "close" is a crime. Go 1.26 follows IEEE-754-2008 for float64; the spec makes no apology: exact decimal arithmeti

heading: Integer Minor Units
text: Before the type definitions — the difference between float books and integer books, posted side by side: The fix is elegant and has been industry standard since before most of us were born: store money as an integer count of the smallest unit your currency supports . For USD, that's cents: $14.99 → 1499. For JPY (no minor unit), ¥1400 → 1400. For KWD (Kuwaiti Dinar, three decimal places), 1.500 KWD → 1500. Integer arithmetic is exact — no rounding, no drift, no surprises. On the job: Meridian's ledger stores every Transfer amount as int64 minor units alongside a three-letter ISO 4217 currency code. Passing a bare float64 dollars value to a ledger function is a compile-time type error. That's intentional. The minor unit of a currency is its smallest indivisible subdivision: the cent for USD (1/100 of a dollar), the yen for JPY (JPY has no minor unit — ¥1 is the smallest unit), the fil for KWD (1/1000 of a dinar). Storing money as an integer count of minor units means $14.99 is stored as 1499 (an int64), not 14.99 (a float64). Because integers have no fractional part, every addition and subtraction is mathematically exact — no IEEE-754 rounding path is involved. This is the foundatio

heading: The Money Type
text: Here is the correct foundation for every financial amount in Meridian's service: int64 holds values from −9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to +9,223,372,036,854,775,807. In USD cents, that's roughly ±92 quadrillion dollars (9.2 quintillion cents ÷ 100). If Meridian's ledger holds more than $92 quadrillion in a single entry, the data type is the least of your problems.

heading: Arithmetic is Exact
text: int64 range is enormous, but it is not infinite. The full int64 range in cents tops out around $92 quadrillion, so only an absurd aggregate could overflow it. In practice, each individual ledger entry is nowhere near that limit. If a single row in Meridian's ledger table holds more than $92 quadrillion, that row is the least of your problems. Use int64 — it's the right tool. For interest accrual or fee calculations that produce fractional cents , you temporarily need more precision. That's what the next section is for.

heading: Decimal Libraries
text: Integer cents are perfect for storing and adding amounts. But some calculations genuinely need more precision: Interest: 7.5% annual rate on a balance, accrued daily → fractional cents at each step FX conversion: 1 USD = 0.9241 EUR → the converted amount has sub-cent precision before you round to storage Tax: some jurisdictions compute to three decimal places before rounding For these cases, you need a decimal arithmetic library — not floats, a library built specifically for base-10 exact arithmetic. On the job: In Meridian's interest accrual job, every daily calculation goes through shopspring/decimal (or math/big.Rat in the stdlib version). The result is rounded explicitly to whole cents before being written to the ledger. There is never a stage where a fractional cent lives in an int64 — it lives in the decimal type until the moment it's rounded. A decimal library performs arithmetic in base 10 rather than base 2. shopspring/decimal represents a number as a big.Int mantissa plus an integer scale (number of decimal places), so 0.1 is stored as 1 × 10^-1 — exactly. math/big.Rat from the standard library stores a fraction as a numerator and denominator big.Int pair, so 1/10 is stor

heading: shopspring/decimal
text: The community standard for Go decimal arithmetic. Internally it represents a number as a big.Int mantissa plus a scale (number of decimal places). All arithmetic is exact up to any precision you specify.

heading: math/big.Int and math/big.Rat
text: The standard library's arbitrary-precision integers and rationals. No external dependency. Slower than shopspring/decimal for typical use (more allocations, no caching), but zero-dependency and sufficient for many cases. As of Go 1.26, math/big remains the canonical standard-library path for exact arithmetic without external packages. int64 minor-unit integer. Zero allocations. Exact addition/subtraction/comparison. The default for ledger storage, transfer amounts, and anything that doesn't need sub-cent math. Base-10 arbitrary precision. Clean API, idiomatic, handles all rounding modes. One external dependency. Right for interest, tax, and FX conversion where you compute in decimal before rounding back to cents. Stdlib arbitrary precision (Go 1.26). Zero dependencies. More verbose API. Right when you can't add dependencies and need exact rational arithmetic for a bounded calculation. Never mix decimal-library values with float64. decimal.NewFromFloat(0.1) does NOT give you 0.1 exactly — it gives you the float's inexact binary value wrapped in a decimal type. Use decimal.NewFromString("0.1") or decimal.NewFromInt with integer cents only.

heading: When to Use Which
text: Situation Tool --- --- Storing amounts in a ledger int64 minor units Adding/subtracting amounts int64 minor units Comparing amounts int64 minor units Computing a percentage fee shopspring/decimal or big.Rat, round → int64 Interest accrual, daily/monthly shopspring/decimal or big.Rat, round → int64 FX conversion shopspring/decimal or big.Rat, round → int64 Everything in storage/wire int64 minor units The pattern is always: compute in decimal precision → round explicitly → store as integer minor units.

heading: Currency Types and Safety
text: We've been using a string for currency codes. That's a footgun. The type system can prevent an entire class of bugs for free — and in fintech, free bug prevention is the best kind. On the job: Meridian's Transfer type has Amount Money where Money.Currency is a Currency struct. A function that adds two Money values with different currencies returns error. A compile-time phantom-type approach (Exercise 4) goes further and catches mismatches before the binary is built.

heading: Minor-Unit Exponents
text: The minorExp field tells you how many decimal places separate the major unit from the minor unit. This is codified in ISO 4217 : Currency Code minorExp Example --- --- --- --- US Dollar USD 2 100 cents = $1.00 Euro EUR 2 100 cents = €1.00 Japanese Yen JPY 0 ¥1 = ¥1 (no minor unit) Kuwaiti Dinar KWD 3 1000 fils = 1 KWD Bahraini Dinar BHD 3 1000 fils = 1 BHD minorExp matters when you convert between display format and storage, when you compute FX rates, and when you interpret amounts from an external API. An API that sends means ¥1,000. The same means 1.000 KWD. Never assume exp = 2. A Money value without its currency is meaningless — and dangerous. In Meridian's database schema, every amount column has a corresponding currency column on the same row. Every API response carries both. Never pass a bare int64 across a boundary and expect the receiver to know the currency from context.

heading: Rounding Modes
text: We've arrived at the part that trips up even experienced fintech engineers, because rounding is not a technical decision — it's a legal one . On the job: When Meridian computes a 1.5% platform fee on a $9.99 transaction, the fee is 9.99 × 0.015 = 0.14985 — not a whole number of cents. Which direction you round is specified in your contracts, your terms of service, and possibly your regulatory framework. If you haven't checked, you're guessing. A rounding mode determines what happens when an arithmetic result falls exactly halfway between two integers (the x.5 case). The two modes that matter most in fintech: Half-up (round half away from zero): 0.5 → 1, 1.5 → 2, 2.5 → 3. What most people call "normal rounding." Simple, but it introduces a systematic upward bias because every tie-break goes the same direction. Common in everyday retail math. Half-even (banker's rounding): 0.5 → 0 (rounds to even), 1.5 → 2 (rounds to even), 2.5 → 2 (rounds to even), 3.5 → 4 (rounds to even). When a value is exactly halfway, it rounds to the nearest even integer. Over a large dataset, half the tie-breaks go up and half go down, so the bias cancels out. Mandated by IEEE-754 as the default rounding mode

heading: The Four Modes You Need to Know
text: Rounds 0.5 up always. What most people think of as "normal rounding." Simple, but introduces systematic upward bias over large datasets. Common in retail. Rounds 0.5 to the nearest even integer. 0.5→0, 1.5→2, 2.5→2, 3.5→4. Eliminates systematic bias because half the tie-breaks go up, half go down. Mandated by IEEE-754 and many financial regulations. Always round down. Favors the payer in a fee context. Used in some tax computations. Always round up. Favors the payee. Sometimes legally required for certain fee types. You do not get to pick the rounding mode based on what makes your math cleaner. The rounding mode for interest, tax, and fee calculations is defined in your regulatory framework, your contracts, and your terms of service. In the US: IRS Publication 538 specifies rounding for tax. In the EU: SEPA payment scheme rules define rounding for transfers. If you're not sure, ask your compliance team — then document the answer in code comments with a citation.

heading: The Penny Allocation Problem
text: Here is a scenario every payment system faces: splitting a total across multiple recipients where the total doesn't divide evenly . Meridian takes a $10.00 payment and splits it to three merchants: 33.33%, 33.33%, 33.34%. Or maybe three equal parts — but 10.00 / 3 = 3.333…, and you can't store a third of a cent. On the job: If your split function loses a penny, the Meridian ledger's debit and credit sides won't balance. Auditors call that a discrepancy. Regulators call that an incident. The penny-allocation problem (also called the largest remainder method) arises when you split an integer total among N recipients and the total is not evenly divisible by N. Naive division truncates, losing the remainder entirely — 1000 / 3 = 333 × 3 = 999, one cent vanished. The correct algorithm is: give everyone floor(total/N), then distribute one extra minor unit to each of the first total % N recipients. The result: every share is either floor(total/N) or floor(total/N) + 1, and all shares sum to exactly total. Not a single minor unit is created or destroyed. This is the only correct way to split an indivisible total. The naive approach: The correct approach — penny allocation (also called the

desc: Debits and credits, accounting invariants, append-only immutability, and modeling a ledger in Go with enforced invariants.
text: Listen up, sport. Every payment system that has ever collapsed — every bank that "lost" money, every fintech startup that burned through investor cash and couldn't explain where it went — shared one common sin: they stored money in a way that let the books get out of balance without anyone noticing. Double-entry accounting is the immune system that has protected financial records for seven hundred years . The earliest full double-entry records are Florentine, around 1300; Luca Pacioli first set the method down in print in Venice in 1494 — and it still powers every bank, brokerage, and payments company on Earth today. And you're going to implement it — correctly, in Go, with invariants the compiler and runtime both enforce. No wiggle room. No "oh we'll check that later." Later is where money goes to disappear. You're lucky I'm the one teaching you this.

heading: Debits and Credits
text: Let me set the scene with a concrete scenario — because abstract accounting jargon is how you end up confused and I end up disappointed. The scenario: You're building the ledger for Meridian, a payments platform. Alice has a checking account with $200 in it. She sends $50 to Bob. How do you record that without creating or destroying any money? This is exactly the problem double-entry accounting solves. Let's build up to the answer one idea at a time. Double-entry means every financial event is recorded as at least two entries that exactly cancel each other out. When Alice sends Bob $50, one entry subtracts $50 from Alice and another entry adds $50 to Bob — the two together sum to zero. Nothing is created; nothing is destroyed. The system catches unbalanced postings the instant they're written, not weeks later when a discrepancy shows up in a report. This is why ledgers don't lose money silently. A debit records value flowing into an asset or expense account (or out of a liability or equity account). In our convention: debit entries carry a positive signed value. When Bob receives $50, his checking account — an asset — is debited: +5000 cents. Think of it as the account being "loade

heading: Seeing the problem first — the unbalanced single-entry world
text: Before the code, watch what actually goes wrong when a payment system skips the second leg. On the job: In production, a single-sided entry that persists to the database will corrupt account balances, trigger false fraud alerts, and create phantom discrepancies that take hours of manual reconciliation to diagnose — and sometimes never get explained. Enforcing the zero-sum invariant at the constructor level means this class of bug is caught before the first database round-trip.

heading: Every account is a bucket
text: An account is a named bucket that tracks the flow of value. In Meridian's ledger, examples include: alice:checking — Alice's checking balance bob:checking — Bob's checking balance platform:revenue — The platform's fee income platform:liability:user-funds — Money the platform holds on behalf of users Every movement of value touches at least two accounts. That's the fundamental rule. When Alice pays Bob $50, money leaves one bucket and enters another. We call each touch an entry .

heading: Debits and credits — defined for engineers
text: These words carry enormous historical baggage (generations of accounting students have memorized them with flashcards). I'm going to define them operationally so they're actually useful: A debit records value flowing into an account (for asset/expense accounts), or flowing out of a liability/equity account. The word "debit" literally means "he owes" in Latin. In Go, you'll model it as EntryDebit. A credit records value flowing out of an asset account, or flowing into a liability/equity account. Latin for "he trusts." In Go: EntryCredit. Things the entity owns or is owed — cash, receivables. A debit increases an asset account. A credit decreases it. Things the entity owes others — deposits held, loans payable. A credit increases a liability. A debit decreases it. The owner's residual claim (assets minus liabilities). Behaves like a liability for debit/credit purposes. Revenue: credits increase it (earning more). Expenses: debits increase them (spending more). The debit-increases-assets / credit-increases-liabilities rule trips up every engineer on first contact. The shortcut: think of debits and credits as directions on a number line , not as "add" and "subtract." The direction's ef

heading: The accounting equation — for engineers, no MBA required
text: Every double-entry system is built on one identity that must hold at all times: Assets = Liabilities + Equity . Translated for engineers: everything the entity has (assets) equals everything it owes (liabilities) plus everything the owners claim (equity). It is a conservation law — like conservation of energy, but for money. Any transaction that preserves this identity can be verified mechanically, which is exactly what we will do in Go. Here's how it applies to Meridian's Alice→Bob transfer: Account Type Effect --- --- --- alice:checking Asset (Alice's) Decreases by $50 — credit bob:checking Asset (Bob's) Increases by $50 — debit Two entries. Two accounts touched. And critically: the sum is zero — one entry takes $50 away, the other adds $50 back. No money created. No money destroyed. The books balance.

heading: The Balance Invariant
text: The beating heart of double-entry is one mathematical rule that must be true at every instant, not just at month-end: For every transaction, the signed sum of all entry amounts is zero. Debits are positive, credits are negative (by our convention). A $50 transfer from Alice to Bob produces two entries: +5000 and −5000. Their sum is 0. This is not accounting policy — it is a conservation law. It means value cannot appear from nowhere and cannot vanish into a void. Enforcing this at the Go constructor level means an unbalanced transaction is a compile-time-detectable error, not a silent database bug. Why does this matter for engineers? 1. Self-checking: If you record a $50 credit but forget the matching debit, the sum is -$50, not 0. The invariant fails. You catch the bug before it hits the database. 2. Audit trail: Given any set of ledger entries, you can verify their correctness by summing them. No external oracle needed — the data checks itself. 3. No "orphan" money: A naive system where you UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 50 WHERE id = alice can crash between the debit and credit, leaving Alice $50 poorer with Bob none the richer. Double-entry records both sides atomicall

heading: Animating a multi-leg transaction
text: Real payments often touch more than two accounts. Here's a $50 payment where Meridian takes a $1 fee: In most systems, the balance invariant is enforced by a mix of application code, database constraints, and hope. If you have a function postEntries(entries []Entry) that just inserts rows, a caller can accidentally pass only one side of a transfer. The database doesn't know about double-entry; it will happily store the unbalanced entries. The bug surfaces hours later as a mysterious discrepancy in an account balance. In Go, we can do better: enforce the invariant at the construction site of a Transaction. The only way to create a valid Transaction is through a constructor that rejects unbalanced input with an error. There is no way to construct a Transaction with entries that don't sum to zero — not through a bug, not through a forgotten check, not through a code path you didn't test. This is the Go proverb "make illegal states unrepresentable" in its purest fintech form. The compiler doesn't know about accounting, but the constructor does. And once the constructor runs, the type itself carries the proof of validity. As of Go 1.26, there's nothing magical happening — this is just i

heading: Append-Only Immutability
text: Here's the part that makes every SQL engineer uncomfortable the first time they hear it. Ledger entries are never updated. Ledger entries are never deleted. Not "try not to update them." Not "only update them in emergencies." Never. Full stop. An append-only ledger is one where entries can only be added, never modified or removed. Every entry is a fact about the past — "$50 left Alice's account at 14:03:22 UTC on June 3rd" — and facts about the past do not change. If an error must be corrected, you post a new entry that undoes the old one. The original is never touched. This gives you a tamper-evident history: an auditor can scan every entry from genesis to now and verify that nothing was silently altered.

heading: Why immutability matters
text: The ledger is not a scoreboard showing current values — it is a complete history of every event that ever happened . Every entry is a fact about the past, and facts about the past do not change. $50 left Alice's account on June 3rd. That happened. You cannot un-happen it. This matters for three reasons engineers care about: 1. Audit. A regulator, an auditor, or your own on-call engineer can look at the ledger and reconstruct the state of every account at any point in time. If entries could be edited, that history would be corrupted — you'd have no way to know whether a balance today reflects legitimate transactions or a backdated edit. 2. Correctness. Derived balances (computed by summing entries) are always reproducible. You can recompute any account's balance from scratch and get the same answer. If entries were mutable, two replicas might compute different answers. 3. Concurrency safety. Immutable data has no write conflicts. Multiple readers can scan the ledger simultaneously without any locking on the entries themselves (though inserting a new transaction still requires a careful write — covered in the next chapter, Transactions, Consistency & Sagas). On the job: Regulators un

heading: Corrections are new entries
text: A reversal (also called a compensating entry or compensating transaction) is a new transaction that exactly undoes a prior transaction. Every entry in the original is replicated with its debit/credit direction flipped, producing a new transaction that also sums to zero. The original is preserved in the log; the reversal sits next to it, timestamped, auditable. This is the only correct way to correct a mistake in an immutable ledger. So what happens when someone makes a mistake? Say a $50 transfer was posted to the wrong account. In a mutable system, you'd UPDATE the entry. In Meridian's immutable ledger, you: 1. Post a reversal (a compensating entry that exactly undoes the original). 2. Post the correction (a new transaction with the right accounts). The reversal is a first-class event — it appears in the audit log, it carries a timestamp, and it can reference the transaction it's reversing. An auditor reading the ledger can see exactly what happened: the original transfer, when it was discovered to be wrong, and when the correction was posted. If this sounds like event sourcing — it is. A double-entry ledger is one of the oldest event-sourced systems in existence. Each entry is an

heading: Computing Balances
text: Now that we have an append-only ledger full of entries, how do we answer the most fundamental question: what is Alice's balance right now? Two strategies, two trade-offs.

heading: Strategy 1 — Derived (event-sourced) balance
text: Sum all entries for the account from the beginning of time: Advantages: The balance is always correct — it's computed from the authoritative source of truth. No denormalization to get out of sync. You can compute the balance at any point in time by filtering entries by timestamp. Disadvantages: For an account with millions of entries, this is O(n) per call. At high transaction volume, this becomes slow. In a production database, you'd add an index on (account id, posted at) and query only the relevant partition — but it's still a full scan of that account's history.

heading: Strategy 2 — Cached (materialized) balance
text: Store a running total alongside the entries. On each new transaction, update the cache atomically in the same database transaction: Advantages: O(1) balance reads — just read the balance cents column. Essential at high transaction volume. Disadvantages: The cached balance and the derived balance can become inconsistent if there's a bug in your write path. You need to verify the cache periodically by recomputing from entries (a reconciliation job — covered in the Auditability & Compliance chapter). On the job: Production ledgers at Meridian-scale use cached balances for fast reads and run a nightly reconciliation job that compares cached totals to derived sums. Any discrepancy is a P1 alert — it means a write-path bug persisted an unbalanced state. Always correct. O(n) cost. Use for low-volume accounts, historical queries, and audit verification. O(1) cost. Can drift. Use for high-volume accounts when you also run periodic reconciliation to catch discrepancies. A scheduled job that recomputes derived balances and compares them to cached balances. heading: ACID & Isolation Levels
text: Before a single dollar moves, you need to understand the contract your database is making with you. That contract has four clauses. Every professional knows them cold. ACID is the set of four guarantees a database transaction makes: A tomicity (all operations in the transaction succeed together or none are visible), C onsistency (every transaction takes the database from one valid state to another — your invariants hold before and after every commit), I solation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's in-progress work), and D urability (once a transaction commits, it survives crashes). You care about ACID because without it, concurrent money movement corrupts balances silently — no exception thrown, no error logged.

heading: The four properties
text: A transaction is a group of operations that the database treats as a single unit. You've used them: BEGIN → do work → COMMIT (or ROLLBACK). The database promises four things about that unit: All operations in a transaction succeed together, or none of them are visible. A transfer that posts a debit and a credit either completes both or neither. No half-posted transfers. Ever. Every transaction must take the database from one valid state to another. Your invariants — like "debits must equal credits" — hold before and after every commit. The DB enforces constraints; you enforce your domain rules in the transaction. Concurrent transactions must not see each other's in-progress work. The degree to which they're shielded is the isolation level. This is the one that bites people in fintech. Once a transaction commits, it's permanent. A crash, a power cut, a cosmic ray — the committed data survives. The write-ahead log (WAL) is how Postgres makes this true. Atomicity and durability are either on or off — you don't configure them. Isolation is a dial.

heading: Isolation levels and the anomalies they prevent
text: An isolation level controls how much a transaction can see of concurrent in-progress work from other transactions. The SQL standard defines four levels — Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable — each buying protection against a specific class of anomaly. Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more contention; lower isolation means more concurrency but more subtle bugs. Postgres defaults to Read Committed , which is safe for many workloads but not for concurrent balance updates. The SQL standard defines four isolation levels. Each one buys protection against specific anomalies. Here they are, strongest to weakest: You read a row that a concurrent transaction has modified but not yet committed. If that transaction rolls back, you saw data that never existed. Postgres doesn't allow this at any isolation level. You read a row, a concurrent transaction commits a change to it, you read it again and get a different value. Two reads of the same row in one transaction return different data. You run a query with a WHERE clause, another transaction inserts rows that would match, you run the same query and get more rows. The "phantom" rows appeared between your

heading: The Lost-Update Problem
text: Enough theory. Let's watch the disaster happen in real time. The lost-update problem occurs when two transactions both read the same value, each independently computes a new value based on that read, and both write back — so the second write silently overwrites the first. No error is raised. No constraint is violated. The database happily commits both transactions. In a balance update, this means real money either disappears or gets created from nothing. On the job: At Meridian, POST /transfers is hit by payment processors, mobile clients, and batch jobs simultaneously. Any read-compute-write pattern on accounts.balance cents without a lock is a lost-update waiting to happen — and it only manifests under load, not in unit tests. Two customers are pulling money from the same account simultaneously. Gwendolyn wants to send $30. Marcus wants to send $40. The account has $100. After both transfers succeed, the balance should be $30. Watch what happens without any locking: That's the lost-update problem. In a real system it means real money either disappears or gets created from nothing. No exception is thrown. No error is logged. The database happily committed both transactions. It was

heading: Pessimistic Locking
text: The fix for the lost-update problem at the database level is pessimistic locking: acquire a lock on the row before you read it, hold that lock until you commit. No other transaction can read or write that row while you hold the lock. You're pessimistic — you assume someone will race you, so you prevent it up front. Pessimistic locking means acquiring an exclusive lock on a resource before reading it, holding that lock for the duration of the transaction. In Postgres, the SQL clause is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. It says: "read this row AND lock it — no other transaction may lock or write it until I commit or roll back." You're paying the overhead of lock management on every read, whether or not there's a race. The payoff: zero possibility of a lost update on that row. On the job: Use pessimistic locking on Meridian's account rows any time you do a read-compute-write on balance cents. High-volume accounts (a prize pool, a merchant settlement account) can see hundreds of concurrent transfers — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is the only correct tool there. In Postgres (and most SQL databases), the spell is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. The FOR UPDATE clause does two things: 1. It reads the row and acquire

heading: Optimistic Locking
text: Pessimistic locking is correct, but it serializes all writes to a row. If contention is low — most of the time nobody races you — you're paying the overhead of lock management and blocking for a scenario that rarely happens. Optimistic locking assumes you won't be raced, and detects the collision after the fact instead of preventing it up front. Optimistic locking lets a transaction proceed without acquiring any lock, then checks at commit time whether the data changed under it. The standard implementation adds a version column — an integer that increments on every update. At write time, the UPDATE includes WHERE version = $old version: if zero rows are affected, another transaction won the race and changed the version first. The current transaction retries from scratch. Optimistic locking wins when contention is low (most writes don't race); it degrades into a thundering-herd problem when contention is high. On the job: Optimistic locking is the right choice for Meridian's user profile updates or currency preferences — fields that are rarely written concurrently. It's the wrong choice for balance cents on a high-volume account. The pattern uses a version column : an integer that i

heading: When to choose optimistic vs. pessimistic
text: Contention is high — the same account is hit by many concurrent transfers. A payment processing queue where many workers drain one account. You cannot afford retries (strict latency SLAs). The operation has expensive side effects you don't want to repeat. Contention is low — most transfers hit different accounts. You're writing a distributed system where lock-holding across network calls would be disastrous. Retries are cheap and safe. The happy path (no conflict) must be as fast as possible. Never use optimistic locking for the account balance if your service handles burst traffic on popular accounts (e.g., a prize account hit by 10,000 concurrent claimants). At high contention, every transaction retries repeatedly, and you've turned a locking problem into a thundering-herd problem. Use FOR UPDATE there.

heading: Safe Concurrent Transfers
text: Now we put it all together. A production transfer between two accounts — with both sides locked, a funds check, and the double-entry ledger posted inside the same transaction. But first: deadlocks . A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are each waiting for a lock held by the other, forming a cycle in the wait-for graph. Neither can proceed. Example: TX 1 locks account A then waits for account B; TX 2 has locked account B and is waiting for account A. Postgres detects this within deadlock timeout (default 1 second) and aborts one transaction with ERROR: deadlock detected. The aborted transaction must be retried from scratch. Prevention is better than detection — lock multiple rows in a deterministic order. On the job: Deadlocks between transfers are the most common liveness bug in fintech database code. They're invisible in single-threaded tests and emerge under concurrent load. The fix costs one comparison. If TX 1 locks account A then tries to lock account B, while TX 2 locks account B then tries to lock account A — they deadlock. The fix is a deterministic lock order: always lock accounts in ascending order of their ID, regardless of which is the sender and which is th

heading: Sagas & Compensating Actions
text: ACID transactions are powerful, but they have a hard limit: they work when all the operations you need to make atomically live inside one database . Reality is messier. Consider this Meridian transfer: debit the user's wallet in the ledger service, then credit their external bank account via the ACH network. These are two different systems. You cannot put them in one BEGIN/COMMIT block. If the ACH call succeeds but the ledger service crashes before recording it, or vice versa — you have a split-brain transfer. This is the problem sagas solve. Forward until something breaks, then compensate BACKWARD — the whole shape of a saga in one run: A saga is a sequence of local ACID transactions, one per service or system, each of which commits independently. Instead of one global atomic commit across multiple systems (which is impossible without a distributed coordinator), a saga achieves eventual consistency — with the guarantee that if any step fails, every preceding step is reversed by a compensating action . A saga is not a hack; it's the correct model for multi-system money movement, used in production at every major payments company. On the job: Meridian's cross-bank transfer is a saga

heading: What a saga is
text: A saga is a sequence of local transactions , where each step commits to its own database. Instead of a global atomic commit, you get eventual consistency — with the guarantee that if any step fails, every preceding step is undone by a compensating action . A compensating action (also called a compensating transaction) is a new, committed database transaction that reverses the business effect of a previously committed step. It is NOT a ROLLBACK — that would make the change invisible. A compensation is a new ledger entry that is permanently visible in the audit log. Example: a debit of $200 is compensated by a credit of $200 — both appear in the ledger, and together they net to zero. This is mandatory for regulated financial systems: auditors need to see what happened and that it was corrected, not a sanitized view where the failure never occurred. Every step has a companion: Forward Action Compensating Action --- --- Debit sender wallet Credit sender wallet (reverse debit) Reserve funds in escrow Release escrow hold Submit ACH transfer Initiate ACH return / reversal Notify recipient Send "transfer failed" notification A compensating action is not a rollback — it's a new, committed t

heading: Orchestration vs. choreography
text: Orchestration uses a central saga orchestrator — a dedicated service or state machine — that knows the full step sequence, calls each step, and triggers compensating actions on failure. The orchestrator is the single source of truth for saga state. Choreography uses no central coordinator: each service publishes events ("DebitSucceeded") and subscribes to events from others ("ACHFailed"), and the saga emerges from the event flow. Orchestration is easier to reason about and observe; choreography is more decoupled but harder to trace. For money movement at Meridian, prefer orchestration — a money transfer needs a clear, auditable state machine. On the job: Choreography sounds elegant until you have to debug a half-executed saga in production at 2am. An orchestrated saga has a saga state table — you can query it. A choreographed saga's state is implicit in a dozen event handlers across five services. A central saga orchestrator (a dedicated service or state machine) knows the full sequence. It calls step 1, waits for success, calls step 2, and so on. If any step fails, it calls the compensating actions in reverse order. The orchestrator is the single source of truth for saga state. Ea

heading: Combining the saga with the transactional outbox
text: There's a subtle bug lurking in a naive saga implementation: what if the orchestrator successfully calls DebitSender but crashes before it can record that step 1 succeeded and trigger step 2? On restart, does it retry step 1 (double-debit!) or skip it (inconsistent)? The answer is the transactional outbox — covered in depth in the Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics chapter. The short version: every state transition in the saga is written to an outbox table inside the same local ACID transaction as the saga state update. A separate outbox relay process reads unprocessed outbox records and fires the next saga step (or the compensating action) reliably — with at-least-once delivery and idempotent handlers. If the orchestrator crashes, the relay picks up where it left off, using the outbox as a durable work queue. A database ROLLBACK is invisible: it undoes changes as if they never happened, and nothing appears in the audit log. A saga compensation is the opposite: it is a committed transaction that explicitly reverses a business effect, and both the original action and the compensation are permanently visible in your ledger. desc: Idempotency keys, deduplication, at-least-once vs exactly-once, safe payment retries, and the transactional outbox pattern.
text: Listen up, sport — because what I'm about to teach you is the difference between a payment system that works and one that silently double-charges customers at 3am while your on-call engineer stares at a dashboard in horror. Here's the thing: networks lie. Clients retry. Servers crash mid-write and come back up not knowing if they succeeded. In this environment, "just don't send the request twice" is not a strategy — it's a wish. What you need is a system that can receive the same request a hundred times and produce exactly the outcome it would have produced once. That property has a name: idempotency . And it's not optional in fintech. It's the floor. By the end of this chapter you will understand idempotency keys, deduplication, the honest truth about exactly-once semantics, safe retry patterns, and the transactional outbox — the pattern that keeps your database and your message broker from ever disagreeing about what happened. I built systems like this. You're about to learn how. Pay attention.

heading: Why idempotency matters
text: The scene that motivates this whole chapter — one webhook, delivered three times: An operation is idempotent if applying it multiple times produces the same result as applying it once. A payment "charge $149.99 for order 4201" must be idempotent: if the client retries after a timeout, Meridian charges once , not twice. We need idempotency because networks retry, and a retried charge that is not idempotent creates money out of nothing — it is a bug that shows up in production under load, not in unit tests. On the job: you hit idempotency the moment any client can retry a mutating call — mobile apps, service-to-service RPCs, background workers, webhook processors. Every POST /v1/charges at Meridian must be idempotent. Every event consumer must be idempotent. Getting it wrong means duplicate charges, double-booked transfers, and a support queue that grows faster than your team. Let me set the scene with the exact scenario that wakes fintech engineers up at night. A customer clicks "Pay Now" for a $149.99 subscription. Meridian's mobile client sends a POST /v1/charges to the payment API. The request crosses the Atlantic, the server processes the charge, deducts the balance, writes the

heading: Idempotency keys
text: An idempotency key is a unique token that the client generates once per logical operation — not per HTTP request. The client sends it with every attempt, including retries. The server stores the mapping from key → result. On a repeated key, the server returns the stored result without re-executing the operation. The key is usually a UUID v4 or ULID. It must be unique per logical operation — not per session and not per user. On the job: Stripe, Adyen, and every mature payments API require an Idempotency-Key header on all mutating calls. If you forget to send one, retries become double charges. If you regenerate the key on retry (a common bug), idempotency is silently defeated. An idempotency key is a unique token the client generates for each logical operation — not each HTTP request. The client sends the key with every request, including retries. The server stores the mapping from key to result. On a repeated key, the server returns the stored result without re-executing the operation. The lifecycle of an idempotency key has three states: 1. In-flight — the key has been seen but the operation has not finished yet. 2. Completed — the operation finished; the result is stored and will

heading: Claiming a key atomically — the race condition
text: Here is where amateurs get it wrong. What happens when two copies of the same retry arrive simultaneously — say, a client is using HTTP/2 and fires two parallel attempts? You cannot let both of them race to process the charge. The solution is a unique constraint on the idempotency key column and an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT clause. This is the database's atomic test-and-set. Only one insert wins; the loser finds the row already exists and knows it must wait for the winner to finish, then return the stored result. ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING is atomic at the database level — it cannot race with another identical insert. The unique index on key guarantees only one insert succeeds. This is not application-level locking; it is a hard database guarantee. Now the full handler flow — a runnable in-memory demonstration: The in-memory store above uses a mutex to serialize Claim — safe enough for demonstration, but it has a critical weakness: it is not durable . If the process crashes between Claim and Complete, the key is stuck as an empty placeholder. On restart, the key entry is gone and a new request could re-execute the charge. The database-backed version is durable and atomic in a deeper

heading: The concurrent race test — a mandatory Meridian verification
text: The most important test for an idempotency system is not a sequential one. It is a concurrent one: fire N identical requests simultaneously and verify that exactly one charge occurs. Run this with -race always. If there is a data race in your idempotency logic, the race detector will find it. This test must be green before any payment handler ships.

heading: Deduplication
text: Deduplication is the practice of detecting and discarding duplicate messages or events before they can be processed twice. Where an idempotency key is client-supplied (your own mobile app, your own service), a natural dedup key comes from the event payload itself — the card network's authorization ID, a bank's ACH trace number, a webhook's event id. Both strategies use the same underlying primitive: an atomic insert into a table with a unique constraint. On the job: dedup keys matter most at event consumer boundaries. A payment processor (Stripe, Adyen) delivers webhooks at-least-once — your consumer will receive the same payment intent.succeeded event more than once during network blips and retries. Without deduplication, you credit the customer twice. Idempotency keys work when clients cooperate — they generate and send the key. But what about deduplication at the message or event level, where the producer may be a third-party system or a broker delivering events at-least-once? Message-level deduplication uses a different strategy: you build a dedup table that records which messages you have already processed, keyed by a natural key — an identifier that comes from the event paylo

heading: At-least-once vs exactly-once
text: These are the three delivery guarantees a messaging system can offer: At-most-once : fire and forget — the message may never arrive. No retries. Used where loss is acceptable (telemetry, UDP). At-least-once : the message will arrive, but may arrive more than once . The sender retries until it gets an acknowledgement. This is the standard for reliable systems — Kafka, SQS, most webhook implementations. Exactly-once delivery : the message arrives exactly once, never duplicated, never lost. Theoretically impossible in an asynchronous distributed system (see the Two Generals Problem and FLP impossibility). What brokers call "exactly-once" is always at-least-once + a dedup layer. Exactly-once processing — also called effectively-once — is the achievable goal: at-least-once delivery combined with an idempotent handler. The broker may deliver the message twice; the handler detects the duplicate (via a dedup table or idempotency key) and makes the second delivery a no-op. The effect on your system is as if the message was processed exactly once. On the job: "we need exactly-once delivery" is a common requirement in payments. The correct response is: "we implement at-least-once delivery wit

heading: Safe payment retries
text: Retries without idempotency are dangerous. Retries with idempotency plus proper backoff are the standard for resilient payment systems. The retry strategy for payment API calls combines three things: 1. Idempotency key — same key on every retry, so the server can absorb duplicates. 2. Exponential backoff — wait longer after each failure to avoid hammering a struggling upstream. 3. Jitter — randomize the backoff slightly so a fleet of clients does not retry in lockstep (the "thundering herd"). The canonical backoff formula: sleep = base 2^attempt + random jitter. Not every error is retryable. A 400 Bad Request (invalid card number) is permanent — retrying it will not fix it. A 500 Internal Server Error or a network timeout is transient — worth retrying. Your retry logic should inspect the error type and only back off on transient failures. Retrying a permanent error wastes time and burns your idempotency key's retry window. As of Go 1.26, errors.AsType[T] provides a generic helper for unwrapping typed errors — useful when your payment processor client returns a typed APIError carrying a status code, letting you branch on transient vs permanent without a manual type assertion. heading: The transactional outbox
text: The dual-write problem occurs when you need to update two separate systems atomically — typically a database and a message broker — but have no distributed transaction spanning both. If the process crashes between the two writes, one system is updated and the other is not: either the event is lost (DB committed, broker publish never happened) or a phantom event exists (broker published, DB rolled back). There is no network call that can make two independent systems commit together without a coordinator. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem without a distributed transaction. Instead of writing directly to the message broker, you write the event to an outbox table inside the same database transaction as the business change. A separate relay process polls unsent outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, then marks them sent. The DB transaction guarantees atomicity between the business write and the outbox write. The relay delivers at-least-once (it may publish twice if it crashes between publish and mark-sent), but your consumers are idempotent — so that is fine.
