desc: The broker-agnostic mental model: queues vs topics, producers/consumers, push vs pull, delivery guarantees, ordering, acks and dead-letter queues.
text: Listen up, sport. You've got a payment service that fires off a payment.completed event — and your ledger service, your notifications service, and your analytics pipeline all need to hear about it right now . The naive move? Call all three directly, in sequence, from inside the payment handler. Then one of them is slow. Or down. Suddenly a perfectly good payment is timing out, or worse, half your side effects ran and half didn't. That's not a system. That's a house of cards in a hurricane. A message broker exists specifically to save you from that fate. By the end of this chapter you'll understand exactly how it does that — queues, topics, delivery guarantees, acknowledgements, dead-letter queues, and back-pressure — without needing to name a single vendor. These are the concepts Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS, and every other broker are built on. Learn the foundation here, and those tools become obvious. You're exceptionally lucky I'm the one teaching you this.

heading: What a Broker Is
text: Let's nail the problem before we build the solution. Here's the scene: Your payments service just settled a payment.completed event for order ORD-7823. Three things need to happen: 1. The ledger service posts the double-entry accounting lines. 2. The notification service emails the customer. 3. The analytics pipeline records the conversion. The synchronous version — calling each service directly from the payment handler — looks like this: That err chain is a lie dressed as safety. If notifier.Send is down for a rolling deploy, you've got ledger entries with no notifications. If analytics.Record times out at 2 a.m., you've got a partially applied side-effect set with no idempotency key to replay safely. You've tightly coupled three independent services behind a single synchronous call chain. On the job: You hit this pattern the moment your payment handler has more than one downstream side effect. The failure mode — partial execution with no clean retry path — is one of the most expensive bugs to debug in production, because the ledger and the notification system are now out of sync with no record of why. A message broker is an intermediary that accepts messages from producers and de

heading: Queues vs Topics
text: Here's where most developers get confused. A broker can operate in two fundamentally different modes, and knowing which one you want is the difference between a system that works and one that loses data silently. A queue is a point-to-point channel where each message is delivered to exactly one consumer from a competing pool. Multiple workers read from the same queue; each message goes to whichever worker has capacity. Use a queue when you want to distribute work across a pool — receipt emails, report generation, image resizing — and each job should be done once, not N times. A topic is a publish/subscribe channel where each message is delivered to every subscriber independently . Each subscriber gets its own copy; the broker tracks each subscriber's progress separately. Use a topic when multiple independent downstream services all need the same event — a payment.completed event that ledger, notifications, and analytics all need to handle. Fan-out is what a topic does: one published message is copied and delivered to every subscriber. It's the messaging equivalent of broadcasting — the producer sends once, N consumers each receive once. Contrast with a queue, where one message goes

heading: The Work Queue: one message, one worker
text: In a work queue (also called a point-to-point queue), a message is consumed by exactly one worker . You have multiple workers competing for messages; each message goes to one of them. This is load distribution. Picture Meridian's receipt-email job queue. You enqueue one job per completed payment. You run three worker pods. Each job gets picked up by whichever pod has capacity — you don't want all three workers processing the same email.

heading: The Topic: one message, every subscriber
text: In a topic (publish/subscribe), a message is delivered to every subscriber independently . This is fan-out. Back to Meridian's payment.completed event: ledger, notifications, and analytics all need it. They're independent subscribers on the same topic. Each gets their own copy of the message.

heading: Queue vs Topic side by side
text: One message → one consumer. Used when you want to distribute work across a pool (receipt emails, image resizing, report generation). Adding workers scales throughput. One message → all subscribers. Used when multiple independent systems need the same event (payment events going to ledger + notifier + analytics). You care about one worker owning each delivery attempt. Pair it with acking, retries, and idempotency when the job must survive crashes. Multiple independent downstream services need the same information. The producer shouldn't know or care who they are. Some brokers blur the line — Kafka topics with consumer groups give you queue semantics within a group and fan-out across groups. The mental model still holds: within a group it's work-queue distribution; across groups it's fan-out. Get this chapter's model right and Kafka makes immediate sense.

heading: Producers, Consumers & Delivery
text: Now let's name the actors cleanly. A producer is any service or process that sends messages to the broker. A consumer (or subscriber) is any service or process that reads messages from the broker. These roles are asymmetric by design — the producer needs to know the destination (topic name or queue name); the consumer only needs to know what it wants to read. The payment service is a producer; the ledger service, the notification service, and the analytics pipeline are each consumers. A producer is anything that sends messages to the broker. A consumer (or subscriber) is anything that reads them. These roles are asymmetric by design — the producer needs to know the destination (topic name or queue name); the consumer only needs to know what it wants to read.

heading: Push vs. Pull
text: Push delivery : the broker sends messages to consumers as soon as they arrive — the broker initiates. Low latency, but the broker needs to track consumer state and risks overwhelming a slow consumer with more messages than it can handle. Pull delivery : the consumer polls the broker when it is ready for more messages — the consumer initiates. The consumer controls its own ingestion rate, which naturally provides back-pressure. Kafka, SQS, and most high-throughput production systems use pull. On the job: Push vs pull is not just a configuration choice — it determines who owns the flow-control signal. In a push system, a slow consumer that can't keep up either drops messages or crashes under load. In a pull system, the slow consumer simply stops pulling; the broker buffers and the system degrades gracefully. For Meridian's ledger consumer — which involves a DB write on every event — pull is the right default. There are two ways a message gets from broker to consumer: Push : the broker sends messages to consumers as soon as they arrive. Low latency, but the broker needs to track consumer state and risks overwhelming a slow consumer. Pull : the consumer polls the broker when it's ready

heading: Delivery Guarantees
text: Now for the part that bites every system at scale. When you publish a message, what promise does the broker make about whether (and how many times) a consumer processes it? On the job: Delivery guarantee mismatches are silent killers. A team that thinks they're running at-least-once but accidentally configured at-most-once will lose financial events with no error, no alert, and no stack trace. Define the guarantee explicitly in your service contracts. There are three tiers: The producer sends the message and moves on. No retry. If the network drops, if the broker crashes, if the consumer dies mid-processing — the message is gone . No duplicate risk, but possibly no delivery either. Appropriate for metrics, telemetry, and health pings where a missed sample is acceptable. Never appropriate for financial events. The broker retains the message until the consumer acknowledges it. If the consumer crashes before acknowledging, the broker redelivers. The consumer may process the same message more than once. This is the correct default for financial events — paired with idempotent consumers (see Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics), it becomes safe. The cost of redelivery is paid; the cost

heading: At-most-once (fire and forget)
text: The producer sends the message and moves on. No retry. If the network blips, if the broker crashes, if the consumer dies before processing — the message is gone . No duplicate. But possibly no delivery either. Use case: metrics, telemetry, system-health pings where a missed sample is fine. Never use this for financial events.

heading: At-least-once (the workhorse)
text: The broker retains the message until the consumer acknowledges it. If the consumer crashes before acking, the broker redelivers. The consumer may process the same message more than once. This is the default for most production systems. The trade-off: you must make your consumers idempotent — processing the same message twice must produce the same result as processing it once. We covered exactly how to do this with idempotency keys in Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics. The two chapters are designed to work together.

heading: Exactly-once (expensive and conditional)
text: The effect happens exactly once, with duplicates suppressed and losses avoided. In theory. In practice, true end-to-end exactly-once effects require coordination between the broker, the consumer, and its downstream store — it's expensive, limits throughput, and often depends on broker-specific features (Kafka's idempotent producer + transactional API, for example). In fintech, the pragmatic answer is " effectively exactly-once ": use at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers. You may receive a message twice; you handle it as if it arrived once. This is the pattern the industry uses — the outbox pattern from the previous chapter is exactly this. Send and forget. May lose messages. Zero duplicate risk. Fine for metrics; catastrophic for payments. Broker retains until acked. May redeliver. Consumers MUST be idempotent. The correct default for financial events. No loss, no duplicates. Expensive and broker-specific. In practice, implemented as at-least-once + idempotent consumers ("effectively once"). Never use at-most-once for any financial event. A missing payment.completed means the ledger never posts. "It probably got there" is not an auditing strategy.

heading: Ordering & Acknowledgements
text: Two more pieces of the mental model that trip up engineers in production. An acknowledgement (ack) is the signal a consumer sends to the broker to say "I have finished processing this message and the result is durable." Only after receiving an ack does the broker discard the message. A negative acknowledgement (nack) tells the broker "I failed to process this — redeliver it." The timing of the ack is critical: ack on receipt (before processing) means a crash during processing silently loses the work. Ack after the commit to durable storage is the correct pattern. On the job: The single most common ack bug is acking on receipt — the moment the message arrives in your process, before you've done anything with it. It looks harmless; it's catastrophic under failure. Add a code review checklist item: "Where does this consumer ack? Is it after the DB commit?"

heading: What an ack really means
text: The naive implementation acks a message when it's received — the moment it lands in the consumer's process. That's wrong. An ack must mean " I have finished processing this message and the result is durable. " If you ack on receipt and then crash while writing to the database, the broker thinks you're done. It discards the message. The work was never done. You've silently lost a financial event. Ack after processing. Ack after the commit. Not before.

heading: Ordering guarantees
text: Global ordering across all producers and all consumers is extraordinarily expensive — it requires a single sequential bottleneck. Most brokers don't provide it. What they do provide is per-partition or per-queue ordering. Within one partition, messages from one producer arrive at consumers in the order they were sent. Across partitions, all bets are off. For fintech, this usually means: use a partition key tied to the entity being modified (e.g., account ID). All events for account ACC-42 go to the same partition, so they're processed in order. Events for different accounts can be processed in parallel across partitions. Here's the precise mechanism. When a broker delivers a message, it starts an ack timer (the visibility timeout in SQS, the ack deadline in Pub/Sub, the session timeout in Kafka). During this window the message is invisible to other consumers — it's been handed off to one. If the consumer acks within the window: the broker discards the message. Done. If the consumer does NOT ack within the window (crash, timeout, slow processing): the broker's timer fires. The message becomes visible again and is redelivered to another consumer (or the same one, recovered). This is

heading: Dead-Letter Queues & Back-pressure
text: Two more production essentials that every system eventually needs. A dead-letter queue is a separate queue where messages are routed after they have exceeded their maximum retry count. Instead of retrying a failing message forever (blocking everything behind it) or silently discarding it, the broker moves it to the DLQ. Operations teams can then inspect it, diagnose the root cause, fix the underlying issue, and replay the message — or discard it with an audit trail. Without a DLQ, one malformed message (a poison message) can halt an entire consumer indefinitely. Backpressure is the mechanism by which a consumer signals upstream producers to slow down when it cannot keep up. Without backpressure, producers publish faster than consumers can process, messages pile up, and the broker's buffer — memory or disk — fills until something crashes. In Go, a buffered channel is a built-in backpressure mechanism: once full, sends block and the producer stalls naturally. Real brokers implement backpressure through fetch-size limits, consumer-lag monitoring, and flow-control protocols. On the job: DLQs and backpressure are the two features teams skip when they're moving fast — and the two they be

heading: Dead-letter queues (DLQs)
text: What happens when a message fails processing not because of a transient glitch, but because it's genuinely bad — a malformed payload, a missing field, a downstream service that rejects it every single time? Without a DLQ, that message retries forever, clogging the queue for every other message behind it. That's called a poison message , and it will bring your consumer to its knees. A dead-letter queue is where messages go after they've exceeded their retry limit (max delivery attempts). Instead of retrying forever or discarding, the broker routes the message to a separate DLQ. There, ops teams can inspect it, fix the underlying issue, and replay it — or discard it with an audit trail.

heading: Back-pressure
text: What happens when producers are publishing faster than consumers can process? Messages pile up. Memory fills. The broker's disk fills. Consumers start lagging further and further behind. Backpressure is the mechanism that signals upstream — "slow down, I'm full." Without it, the buffer grows unbounded until something crashes. In Go, a buffered channel is a built-in backpressure mechanism. Once it's full, the send blocks. The producer stalls. That's backpressure — the consumer's capacity limits the producer. Real brokers implement back-pressure through fetch size limits (consumers request N messages at a time), consumer lag monitoring, and flow control protocols. The mental model — "consumer capacity limits producer rate" — is the same whether the backpressure signal travels through a buffered channel or a Kafka consumer-group lag metric. Messages that fail processing after max retries are routed here instead of retrying forever. Enables inspection, debugging, and replay without blocking the main queue. chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
desc: Before you reach for a broker: an in-process, type-safe pub/sub event bus built from channels, generics and reflection — the actor model, total event ordering, and backpressure — grounded in decoupling Meridian's modules and read against Tailscale's production util/eventbus.
text: Listen up, sport. Last chapter I handed you the whole broker-agnostic mental model — topics, fan-out, acks, backpressure — and you earned it. But here's the thing nobody tells you before they sell you a Kafka cluster: you might not need a network at all. Meridian isn't six services yet. Right now it's one binary : the transfers module, the ledger module, the notifications module, the fraud module — all running in the same process, sharing the same memory. And they're calling each other directly, which means they're welded together. Change one, recompile all. One slow module stalls the request. That's not architecture, that's a single point of seizure. An in-process event bus breaks that weld without a broker, without a network hop, without serialization. Same publish/subscribe model you just learned — but the "wire" is a Go channel and the "message" is a struct that never leaves the heap. Tailscale runs exactly this pattern in production to keep their daemon's subsystems from strangling each other, and by the end of this chapter you'll have built it yourself, from channels up through generics and reflection, and then read theirs and understood every line. I've decoupled bigger syst

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: The Coupling Problem
text: Let's see the weld before we cut it. Meridian's monolith settles a transfer. The instant POST /transfers commits, four things must happen: the ledger posts the double-entry lines, the notifier emails a receipt, the fraud module updates its rolling risk score, and the analytics module records the conversion. Today the transfers handler just... calls all four. Look at what this Handler now knows . It imports ledger, notifier, fraud, and analytics. It knows the order they run in. It knows their method names. Add a fifth consumer — a webhook dispatcher — and you edit this function and recompile the transfers module to teach it about a module it has no business knowing. That is the definition of tight coupling : a change there forces a change here . On the job: you hit this the moment a second module cares about something the first module did. The transfers handler should know how to move money. The instant it also has to know who's watching it move money, every new feature becomes a surgery on the hottest code path you own — and a slow notifier turns a successful transfer into a timed-out request. An event bus is an in-process publish/subscribe mediator. A component publishes a typed e

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: A Naive Channel Bus
text: Let's build the simplest thing that works, then watch it fail in an instructive way. You already know channels are Go's in-process pipe. So the crudest possible bus is: keep a slice of subscriber channels; to publish, send the value to each one. Here it is, carrying Meridian's TransferCompleted event to a ledger listener and a notifier listener. That works. It decouples transfers from ledger and notifier — exactly what we wanted. So what's wrong with it? It carries one type. The day the fraud module wants to hear about AccountFrozen, and the analytics module wants LimitRaised, you are writing AccountFrozenBus and LimitRaisedBus, each an identical copy-paste with the type swapped. A bus per event type is not a bus — it's a parking lot full of one-seat cars. We want one bus that any module can publish any event type onto, and subscribers pick out only the types they asked for. Two instincts are both half-right, and seeing why each fails is the whole lesson: One bus, one chan any, send anything. But now every subscriber receives every event and must type-assert each one in a giant switch — and the bus has thrown away which channel wants which type. We lost routing. Bus[T] is type-safe

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Typed Edges with Generics
text: Here's the design in one sentence: the caller only ever touches Publisher[T] and Subscriber[T]; inside, everything is boxed to any and routed by reflect.Type. Start with the typed facades. A Publisher[T] is a thin wrapper that knows its event type T and forwards values into the untyped bus. A Subscriber[T] is a thin wrapper that pulls untyped values out and asserts them back to T before the caller sees them. The type safety lives entirely at these two edges. Notice what the caller sees: p.Emit(TransferCompleted ) won't compile if you hand it an AccountFrozen. for ev := range sub.Events() gives you a TransferCompleted, statically — no assertion, no , ok, no switch. The generics buy compile-time safety at the call site . The reflection we're about to add buys runtime routing in the core . Neither could do the other's job.

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Routing by Type
text: Now the core. The bus keeps a map from event type to the list of subscriber channels that want that type. The key is a reflect.Type — Go's runtime handle for "the type TransferCompleted," usable as a comparable map key. One bus. Two event types. Each event reaches only its type's subscriber, with full static typing at both ends. That's the whole trick — and it's the architecture Tailscale ships. Three mechanics make this work, and each has a price worth knowing. 1. Boxing into any. When Emit passes v T to publish(v any), Go puts v into an interface value: a two-word pair (type-pointer, data-pointer). The type-pointer references the runtime. type for TransferCompleted; the data-pointer references the value (heap-allocated if it escapes, which here it does because it flows through a channel into another goroutine). So each published event is one small interface header plus, usually, one heap allocation for the value. That's the cost of erasing the static type — and it's why a hot path that fires millions of events still measures this. 2. reflect.Type as a map key. reflect.TypeOf(v) reads the type-pointer straight out of that interface header — it's nearly free, just a field read. The

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Backpressure & the Pump
text: Our teaching bus has a hidden flaw, and it's the same one every real bus must answer: what happens when a subscriber is slow? In our publish, the fan-out loop does ch Backpressure is the resistance a slow consumer exerts back on its producer. When a subscriber can't keep up, its buffer fills; once full, the producer must either block (wait — preserving every event, at the cost of slowing the producer), drop (discard events — protecting the producer's speed, at the cost of losing data), or grow an unbounded buffer (preserve everything and stay fast — at the cost of unbounded memory, i.e. an eventual OOM). There is no fourth option; every event bus picks among these three, and the choice is the design. The naive answer — make every channel buffer enormous, or unbounded — just trades a stall for an out-of-memory crash under sustained load. The production answer is a single dispatch goroutine (call it the pump ) with a bounded internal queue, that imposes a clear ordering and a predictable backpressure point. One goroutine owns the timeline: it reads published events one at a time and hands each to the right subscribers. Because one goroutine sequences everything, you get a property th

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: The Actor Model
text: Step back from channels for a second, because the bus is really a vehicle for a design discipline , and that discipline has a name. The actor model structures a program as independent actors , each owning its own private state, that never touch each other's memory. An actor changes the world in exactly two ways: it emits messages, and it reacts to messages it receives. There is no shared mutable state to lock, because there is no sharing — coordination happens entirely through message passing. An event bus is the message-passing substrate; each subscribing module is an actor. Tailscale's bus documentation says it plainly: structure each component to hold authority over its own state and interact with everything else only by emitting and receiving events. The ledger module owns the ledger. Nobody reaches into it; they publish facts, and it decides what to do. The fraud module owns its risk scores. Nobody mutates them; they publish TransferCompleted and fraud updates itself . This is why the bus guarantees a total order ("one true timeline," in their docs): if every actor only reacts to a single, agreed sequence of events, then every actor sees the same history, and the system as a w

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Why So Many Parts
text: Here's the honest thing about reading util/eventbus cold: it looks like overkill . There's a Bus, a Client, a subscribeState, a subscriber interface, a Subscriber[T], a subscriberCore, a SubscriberFunc[T], a PublishedEvent, a DeliveredEvent, and a tangle of methods named dispatch, dispatchFunc, and dispatchTyped that call each other . The natural reaction is "why on earth does an event bus need ten types?" The answer is the best kind of lesson Go has to offer: every one of those parts exists to fix a specific problem the previous version created. Nobody designed this all at once. It grew, one forced move at a time. So let's grow it the same way — start from the naive bus you already built, and at each step, break it, see exactly why it breaks, and add the one part that fixes it. By the end, all ten types will feel not just sensible but inevitable . We'll keep using Meridian's two event types — TransferCompleted and AccountFrozen — as our stand-ins for any two unrelated events on one bus.

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 1 → the pump: ordering across publishers
text: You already met this in "Backpressure & the Pump," but now it's the first domino , so look again. In the naive bus, publish itself walks the subscriber slice and sends. So if the transfers goroutine and the fraud goroutine both publish at the same instant, each is running publish independently, sending to subscribers at its own pace. A subscriber listening to both types can see them interleaved in any order — and worse, two different subscribers can disagree on the order. For a stream of money events, "no agreed order" is a non-starter. The fix is the single pump goroutine: publishers stop sending directly and instead drop their event into one channel; one goroutine drains that channel and does all the delivery. Because one goroutine decides "next," there is now exactly one order — the "one true timeline."

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 2 → non-generic wrappers: the pump can't type-assert
text: Now the move that shapes everything else , and the single most important idea in this whole codebase. Watch what happens when we try to write the delivery step inside pump. To deliver, the pump must take the boxed any event and send it on a subscriber's typed channel — which means it must do the assertion evt.(TransferCompleted). But to write evt.(T), the code needs T in scope. And here's the wall: A type parameter like the T in func SubscribeT any exists only inside that generic function or method . A plain, non-generic function has no T — there is no type variable for it to name. So you can box a value into any anywhere, but you can only un box it with v.(T) somewhere that T is a visible type parameter. This is the constraint the entire bus is built around. The pump is a method on Bus. Bus is not generic — it has to hold subscribers of many event types at once, so it can't carry a single T. Therefore the pump has no T, therefore it cannot write evt.(T). The code simply won't compile. So the type assertion cannot happen in the bus . It can only happen back out at the edges, inside a generic function where T is in scope. Every awkward-looking part that follows is a consequence of s

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 3 → the Client: ordering across subscriptions
text: We fixed ordering across publishers with one pump. But if every call to Subscribe spins up its own subscribeState with its own goroutine, then a component that subscribes to both TransferCompleted and AccountFrozen has two independent goroutines pulling events — and they can fall out of order relative to each other again. The "one true timeline" leaks at the subscription boundary. The fix is the Client: a named handle that owns one subscribeState and therefore one dispatch goroutine, no matter how many event types it subscribes to. All of that client's subscriptions are served by that single goroutine, so they're delivered in the one true order. This is also why Bus.Client(name) wants a human name: it's the unit of "an actor," and the name shows up in the debugger so you can see which subsystem is behind a slow subscriber. To make the non-generic subscribeState able to call the generic Subscriber[T] it routes to, we need a contract between them that doesn't mention T. That's the subscriber interface : An interface is a set of method signatures; any type implementing those methods satisfies it, and you can hold it in a variable whose static type is the interface — without knowing th

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 4 → the queue + multi-way select: a slow subscriber can't stall the pump
text: The subscribeState delivers to a Subscriber[T] over a single channel. If that subscriber is slow and its channel fills, the send blocks — which blocks the subscribeState's goroutine, which blocks the bus pump feeding it, which blocks every publisher. One sluggish handler freezes the whole bus. The fix is to never let the delivering loop get stuck. The dispatch loop runs a multi-way select : one case tries to send the current event to the subscriber; another case, in the same select, keeps accepting newly-arriving events into an internal queue so the upstream pump is never blocked just because this one subscriber is slow; a third case handles shutdown. acceptCh() is a small function that returns the inbound channel — or nil when the queue is full, which (since a receive on a nil channel blocks forever) is exactly how you re-enable backpressure once the buffer is genuinely exhausted. (In our teaching bus we used a buffered channel for the same effect; this is the grown-up version with an explicit queue and an explicit "still accepting" case.)

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 5 → the subscriberCore: one itab instead of one per event type
text: Now a pure-Go cost problem, and the reason there's a subscriberCore at all. Subscriber[T] implements the subscriber interface. But Subscriber[TransferCompleted] and Subscriber[AccountFrozen] are different concrete types , so Go generates separate interface plumbing for each. When a concrete type is stored in an interface, Go builds an itab — an interface method table mapping the interface's methods to that concrete type's implementations, so a call like sub.dispatch(...) can find the right code at runtime. There's one itab per (interface, concrete type) pair. If Subscriber[T] implements subscriber, you get a fresh itab for every event type T ever used — plus a generic method body (a "stencil") per type shape. Each is only tens of bytes, but Tailscale's node software ships on every device and defines many event types, so "per-type" overhead in the binary is real and worth removing. The fix is to make a single, non-generic type implement the interface, so there's exactly one itab regardless of how many event types exist. That type is subscriberCore: But subscriberCore is non-generic — it still can't do the assertion itself. So how does its dispatch reach the one place that can , the

chTitle: In-Process Pub/Sub: Building an Event Bus
heading: Problem 6 → SubscriberFunc: a friendlier API
text: Last part, and this one's a convenience, not a correctness fix. With Subscribe[T], the caller gets back a Concurrent publishers → no agreed order. One goroutine draining one channel imposes the single "true timeline." The non-generic pump can't do evt.(T). Carry events in PublishedEvent/DeliveredEvent and route to a non-generic subscribeState; defer every assertion to a generic edge. Per-subscription goroutines reorder across subscriptions. One Client = one subscribeState = one goroutine = ordered across all its subscriptions. A non-generic subscribeState must call a generic subscriber. The subscriber interface is the bridge that names no T. A slow subscriber stalls the whole pump. A multi-way select keeps accepting into a queue so upstream never blocks on one laggard. One itab per Subscriber[T] bloats the binary. A single non-generic subscriberCore implements the interface once; a closure captured where T lives reaches dispatchTyped for the assertion. Now re-read the file listing from the top of this section. Bus, Client, subscribeState, subscriber, Subscriber[T], subscriberCore, SubscriberFunc[T], PublishedEvent, DeliveredEvent, dispatch/dispatchFunc/dispatchTyped — not overkill.

Add a third Meridian event type, LimitRaised , a subscriber for it, and publish one — without changing a single line of Bus, Publisher, Subscriber, or Subscribe. The point: a correct bus is closed to modification and open to new event types. That you added a whole new event flow with only application code — no edit to the bus — is the proof the design is right. The map[reflect.Type] keys itself on the new type automatically; Subscribe[LimitRaised] registers under a key that didn't exist a moment ago and the pump routes to it with no special case. desc: Event sourcing, CQRS, the outbox and reconciliation; then Kafka deep: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, rebalancing and partition-key design.
text: Listen up, sport. We just covered the theory of messaging — topics, queues, delivery guarantees. Adorable foundation. Now we're going to build something that actually runs real payments at scale, because theory without architecture is just philosophy, and philosophy doesn't clear ACH. You are going to leave this chapter understanding why the payments system you're building stores facts instead of states, why your read models are separate from your write models, and — most importantly — how Kafka turns a partition offset into one of the most elegant ordering guarantees in distributed systems. By the time we're done, you'll be able to design partition keys like you've been doing it for years. Which you haven't. But you will. Let's go.

heading: The Event-Driven Paradigm
text: In event-driven architecture , services communicate by publishing and consuming events — immutable records of things that happened — through a durable broker instead of calling each other directly. The producer fires and forgets; consumers react on their own schedule. This decouples operational availability: a crashed consumer doesn't block the producer, and new consumers can replay the event log without any producer changes. We need it because synchronous HTTP coupling turns every downstream outage into a payments outage. Here's the scene: your payments system has a dozen services — account-service, ledger-service, notification-service, fraud-service, analytics-service. Every time a payment completes, all of them need to know. The naïve implementation has payment-service making five synchronous HTTP calls in sequence. You ship it. Three weeks later, notification-service has a bad deploy, and suddenly payments stop processing because your synchronous call is timing out. You've coupled your write path to the operational health of every downstream consumer. That's not architecture. That's a hostage situation. Event-driven architecture breaks that coupling. The rule is simple: produce

heading: Events are facts, not commands
text: An event is an immutable, timestamped record of something that already happened: payment.completed, account.credited. It is not a command and carries no expectation of a response. Events are facts — you cannot un-publish them, and consumers must handle them idempotently because a broker may deliver them more than once. An event is an immutable record of something that happened in the past. It is not an instruction. Tells a service what to do. ProcessPayment. SendEmail. The producer knows the consumer and expects a response. Records what happened. payment.completed. account.credited. The producer knows nothing about consumers — it just records the fact. Asks for current state. Separate from both — we'll formalize this split with CQRS. The naming matters. send payment email is a command disguised as an event — you're still coupling the producer to the consumer's behavior. payment.completed is a true event: the producer's job ended when the payment completed. What happens next is none of its business.

heading: The benefits — and the real costs
text: I will not sugarcoat this. Event-driven systems are genuinely powerful and genuinely hard to reason about. Know both before you commit. Temporal decoupling: producer and consumer don't need to be up at the same time. Operational independence: a consumer crash doesn't take down the producer. Fan-out at no producer cost: ten consumers read the same event; the producer published once. Audit trail: every event is a permanent record of what happened. Eventual consistency: consumers may lag seconds or minutes behind. Harder to trace: a request doesn't have a single call stack — it fans out across services and time. Schema evolution is painful: you can't change an event's shape without coordinating every consumer. Debugging is non-trivial: the action and its effect are separated in time. Let's animate what the decoupling looks like at runtime. Compare the synchronous approach to the event-driven one: A distributed system is eventually consistent when all replicas or consumers will converge to the same state, given enough time and no new updates. It does not mean "broken" or "wrong" — it means "not yet." In Meridian's ledger, a payment.completed event processed by the projection worker 200

heading: Event Sourcing
text: Event sourcing is the practice of storing an entity's history as an ordered, append-only sequence of events rather than storing the entity's current state. The current state (e.g., an account balance) is derived by replaying those events from the beginning — or from the most recent snapshot. We need it in fintech because an append-only event log is intrinsically auditable, immutable, and replayable: regulators love it, and it makes "what happened to this account?" a query rather than a forensic investigation. Most databases store current state . Your accounts table has a row per account with its current balance. That's the snapshot you care about today — but it silently discards everything that happened to get there. Event sourcing flips this. Instead of storing the current state of an entity, you store the complete sequence of events that happened to it. Current state is derived by replaying the event log. This is not new to you. The double-entry ledger in Double-Entry Ledgers (Part 3) was event sourcing in disguise: every transaction was an immutable entry; the balance was a sum over those entries. Event sourcing is that pattern applied universally. On the job: You reach for even

heading: The event store
text: The source of truth is the event store — an append-only log of events for each entity. To get an account's balance, replay the events:

heading: Snapshots: don't replay ten million events
text: Replaying the full history is elegant but impractical once an account has ten million events. The solution is snapshots : periodically serialize the derived state and store it alongside the event log. To rebuild state, load the most recent snapshot and replay only the events that occurred after it. Traditional state-storage systems have a deeply uncomfortable property: you can update or delete a row . In fintech, this means you can silently lose history — an accidental UPDATE accounts SET balance = 0 WHERE id = $1 is catastrophic and potentially undetectable. Event sourcing makes this class of bug impossible : the event log is append-only. You can never modify a past event (your schema enforces it with no UPDATE/DELETE grants on the events table). Every balance change is recorded as a new event. Auditors love this. Regulators love this. Your on-call engineers love this because "what happened to this account?" is just a query. The Go implementation leans on this naturally: events are value types (no pointers that could be mutated), the slice is iterated with range (copying values, not sharing pointers), and the running total is a plain int64 — no rounding, no float drift. As of Go 1

heading: CQRS
text: CQRS separates the model that handles writes (the command side — enforces invariants, appends events) from the models that serve reads (the query side — projections optimized for specific query shapes). We need it because the write model optimizes for correctness and the read model optimizes for query performance; trying to do both in one table produces neither. The eventual consistency window between "command succeeds" and "projection updated" is the main trade-off. Event sourcing raises an immediate problem: if the balance is computed by replaying events, how do you efficiently answer "show me all accounts with balance $10,000" or "show me this user's transaction history paginated"? You don't query the event store for that. You project events into purpose-built read models. This is CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation. The insight is simple: the model that handles writes (commands) should be separate from the models that serve reads (queries). They optimize for different things. On the job: You hit CQRS when your dashboard queries start timing out against the same table your transfer handler writes to. The tell is asymmetric load: thousands of balance reads per second

heading: When CQRS is overkill
text: I respect you too much to pretend CQRS is always the right call. It adds real complexity: you now have two models to maintain, event-to-projection consistency lag, and projection rebuild procedures. For a small internal admin tool with five users? Use a single model and call it a day. CQRS shines when: Read and write loads are asymmetric (many reads, few writes — typical for fintech dashboards) Different queries need radically different data shapes (transaction history vs. aggregate balances vs. fraud signals) You need auditability (the event store is your audit log for free) You're already doing event sourcing There is a window between "command succeeds" and "projection updated" during which a read might return stale data. In most fintech systems this is acceptable (showing a slightly stale balance on a dashboard is fine). For operations that depend on the current balance — like a new transfer — you read from the write model (or replay events for that account), not from the projection. Know the difference and design explicitly.

heading: Transactional Outbox & Reconciliation
text: We covered the outbox pattern in Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics (Part 3) . Let's revisit it in the event-driven context, then go deeper on the reconciliation side — because the outbox solves "did I publish?" and reconciliation solves "do our systems agree?" Reconciliation is the periodic process that compares two systems — the authoritative source (e.g., Meridian's event store) and a downstream system (e.g., a balance projection or a partner bank's ledger) — diffs the two, and emits corrections for any drift. We need it because bugs, crashes, and redelivered messages mean systems drift over time even when each individual step was correct. Reconciliation is the safety net that proves eventual consistency actually converges. On the job: You need reconciliation whenever two systems must agree on a number that has financial meaning — your ledger vs. a partner bank's settlement report, your balance projection vs. the event store replay. The failure mode without it is silent drift accumulating until a customer notices a wrong balance.

heading: The outbox: atomic write + publish
text: The core problem: you want to update your database and publish an event to Kafka in one atomic operation. These are two different systems. You cannot do a distributed transaction across them cheaply. So you use the transactional outbox : 1. In a single database transaction: update your entity state AND insert a row into an outbox table. 2. A separate outbox worker reads undelivered outbox rows and publishes them to Kafka. 3. Once published (and acknowledged by Kafka), mark the row as delivered.

heading: Reconciliation: when eventual consistency needs a safety net
text: The outbox solves the publish problem. But what about drift between systems over time? Bugs, crashes, and network glitches mean that sometimes a consumer processes an event twice, skips one, or applies it out of order. Reconciliation is the periodic process that compares two systems and fixes the drift. In fintech, the canonical reconciliation pattern is: 1. Compute expected state from the authoritative source (your event store). 2. Query actual state from the system being reconciled (e.g., the balance projection, or a partner bank's API). 3. Diff the two and identify discrepancies. 4. Emit correction events or trigger repair actions for anything that doesn't match. When a consumer lags and the projection shows a balance that's $50 lower than the event store says it should be, that's not a bug — that's the system being temporarily inconsistent, heading toward eventual consistency. Your job as the engineer is to: 1. Know which invariants must be strongly consistent (a transfer must see the authoritative balance before it executes). 2. Know which can be eventually consistent (the balance projection shown on a dashboard can lag by seconds). 3. Have a reconciliation job that detects an

heading: Kafka Deep Dive — Part 1
text: Apache Kafka is a distributed, durable, high-throughput event streaming platform. A Kafka cluster is a set of broker servers that store event streams in durable, append-only topic partitions . Producers write to topics; consumers read from them at their own pace. Kafka is the dominant event broker in fintech because it gives you: durable storage (events survive broker restarts), replay (consumers can re-read from any offset), fan-out (many consumer groups read the same topic independently), and — with careful partition-key design — per-entity ordering guarantees. The two major Go clients are segmentio/kafka-go and twmb/franz-go; this chapter uses segmentio/kafka-go for examples. With the paradigm and patterns in place, let's go deep on the actual technology. Kafka is the dominant event streaming platform in fintech, and for good reason: it gives you durability, scale, and — with the right partition-key design — per-entity ordering. Understanding why requires understanding its internal model precisely. On the job: You reach for Kafka when you need durable, replayable, high-throughput event streams that fan out to multiple independent consumer groups. The failure mode of getting the

heading: Topics, partitions, and offsets
text: A topic is the logical name for a stream of related events: account.events, payment.completed. A topic is divided into one or more partitions . You publish to a topic by name; the broker routes each message to a specific partition based on the message key. A partition is the physical unit of storage and parallelism in Kafka. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log on disk. Ordering is guaranteed within a partition — messages in partition 3 are always delivered in the order they were produced. Messages across different partitions have no ordering relationship. Each partition is owned by exactly one consumer in a consumer group at a time, which makes the partition both the unit of ordering and the unit of parallelism. An offset is the monotonically increasing integer position of a message within a partition. Offset 0 is the first message; offset 100 is the 101st. Consumers track their progress through a partition by tracking the last offset they processed. If a consumer restarts, it resumes from its committed offset — no message is lost and no message before that offset is re-processed. A topic is the logical name for a stream of related events. payment.completed. account.event

heading: Consumer groups: the unit of parallel consumption
text: A consumer group is a named set of consumer instances that cooperatively read a topic. Kafka's group coordinator distributes partitions across the group's members so that each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in the group at any time. Multiple independent groups can read the same topic simultaneously — each gets its own cursor (offset) per partition. Adding consumers to a group scales throughput up to the partition count; excess consumers sit idle. A consumer group is a set of consumer instances that share the work of reading a topic. Kafka distributes partitions across the group members. The rules: Each partition is assigned to at most one consumer within a group at a time. Multiple groups can read the same topic independently (fan-out at zero producer cost). Adding consumers to a group scales throughput — up to the partition count. A group with more consumers than partitions means some consumers are idle. Each partition is a directory on disk containing log segment files — append-only files where new messages are written sequentially. Kafka never overwrites. Writes are sequential and therefore fast (sequential disk I/O saturates a modern SSD at GB/s). An offset is ju

heading: Rebalancing: when consumers join and leave
text: A rebalance is the process by which the Kafka group coordinator redistributes partition ownership among a consumer group's members. It is triggered whenever the group membership changes: a consumer joins, crashes, or leaves, or a new partition is added. During a rebalance, some partitions briefly pause while ownership transfers. The modern cooperative-sticky strategy minimizes the pause by only revoking the partitions that must change hands — consumers retain their other partitions and keep processing. The classic "eager" strategy revoked all partitions from all consumers and is now deprecated for most use cases. A rebalance happens whenever the consumer group's membership changes: a new consumer joins, an existing one crashes, or one leaves gracefully. During a rebalance, partition ownership is redistributed. This is the part fintech engineers must understand cold, because a rebalance during high-throughput payment processing has real consequences. On the job: A rebalance caused by a consumer crash during ledger projection means some partitions briefly stop advancing. If offset commits were incomplete, those messages replay from the last committed offset on restart. Your UpdateBal

heading: Delivery semantics and idempotent producers
text: An idempotent producer is one configured so that retried produce requests cannot result in duplicate messages at the broker. Kafka achieves this by assigning the producer a producer ID (PID) and tracking a sequence number per partition. If the producer retries a message after a transient failure, the broker recognizes the duplicate PID + sequence-number pair and discards it. For a payment event stream this is not optional — a non-idempotent producer can double-publish payment.completed events under network flaps, leading to double charges. Requires acks=all (RequireAll in kafka-go). Kafka supports three delivery semantics. Know exactly what you're buying: Producer doesn't retry on failure. A message may be lost if the broker crashes before acknowledging. Fast. Never acceptable for payments. Producer retries until it gets an ack. A message may be delivered more than once if the ack is lost after the message was stored. The default. Requires idempotent consumers. Idempotent producer + transactional API. Kafka assigns a producer ID and sequence number to detect and deduplicate retried messages at the broker. Complex to configure; correct for financial message flows. On the job: Most f

heading: Partition-key design: the most important decision you'll make
text: The partition key is a string value attached to each Kafka message that determines which partition it lands in. The broker (or client) hashes the key and takes the result modulo the partition count: partition = hash(key) % numPartitions. The same key always produces the same partition — this is the property that gives you ordering guarantees. For Meridian's account event stream, the right key is the account ID : all events for ACC-001 hash to the same partition, in the order they were produced, processed by one consumer. This is where theory becomes operational. The partition key determines two things simultaneously: which partition a message lands in, and therefore which consumer processes it. Getting this wrong either loses per-account ordering or creates hot spots. On the job: The wrong partition key in a payments system means events for the same account land in different partitions, processed by different consumers in undefined order. A debit can be applied before a credit. The balance projection goes negative. Your reconciliation job catches it — but only after the damage is done. The rule for a payments system: key by account ID . Why? Because ordering guarantees are per-part

heading: The hot-spot problem: choosing keys wisely
text: There is a trap. If your payments system processes accounts of wildly different sizes — a retail customer sends 10 payments a day, a corporate customer sends 100,000 — and they both happen to hash to partition 2, partition 2 processes orders of magnitude more work than others. One consumer instance handles a disproportionate share of the load. This is a hot partition . For fintech, account ID is almost always the right partition key because: 1. It distributes load reasonably well across thousands of accounts. 2. It keeps all events for one account ordered in one partition. 3. A "hot" corporate account only affects one partition, not all of them. You cannot easily decrease the partition count of a live topic (it requires consumer-group rebalancing and potential ordering disruption). Start with more than you think you need — 12 or 24 for a payment events topic is not unusual. Partitions are cheap. Re-partitioning a live system is expensive and risky. This is one of the few places where "over-provision at the start" is the right answer.

heading: Putting it all together: a Go consumer for ledger projection
text: This is the real-world integration — a Go consumer group that reads account.events keyed by account ID and updates the balance projection. This requires a real Kafka cluster, so it's clearly labeled as non-runnable reference code: The ordering of "process then commit" versus "commit then process" is the core of Kafka's delivery guarantee: Commit before processing (at-most-once): If the consumer crashes between the commit and the actual DB write, the offset is already advanced. On restart, the message is skipped. The balance projection is missing that update. For a payments system, this is unacceptable. Commit after processing (at-least-once): If the consumer crashes between the DB write and the commit, on restart it will re-read and re-process the same message. This is why UpdateBalance must be idempotent — the sequence number check ensures a second application of the same event is a no-op rather than double-crediting an account. Exactly-once: Kafka transactions can make Kafka writes and offset commits atomic inside Kafka, which is powerful for read-process-write pipelines that stay within Kafka. They do not automatically include an external Postgres write in the same atomic transa

desc: The Publisher/Subscriber abstraction, messages and the Router, middleware, and implementing CQRS, event sourcing and the outbox with Watermill.
text: Listen up, sport, because I'm only going to say this once: the single stupidest thing a payments engineer can do is couple their business logic directly to a message broker. Today you change Kafka's config and everything rebuilds. Tomorrow your compliance team mandates a different broker and you're rewriting handlers — as if handlers have anything to do with brokers. That is not a problem I have. Ever. Watermill fixes this. It gives you a clean, broker-agnostic Publisher/Subscriber layer so the same handler code runs on Kafka in production and on an in-memory channel during your test suite. Swap brokers by swapping one constructor call. Your logic stays pristine. That's not convenience — that's correctness by design. By the end of this chapter you will have: the Publisher/Subscriber abstraction wired into your brain, the Router (the heart of the whole thing) animated step by step, middleware layered the right way, and a complete CQRS/event-sourcing/outbox flow. We're building Meridian's payments service. Let's go.

heading: Why Watermill
text: Watermill (github.com/ThreeDotsLabs/watermill) is a third-party Go library for building event-driven services. It defines a thin Publisher / Subscriber interface that any message broker can implement, then provides a Router that dispatches messages to handler functions with composable middleware. The payoff: swap Kafka for NATS or an in-memory channel by changing one constructor call — your handlers never notice. Here's the problem we're solving, and it's embarrassingly common. Meridian's payments service publishes a payment.completed event to Kafka. The ledger-projection handler, the notification handler, and the fraud-check handler all subscribe to it. Beautiful. Then someone decides that for the settlement flow you need NATS Streaming, and for the test suite you absolutely cannot be spinning up a real Kafka cluster in CI. Now you have three message-broker SDKs, three sets of connection boilerplate, three subtly different delivery semantics to manage, and a handler that reads Kafka-specific kafka.Message types instead of a clean domain event. You have built infrastructure coupling into your business logic. On the job: Broker migrations are more common than they sound — compliance

heading: Publisher and Subscriber
text: The Publisher/Subscriber abstraction is Watermill's core. Two small interfaces — Publisher (send messages to a topic) and Subscriber (receive messages from a topic) — hide every broker behind the same contract. Kafka, NATS, RabbitMQ, and the in-process GoChannel all satisfy the same two interfaces. Your handlers, Router, and middleware operate exclusively against these interfaces and are therefore broker-agnostic. Everything in Watermill descends from two interfaces. If you understand these, you understand everything that follows. Two interfaces. That's the whole broker abstraction. Any broker that can publish and consume messages can satisfy these two interfaces, and Watermill ships adapters for the most common ones. But let's look at what travels over those channels.

heading: The message.Message
text: A message.Message is Watermill's universal message envelope. It carries a UUID (the idempotency key), Metadata (a map[string]string for trace IDs and headers), and a Payload ([]byte — usually JSON or Protobuf). Critically, it owns the delivery acknowledgement: calling msg.Ack() tells the broker the message was processed successfully; calling msg.Nack() asks for redelivery. The Router calls Ack or Nack on your behalf — handlers just return nil or an error. A Watermill message.Message is a tiny struct with four fields: The Ack() and Nack() calls are the hooks that drive Watermill's at-least-once delivery. We'll animate exactly how the Router uses them in the next section — but the key point right now is that Ack/Nack are on the message, not the consumer . Your handler doesn't call any broker-specific API; it just returns nil (which the Router translates to Ack) or an error (which the Router translates to Nack and optionally retries). On the job: A handler that swallows errors and returns nil always Acks — even on failures. You will silently lose payment.completed events and the ledger will be wrong. Return errors honestly; let the Router and middleware decide what to do with them.

heading: The GoChannel — your test double
text: Watermill ships github.com/ThreeDotsLabs/watermill/pubsub/gochannel. It is a fully in-process Publisher/Subscriber backed by Go channels. No network, no broker, no Docker. It implements exactly the same Publisher and Subscriber interfaces as the Kafka adapter, which means: The handler doesn't change. The Router doesn't change. The middleware doesn't change. Only the constructor changes. This is the entire value proposition — don't let anyone tell you it's more complicated than that. --

heading: The Router
text: The Router is Watermill's central dispatcher. You register handlers with it (AddHandler), add middleware globally (AddMiddleware), then call router.Run(ctx). The Router spawns one goroutine per handler, feeds it messages from the subscribed topic, runs the composed middleware chain, and calls msg.Ack() or msg.Nack() based on the handler's return value. You do not manage goroutines, channels, or Ack/Nack directly — the Router owns all of that. The Router is the heart of Watermill. It's the component that watches subscriber channels, dispatches incoming messages to the right handler, manages the Ack/Nack lifecycle, and runs your middleware chain. Every production Watermill service has exactly one Router.

heading: Handler registration
text: The handler signature is one of the cleanest things in Go: Notice: no broker types, no Kafka offsets, no NATS subjects. Just a function. This is what broker-agnostic looks like in practice.

heading: The Router dispatching a message through middleware to a handler
text: When router.Run(ctx) is called, the Router spawns one goroutine per registered handler . Each goroutine sits in a loop: for msg := range subscriberChannel. When a message arrives, it calls the composed middleware chain (which wraps your HandlerFunc). On success it Acks; on final failure it Nacks. The key implementation detail: middleware composition is just function wrapping . The Router's internal type is: When you call router.AddMiddleware(m1, m2, m3), the Router builds a composed handler: This is the exact same pattern as Go's http.Handler middleware — a decorator chain of functions, each wrapping the next. The outermost middleware runs first on the way in, last on the way out. This is why middleware order matters : correlation-ID must be outermost (so it stamps the ID before anything else logs), retry must wrap the inner logic (so it can re-invoke it), and poison-queue must be the innermost wrapper around the handler (so it catches final failures after retry gives up). As of Go 1.26, the goroutine-per-handler model is efficient: goroutines are cheap (a few KB of initial stack, grown dynamically), and the GMP scheduler multiplexes them onto OS threads without you thinking about

heading: Middleware
text: A message's path through the chain — and what happens when the handler keeps failing: In Watermill, middleware is a function of type func(HandlerFunc) HandlerFunc — it wraps a handler with additional behaviour (retry, recovery, tracing) without the handler knowing. Middleware composes by wrapping: m1(m2(m3(handler))). The outermost middleware runs first on the way in and last on the way out, so order determines behaviour . This is the same decorator pattern as Go's http.Handler middleware chain. On the job: Middleware is the correct place for cross-cutting concerns (retry, DLQ, trace IDs). A handler that implements its own retry loop is not testable, not reusable, and silently breaks when you add a second handler that needs the same logic. Middleware is where Watermill goes from "nice abstraction" to "production-grade infrastructure." The four middlewares you'll use in every payments service:

heading: 1. Retry
text: This directly applies the retry-with-backoff-and-jitter pattern from "Reliability Patterns (Part 2)" — but now it's middleware, applied uniformly to every handler in the Router, without each handler needing to implement its own retry loop.

heading: 2. Poison Queue (Dead-Letter Queue)
text: This implements the DLQ pattern from "Event-Driven Architecture & Kafka (Part 3)." The key insight: a message that fails repeatedly is not the same problem as a message that fails transiently. Transient failures get retried. Poison messages (bad payload, schema mismatch, unexpected data) should be parked for investigation — not looped forever. The PoisonQueue middleware makes this automatic. On the job: Without a DLQ, a single malformed payment.completed event can stall an entire consumer group. The partition offset never advances, the handler loops forever on the bad message, and every subsequent event — valid ones — piles up behind it. The DLQ breaks the loop and lets the partition drain.

heading: 3. Correlation ID
text: The CorrelationID middleware stamps every message with a correlation id in its metadata. When your handler publishes downstream messages (e.g. the ledger entry event), those messages inherit the same correlation ID. You now have a chain from the original payment event all the way through every downstream effect — observable across services, for free.

heading: 4. Recovery
text: Panics in a handler goroutine would crash the goroutine and stall that handler slot forever (messages pile up, offsets never commit). The Recoverer middleware catches panics, logs them as structured errors, and Nacks the message — the Router stays alive and the DLQ catches the bad message.

heading: CQRS, Event Sourcing and the Outbox
text: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) splits a service's write path from its read path. A command mutates state and has exactly one handler (point-to-point). An event announces that state changed and has zero or more handlers (fan-out). In Watermill, the CommandBus routes commands to one handler; the EventBus fans out events to all subscribers. The result: ProcessPayment is a command owned by one service; PaymentCompleted is an event that the ledger, notification, and fraud services each handle independently. The transactional outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem: you must write to the DB and publish an event, but you cannot do both atomically with a single broker call. The solution: write the event to an outbox table in the same DB transaction as your domain write, then have a background process (Watermill's Forwarder ) poll the outbox and deliver to the broker. If the process crashes before delivery, the outbox record survives and the Forwarder retries. You get atomicity without a distributed transaction. On the job: The dual-write problem is the source of "ghost payments" — a payment debited from the account but never reflected in the ledger because the event p

text: Watermill ships a cqrs package that gives you typed command buses and event buses on top of the raw Publisher/Subscriber layer. Think of it as thin, opinionated wiring: Command handler — processes one command, emits events: Event handler — reacts to an event, reads-only on the domain:

heading: The Transactional Outbox with Watermill's Forwarder
text: The transactional outbox pattern ("Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics (Part 3)") ensures that writing to your DB and publishing an event are atomic — you write both in one database transaction, then a background process forwards the event to the broker. Watermill ships the Forwarder component for exactly this. The write path — the "transactional" part: This ties together "Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics (Part 3)" (idempotency key = cmd.PaymentID as msg.UUID), "Event-Driven Architecture & Kafka (Part 3)" (the outbox pattern described for Kafka), and now Watermill's Forwarder as the Go implementation. Under the hood, the Router's goroutine for each handler runs this loop (simplified from the Watermill source): The critical ordering: output messages are published before the input is Acked . This ensures at-least-once delivery of the entire pipeline : if the process crashes after posting the ledger entry but before Acking the input, the input message is redelivered and the handler runs again. This is why your handlers must be idempotent (see "Idempotency & Exactly-Once Semantics (Part 3)") — they will run at least once, and possibly more than once. The msg.Ack() and msg.Nack() c
