heading: THE Classic: Reverse a Linked List (Iterative)
text: If an interview asks exactly one linked-list question, this is it. Three pointers: prev, curr, next. Walk the list, point curr.Next backward, advance all three. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Variations: recursive reverse (O(n) stack space — not O(1)), reverse a sublist, reverse in groups of k.

heading: Floyd's Cycle Detection (Fast & Slow Pointers)
text: Two pointers: slow moves one step at a time; fast moves two. If there's a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow — they'll meet inside the cycle. If fast reaches nil, there's no cycle. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Variations: find cycle start (extend with phase 2), find cycle length.

heading: Merge Two Sorted Lists
text: A classic recursion-or-iteration problem. Compare the two heads; take the smaller one; recurse (or loop). The dummy-head trick eliminates the "what's the head?" special case. Complexity: O(m+n) time, O(1) space (iterative). The dummy-head sentinel is idiomatic — use it whenever "what is the new head?" is a question.

heading: Find the Middle of a Linked List
text: Fast/slow again: when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. Even-length lists: slow lands on the second middle (adjust by stopping when fast.Next == nil for the first middle). Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. A Go ListNode is a heap allocation per node: 16 bytes of ListNode struct plus the allocator header. For a list of N integers, that's N separate heap allocations, scattered across memory, each reachable only via a pointer. Traversal is a cache-miss-per-node on any real dataset, because sequential list nodes are rarely adjacent in memory. A []int of the same N values is one allocation — a contiguous array. Traversal is a sequential memory read, which hardware prefetchers and cache lines handle with ease. For N=1000, a slice traversal may be 10-50× faster than a linked list traversal on modern hardware, purely due to cache behavior. This is why production Go almost never uses container/list for sequences. Slices win. The cases where linked lists win in Go: O(1) mid-list insert/delete when you already have a pointer to the node (e.g., an LRU cache evicting an element — this is the container/list use case); or when elements are very large and copying them on reallocation i

heading: Monotonic Stacks
text: A monotonic stack is a regular slice-based stack with one extra rule: the invariant that elements stay in sorted order (strictly increasing bottom-to-top, or strictly decreasing) is maintained on every push. Before pushing a new element, pop everything that would violate the order. The pop event is not waste — it is the answer: the element being pushed is the next greater (or smaller) element for each thing it evicts. Every element is pushed once and popped at most once, giving O(n) total work for problems that look O(n²) at first glance. Classic applications: next-greater-element, daily temperatures, largest rectangle in histogram, trapping rainwater. Here is where I separate the people who practiced from the people who merely read . heading: Binary Trees & Recursion
text: Let's set a scene you'll actually recognize. You're two hours into an onsite loop. The interviewer slides a piece of paper across the table with a binary tree drawn on it. "Find the maximum depth," they say. Your job isn't to panic — your job is to recognize the pattern in the first five seconds and write clean Go without breaking a sweat. The pattern is this: base case, recurse on children, combine the results .

heading: The TreeNode struct
text: Every LeetCode tree problem hands you this struct. Commit it to muscle memory. No constructor needed. The zero value of a TreeNode is nil, which means "no child." That's the base case for every recursion you'll write. The Go zero value is doing real work here — a leaf node is just &TreeNode with Left and Right already nil.

heading: The recursive mindset
text: Every tree recursion has the exact same skeleton. I don't care which problem it is. The skeleton is: 1. Base case — if the current node is nil, return something sensible (often 0, true, or nil). 2. Recurse left — call yourself on node.Left. 3. Recurse right — call yourself on node.Right. 4. Combine — derive the answer for node from node.Val, the left result, and the right result. Let's animate that skeleton on the simplest useful problem: max depth (also called max height). The key insight: the work happens on the way back up . Going down, you're just asking questions. Coming back up, you're combining answers. Once you feel that rhythm, tree problems become mechanical. Same tree — are two trees structurally identical with identical values? Invert tree — mirror every node's children left-to-right. Symmetric — is a tree its own mirror image? Base case = nil node. Recurse on Left and Right. Combine at the current node. That is the entire genre. O(n) for all four classics — every node is visited exactly once. You cannot do better; you must at least look at every node. O(h) where h is the height of the tree. Each recursive call adds one frame to the call stack, and the deepest path has h frames. Balanced tree: O(log n). Degenerate (linked list) tree: O(n). The isSameTree and isMirror functions check BOTH children being nil first. If you check one nil before the other without checking both, you get a nil pointer panic when you try to read .Val on a nil node. Always guard nil before accessing any field. heading: DFS Traversals
text: DFS — depth-first search — means you go as deep as possible before backtracking. On a binary tree that means you commit to one subtree, recurse all the way to a leaf, then come back up and try the other side. There are three canonical orderings, and they differ only in when you visit the current node relative to its children . Pre-order : visit node → left → right ("process me before my children") In-order : left → visit node → right ("process me between my children") Post-order : left → right → visit node ("process me after my children") Here are all three traversals — recursive AND iterative — in one playground. See how the iterative versions mirror the recursive ones, but use an explicit slice as the stack instead of the call stack.

heading: Why in-order of a BST is sorted
text: This is one of those facts that seems magical until you understand it, and then it's obvious. A BST's defining property says: every node in the left subtree has a value less than the current node, and every node in the right subtree has a value greater than it. In-order traversal visits left subtree → current node → right subtree. That's exactly "everything smaller, then me, then everything larger" — sorted ascending by induction. If you need to recover a sorted sequence from a BST, in-order traversal is O(n) and requires no extra data structure. Serializing a tree (you can reconstruct it from the pre-order list + a BST invariant or structure marker). Also: copying a tree preserving shape — you write the parent before writing the children. Deleting a tree (delete children before the parent, so you never orphan a subtree). Also: evaluating expression trees (evaluate operands before the operator). BST sorted output. Validating a BST: if the in-order sequence is not strictly ascending, the invariant is violated. Iterative post-order is the trickiest of the three. A clean trick: do a "reversed pre-order" (root → right → left) and reverse the output. Or use two stacks. Don't try to do i

heading: BFS by Level
text: BFS — breadth-first search — is the other half of tree traversal. Instead of going deep first, you visit all nodes at depth 1, then all at depth 2, then depth 3, and so on. The data structure that makes this work is a queue : you enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue a node, process it, and enqueue its children. Why a queue and not a stack? Because a queue is FIFO — the first child you enqueue is the first one you process. That gives you level-by-level order. A stack would give you DFS. The "process one level at a time" insight unlocks a whole family of problems. Here's the canonical implementation plus two common variations: right-side view and level averages. The line levelSize := len(queue) is the key to all level-order problems. At the start of each outer loop iteration, len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes at the current level — because we only enqueue children of the current level's nodes. Snapshot it before the inner loop, process exactly that many nodes, and everything you enqueue during the inner loop belongs to the next level. Clean. No sentinel nodes, no two-queue dance. heading: Recursion vs Explicit Stack
text: Here's the thing about recursion: it IS a stack. Your call stack. The Go runtime manages it, grows it automatically, and collapses it when each frame returns. That's convenient right up until the tree has a million nodes in a straight line — then it's a million frames deep and you're leaking memory, or worse, exhausting the goroutine's stack allocation. Converting a recursive DFS to an iterative one is a one-for-one swap: replace the call stack with an explicit slice used as a stack . The algorithm is identical; only the memory manager changes. 0 return out }} / Go goroutine stacks start small (about 2 KB in current Go implementations) and grow dynamically. For typical interview-size trees, you'll never hit the limit. For a degenerate tree with 100,000+ nodes, the exact stack use depends on frame size and compiler/runtime details; it may still be fine, or it may become memory pressure. At very large depths, recursion can exhaust the goroutine stack or the process's available memory. The explicit stack approach moves that memory into a slice you control, where growth and retention are easier to reason about. desc: container/heap in practice, top-K, merge-K, and the running median.
text: Listen carefully, because I'm about to hand you one of the most powerful weapons in the interview arsenal, and most people fumble it because they memorize the API without understanding the mechanism . A heap is not magic. It's an array that lies to you — in the best possible way. It pretends to be a tree while staying flat in memory, and it enforces one iron rule at every insertion and extraction. Learn that rule, internalize the sift-up and sift-down operations, and every "find the top-K," "merge-K," or "running median" problem becomes a pattern you recognize before the interviewer finishes the sentence. Go's container/heap package is, and I say this as someone who could write a better one in an afternoon, clunky . You will implement five methods on a slice type and hand it to the runtime. heading: The Heap Property & Array Representation
text: Here's the thing, sport: every heap tutorial shows you a picture of a tree. Then they show you an array. Then they tell you the tree is the array. And somehow, most people leave still uncertain why. Let me fix that in three steps.

heading: Step 1: the heap property
text: A binary heap satisfies one invariant at every node: a parent's value compares favorably to both its children. There are two flavors: Min-heap : every parent ≤ both children. The smallest value sits at the root (index 0). heap.Pop always gives you the minimum. Max-heap : every parent ≥ both children. The largest value sits at the root. Flip the comparison in Less to turn a min-heap into a max-heap. The invariant does not say anything about ordering between siblings or cousins. That's the key: it's a local guarantee enforced at every parent-child edge, not a global sort. This is precisely why heaps are fast — maintaining a global sort takes O(n log n); maintaining the heap property on one new element takes O(log n).

heading: Step 2: the array representation
text: A complete binary tree can be stored in a flat array with zero wasted space and zero pointers. For a node at index i (0-based): The min (or max) of the entire heap. Peeking is O(1) — just read index 0. Extracting is O(log n). Given index i, left child lives at 2i+1 and right child at 2i+2. No pointers needed — pure arithmetic. Integer division walks back up the tree. Sift-up uses this repeatedly to restore the property after an insert. The array representation only works for a complete binary tree (all levels filled left-to-right). Heaps maintain completeness automatically because Push appends to the end and Pop swaps the root with the last element before shrinking. A seven-element min-heap in array form:

heading: Step 3: sift-up (after insert) and sift-down (after extract)
text: These two operations are the entire mechanism. Everything else — Push, Pop, Fix — is built from them. Sift-up is used after inserting a new element at the end of the array. The new element may be smaller than its parent (in a min-heap), violating the heap property. We fix it by repeatedly swapping with the parent until the property is restored or we reach the root. Sift-down is used after removing the root. The standard trick: move the last element to the root position (to keep the array compact), then sift it down — repeatedly swap with the smaller child until neither child is smaller. Let's animate both. heading: Top-K Problems
text: The pattern: use a heap of size k. Stream elements through it. Maintain only what you need. Pattern name: Fixed-size heap (size k) K largest from a stream of n: keep a min-heap of size k. Pop the maximum when size k. Same complexity. Why a min-heap for k-largest? Because the root of the min-heap is the smallest of the k candidates. If a new element is larger than that minimum, it displaces it. You're always evicting the weakest competitor.

heading: Merge-K Sorted Lists
text: Pattern name: K-way merge with a min-heap You have K sorted arrays (or linked lists). You want one sorted output. The naïve approach — flatten and sort — is O(N log N) where N is the total number of elements. The heap approach is O(N log K). When K ≪ N, that's a massive win. The insight : maintain a min-heap containing exactly one element from each of the K lists — the front element. Each Pop gives you the globally smallest remaining element. Then push the next element from whichever list just donated the minimum.

heading: Merge-K sorted arrays
text: The pattern in four sentences: 1. Push the first element of every list into a min-heap along with a cursor (which list, which index). 2. Pop the global minimum. Append to output. 3. Advance that list's cursor by one. Push the next element from the same list into the heap (if it exists). 4. Repeat until the heap is empty. The heap never holds more than K elements — one per list. Each of the N total elements does one push and one pop: O(N log K). Common variations: Merge-K sorted linked lists (LeetCode 23): same algorithm; store ListNode in the heap instead of a cursor struct Find the smallest range covering one element from each of K lists: add a max-tracker alongside the heap External sort (sorting a file larger than RAM): split into K sorted chunks on disk, merge-K them in streaming fashion In production, merge-K shows up whenever you have multiple shards of sorted data that need to be combined: log aggregation across servers, merging sorted result sets from distributed databases, combining time-sorted event streams. The heap is your answer every time. Once you see the pattern, you can't un-see it.

heading: Running Median
text: This is the interview problem that separates the "knows heaps" engineer from the "lives heaps" engineer. It is one of the most beautiful two-heap patterns ever devised. The problem : numbers arrive one at a time in a stream. After each insertion, return the current median. Why it's hard : a median is the middle value of a sorted sequence. Maintaining a fully sorted structure is O(log n) per insert but requires sorting, and you can't just binary-search an unsorted stream. The insight — two heaps as a balanced partition: Keep two heaps that partition all seen numbers at every moment: lo : a max-heap holding the smaller half of all numbers. Its root is the largest of the small numbers. hi : a min-heap holding the larger half. Its root is the smallest of the large numbers. The invariant: lo.Len() - hi.Len() ≤ 1. When the sizes differ by at most 1, the median is: lo.root (if lo is larger) hi.root (if hi is larger) (lo.root + hi.root) / 2 (if sizes are equal) Insertion algorithm: 1. If the new number ≤ lo.root, push to lo. Otherwise push to hi. 2. Rebalance: if one heap exceeds the other by more than 1, pop from the larger and push to the smaller. lo.root(5), goes to hi. chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
desc: Adjacency lists, BFS/DFS, topological sort, union-find, and shortest paths with Dijkstra.
text: This is interview prep — say that out loud so you're not confused when things get intense. Graphs are the boss level of the algorithms round. They show up in build systems, social networks, navigation, dependency resolution, network routing — the interviewer knows this, and so now you will too. BFS, DFS, topological sort, union-find, Dijkstra: five tools. Each one is exact and non-negotiable. Learn the shape of each, know which one to reach for, and you walk out of the loop with an offer. I've guided people through far worse. Try to keep up.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Representing Graphs
text: Before you can traverse a graph, you need to hold one in memory. There are exactly two standard representations, and the choice matters. The setup. Imagine you're building the dependency resolver for a Go module system. Packages are nodes. A directed edge from package A to package B means "A imports B." You need to figure out which packages to compile first — and whether there's a circular dependency that would make compilation impossible. This graph problem is the spine of every section in this chapter. A graph is a set of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. An adjacency list represents it by storing, for each node, the list of nodes it connects to — in Go, either [][]int (nodes numbered 0…N-1) or map[int][]int (arbitrary node IDs). Space is O(V+E), making it the right default for any graph where edges are far fewer than V². Without a graph structure you cannot express dependency order, reachability, or routing — all of which come up constantly in distributed backend systems.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Adjacency List vs. Adjacency Matrix
text: An adjacency list stores, for each node, the list of its neighbors. In Go that's either map[int][]int (sparse graphs, arbitrary IDs) or [][]int (dense graphs, nodes numbered 0…N-1). An adjacency matrix is a 2-D boolean (or weight) array: matrix[u][v] = true if there's an edge from u to v. O(V + E). Each edge stored once (directed) or twice (undirected). The right default for sparse graphs (most real ones). O(V²). Even if there are only 10 edges in a 1000-node graph, you allocate a million cells. Wasteful when edges are sparse. List: O(degree) — scan neighbors. Matrix: O(1) — just index in. Matrix wins for dense graphs where you ask "does edge u→v exist?" millions of times. List: O(degree) — exactly as many steps as you have neighbors. Matrix: O(V) — you must scan an entire row even if only two cells are set. Add a weight: list stores []Edge where Edge has to int and weight int. Matrix stores the weight directly at matrix[u][v]. Never use adjacency matrix for graphs where V is large and edges are sparse — the O(V²) allocation alone will TLE or OOM. In interviews, state your choice and justify it. chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: BFS and DFS
text: Before the code, watch BFS work the settlement network — level by level, never skipping ahead: Two traversals. Every graph problem is secretly one of these — or a clever hybrid. The scenario. Your module graph is loaded. You want two things: (1) the minimum number of hops from package main to any dependency (to prioritize shallow compilation), and (2) whether any connected component is an island (never reachable from main). BFS answers (1). DFS answers (2). BFS explores a graph level by level , visiting all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1. It uses a FIFO queue, and the first time a node is dequeued its recorded distance is the shortest possible. That property makes BFS the go-to algorithm for shortest paths in unweighted graphs . If you skip BFS and use DFS for shortest-path, you'll get a path — just not the shortest one, and the bug will be silent.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: BFS — Breadth-First Search
text: BFS explores the graph level by level , starting from a source. It visits all nodes at distance 1 before any at distance 2 — which is exactly why it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. The data structure driving it is a queue (FIFO). In Go, a slice used as queue[0] (dequeue front) + append (enqueue back) is the standard BFS queue. It's O(1) amortized append and O(n) overall dequeue, which is fine for interview use; container/list gives true O(1) dequeue if allocations matter. Classic BFS problems: number of islands (treat each cell as a graph node, 4-directional neighbors), clone graph, word ladder (word = node, one-letter-diff = edge), rotting oranges (multi-source BFS). DFS follows one path to its end before backtracking to try another. It runs naturally on the call stack (recursive) or an explicit stack (iterative). DFS does not guarantee shortest paths, but it excels at cycle detection , connectivity , and topological ordering — problems where you need to know whether a path exists, not how short it is. Miss a cycle in a dependency graph and you compile forever; miss it in a payment DAG and you get circular settlement references.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: DFS — Depth-First Search
text: DFS dives as deep as possible along one path before backtracking. It's naturally recursive and naturally expresses problems about connectivity , cycle detection , and ordering . Recursive DFS is cleaner and the default in interviews. Iterative DFS (explicit stack) avoids stack overflow for extremely deep graphs. Cycle detection in an undirected graph: During DFS, if you reach a neighbor that is already visited and is not the parent of the current node, you've found a back edge — a cycle. Cycle detection in a directed graph: Track three states per node: unvisited (0), in-stack (1), done (2). If you reach a node that's in-stack, the graph has a cycle. BFS works by expanding a frontier — all nodes at distance d are settled before any node at distance d+1 is enqueued. The moment you enqueue a node, you record its distance, and since it's the first time you've touched it via BFS, that distance is the minimum. No node at a shorter distance is waiting behind it in the queue — BFS's FIFO property guarantees this. DFS, by contrast, dives arbitrarily deep along one path. It might find a path of length 10 to a node before discovering a path of length 2. The traversal order has nothing to do w

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Topological Sort
text: A topological sort of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is a linear ordering of all nodes such that for every directed edge u→v, u appears before v in the result. It only exists when the graph has no cycles — a cycle means "A depends on B depends on A," which has no valid ordering. In production: your build system, package manager, and database migration runner all need topological order. Get it wrong and you compile a package before its dependency compiles, or run a migration that references a table that doesn't exist yet. A topological sort of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) is an ordering of nodes such that for every directed edge u→v, u comes before v. It only exists if the graph has no cycles. The scenario. Your Go module resolver needs to compile packages in dependency order. If package A imports B and C, and B imports C, then C must be compiled first, then B, then A. That ordering is a topological sort. The algorithm also doubles as cycle detection: if the graph has a cycle, no valid ordering exists and the build fails.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Kahn's Algorithm (BFS-based, in-degree method)
text: In-degree of a node is the count of edges pointing into it. Nodes with in-degree 0 have no unresolved dependencies — they can go first. The algorithm: 1. Compute in-degrees for all nodes. 2. Enqueue all nodes with in-degree 0. 3. While the queue is non-empty: dequeue a node, append it to the result, decrement the in-degree of each neighbor. If a neighbor's in-degree drops to 0, enqueue it. 4. If the result length equals V, you have a valid topological order. If not, a cycle exists. An alternative to Kahn's is DFS post-order: run DFS, and after fully exploring a node (all descendants visited), push it onto a stack. Reverse the stack at the end. Both give valid topological orderings. Kahn's is preferred in interviews because it naturally surfaces the cycle (the count check) and is easier to reason about under pressure. The DFS version is elegant but the cycle detection is subtler.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Union-Find (DSU)
text: Disjoint Set Union (also called Union-Find) answers one question with near-O(1) amortized speed: do two nodes belong to the same connected component? The scenario. You're processing Kafka events that represent new "package imports" appearing live. After each event, you need to answer: "Is package X in the same compilation unit as package Y?" Union-Find lets you answer this in effectively constant time, even after thousands of merges.

chTitle: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Topo Sort & Dijkstra
heading: Find + Union with Path Compression + Union by Rank
text: Every node starts as its own "root." find(x) returns the root of x's component, applying path compression on the way back — every node on the path is attached directly to the root, flattening the tree. union(x, y) merges two components by rank (tree height) — always attaching the shorter tree under the taller one to keep the trees flat. Together, path compression + union by rank give amortized O(α(n)) per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant for any input size you'll ever see in practice. Without any optimization, find could traverse a chain of n nodes — O(n) worst case if every union makes a linked list. Path compression flattens that chain: every node encountered during find is re-attached directly to the root. The next find on any of those nodes is O(1). Union by rank prevents the chain from forming in the first place. The rank is an upper bound on the tree height. By always merging the shorter tree under the taller one, the maximum height grows only as log(n). With both optimizations, the amortized cost per operation is O(α(n)) — the inverse Ackermann function. For any realistic n (up to 10^80), α(n) ≤ 4. It's effectively constant. As of G

heading: Dijkstra
text: BFS counts hops; Dijkstra weighs them. Watch it relax edges outward from Meridian, always expanding the cheapest known node: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source node to every reachable node in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights . It is BFS with a min-heap (priority queue) replacing the plain FIFO queue — instead of "fewest hops," it greedily processes "lowest accumulated cost." The crucial constraint: all edge weights must be non-negative . One negative edge breaks the greedy assumption and silently produces wrong answers. In production: route optimisation (cheapest transfer corridor between settlement banks), network latency modelling, CDN path selection. Use BFS when edges are unweighted; Bellman-Ford when weights can be negative. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source to all nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative weights . It's BFS with a min-heap instead of a plain queue — each time you pull the next node, it's the globally closest unvisited node. The scenario. chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: The scenario
text: You're a backend engineer at a trading platform. You have a sorted slice of int64 timestamps representing when limit orders were placed (millions of them, sorted ascending). A client asks: "Does order with timestamp T exist?" A linear scan is O(n) — that's millions of comparisons on every request. The market moves in microseconds. You need O(log n). That's binary search. The idea: the array is sorted , so at any point you can look at the middle element and eliminate half the remaining search space in one comparison. Repeat until you find it or run out. On the job: every sorted data lookup that needs sub-millisecond latency — index lookups, sorted caches, range queries on sorted IDs — reaches for this. Get the boundary wrong and the service either returns stale data or spins in an infinite loop under load. Binary search finds a target in a sorted collection in O(log n) by repeatedly halving the live search interval. At each step, compare the middle element to the target: if equal, done; if the middle is smaller, the target must be in the right half; if larger, the left half. Because the data is sorted, one comparison eliminates half the remaining candidates. Without sortedness the h

heading: The three things that kill attempts
text: Is it lo mid := (lo + hi) / 2 overflows when lo and hi are both large int values close to math.MaxInt. The safe form — always — is mid := lo + (hi-lo)/2. In Go, int is 64 bits on modern hardware, so overflow is rarer than in C, but write the safe form anyway: it's the same typing cost and it's always correct. When nums[mid] is too small, you set lo = mid + 1 — because mid itself is eliminated. When it's too big, hi = mid - 1 — same reason. If you write lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1, the interval can stop shrinking and you spin forever on two equal elements. The infinite-loop trap: mid := lo + (hi-lo)/2 rounds down , so when lo == hi - 1, mid equals lo. If your update says lo = mid (not lo = mid + 1), the loop never makes progress. Always write lo = mid + 1 and hi = mid - 1 — both sides eliminate mid from future consideration. The three rules that make binary search correct every time: (1) Loop condition — use lo

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: The scenario
text: Same order-timestamp system. Now the client asks: "Give me the first order placed at or after timestamp T, and the last order placed at or before T." That's lower-bound and upper-bound — the pair of building blocks that make every boundary query possible.

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Lower bound: first occurrence (or insert position)
text: The lower bound answers: "What is the leftmost index where nums[i] = target?" This is also called the "search-insert position" — if target isn't present, it's where you'd insert it to keep the array sorted. Reframe: we want the leftmost position where the predicate nums[i] = target is true . The structure: the array looks like [false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true] — all the falses on the left, all the trues on the right. Binary search finds the boundary. Notice the template changed: hi = len(nums) (not len-1) and the condition is lo < hi (not lo <= hi). Why? Because the answer could be "insert at position len" — one past the end — and we need hi to be able to hold that. The invariant is now: "the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]" where both endpoints are possible, and we stop when lo == hi.

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Upper bound: last occurrence
text: Upper bound answers: "What is the leftmost index where nums[i] target?" Then the last occurrence of target is at index upperBound - 1. A lower bound is the first index where nums[i] = target — the leftmost place the target could sit. An upper bound is the first index where nums[i] target — one past the last occurrence. Together they bracket the exact range of any value in a sorted slice, including duplicates. Go's sort.Search(n, f) is the stdlib spelling of lower bound: it finds the smallest index in [0, n) where a caller-supplied monotone predicate f first becomes true. If f is false for every index, sort.Search returns n — a past-the-end sentinel, not -1. You must always guard the result: if i == len(nums) nums[i] != target .

chTitle: Binary Search: On Data and On the Answer
heading: Go's stdlib: sort.Search
text: Go's standard library gives you a generic lower-bound via sort.Search(n, f). It returns the smallest index i in [0, n) for which f(i) is true, assuming f is false for indices before the answer and true after. It uses the same lo Both lowerBound and sort.Search share one mental model: the predicate partitions the index space into [false … false true … true], and you're finding the leftmost true . Once you see binary search as "find the leftmost true on a monotone predicate," every variant falls out naturally — including the answer-space searches in section 4.

heading: The scenario — and the big idea
text: Your platform needs to split a giant log file of n order events into k sequential chunks for parallel processing, minimizing the size of the largest chunk. Or: given a cargo ship with capacity W, find the minimum number of days to ship all packages when you load packages in order. Or: Koko the bear eats bananas from n piles — at speed s bananas/hour — and you need the minimum speed that lets her finish all piles within h hours. These problems look nothing like "search a sorted array." But they share one structure: the answer is a number, and the feasibility of a given answer is monotone. Instead of searching a sorted array for a value, you binary-search the range of possible answers for the minimum (or maximum) that satisfies a feasibility condition. The condition must be monotone : if answer x works, then every answer larger than x also works (or every answer smaller, depending on direction). desc: Permutations, combinations, subsets, N-queens, and pruning the decision tree.
text: Listen up, because this is the part of the interview circuit that separates the pretenders from the genuinely dangerous. Backtracking. The decision tree. The art of committing to a choice, going all the way down, and — when the universe says no — calmly stepping back and trying the next thing. Like me. Always in control. This chapter is interview prep . We are not building production systems here. We are building the pattern-recognition muscle that lets you stare at "generate all permutations" at 10am on a whiteboard and not flinch. Every solution ships runnable. Every complexity is honest — and yes, most of these are exponential. That's not a bug. It's the shape of the search space. Buckle up, sport.

heading: The scenario: generating PIN codes under a constraint
text: You're on the fraud team at a payments startup. A compromised POS terminal issued PINs following a now-known pattern: no digit appears more than once. You need to enumerate every valid 4-digit PIN from a given digit pool so your security scanner can cross-reference against transaction logs. The search space is manageable — but you need all of them, correct and fast. That's backtracking. A systematic search strategy that commits to one choice, recurses into the remaining search space, then undoes that choice before trying the next option. It is the correct algorithm whenever you need to enumerate all valid configurations (every valid PIN, every permutation, every placement of N-queens) and there is no shortcut that avoids examining each possibility. Why it matters: without the un-choose step, you cannot reuse the same path variable across branches — each branch would see the side effects of all previous branches. The conceptual tree that backtracking traverses depth-first. Each node is a partial state (a path built so far); each edge is one choice (append digit 3). Leaves are either complete solutions (record them) or dead ends (backtrack). The tree is never materialized in memory —

heading: Three moves, one recursion
text: Every backtracking algorithm is exactly three moves repeated until the answer space is drained: 1. Choose — pick one option from the available choices at the current decision point. 2. Explore — recurse deeper, making the next choice inside the reduced search space. 3. Un-choose — undo the choice after the recursion returns, restoring the state for the next option. The mental picture is a decision tree . Each node is a partial state; each edge is one choice. You walk depth-first from the root toward the leaves. When you hit a leaf (a complete solution) you record it. When you hit a dead end (constraint violated, no options left), you backtrack — climb back up one level and take the next branch. You exhaust the entire tree.

heading: The universal Go skeleton
text: The append([]int , path...) copy on the base-case line is the most important line in this entire chapter. Go slices are headers over a shared backing array. If you write result = append( result, path), every collected result ends up pointing at the same underlying array — and you'll watch your answers silently corrupt as later mutations overwrite earlier ones. We'll show this trap live in the UnderTheHood block. A Go slice is a three-word value: (pointer, length, capacity). Backtracking mutates the same underlying array in-place across every recursive call — appending to grow path, then shrinking len to un-choose. If you store the slice header without copying (result = append(result, path)), every stored result shares that same array and will be overwritten by future mutations. Fix: slices.Clone(path) or append([]int , path...) allocates a fresh array snapshot that backtracking can never touch. Why it bites everyone: the bug is invisible when you look at results immediately — they look correct. heading: Generate all subsets (the power set)
text: Scenario: An options-pricing engine needs to evaluate the PnL impact of every possible subset of a risk-factor set. Given n factors, that's 2^n subsets. Small n, enormous business value — enumerate them all. Pattern: At each element, make a binary choice — include it or exclude it. Use a start index to march forward through the array without revisiting earlier elements (prevents duplicates). Complexity: Time O(2^n n) — 2^n subsets, each takes O(n) to clone. Space O(n) call stack + O(2^n n) for results. Variations: Subsets with duplicates (LeetCode 90): sort first, then skip duplicates at the same recursion level with if i start && nums[i] == nums[i-1] . Subsets of a given size k : add if len(path) == k as your leaf condition.

heading: Combinations: choose k from n
text: Pattern: Same start-index trick, but only record when len(path) == k. Complexity: Time O(C(n,k) k) — number of combinations times the clone cost. Space O(k) call stack.

heading: Combination Sum: reuse allowed
text: Scenario: A cashier system needs every way to make exact change for a target amount using a given coin denominations set, with unlimited coins per denomination. Key difference from combinations: pass i (not i+1) to allow reusing the same element. Complexity: Time O(N^(T/M)) where T is target and M is the smallest candidate — roughly exponential in depth. Space O(T/M) call stack. Pass start to avoid revisiting earlier elements and generating duplicate sets. The single biggest source of confusion in this family of problems. Pass i to allow reuse (combination sum), i+1 to forbid it (combinations, subsets). One character, two entirely different problems. Sort candidates before backtracking so you can break early when the current candidate already exceeds the remaining budget. Free pruning. Subsets with duplicates (LeetCode 90): sort first, then skip at the loop level with if i start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]. The i start guard is crucial — it skips duplicates only at the same depth, not across depths. --

heading: All orderings of distinct elements
text: Scenario: A payments router needs to try every ordering of settlement channels to find which sequence has the lowest total fee. Given n channels, there are n! orderings. Pattern: Unlike subsets, permutations care about order. Use a used boolean array (indexed by position in nums) to track which elements are already on the path. Complexity: Time O(n! n) — n! permutations, O(n) to clone each. Space O(n) for the used array and call stack.

heading: Permutations with duplicates
text: When nums contains repeated elements, the naive algorithm generates duplicate permutations. The fix: sort first, then skip an unused element if it equals its predecessor (and that predecessor is unused at this level). Complexity: Time O(n! n) worst case, but pruning eliminates duplicate branches early. heading: N-Queens: the classic
text: Scenario: A hardware security module (HSM) needs to place n independent signing threads on an n x n grid of processing slots such that no two threads share a row, column, or diagonal — to prevent timing-based side-channel attacks. Model it as N-queens. Pattern: Place one queen per row. For each row, try every column; skip columns/diagonals already attacked. No need for a full board matrix — three boolean arrays (or sets) track which columns and diagonals are occupied. Complexity: Time O(n!) — at row 0 you have n choices, row 1 at most n-1, and so on. Space O(n) for the three mark arrays plus call stack.

Mark cells as visited by temporarily overwriting them (the classic Go trick to avoid an extra visited array), then restore on backtrack. Complexity: Time O(m n 4^L) where L is the word length — we start from every cell and explore 4 directions for each character. Space O(L) call stack. Three bool arrays for columns, \ diagonals, and / diagonals give O(1) conflict checks. No board scanning needed. Overwrite the cell with to mark visited inline; restore on backtrack. Avoids allocating a separate visited grid. For existence problems (word search), return true as soon as any branch succeeds — no need to explore the full tree. In the word search, after restoring board[r][c] = tmp, the OR chain bt(...) bt(...) ... short-circuits — if the first direction finds the word, the others are never called. This is implicit pruning. --

heading: The difference between TLE and AC
text: Skipping an entire subtree of the decision tree the moment you can prove no leaf in it can be valid . Example: in combination sum, once the current candidate exceeds the remaining target (and candidates are sorted), every subsequent candidate also exceeds it — break immediately rather than recurse into each one. Why it matters: pruning does not change the worst-case complexity, but it destroys the constant factor. The difference between TLE and AC on a backtracking problem is almost always a missing pruning condition. Pruning is cutting branches off the decision tree before exploring them — because you can already tell they cannot lead to a valid solution. Without pruning, backtracking is correct but often laughably slow. With it, the same skeleton goes from TLE to milliseconds on real input. The rule: any time you can prove that no leaf reachable from the current node can be valid, return immediately without recursing.

desc: Memoization vs tabulation, 1-D and 2-D tables, and classics: knapsack, LCS, edit distance, coin change.
text: Let me be direct with you, sport, because I respect your time and mine: dynamic programming is the topic that turns a mediocre interview candidate into a puddle on the floor. Every recruiter knows it. Every hiring manager knows it. The candidate who walks in, sees "coin change," and confidently derives the recurrence on a whiteboard in four minutes ? That person gets the offer. That's going to be you. Not because I'm nice — I'm not — but because I refuse to send anyone into an interview who learned DP from a YouTube video and can't explain why the table fills the way it does. This is interview prep . We are not building a payment service today. We're building the one skill that separates engineers who "get" DP from engineers who "memorize" DP — and only one of those groups can handle a problem they've never seen before. By the end, you'll derive the recurrence yourself, every time, from first principles. I set that standard personally.

heading: The DP Mindset
text: Here is the truth about dynamic programming that nobody tells you upfront, because they're afraid it'll sound too simple: DP is just recursion — but you refuse to recompute what you've already solved. That's it. The rest is engineering discipline around how you store the answers and which order you compute them in.

heading: Two conditions: know them cold
text: Before you write a single line of DP code, you must confirm two things about the problem: The same subproblem — the same input to the same recursive call — is solved more than once in the naive recursion tree. For Fibonacci: fib(3) appears as a subtree under both fib(5) and fib(4). That redundancy is what caching eliminates. If every subproblem is unique, divide-and-conquer (merge sort, binary search) is sufficient — DP adds no benefit. The optimal solution to the whole problem can be constructed from optimal solutions to its subproblems . For shortest path: the optimal route from A to C through B requires the optimal route from A to B. Without this property, a locally optimal sub-answer doesn't help you globally — DP gives the wrong answer or no speedup. Greedy algorithms also require optimal substructure, but without the overlap condition. Both must hold. Miss either one and DP gives you the wrong answer, or no speedup at all.

heading: Fibonacci: the gateway drug
text: The simplest example of both conditions is Fibonacci. You've seen it a hundred times. See it again — this time, watch the computation tree. For fib(5), the call tree looks like this: The two approaches to eliminating that waste are memoization (top-down: cache as you recurse) and tabulation (bottom-up: build the table iteratively). We'll cover both in depth. First, the repeatable method for deriving the recurrence — because that's the hardest part and nobody teaches it properly. You write the natural recursion and add a cache — typically a map in Go. On each call, check the cache first; if there's a hit, return the stored answer. If not, compute it, store it, return it. The recursion tree still exists conceptually, but each unique subproblem is computed exactly once. Downside: function-call overhead, potential stack depth, and the cache lookup constant. Upside: you only compute the states you actually reach — useful when the state space is sparse. You fill a table iteratively , starting from the base cases and working toward the answer. No recursion, no call stack. Each cell is filled exactly once, in an order that guarantees its dependencies are already filled. Faster constant fac

heading: How to derive any recurrence (the repeatable method)
text: Every DP problem yields to the same four questions asked in order: 1. Define the state. What does dp[i] (or dp[i][j]) mean ? Write it in English. "The minimum number of coins to make amount i." If you can't say it in one sentence, your state is wrong. 2. Ask: what's the last decision? For each state, think about the last choice made to reach it. For coin change: "the last coin added was denomination c." 3. Write the transition. Express the current state as a function of smaller states: dp[i] = min(dp[i-c] + 1) for all valid c. 4. Identify base cases and the answer. Where does the table start (base case)? Where is your final answer (often dp[n] or dp[m][n])? Apply these four questions to every problem in this chapter. By the fifth time, it'll be automatic. Same smaller problems recur multiple times in the recursion tree. Caching them is the entire speedup. Optimal answer for the whole = built from optimal answers to sub-parts. Greedy has it too, but without overlap. Top-down (memoization): recurse + cache. Bottom-up (tabulation): iterate from base cases up. Same complexity, different code shape. The single most important DP skill. Wrong state = wrong recurrence. Spend 60% of your th

heading: Memoization (Top-Down)
text: Memoization is the easier first step. You write the natural recursion — the one that falls straight out of the recurrence — and then add a cache. When the function is called with the same arguments again, you return the stored answer instead of recomputing.

heading: Climbing stairs
text: Problem: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways to reach step n? State: dp[i] = number of ways to reach step i. Last decision: the last step taken was 1 or 2. Transition: dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] (came from one step below or two steps below). Base cases: dp[0] = 1 (one way to be at ground), dp[1] = 1. Watch the table fill bottom-up — every cell computed exactly once, each from the two cells the gopher already filled:

heading: House robber
text: Problem: Houses in a row, each with a value. You can't rob two adjacent houses. Maximize loot. State: dp[i] = max loot from houses 0..i. Last decision: rob house i or skip it. Transition: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]). Base cases: dp[0] = nums[0], dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]). The naive recursion for Fibonacci creates a binary tree of calls. At depth k, there are up to 2ᵏ nodes — hence O(2ⁿ) total. The key insight is that the number of distinct inputs is tiny : for fib(n), there are only n+1 distinct arguments (0 through n). Each unique argument is computed exactly once and stored. Every subsequent call with the same argument is a map lookup: O(1). So the total work is: (number of distinct states) × (work per state, excluding recursive calls) = n × O(1) = O(n) . This generalizes: if a problem has S distinct states and each state takes T work to compute (assuming child states are already cached), memoization costs O(S × T). For 2-D DP, S = m × n states each taking O(1) to fill → O(m × n) total. In Go (as of 1.24), a map[int]int lookup is O(1) amortized with small constant. For a slice-backed table it's a direct index → faster constant, which is why tabulation is often pre

heading: Tabulation (Bottom-Up)
text: Tabulation flips memoization on its head. Instead of recursing down and caching on the way back up, you fill a table from the base cases upward , ensuring that when you compute dp[i], every smaller state it depends on is already in the table. Advantages over memoization: No function call overhead or call stack — iterative loops are faster in practice. No risk of stack overflow on large inputs (goroutine stacks start small and grow, but deep recursion still consumes stack memory). Easier to spot and apply space optimizations (rolling array — covered in Section 6). The discipline: every tabulation solution needs four labeled components. Say them aloud: 1. State — what does dp[i] mean? 2. Transition — how does dp[i] depend on smaller indices? 3. Base case — what cells are filled before the loop starts? 4. Answer location — which cell holds the final answer?

heading: Fibonacci via tabulation
text: The right panel also shows the space-optimized form (O(1) space) — we'll derive that rigorously in Section 6.

heading: 1-D DP Classics
text: These four problems appear repeatedly in interviews. Each follows the same derivation ritual.

heading: Coin change — minimum coins
text: Problem: Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins to make that amount. Infinite supply of each denomination. State: dp[i] = minimum coins to make amount i. Last decision: the last coin added had denomination c. Transition: dp[i] = min(dp[i-c] + 1) for all c in coins where c Complexity: Time O(amount × len(coins)), Space O(amount). Common variations: count ways (not min), unbounded vs. 0/1 (can't reuse), exact change.

heading: Longest increasing subsequence
text: Problem: Given nums, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (need not be contiguous). State: dp[i] = length of LIS ending at index i. Last decision: which previous element j did we extend from. Transition: dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1) for all j Complexity: Time O(n²), Space O(n). There's an O(n log n) variant using binary search — worth knowing for follow-up questions.

heading: Decode ways
text: Problem: A string of digits ("12" = 'AB', "1" = 'A', "26" = 'Z'). Count the number of ways to decode it. State: dp[i] = number of ways to decode the first i characters. Transition: dp[i] += dp[i-1] if s[i-1] is a valid single-digit decode ('1'-'9'); dp[i] += dp[i-2] if s[i-2:i] is a valid two-digit decode ('10'-'26'). Base cases: dp[0] = 1 (empty string, one way), dp[1] = 1 if s[0] != '0' else 0. Complexity: Time O(n), Space O(n) → reducible to O(1) with two variables. If the problem asks for min/max/count over a linear sequence and each position depends only on a fixed number of earlier positions, it's almost certainly 1-D DP. The giveaways: "you can't pick adjacent," "use at most k items," "partition into segments." Define state, ask last decision, write the transition.

heading: 2-D DP Classics
text: Here's where interviews separate the people who memorized a few problems from the people who actually understand the technique. 2-D DP has the same four-question framework — the table just has two dimensions.

heading: Unique paths on a grid
text: Problem: Robot starts at top-left of an m × n grid, can only move right or down. How many paths to bottom-right? State: dp[r][c] = number of paths from (0,0) to (r,c). Transition: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] (arrived from above or from the left). Base cases: entire top row and left column = 1 (only one way to reach any cell in those). Answer: dp[m-1][n-1]. Complexity: Time O(m × n), Space O(m × n) → reducible to O(n) (see Section 6).

heading: Longest common subsequence (LCS)
text: Problem: Given strings s and t, find the length of their longest common subsequence (not necessarily contiguous). State: dp[i][j] = LCS length of s[0..i-1] and t[0..j-1]. Transition: If s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 (last chars match, extend). Else: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (skip one char from either string). Base cases: dp[0][j] = 0 and dp[i][0] = 0 (empty string has LCS 0 with anything). Answer: dp[m][n]. Complexity: Time O(m × n), Space O(m × n). Variations: Longest common substring (must be contiguous — different recurrence), shortest common supersequence, print the actual subsequence (backtrack through the table).

heading: Edit distance (Levenshtein)
text: Problem: Given words s and t, find the minimum number of operations (insert, delete, replace a single character) to transform s into t. State: dp[i][j] = min operations to transform s[0..i-1] into t[0..j-1]. Transition: If s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (no operation needed). Else: dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (replace, delete from s, insert into s). Base cases: dp[i][0] = i (delete all of s), dp[0][j] = j (insert all of t). Answer: dp[m][n]. Complexity: Time O(m × n), Space O(m × n).

heading: 0/1 Knapsack
text: Problem: Given n items, each with weight w[i] and value v[i], and a knapsack capacity W. Pick items to maximize total value without exceeding capacity. Each item used at most once (0/1). State: dp[i][w] = max value using items 0..i-1 with capacity w. Last decision: include item i-1 or exclude it. Transition: Exclude: dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]. Include (if weights[i-1] Complexity: Time O(n × W), Space O(n × W) → reducible to O(W) (see Section 6). Common variations: unbounded knapsack (items can repeat — use a 1-D DP, iterate capacity forward), fractional knapsack (greedy, not DP), subset sum (values equal weights). For 0/1 knapsack (each item once), when you optimize to 1-D, iterate capacity backward (high to low). This ensures you don't use the same item twice in the same row. For unbounded knapsack (items can repeat), iterate forward . Mixing these up is the 1 knapsack bug in interviews — and yes, I've seen it cost offers.

heading: Space Optimization
text: If you got through Section 5, you know DP. This section is what makes you dangerous : most 2-D DP tables can be reduced to a 1-D array, cutting space from O(m × n) to O(n). Interviewers love asking for this as a follow-up. The key observation: for most 2-D DP problems, dp[i][j] depends only on the previous row (dp[i-1][...]) and/or the current row (dp[i][j-1]). You don't need to keep all m rows — just the current row and the previous row (or often just one row, overwritten carefully).

heading: Rolling array: unique paths (2-D → 1-D)
text: Original: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]. Each cell depends on the row above and the cell immediately to the left. We need only the previous row.

heading: Rolling array: LCS (2-D → 1-D)
text: LCS needs the diagonal element dp[i-1][j-1] as well. We preserve it using a temporary variable: For 0/1 knapsack with a 1-D dp array of length W+1, the transition for item i is: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-wi] + vi). The critical question is: after you update dp[w], does dp[w-wi] still mean "without item i" or "possibly with item i"? If you iterate w from wi to W (ascending), when you compute dp[w], dp[w-wi] was already updated in this same pass — meaning it may already include item i. That gives the unbounded knapsack (each item can be used multiple times). If you iterate w from W down to wi (descending), when you compute dp[w], dp[w-wi] hasn't been updated yet in this pass — it still reflects the state without item i. That gives the 0/1 knapsack . This is a one-line difference that completely changes the semantics. The compiler gives you zero warning. The tests with small inputs often pass either way. This is exactly the kind of subtle correctness bug that kills you on a real coding interview or, worse, in a real scheduling or allocation system. Go 1.24's range n syntax makes the loop direction explicit — use it deliberately. --

heading: Exercises
text: You've watched the table fill. Now you fill it yourself — on the whiteboard in your head first, then in the editor. That's the order. Always. Given an m × n grid of non-negative integers, find the path from top-left to bottom-right (moving only right or down) that minimizes the sum of all numbers along the path. Return that minimum sum. Example: grid = [[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]] → 7 (path: 1→3→1→1→1). Define the state and transition before you write any code. State: dp[r][c] = minimum path sum to reach (r,c). Transition: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]). Base cases: dp[0][0] = grid[0][0], top row and left column fill by cumulative sum. O(m × n) time, O(m × n) space. State: dp[i] = number of combinations summing to i. Transition: for each coin c, dp[i] += dp[i-c] (unbounded → iterate coins in outer loop

heading: The Lab
text: Alright, sport. You've watched me derive every recurrence from scratch. You've seen the tables fill cell by cell. You've got the four questions memorized. Now I want to see you do it — without my hand on your shoulder. This is the test I set personally. I take a very particular interest in whether you pass. Two functions. Four questions each. O(n) space for both. The verifier checks allocation counts, not just outputs — you can't fake your way through this one. I'll know. DP = recursion + cache. It applies when you have overlapping subproblems (same sub-input computed multiple times) and optimal substructure (optimal whole = built from optimal parts). Derive the recurrence in four steps every time: define the state (what does dp[i] mean?), ask what the last decision was, write the transition, identify base cases and answer location. Memoization (top-down): write the natural recursion, add a map cache. Each unique state computed once. Great first step. Tabulation (bottom-up): fill a table iteratively from base cases. No stack overhead, easier to space-optimize. Prefer it in production and in follow-up questions. 1-D DP classics: coin change (min coins), LIS, house robber, decode way

desc: Interval scheduling/merging, greedy-vs-DP intuition, and the common bit tricks.
text: Interview prep. Flag it as such. Three patterns that separate the engineers who studied from the ones who merely coded. Greedy algorithms commit — they make the locally-optimal move and never look back. Interval problems look terrifying until you sort and sweep, and then they're trivially linear. Bit manipulation makes you look like a wizard and runs faster than anything you'd write by hand. I built all of these from scratch in a weekend. You'll learn them in one chapter. Lucky you.

heading: Greedy Algorithms
text: A greedy algorithm makes the locally-optimal choice at each step and never revisits it. No table. No backtracking. It bets that local optima compose into a global optimum — a bet that is mathematically provable for some problems and catastrophically wrong for others. At Meridian, the daily settlement scheduler is greedy: it always dispatches the earliest-deadline transfer first. If two transfers share a window, it picks the one that ends soonest and moves on. That works because the problem has the greedy-choice property (proved below). Coin change with arbitrary denominations does not. When greedy fails vs DP: if an early "good" choice closes off a later "better" path, greedy produces the wrong answer and you need dynamic programming. The tell: can you write an exchange argument showing that swapping a greedy pick for any other pick never improves the outcome? If not, reach for DP. Here's the scenario: you're building a rate-limiter scheduler for a fintech API. You have N pending jobs, each with a deadline, and you can only run one at a time. You want to complete as many as possible without missing a single deadline. There is no time to evaluate every possible ordering — the server

heading: When greedy works — and when it lies to you
text: Not every problem lets you greedy your way to the optimum. Two conditions must hold simultaneously: 1. The greedy-choice property — a globally-optimal solution can always be extended by a locally-optimal choice. The thing you pick now never invalidates an optimal future choice. 2. Optimal substructure — the problem's optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems (same as DP, but greedy doesn't need to explore them; it just commits). When those hold: greedy wins. O(n log n) at worst. No table. No memoization. When they don't hold, greedy lies to you beautifully. The coin-change problem is the textbook execution. With US denominations (25, 10, 5, 1) greedy works: pick the largest coin that fits, repeat. With arbitrary denominations — say and a target of 6 — greedy picks 4, then 1+1, totaling three coins. But 3+3 is two . Greedy failed because the locally-optimal coin (4) closed off the better global path (two 3s). That problem needs dynamic programming. The golden intuition: greedy commits, DP explores . If the problem's choices don't paint each other into corners, commit. If they do, explore with DP. A locally optimal pick never ruins a globally optimal completion.

heading: Classic: Jump Game
text: You're on index 0 of an array. Each element is the max jump length from that position. Can you reach the last index? Pattern: greedily track the furthest reachable index. At each position, if you're past the furthest reachable, you're stuck. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. Variation — Jump Game II: find the minimum number of jumps to the last index. Same greedy sweep, but now you count level "boundaries" like a BFS frontier: track the current level's right edge and the furthest reach; when you step past the edge, increment jumps. Still O(n).

heading: Classic: Gas Station
text: A circuit of gas stations. At station i you gain gas[i] fuel and pay cost[i] to reach the next. Can you complete the circuit, and from which station? Greedy insight: if total gas ≥ total cost, a solution exists. Among all starting points, the valid one is the first position after any prefix whose running total goes negative. Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

heading: Classic: Assign Cookies
text: Each child has a greed factor; each cookie has a size. Assign at most one cookie per child, satisfying as many children as possible (a child is satisfied if the cookie size ≥ greed factor). Greedy: sort both. For each child in ascending greed order, assign the smallest cookie that satisfies them. Two-pointer sweep. Complexity: O(n log n) for the sort; O(n) sweep.

heading: Intervals
text: Merging on a timeline — sort by start, then a single sweep: An interval is a pair [start, end] representing a window of time (or any ordered range). Interval merging folds overlapping windows into one: if window A ends at or after window B starts, they share time and collapse into [min(A.start, B.start), max(A.end, B.end)]. At Meridian, every ACH settlement run has a processing window [open, close]; windows from the same counterparty often overlap, and the reconciliation job must merge them before computing net positions. Getting merging wrong means counting the same transfer twice — or missing one entirely. On the job: you hit interval problems whenever two events share a time range — meeting rooms, lock hold times, DB transaction windows, streaming time-series gaps. The merge/overlap check is everywhere; the pattern is always sort-then-sweep. current merged end 6 — no overlap. heading: Classic: Merge Intervals
text: Given a list of intervals, merge all overlapping ones. Sort by start. Sweep: if the current interval's start ≤ last merged interval's end, extend the merged end. Otherwise, push and start fresh. Complexity: O(n log n) sort + O(n) sweep = O(n log n) . end 6", note: "No overlap. Push [8,10] as a new interval. out=[[1,6],[8,10]]." }, , ]} caption="Sort once, sweep once. Overlap check is O(1) per interval because sorted order makes it local." /

heading: Classic: Insert Interval
text: Given a sorted, non-overlapping list and a new interval, insert it in the right place, merging as needed. No re-sort needed. Three phases: copy everything that ends before the new interval starts; merge everything that overlaps; copy the rest. Complexity: O(n) — single pass, no sort.

heading: Classic: Non-Overlapping Intervals (erase fewest)
text: Remove the minimum number of intervals so that the rest don't overlap. Sort by end time. Greedy: always keep the interval that ends earliest — it leaves maximum room for future intervals. Count every interval you skip. Complexity: O(n log n).

heading: Classic: Meeting Rooms II (minimum rooms)
text: Given meeting intervals, find the minimum number of conference rooms required. Approach 1 — min-heap: sort by start. Maintain a min-heap of room end-times. For each meeting: if the earliest-ending room is free (its end ≤ current start), reuse it (update the heap). Otherwise, open a new room. Heap size at any point = rooms in use. Answer = max heap size ever reached. Approach 2 — sweep line: split into start-events (+1) and end-events (-1), sort all events by time (ends before starts on ties), sweep and track the running count. We'll implement the heap approach — it maps directly to container/heap. Complexity: O(n log n). When intervals are unsorted, checking whether any two intervals overlap is O(n²) — you compare every pair. Sorting by start time turns the problem local: after sorting, the only interval that can overlap interval i is interval i+1 (or the current "active" set). You never need to look backwards. Formally: after sorting, for intervals A[i] and A[j] with i j has A[k].start ≥ A[j].start ≥ A[i].end — so you can stop checking once the gap opens. That's why the sweep is O(n): every interval is touched exactly once. The heap in Meeting Rooms II (O(log n) per push/pop) bump

heading: Bit Manipulation
text: Bit manipulation operates directly on the binary representation of integers using CPU-native instructions — no loops, no allocations. The four operators: & (AND — both bits must be 1), (OR — either bit is 1), ^ (XOR — bits differ), and (left/right shift — multiply or divide by powers of two). At Meridian, each transfer record carries a flags uint32 bitmask: bit 0 = settled, bit 1 = reconciled, bit 2 = disputed. Checking flags & (1 XOR has two key properties: a ^ a == 0 (any value XORed with itself is zero) and a ^ 0 == a (zero is the identity). XOR all values in a list; every value that appears an even number of times cancels to zero; whatever appears an odd number of times survives. At Meridian this detects the single transaction ID that appears without a matching pair in a de-duplication pass — one loop, O(n) time, O(1) space, no hash map. The trick generalises: XOR 0..n against all elements in a slice to find a missing number by the same cancellation logic. New scenario: you're reviewing audit logs for a payment processor. Each transaction is flagged with a bitmask of permission categories. You need to check which permissions are set, toggle experimental flags without touching t

heading: The fundamental operations
text: Every trick reduces to four operators: & (AND), (OR), ^ (XOR), (NOT for bitwise complement — in Go, ^x for a single operand), and the shifts (right). Check bit i. Result is non-zero if bit i is set. The mask isolates exactly one bit position. Set bit i to 1. OR with a mask always sets; cannot clear. Clear bit i to 0. Go's AND-NOT operator (&^) is x & mask from other languages. Toggle bit i. XOR flips it: 0→1, 1→0. Clear the lowest set bit. Brian Kernighan's trick. Loops until zero to count set bits. Isolate the lowest set bit only (two's complement trick). In Go, use &^ (AND-NOT) to clear bits — not & ^ (two separate tokens) and not & (C syntax). Also: unlike C, Go defines shift operations for non-negative shift counts; still keep your mask width explicit and prefer uint for bitmasks to avoid sign-extension surprises on right shifts.

heading: Power-of-two check
text: x & (x-1) == 0 — if x is a power of two, it has exactly one bit set. Subtracting 1 flips that bit to 0 and sets all lower bits. ANDing the two gives zero. O(1).

heading: Count set bits (popcount) — Brian Kernighan's algorithm
text: x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit. Repeat until zero, counting iterations. Complexity: O(k) where k = number of set bits (not O(32)).

heading: XOR tricks — single number
text: Every integer in a slice appears exactly twice, except one. Find it. O(n) time, O(1) space. Why XOR works: a ^ a == 0 (same value cancels), a ^ 0 == a (identity). XOR all values; every duplicate cancels, leaving the single.

heading: Missing number
text: Find the missing number in [0..n] given n elements. XOR 0..n against all elements in the slice — everything cancels except the missing one.

heading: Bitmask for subsets
text: To enumerate all subsets of an n-element set, iterate masks from 0 to (1 XOR as carryless addition. In binary, addition is a + b = (a XOR b) + 2 (a AND b). The XOR term gives the sum bits where no carry occurs; the AND term produces the carry. XOR alone is addition where the carry is always discarded — so 1 XOR 1 = 0 (they cancel) instead of 10 in binary. That's why pairs XOR to zero: they have identical bits, so every position cancels. Why x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit. Consider any integer x whose lowest set bit is at position k. In binary, x ends with ...1 followed by k zeros. Subtracting 1 borrows from position k: it clears the bit at k and sets all bits below it — so x-1 ends with ...0 followed by k ones. The AND of these two patterns gives ...0 followed by k zeros at the low end: all bits below k cancelled (one side has 0s, the other has 1s), and bit k itself became 1 & 0 = 0. Every bit above k is unchanged in both, so the AND preserves them. Net result: exactly the lowest set bit of x was cleared, and nothing else changed. Count how many times you can do this before reaching zero — that's the popcount. Both tricks hold in Go's int (two's-complement, 64-bit on modern ha

desc: Pattern recognition, narrating your approach, on-the-spot complexity analysis, and writing clean, correct, idiomatic Go under time pressure.
text: Listen up. You've done the work. You've mastered complexity, two pointers, hashing, stacks, trees, heaps, graphs, binary search, backtracking, DP, greedy — every weapon in the armory is loaded and ready. Most people stop here and think they're prepared. They're not. Because here's the dirty secret of the coding interview: knowing a pattern and deploying it under pressure, in front of a stranger, while narrating your thinking, with the clock running — that is an entirely different skill. And it is one that almost nobody teaches. I'm going to teach it. This chapter is about the meta-game: reading a prompt and immediately knowing which pattern it's asking for, narrating your process so the interviewer scores your thinking (not just your final code), analyzing complexity on the spot, and writing clean idiomatic Go when your hands are shaking. Then we'll walk one complete problem from first read to final analysis, end to end, the way I'd do it. By the end of this appendix, you will be interview-ready. Not "pretty good." Ready. — This chapter is Appendix Track: the interview craft capstone. If you're here, you've earned it.

heading: Every prompt is wearing a disguise
text: Here's the thing, sport: the people who write interview problems are not trying to trick you. They're using the same signal words, the same shapes, the same structures — over and over. Your job is to strip the costume off the prompt and see the pattern underneath. The moment you recognize the pattern, you have the template. And the template is already in your head. Pattern recognition is the skill of reading a problem prompt and matching its signal keywords and structural shape to a known algorithm template — without having to solve the problem from scratch. A prompt that says "sorted array + two values" fires the two-pointer template; "top K" fires the heap template. The interview win isn't solving novel problems — it's classifying familiar patterns fast, then executing a template you've already internalized. I've distilled the entire signal map into one decision guide. Study it. Then you won't have to think — you'll just know. Two pointers. One starts at the left, one at the right, they move toward each other. Keywords: "sorted," "pair that sums to target," "palindrome check," "remove duplicates in place," "squeeze a window." Binary search if the pointer movement is logarithmic r

heading: The classification decision flow
text: Watch the prompt pass through each signal filter in sequence. The first one that fires is your pattern.

heading: Constraint → complexity guide
text: The constraints are not decoration — they are a secret handshake. The problem setter chose those bounds to guarantee exactly one complexity class works. The n ≤ ... bound in a problem statement is a direct signal from the problem setter: it tells you which complexity class your solution must land in . n ≤ 20 means exponential is acceptable — backtracking over all 2ⁿ subsets. n ≤ 10⁵ means you need O(n log n) or better — a full O(n²) scan will time out. Read the constraint first, derive your required complexity ceiling, then pick the pattern that fits. Skipping this step is how engineers code a correct-but-too-slow solution and fail. Exponential is fine. Bitmask DP or backtracking over all 2ⁿ subsets. This is the "small n" signal — embrace it. O(n³) is the ceiling. Think DP over intervals (edit distance, matrix chain), or triple-nested loops. O(n²) just barely fits. Brute-force two-pointer without optimization, O(n²) DP. You need O(n log n) or better.
