heading: The loop that separates good engineers from great ones
text: The interviewer is not grading whether your first thought is correct. They're grading your process : how you handle ambiguity, how you move from naïve to optimized, and whether you can write clean code while thinking out loud. A candidate who narrates a correct process and writes imperfect code beats a silent candidate who writes perfect code every time. The interview loop is the fixed seven-step process every strong candidate runs on every problem: (1) clarify constraints and edge cases, (2) construct an example and trace the expected output, (3) state the brute-force solution and its complexity, (4) name the pattern and optimize, (5) commit to a target complexity before coding, (6) code while narrating every meaningful decision, (7) test and re-state complexity on the code you actually wrote. The loop matters because interviewers score process, not just the final solution — a structured approach with imperfect code outscores silent genius that produces correct code. Here's the loop. Run it every single interview.

heading: What the interviewer is actually scoring
text: Can you break an unfamiliar problem into known sub-problems? Do you identify the key insight, or do you flounder with edge cases first? Are you narrating your thinking, or silently staring at the board for five minutes? Silence is the fastest way to fail an interview you'd otherwise pass. Does your code handle empty input, a single element, negative numbers, integer overflow? Engineers who only test the happy path scare interviewers. Are names meaningful? Is there unnecessary duplication? Would a reader understand what each function does from its signature? Sloppy names signal sloppy thinking. Never say "I know there's a smarter solution but I'm going to go with the brute force" and then code nothing. Either code the brute force or code the smart solution — always have running code on the board. Partial credit exists; blank boards do not.

heading: Time and space — quickly
text: On-the-spot complexity analysis is deriving time and space complexity in seconds, without paper, while narrating to an interviewer. The mental model: for time , count the outer loop iterations, count the work per iteration, multiply (sequential independent loops add, nested loops multiply). For space , count only the extra memory that grows with input — explicit data structures plus call-stack depth from recursion. State both, unprompted, before and after you code. An engineer who can't narrate complexity is a liability in code review; demonstrating it in the interview proves you think about it habitually. You don't need a math proof. You need a fast, correct mental model that produces the right answer under pressure. Here's how I do it. Time complexity: count the work. Ask three questions in order: 1. How many times does the outer loop run? — call it n. 2. For each outer iteration, how much work happens inside? — constant, log n, n, n log n, or n². 3. Multiply. Add if there are sequential independent loops (they don't multiply). Space complexity: count the extra memory. Ask: what new data structures did I allocate that grow with the input? A result slice of size n → O(n). A recurs

heading: The common classes — and what they feel like
text: No loop. No recursion. Direct index or arithmetic. Classic: hash map lookup (average), swap two variables. The search space halves each step. Classic: binary search, one level of a heap sift. Feels like: "I know which half is wrong and throw it away." One pass, every element touched once. Classic: scan an array, sliding window, BFS over a list. Feels like: "I walk the whole thing exactly once." A sort, or n operations each costing log n (heap insert × n). Classic: merge sort, Dijkstra on a sparse graph. Nested loops. Classic: compare every pair, insertion sort, naive two-sum. Fine for n ≤ 10⁴; death for n = 10⁶. Enumerate every subset or permutation. Classic: backtracking without pruning, brute-force TSP. Only acceptable for n ≤ 20. Recursion depth is space. A DFS on a tree of depth d uses O(d) call-stack frames. For a balanced BST that is O(log n); for a skewed one (worst case) it is O(n). Always state the space from the call stack separately from the space from explicit data structures.

heading: The Go reflexes — drill these until they're automatic
text: Even under interview pressure you must write idiomatic Go. heading: Go interview footguns — see them coming
text: Slice aliasing. When you slice a slice, the two slices share the same backing array. Appending to one can silently mutate the other if there's capacity left. In an interview, if you modify a "copy," use copy() or append([]int , original...) to get a true independent copy. Integer overflow. The problem says values are up to 10⁵. You're summing n = 10⁵ of them. The maximum sum is 10¹⁰ — that overflows int32. Use int (which is 64-bit on every platform you'll interview on) or int64. State the reasoning out loud. Empty input. Before doing anything with a slice, ask: "What happens if len(nums) == 0?" A nums[0] on an empty slice panics. Return a sentinel or a zero value. The interviewer will probe this even if the problem statement doesn't. Go's map is a hash table. Under the hood, as of Go 1.24, the standard runtime uses a Swiss Table-style implementation with groups of 8 slots plus control bytes, not separate linked-list chaining. Lookup is: 1. Hash the key → table/group probe path: O(1) amortized. 2. Compare control bytes first, then full keys only for plausible matches: O(1) for healthy tables. 3. desc: The first cluster of common Go mistakes — the ones that quietly rot a codebase: variable shadowing, deep nesting, init misuse, interface pollution and where to declare interfaces, why `any` says nothing, generics misuse, type-embedding traps, the functional options pattern, and package/tooling hygiene — each shown as the bug, the why, and the idiomatic fix.
text: Welcome to the part of the course where I stop teaching you what to do and start showing you the specific, recurring ways Go engineers humiliate themselves. This is a catalog — a field guide to the mistakes I see in real codebases, the ones that pass review because they compile , then quietly rot the thing from the inside. This first chapter is about structure and APIs : the decisions that don't crash today but make every future change harder. Variable shadowing that ships a nil client to production. Interfaces bred like rabbits until nobody can find the actual code. any smeared across a signature so the compiler can't help you. We go bug → why → idiomatic fix, every time, grounded in Meridian's backend. Each fix also points back to the deep chapter where the topic lives. Don't just read it. Internalize it. I'd hate to see your name on one of these. Let's go.

heading: Shadowing & Nesting
text: Two readability mistakes that cause real bugs. First, variable shadowing — re-declaring a name in an inner block so writes never reach the outer one. Shadowing happens when a variable declared in an inner block has the same name as one in an outer block — the inner one hides the outer for that block. The trap: writing x, err := f() inside an if creates a new x (because := declares), so assignments never reach the outer x. Why it matters: the outer variable keeps its zero value (often nil), and you ship a nil client, an empty config, or a dropped result — with zero compiler complaint. Caller gets nil and panics on first use." } ]} caption="Fix: in the tracing branch, write client, err = traced() (assign, declaring err separately) so the OUTER client receives the value. heading: init & Accessors
text: An init() function runs automatically at package load, before main. The mistakes: using it for work that can fail (it can't return an error — you're forced to panic), for things that need ordering or configuration (init order across files is fragile), or for setting up global state that makes the package hard to test . Why it matters: init hides setup and removes your ability to handle failure gracefully. Prefer an explicit constructor (NewX() ( X, error)) you call from main, where you control order and errors. init has real uses (registering a database driver via blank import, setting up //go:embed data), but "open the DB connection in init" is a classic trap — if it fails, your whole binary panics on startup with no recourse. Make it explicit instead: Can't return an error → must panic. Runs implicitly, so failures are invisible and order across files is brittle. Hard to test (no way to skip it). Reserve for driver registration and trivial table setup. ⚠ Don't put db.Open / network calls in init. Use func NewStore(ctx) ( Store, error) and call it from main, where you can log, retry, and fail cleanly. Mistake 4 is overusing getters and setters . Go is not Java — a plain exported f

heading: Interface Pollution
text: The single most common Go API mistake. Engineers coming from other languages create an interface for everything , "just in case" — one interface, one implementation, mock for tests. That's interface pollution , and it adds indirection that buys nothing. Interface pollution is creating interfaces with no real abstraction value — typically one interface per concrete type, defined preemptively. Go's rule is the opposite of nominal languages: discover interfaces, don't design them up front. And declare an interface on the consumer side (the package that uses the behavior), not the producer side (the package that implements it). Why it matters: producer-side interfaces force every consumer to depend on the producer's abstraction; consumer-side interfaces stay small (often one method) and let any type satisfy them implicitly. The proverb: accept interfaces, return structs. Two siblings of this mistake: returning interfaces ( 7) — return the concrete type so callers keep full access and you don't lock the abstraction; and any says nothing ( 8) — next section. Most Go code needs far fewer interfaces than people write. When you do need one, it'll be small and it'll appear where it's used. D

heading: any & Generics
text: any (the alias for interface ) is sometimes necessary, but reaching for it to mean "some type" throws away everything the compiler can do for you. Since Go 1.18, generics give you "some type" with type safety. Generics are not free and not always clearer. Use them when you're writing the same logic over many types — generic data structures (a typed Set[T], a Heap[T]), or functions over slices/maps/cmp. Don't use them when an interface with a method already expresses the behavior (if you only ever call w.Write, take an io.Writer, not a type parameter), or for a one-off. The smell: a type parameter that appears once, or constraints that just re-state an existing interface. Rule of thumb — reach for generics for containers and algorithms , interfaces for behavior . Full treatment: Generics in Go, In Depth.

heading: Embedding & Options
text: Type embedding ( 10) promotes an embedded type's fields and methods to the outer type. Powerful, but two traps: you can accidentally promote methods you didn't mean to expose (embedding a sync.Mutex makes Lock/Unlock part of your public API), and you can leak an embedded type's behavior in ways that break invariants. Embedding is for is-a composition where promoting the methods is the point (embedding io.Reader in a wrapper). It is not a shortcut for "give me these fields." ⚠ Embedding sync.Mutex exports Lock()/Unlock() on your struct — callers can now lock your internals. Make it a named field (mu sync.Mutex), not embedded. The positive pattern in this group is 11: functional options — the idiomatic way to build a configurable constructor without a giant parameter list or a mutable, half-built config struct: This is the pattern behind so many real Go libraries (gRPC, the AWS SDK, slog handlers). It beats a Config struct (which can be passed half-initialized) and a builder (more ceremony). Deep dive: Design Patterns, the Go Way.

heading: Packages & Tooling
text: The last cluster ( 12–16) is hygiene — boring, and the difference between a codebase people enjoy and one they dread. Don't cargo-cult a deep pkg//internal/ tree on day one. Start flat; grow structure when the package boundaries actually emerge. Organize by domain , not by technical layer. A package named utils, common, or helpers is a code smell — it's a junk drawer with no cohesion. Name packages for what they provide (money, ledger), and the contents follow. Don't shadow a package name with a variable (json := ... then you can't call json.Marshal). And avoid two imported packages with the same name without an alias. Exported identifiers need doc comments, starting with the name (// Charge debits...). It's not bureaucracy — it's what go doc and your editor show. go vet + golangci-lint catch a huge fraction of this chapter automatically — shadowing, unchecked errors, suspicious constructs. Not running them is choosing to ship known bugs. ⚠ Wire the linters into CI, not just your laptop. A check that's optional is a check that's skipped under deadline. Shadowing is legal Go: re-declaring a name in a nested scope is a deliberate feature (it's how if v, ok := m[k]; ok works). So the

A slice that shares memory with another and overwrites it behind your back. A "small" slice that pins a megabyte of RAM forever. A map that never gives memory back. A float that says ₦0.30 isn't ₦0.30. This is the tier where Go's biggest sharp edge lives: slices are a window onto a shared backing array , and if you don't understand that, append will eventually eat your data. heading: Numbers
text: Three quick traps before the slices. Integer overflow ( 18): Go's fixed-width integers wrap silently — no panic. Float imprecision ( 19): binary floats can't represent most decimals exactly. And octal literals ( 17): a leading 0 means octal, so 0o600/0600 is 384, not 600. 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 is not a Go bug — it's how IEEE-754 binary floating point works in every language. For a ledger, that imprecision is catastrophic : fractions of a cent drift, and the books stop balancing. The rule, shouted throughout Part 3: represent money as integer minor units (cents, kobo) in int64, or a decimal library — never float64. And when you do arithmetic on user-supplied integers (a transfer amount × a quantity), check for overflow on the way in. See Representing Money — Never Use Floats.

heading: Length & Capacity
text: The foundation for everything that follows. A slice is not an array — it's a small header describing a window onto one. A slice header is three words: a pointer to a backing array, a length (how many elements you can index, len), and a capacity (how many elements exist from the pointer to the end of the backing array, cap). Why it matters: len is what you iterate; cap is the spare room append can fill without allocating . When append fits within cap, it writes in place into the shared array (fast — but it can clobber another slice viewing the same array). When it exceeds cap, it allocates a new array and copies. Almost every slice bug comes from not tracking cap. A related efficiency mistake ( 21) is growing a slice from empty when you know the size: preallocate with make([]T, 0, n) so append doesn't reallocate-and-copy repeatedly as it grows.

heading: nil vs Empty
text: A nil slice and an empty slice both have length 0, but they are not identical — and confusing them causes JSON bugs and pointless nil checks. Pointer is nil, len 0, cap 0. Marshals to JSON null. Perfectly usable — you can append to it, range it, take its len. Non-nil pointer, len 0, cap 0. Marshals to JSON []. Behaves the same for len/range/append. ⚠ Check emptiness with len(s) == 0, never s == nil — an empty-but-non-nil slice is also "empty," and s == nil would miss it.

heading: Append & Aliasing
text: The big one. Because append reuses spare capacity in place , appending to a slice that shares a backing array with another slice can silently overwrite the other's elements. And 24, copying correctly : copy(dst, src) copies only min(len(dst), len(src)) elements — so copying into a nil or too-short dst silently copies nothing or fewer than you think. Size the destination: dst := make([]T, len(src)).

heading: Memory Leaks
text: Slices and maps both pin memory in non-obvious ways. Re-slicing keeps the entire backing array alive, even if your slice views only a few elements — because the slice header still points into that array, the garbage collector can't free it. So returning huge[:3] from a function pins all of huge in memory. Why it matters: a long-lived small slice carved from a short-lived huge buffer leaks the whole buffer. Fix: copy the few elements you need into a right-sized slice (out := make([]T, n); copy(out, huge)), so the big array becomes collectible. The same applies to substrings (a substring shares the original string's bytes — covered next chapter). Maps have their own leak ( 28): deleting entries does not shrink a map's internal storage back to its small form. If a map grows to a million entries and you delete all but ten, it can still retain storage sized for the high-water mark. If you have a map that spikes huge then shrinks, periodically recreate it (copy the survivors into a fresh map) to actually release memory. A small re-slice pins the whole backing array. Copy out the elements you keep. Watch for this when caching a few bytes/items carved from a large buffer or response. delet

heading: Maps & Comparisons
text: Two more. Map initialization ( 27): like slices, give make(map[K]V, hint) a size hint when you know roughly how many entries you'll add, to avoid repeated rehashing as it grows. And comparing values ( 29): == works on comparable types (numbers, strings, booleans, pointers, and structs/arrays of comparable fields) but does not compile for slices, maps, or functions. A slice value is literally a 3-word struct — — passed by value (so a slice argument is a copy of the header sharing the same backing array; that's why a function can mutate your elements but not your length). When append exceeds cap, the runtime allocates a bigger array: historically it doubled capacity for small slices and grew by 1.25× once large (the exact threshold has shifted across versions; don't rely on a specific factor — rely on preallocating). That growth-and-copy is why make([]T, 0, n) matters in a hot loop. Maps are hash tables; deleting entries removes mappings but does not compact the map's internal storage back to its small form, so a map can retain memory sized for its high-water mark — hence the "rebuild to reclaim" trick. As of Go 1.21+, prefer the slices and maps packages (slices.Equal, slices.Contain

text: Two chapters ago we did the mistakes that make code ugly . Last chapter, the ones that lose data . This one is the worst of both worlds: bugs that look completely reasonable, compile without a whisper, and then do nothing you asked. You write acc.Balance += fee inside a range loop, run it, and the balances don't change — because range handed you a copy . You append a UUID to a cache and somehow pin a 4KB log line in memory forever. You call TrimRight(name, "Inc") and it eats the "c" off "Acme Public" too. This is the control-flow and strings tier. The through-line: in Go, a range value is a copy, and a string is a window onto shared, immutable bytes — and almost every mistake here comes from forgetting one of those two facts. Bug → why → idiomatic fix, grounded in Meridian's backend, every time. I have watched people fight the range-copy bug for hours . You're going to see it once and never again. Let's go.

heading: Range Copies
text: The most reliably surprising thing about Go's range loop: the value variable is a fresh copy of each element, every iteration. So mutating it does nothing to the underlying data. In for i, v := range s, the second variable v is a copy of s[i], not a reference to it. Each iteration assigns a new copy into the same variable v. Why it matters: if v is a struct and you write v.Field = x, you mutate the copy — the element in s is untouched. To mutate the real element, index it (s[i].Field = x) or make the slice hold pointers ([] T), so the copy is a pointer to the shared value. Watch a fee that should hit three accounts hit nothing — because each acc is a throwaway copy: The two idiomatic ways to actually write through: index the element, or hold pointers so the copied value is a pointer to shared memory.

heading: Range Args & Pointers
text: Two more range traps. First ( 31): the range expression is evaluated exactly once , before the loop starts — Go copies it into a hidden temporary and iterates over that . Second ( 32): the classic pointer-of-loop-variable trap, which Go 1.22 mostly closed but didn't fully erase. In for i, v := range expr, expr is evaluated a single time before iteration begins, and a copy of it is what the loop walks. Why it matters: for an array (a value type), the loop iterates over a copy — so writing arr[2] = x mid-loop won't be seen by the range. For a slice , the header is copied but it points at the same backing array, so the bound (the length) is fixed at the start even if you append. For a channel , it's read once and ranged until closed. The array case is the sharp one — because an array is a value , ranging over it iterates a frozen copy: Now the famous one. Before Go 1.22, the loop variable was shared across all iterations , so taking &v always gave the same address — and you'd end up with a slice of pointers all aimed at the final element. As of Go 1.26, loop variables are per-iteration (the change landed in Go 1.22 ): each iteration of for , v := range s gets its own v, so &v now give

heading: Maps, break & defer
text: Three independent control-flow traps in one section. Map iteration order ( 33) is unspecified; break ( 34) leaves the innermost statement, which may not be your loop; and defer in a loop ( 35) stacks up until the function returns, not the iteration. Ranging a map visits keys in an unspecified order that may change from one iteration to the next. Two further rules: don't assume insertion order is preserved, and an element added during iteration may or may not appear in that same loop. Why it matters: code that "works" because the map happened to iterate in a convenient order is a flake waiting to happen. Sort the keys if you need order; avoid mutating the map you're ranging — build a second map. Iteration order is unspecified and may vary. Need deterministic output? Collect keys into a slice, slices.Sort it, then range the keys. Never rely on insertion order. break (and continue) act on the innermost for/switch/select. A break inside a switch inside a for exits the switch, not the loop. Use a label . defer runs at function return, not at the end of the loop body. Deferring f.Close() per file in a loop keeps every handle open until the whole function exits. ⚠ Don't insert into a map

heading: Runes & Iteration
text: One string, two iterations — index walks BYTES, range walks RUNES: On to strings — and the first thing to internalize: a Go string is a read-only sequence of bytes , not characters. A rune is the character. Confusing the two breaks the moment you touch anything outside ASCII. A string in Go is an immutable sequence of bytes . A rune is a Unicode code point (an alias for int32). Text is commonly UTF-8, and Go source string literals are UTF-8, but a string value can contain arbitrary bytes. Why it matters: len(s) is the byte count, not the character count — len("汉") is 3. And s[i] indexes a byte (type byte), not a character. The naira sign ₦, an accented é, an emoji — each is multiple bytes in UTF-8, so byte-indexing can split them into garbage. This directly causes the inaccurate iteration mistake ( 37). A plain index loop for i := 0; i i is the byte index where each rune begins (it jumps by the rune's byte width — 1, 2, 3, or 4), and the value is the rune. s[i] is still a single byte . Use the value variable for the character. Iterates bytes . s[i] is a byte. Correct only for pure-ASCII data; on multi-byte text it slices code points apart. Use this only when you genuinely want byte

heading: Trim, Concat & Convert
text: Three string-API mistakes that waste correctness or performance. Trim misuse ( 38) is a correctness bug; concatenation ( 39) and useless conversions ( 40) are performance bugs that allocate behind your back. First, trim. TrimLeft/TrimRight take a cutset — a set of characters to strip from the end — not a literal suffix. People reach for TrimRight(s, "Inc") expecting it to remove the word "Inc", and instead it strips any trailing I, n, or c: Next, concatenation. Strings are immutable , so s += x in a loop allocates a brand-new string every iteration — O(n²) copying. strings.Builder writes into a growable byte buffer and produces the final string once: strings.Builder holds an internal []byte and appends to it — so it suffers the same regrow-and-copy as any slice. If you can compute the final byte length up front (sum the len of each part), call sb.Grow(total) once before the loop to preallocate, exactly like make([]T, 0, n) for a slice. For just a handful of strings, plain += or fmt.Sprintf is fine and more readable — reach for Builder once you're concatenating more than 5 strings, especially in a loop. Finally, useless conversions ( 40). Most I/O is []byte (io.Reader, io.ReadAll).

heading: Substrings & Leaks
text: The string sibling of last chapter's slice-capacity leak — and the subtlest mistake in the chapter. A substring shares the original string's backing bytes . So slicing 36 bytes out of a 4KB log line keeps the entire 4KB alive for as long as you hold the substring. A string is internally a pointer to bytes plus a length. A substring s[a:b] creates a new header pointing into the same bytes — no copy (the Go compiler shares the backing array for speed). Why it matters: if you keep the small substring but drop the original, the garbage collector cannot free the original's bytes — your tiny substring pins the whole thing. To release the rest, force a copy: strings.Clone(s[a:b]) or the string([]byte(s[a:b])) round-trip, which allocates a fresh, right-sized backing array. One more trap stacked on top: s[:5] takes the first five bytes , not the first five characters. On "Hêllo" (where ê is two bytes) s[:5] cuts the ê in half and yields invalid UTF-8. To take the first five characters , convert first: string([]rune(s)[:5]). Bytes versus runes follows you everywhere in Go strings — substrings included. A range loop is syntactic sugar the compiler rewrites into a classic indexed loop with a h

(For a slice of structs you'd write prices[i].Field = ...; the same rule applies.) This is the 30 mistake in its purest form. This is meant to stop scanning at the first failed charge, but it scans every charge. Fix it with a label. The bare break exited the switch, not the for, so the loop kept going. desc: Function, method, and error-handling mistakes: choosing value vs pointer receivers, named result parameters and their deferred-mutation side effects, the typed-nil receiver that makes err != nil lie, taking an io.Reader instead of a filename, how defer evaluates its arguments and receiver up front; then error management — when to panic, wrapping with %w, checking with errors.Is/errors.As instead of ==/type assertion, not handling an error twice, and not swallowing deferred Close errors.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Most of the bugs in this chapter don't crash, don't get flagged, and don't even look wrong. They smile at you in review. Then they ship — and they lie. A function returns "no error," your if err != nil agrees, and a failed transfer gets recorded as a success. That's not a typo. That's a betrayal , dressed up as working code. This chapter is about functions, methods, and errors — the connective tissue of every Go program, and the place where Go's small, sharp design choices punish anyone who skims. Which receiver to use. Why a named return can be quietly rewritten by a deferred closure. The famous typed-nil trap where a nil pointer wrapped in an error interface is somehow not nil. When to panic versus return. And the modern error machinery — %w, errors.Is, errors.As — that you are almost certainly using wrong if you learned Go before 1.13. Bug → why → idiomatic fix, every time, grounded in Meridian's payments backend. Read it twice. I'd hate for one of these to settle the books wrong on your watch. Let's go.

heading: Receivers
text: A method's receiver is the value the method is attached to — func (c Customer) Validate(). It can be a value (c Customer, a copy) or a pointer (c Customer, an address). Mistake 42 is not knowing which to reach for — and, worse, mixing both on the same type. A value receiver gets a copy of the value; mutations inside the method are local and vanish when it returns. A pointer receiver gets the address , so mutations persist on the original. Why it matters: pick value when the method only reads and the type is small; pick pointer when the method must mutate the receiver, when the struct is large (copying is wasteful), or when the type contains something that must not be copied (a sync.Mutex, or any embedded sync type). The hard rule: don't mix receiver kinds on one type — if any method needs a pointer, give them all pointer receivers, so the method set stays consistent. Here's the trap in miniature: Meridian's Account.Deposit looks like it works, but a value receiver copies the account, mutates the copy, and throws it away. The balance never moves. The method mutates the receiver, or the receiver embeds a type that can't be copied (sync.Mutex, sync.WaitGroup). A value receiver here is

heading: Named Results & Defer
text: The defer trap in four beats — arguments freeze at defer time, the call fires at return time: Two related features, two related mistakes. Named result parameters ( 43) let you name your return values in the signature; they're pre-initialized to zero and enable a naked return. Unintended side effects ( 44) is what happens when a named return interacts badly with defer. A named result parameter is a return value given a name in the signature: func get(addr string) (lat, lng float32, err error). It's a real variable, initialized to its zero value when the function begins, and a bare return (a naked return ) returns whatever those named results currently hold. Why it matters: names document the return order (which float32 is latitude?), and a deferred closure can read and modify the named result before the function actually returns — which is the whole basis of clean defer-based error handling. The cost: naked returns in a long function force the reader to track invisible state. Use named results when they genuinely add clarity — multiple results of the same type (so the names disambiguate order), or when you need a defer to touch the return value. Don't slap a name on a lone (err erro

heading: The Typed-Nil Trap
text: Mistake 45, and the most infamous gotcha in the language. You return a nil pointer as an error, your caller checks if err != nil — and it's true . A clean validation reports failure. A successful operation gets rolled back. An interface value is a pair : a type and a value . An interface is nil only when both are nil. A typed nil is a nil pointer (value = nil) carrying a concrete type (type = MultiError) — so when you assign it to an interface like error, the interface holds (type: MultiError, value: nil). The type half is non-nil, so the interface is not nil . Why it matters: returning a var m MultiError as an error makes err != nil true even when m is nil — your success path is reported as a failure. Fix: return the nil interface explicitly (return nil), never a typed nil pointer. Here is Meridian's customer validator. It returns nil errors for a clean customer — except it doesn't, because it returns a typed-nil MultiError. The demo prints output instead of dying, so you can see the lie: Why does it happen? A method is sugar for a function whose first argument is the receiver, and a nil pointer is a perfectly valid receiver — ( MultiError)(nil).Error() doesn't crash, it just oper

heading: io.Reader & Panic
text: Two design mistakes that sit on either side of "how do functions talk to the outside world." 46: taking a filename as input. A function that accepts a filename string and opens it itself is welded to the filesystem — you can't feed it an HTTP body, a string, a gRPC stream, or a test fixture without writing a temp file. Accept an io.Reader instead and the data source becomes the caller's problem. io.Reader is the one-method interface Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) — "give me bytes from somewhere." Accepting an io.Reader instead of a filename abstracts the source : a file ( os.File), an HTTP body (req.Body), an in-memory string (strings.NewReader), or a network socket all satisfy it. Why it matters: the function becomes reusable across every byte source and trivially testable — a unit test feeds strings.NewReader("...") with no temp file, no disk, no cleanup. Open the file at the edge of your program; pass the reader inward. 47: how defer evaluates its arguments and receiver. A defer's arguments — and its method receiver — are evaluated at the defer statement , not when the deferred call finally runs. So defer notify(status) captures status now , even though the call happens at re

heading: Wrapping & Checking Errors
text: The modern error machinery, and the three mistakes people make once they start using it ( 49, 50, 51). Since Go 1.13, fmt.Errorf with the %w verb wraps an error — adds context while keeping the original reachable. With %v it merely transforms — adds context but severs the chain. Wrapping an error packs it inside another error that still exposes the original via an Unwrap() method — produced by fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err) (the %w verb, since Go 1.13). The wrapper adds context ("charging account 42:") while the source error stays reachable down the chain, so callers can still match it with errors.Is/errors.As. Using %v instead transforms the error: you get the context string but the chain is cut and the source is gone. Why it matters: wrap (%w) when callers should be able to detect the underlying cause; transform (%v) when the cause is an implementation detail you don't want to leak as part of your API. always false} good= badLabel="%v (transform, chain cut)" goodLabel="%w (wrap, chain intact)" / Once you wrap, you must change how you check. The naive == for a sentinel and a type assertion for a typed error both look only at the outermost error — so wrapping breaks them. The right

heading: Handling Errors Once
text: The last cluster ( 52–54) is about discipline: handle each error exactly once , never ignore one silently, and never let a deferred Close swallow its own failure. 52: handling an error twice. Logging an error and returning it means it gets logged again by every caller up the stack — the same failure smeared across a dozen log lines, making one incident look like ten. Do one : either handle it here (log/recover and stop), or add context and return it for someone above to handle. Not both. the // caller logs it again, and so on. // One failure, N noisy log lines. if err != nil } good= badLabel="Log AND return (double noise)" goodLabel="Wrap and return (handle once)" / 53: not handling an error. The blank-identifier ignore — = doThing() or just dropping the returned error — discards information about a real failure. If you truly mean to ignore it, make that intent explicit and loud: assign to with a comment explaining why it's safe. Most of the time, "I'll ignore this" is "I forgot to handle this." 54: not handling defer errors. The classic: defer f.Close() throws away whatever Close returns. First, Credit mutates w.Cents — a value receiver would update a copy and discard it. Second, Wallet embeds a sync.Mutex, which must not be copied (copying a mutex breaks its locking; go vet flags it). Either reason alone forces a pointer receiver; together they make it unambiguous. And by the consistency rule, every method on Wallet should then take Wallet. This factory returns a typed-nil when no config is needed, so callers' if h != nil wrongly passes. Fix it. Returning h (a traceHook) when it's nil produces an interface of (type: traceHook, value: nil) — non-nil, so the caller's h != nil guard passes and then dereferences a nil pointer. The fix is to return the nil interface literally when there's nothing to return, so the interface's type half is also nil. desc: The concurrency mistakes that cause the worst production bugs: confusing concurrency with parallelism, assuming concurrency is always faster, choosing channels vs mutexes, data races vs race conditions and the Go memory model, context propagation and cancellation, goroutine leaks, nondeterministic select, notification and nil channels, channel sizing, WaitGroup and sync.Cond misuse, errgroup, data races from append, and the copied-mutex trap that go vet catches.
text: Here's the thing, sport. Everything in this course so far has been a warm-up. The mistakes were embarrassing — a shadowed variable, an append that clobbers its neighbor — but they were honest, single-threaded embarrassment. You could stare at the code and see the bug. Those days are over. This is concurrency. This is where a bug doesn't live in the code — it lives in the timing . The program runs ten thousand times and passes. It runs the ten-thousand-and-first time, on a busy production box, with two requests arriving a microsecond apart, and it corrupts a customer's balance, or leaks a goroutine every minute until the box falls over at 3 a.m. and nobody can reproduce it. These are the bugs that get people paged . I don't get paged. I'm going to teach you how to not get paged. We go bug → why → idiomatic fix, grounded in Meridian's backend, where two transfers racing on one account is not a thought experiment. I will make the interleavings so concrete you can watch them. Read every timeline. Run every snippet. The compiler will not save you here — and neither will hope. Let's go.

heading: Concurrency vs Parallelism
text: Before a single channel, the two foundational confusions. People use "concurrency" and "parallelism" as synonyms. They are not, and getting this wrong is why people reach for goroutines that make their code slower . Concurrency is about structure : dealing with many things at once — decomposing a program into independently-executing tasks (goroutines) that can make progress in overlapping time windows. Parallelism is about execution : doing many things at the same instant — tasks literally running on separate CPU cores. Concurrency is a design property; parallelism is a runtime property. Why it matters: concurrency enables parallelism but doesn't guarantee it. You can have concurrency on a single core (the scheduler interleaves goroutines), and a well-structured concurrent program will scale to more cores — but a badly-structured one won't, no matter how many cores you throw at it. As Rob Pike put it: concurrency is dealing with lots of things at once; parallelism is doing lots of things at once. The second confusion is the dangerous one for performance: assuming concurrency is always faster ( 56). Goroutines aren't free. Each one costs a stack, scheduling overhead, and — if it com

heading: Races & the Memory Model
text: The heart of the chapter. Two terms people use interchangeably — and they are not the same bug. A data race occurs when two or more goroutines access the same memory location concurrently , at least one access is a write , and there's no synchronization ordering the accesses. Data races are serious program errors: Go may report the race and terminate, and otherwise the memory model gives only limited guarantees about what a racing read may observe. A race condition is broader: the program's correctness depends on the relative timing or interleaving of goroutines, even if every individual access is properly synchronized. Why it matters: you can eliminate every data race (lock everything) and still have a race condition (the lost-update bug from the Scene — each access is atomic, but the read-modify-write as a whole isn't). Fixing data races is mechanical (synchronize). Fixing race conditions requires thinking about which interleavings are valid . Here's the lost-update race condition as an interleaving. Both goroutines synchronize each individual read and write — there's no data race — yet the result is still wrong, because the read and the write aren't atomic together : Now the loa

heading: #57 — channels or mutexes?
text: Both synchronize. Choosing wrong makes code awkward, not incorrect — but the awkwardness compounds. The rule of thumb: Use a sync.Mutex (or RWMutex) when goroutines access shared memory in place : a counter, a cache map, a balance. The data stays put; you serialize access to it. Smallest, fastest tool for "many goroutines touch one struct." Use a channel when you're passing data between goroutines, signaling, or orchestrating a pipeline/stages. "Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating" — when the design is about flow and ownership handoff, a channel is clearer than locks. ⚠ A channel is not a "better mutex." Using a buffered channel of size 1 as a lock works but is slower and obscures intent. Guarding a plain field? Reach for the mutex.

heading: Context & Cancellation
text: A context.Context is how Go propagates deadlines, cancellation, and request-scoped values across API boundaries and goroutines. Misunderstanding it ( 60) and propagating the wrong one ( 61) are two of the most common real-world concurrency bugs. A context carries three things down a call tree: a deadline (cancel automatically at a time / after a duration), a cancellation signal (cancel manually via a cancel func, e.g. the client disconnected), and request-scoped values (a request ID, an auth subject). The cancellation arrives as a channel: ctx.Done() returns a receive-only channel that's closed when the context is cancelled or its deadline passes; ctx.Err() then tells you which. Why it matters: any function doing blocking work (a DB query, an HTTP call, a long loop) should take ctx as its first argument and watch ctx.Done(), so when the caller gives up, the work stops instead of running to completion against a client that's already gone. The whole point is the select on ctx.Done() — it lets a blocking operation bail out the instant the context is cancelled: Now the subtle one — 61, propagating an inappropriate context. A request's context is cancelled when the request ends. So if y

heading: Goroutine Leaks
text: The signature concurrency bug. Goroutines are so cheap to start that people start them without a plan for when they stop ( 62) — and a goroutine that never stops is a leak. A goroutine leak is a goroutine that never terminates — it's blocked forever on a channel send/receive, a mutex, or an infinite loop with no exit. Why it matters: each leaked goroutine pins its stack (minimum 2 KB, growable) plus every variable it references on the heap plus any resources it holds open — a DB connection, an HTTP body, a file. A handler that leaks one goroutine per request leaks memory and file descriptors linearly with traffic , until the process is OOM-killed or runs out of FDs. Leaks don't crash on the test that creates them; they crash the box hours later under load, far from the cause. Every goroutine you start must have a guaranteed exit path. The classic leak: a goroutine sends on an unbuffered channel, but the receiver gave up early (returned on an error, or its context was cancelled). With no one to receive, the sender blocks on that send forever : Here's the leak and both fixes, made runnable. We detect the leak deterministically with a counter — no -race needed: For years, the most-ste

heading: Channels & select
text: Channels are the part everyone thinks they understand and quietly doesn't. Four mistakes that bite even experienced people. 64 — select with multiple ready channels is nondeterministic. People write the "priority" case first and assume it wins. It doesn't: when more than one case is ready, select picks one via a uniform pseudo-random selection . Ordering the cases means nothing. To get real priority, you nest selects: try the high-priority channel alone first (with a default), then fall back to selecting on both. 65 — use a notification channel (chan struct ) for signals with no data. When a channel exists only to signal an event — "shutdown now," "this is done" — the value carried is meaningless. Don't use chan bool (a reader wonders: does false mean something?). Use the empty struct. A notification channel is a channel used purely for signaling , carrying no data — declared chan struct . The empty struct struct occupies zero bytes , so the channel communicates only the fact of a send or, more often, a close . The idiom: close(done) to broadcast a one-time signal to every receiver at once (a closed channel is always receivable, immediately, for all goroutines). Why it matters: cha

heading: sync, WaitGroup & errgroup
text: The sync package and its friends. Powerful, and full of foot-shaped holes. 71 — misusing sync.WaitGroup: call Add in the parent, before the goroutine. A WaitGroup waits for n operations. The classic bug is calling wg.Add(1) inside the goroutine — which races with wg.Wait(): if Wait runs before the goroutine's Add, the counter is still 0 and Wait returns immediately, before the work is done. As of Go 1.25, wg.Go(func() ) is the idiom: it increments the counter before launching the goroutine and calls Done when the function returns, so the "Add too late" race is impossible by construction. The Go 1.25 vet waitgroup analyzer also flags an Add call inside a goroutine. 72 — forgetting sync.Cond. Sometimes you need to broadcast "this condition changed" to many waiting goroutines, repeatedly. A channel send goes to only one receiver (round-robin), so it can't fan out an update to N listeners. A close broadcasts but only once . sync.Cond is the right tool: waiters call Wait() (which atomically releases the lock and sleeps), and the updater calls Broadcast() to wake them all. 73 — not using errgroup. chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
desc: The final cluster of Go mistakes: standard-library traps (time.Duration units, time.After allocation churn, JSON and SQL pitfalls, unclosed HTTP/SQL/file resources, missing return after http.Error, timeout-less default HTTP client and server), testing mistakes (categorizing tests, the -race flag, table-driven tests, not sleeping, injecting a clock, httptest, accurate benchmarks), and optimization fundamentals (CPU caches and false sharing, struct alignment, stack vs heap and escape analysis, reducing allocations, inlining, pprof and the tracer, the GC, and running Go in containers with a container-aware GOMAXPROCS).
text: Here's the thing, sport. You've made it to the end. Ninety-nine mistakes behind you, and you're still standing — barely, but standing. I'm almost impressed. Almost. This is the final chapter of the gauntlet, and it's the one that separates people who write Go from people who run it in production at three in the morning when a payment gateway goes slow and your service quietly strangles itself to death. The standard library will hand you a loaded gun and a warm smile: a default HTTP client with no timeout, a time.After that allocates a fresh timer every loop iteration, a sql.Open that swears it connected and didn't. Then we get to testing — the thing separating engineers I trust from engineers I tolerate — and finally optimization , where you learn how the machine actually works: cache lines, escape analysis, the garbage collector, and why your beautiful Go binary thinks it has 64 CPUs inside a container that gave it one. We go bug → why → flawless fix, grounded in Meridian's backend, same as always. Twenty-six mistakes; we'll do the fourteen that matter most, and we'll do them right . This is the last time I get to watch you work. Don't embarrass us. Let's go.

chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
heading: Time & Resources
text: We open with the most embarrassing bug on this list — one a child could avoid, yet I see it in real ledgers. Mistake 75: passing a raw integer where a time.Duration is expected. A time.Duration is an int64 counting nanoseconds , not seconds. So time.Sleep(1000) sleeps 1000 nanoseconds — one microsecond — not one second. You must multiply by a unit constant: 1000 time.Millisecond, 5 time.Second. Why it matters: the bare literal compiles fine (it's an untyped constant convertible to Duration), so a config that reads timeout := 30 and passes it as 30 nanoseconds will look set and behave as if it's basically zero. Always attach a unit; never pass a naked number. Let's make the arithmetic undeniable. Run it: Now mistake 76 , the subtle one: time.After inside a hot loop. time.After(d) returns a channel that fires after d — convenient for a one-shot timeout. Since Go 1.23, an unreferenced abandoned timer can be garbage-collected before it fires, so this is no longer the old pre-Go 1.23 timer-retention trap. But every call still allocates a fresh timer. heading: JSON & SQL
text: Mistake 77: JSON traps. Three bite people constantly. First, type embedding can shadow MarshalJSON : if you embed a type that implements json.Marshaler, the outer struct inherits that method — so marshaling your wrapper silently calls the inner type's custom marshaling and drops your own fields. Second, time.Time carries a monotonic-clock reading that survives in memory but is stripped on marshal, so a round-trip through JSON produces a Time that is != the original (use .Equal, never ==). Third, decoding arbitrary JSON into map[string]any turns every number into a float64 — so a transaction amount of 100 comes back as float64(100), and large integer IDs lose precision past 2^53. A time.Time you read from time.Now() includes a monotonic-clock component. json.Marshal writes only the wall-clock part, so the value you unmarshal lacks the monotonic reading and compares unequal with == even though it's the same instant. The rule: compare instants with t1.Equal(t2), never t1 == t2. The same applies after any serialization round-trip (a DB write, a gob, a protobuf). As of Go 1.25 there's an experimental encoding/json/v2 (behind GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2) that fixes several long-standing v1 sharp

chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
heading: HTTP Pitfalls
text: Mistake 80: forgetting return after http.Error. http.Error writes a status code and body — but it does not stop your handler. Execution falls straight through to the rest of the function, which then tries to write a second response (Go logs http.superfluous...WriteHeader call) and, worse, runs the success logic you meant to skip. The fix is one keyword: return. And the big one, 81: the default HTTP client and server have no timeouts. You saw the Scene: a slow upstream and http.DefaultClient (timeout zero == infinite) means requests block forever, leaking a goroutine and a connection each. Same on the server side — the default http.Server has no ReadTimeout/WriteTimeout/IdleTimeout, so a slow-loris client that dribbles bytes can hold connections open indefinitely. Set timeouts on both sides. (These servers can't bind a port in the offline sandbox, so they're illustrative, not runnable.) &http.Client bounds the whole request (dial + write + read). For finer control, use a context.WithTimeout per request — it also propagates cancellation to the server. Set ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout on your http.Server. chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
heading: Testing
text: Now the part I care about most. Anyone can make code that works once . Tests are how you prove it keeps working — and the mistakes here are about leaving the safety off. Mistake 83: not enabling -race. Go ships a data-race detector. Run go test -race ./... and it instruments memory access to catch two goroutines touching the same variable without synchronization — the exact bug class from the concurrency chapter. It's not on by default (it slows execution and inflates memory), so a team that never passes -race is choosing not to find its races. Wire it into CI. Mistake 85: not using table-driven tests. When you test the same function across many inputs, a table of cases plus subtests beats copy-pasted test functions — you add a case by adding a row, and t.Run gives each case a name in the output. The logic is plain Go we can run offline (the sandbox has no go test, so we exercise the table from main): Two more that ruin test suites. Mistake 86: sleeping in unit tests. A time.Sleep(100 time.Millisecond) to "wait for the goroutine" is flaky (too short on a loaded CI box, slow everywhere else). chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
heading: Caches & Memory
text: Welcome to the machine. Optimization in Go starts with one truth: the CPU is fast , and main memory is slow — so performance is mostly about feeding the CPU from cache, not RAM. The CPU doesn't read one byte from memory — it reads a fixed-size block called a cache line (64 bytes on essentially every modern CPU) into fast L1/L2 cache. Why it matters: accessing data that's already in a loaded cache line is 100× faster than fetching from main memory. So memory layout determines speed . Iterating a contiguous slice is fast (each fetched line carries the next several elements); chasing pointers all over the heap is slow (each access may miss cache and stall the CPU). This is why a slice-of-values often crushes a slice-of-pointers for hot loops. Mistake 91: ignoring CPU caches — specifically, struct-of-slices vs slice-of-structs. If a hot loop only reads one field from each element, a slice of structs wastes cache: every loaded line drags along the fields you don't touch. Splitting into parallel arrays (one slice per field, "struct of arrays") packs the field you scan contiguously, so each cache line is all useful data. chTitle: Go Mistakes: Standard Library, Testing & Optimizations
heading: Allocations & Containers
text: The last cluster — squeezing allocations, understanding the GC, and the mistake that quietly halves throughput in every containerized Go service. Mistake 96: not reducing allocations where it counts. In a hot path, fewer allocations means less GC work and better cache behavior. Levers: reuse buffers with sync.Pool (a free-list of temporary objects), preallocate slices and maps with a size hint, pass values that don't escape, and shape APIs to write into a caller-provided buffer (AppendFormat-style) instead of returning a fresh allocation each call. Mistake 97: inlining — the compiler can paste a small function's body into its caller, erasing call overhead and enabling further optimizations (including keeping values on the stack). Tiny, hot functions inline automatically; giant ones don't (they exceed the inliner's budget), which is one more reason to keep hot functions small. A pool of reusable temporaries (e.g. bytes.Buffers in a request handler). Get borrows, Put returns. Cuts allocations on hot paths — but objects can be reclaimed by GC at any time, so only use it for transient , reconstructible objects, never for state you need to keep. chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
desc: The OWASP Top 10 from the attacker's side of the table: one real, publicly documented breach or bounty per category — First American (IDOR, 885M files), Adobe (3DES-ECB passwords), Heartland (SQL injection), Starbucks (race-condition design flaw), Tesla (open Kubernetes console), Equifax (CVE-2017-5638), Instagram (rate-limit bypass), event-stream (npm supply chain), Target (ignored alerts), Capital One (SSRF to cloud metadata) — each paired with the Go pattern that defends against it and the bug-hunter's recon-and-test methodology.
text: Here's the thing, sport. You can read the OWASP Top 10 as a checklist and forget it by lunch. Or you can read it the way the people who get paid to break things read it: as ten doors, each of which a real company left open, and each of which cost real money to close. That's this guide. Ten categories. Ten real, publicly documented cases — a title insurer that leaked 885 million files by letting you change a number in a URL, a password breach decrypted because the vendor encrypted instead of hashed, a $250-million card heist that started with one SQL injection, a researcher who minted free money on a coffee gift card with a race condition, and a bank that lost 106 million records to a single forged internal request. For each, I'll show you how a bug-hunter would find it, the exact mechanism, and the Go that would have shut the door. The Broken Access Control chapter went deep on category one; this guide is the panorama — every category, attacker-first, with the defense in your hands by the end. This is the appendix. No Meridian scaffolding, no narrative arc. Just the ten ways systems actually fall, the receipts to prove each one happened, and the code to make sure it's not yours nex

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: How to Hunt
text: Before the ten doors, the method. Every large-scale access-control haul — the Google one in the previous chapter, the bug-bounty careers built on the cases below — runs the same loop. It is not magic; it is bookkeeping applied adversarially. The asymmetry never changes: the hunter needs one missing check; the defender must assert every present one. The ten sections below each pair a real open door with the Go that keeps it shut — read them as both the offense to understand and the defense to ship. Every case in this guide is publicly documented — breach disclosures, DOJ indictments, Senate reports, researcher write-ups, vendor post-mortems. The primary sources are listed at the end so you can read the originals. Nothing here is invented; the figures are the ones in the public record. --

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A01 · Broken Access Control — First American Financial
text: Failure to enforce what an authenticated (or unauthenticated) principal may do — IDOR/BOLA, missing function-level checks, privilege escalation, cross-tenant access. OWASP's 1 risk since 2021. The Broken Access Control chapter covers the full taxonomy; this is the canonical breach. The case — First American Financial, 2019 ( 885,000,000 files). A real-estate title insurer published document images at URLs like …/DocumentLink?id=000000075. The ID was sequential , and there was no authentication on the page at all. Change the number up or down and you got someone else's document — and the documents held Social Security numbers, bank statements, driver's licenses, mortgage and tax records, and wire receipts. The lowest valid ID pointed at a 2003 transaction; the highest was around 885 million . A bug-hunter's entire exploit was a for loop over an integer. (Reported by Brian Krebs.) That is the loop from the last section in its purest form: recon found one document URL, mapping noticed the ID was sequential, probing as "not the owner" returned the file anyway, and the impact was the entire archive. Whenever an object ID appears in a URL, a hidden field, or a JSON body, the first test i

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A02 · Cryptographic Failures — Adobe
text: Sensitive data protected by the wrong primitive, a weak mode, a reused key, or — worst — not protected at all. Includes storing passwords reversibly, using ECB mode, hardcoding keys, and weak randomness (covered in Security for Financial Systems ). The case — Adobe, 2013 (153,000,000 accounts). Adobe stored passwords with 3DES in ECB mode , using the same key for every password , and stored each user's password hint in plaintext . Three compounding errors. ECB enciphers each block independently, so two users with the same password got the same ciphertext — and the plaintext hints ("name of my dog", "all zeros") gave researchers a crib. With one key, identical ciphertexts, and millions of known plaintexts, the community reconstructed a top-100 password list from the dump. The lesson isn't "use a stronger cipher." It's that passwords must never be encrypted at all — they must be slow-hashed with a salt, so there is no key to steal and nothing to decrypt. This snippet shows the ECB failure directly: identical plaintext blocks leak as identical ciphertext. --

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A03 · Injection — Heartland Payment Systems
text: Untrusted input interpreted as code or structure rather than data — SQL, OS command, LDAP, path traversal, XSS. The Application Security Baseline chapter (Part 2) covers the family; this is the most expensive instance. The case — Heartland Payment Systems, 2008 ( 130,000,000 cards). Albert Gonzalez and accomplices used SQL injection against web applications to get a foothold, then planted packet sniffers that captured card data flowing across the network. Across Heartland, Hannaford, 7-Eleven and others, the indictment put it at 130 million card numbers — at the time the largest such case in US history. Gonzalez was sentenced to 20 years. The entry point — the thing that turned a public website into network access — was untrusted input concatenated into a query. The mechanism is always the same: a value the user controls lands inside the query string , so the attacker ends the data and starts writing SQL. The fix is a parameterized query , where the template and the values travel separately and the driver guarantees the value is never parsed as SQL. "We escape the input" is not the fix — escaping is a blocklist you will eventually get wrong (encodings, edge cases, second-order inje

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A04 · Insecure Design — Starbucks Gift Cards
text: A flaw in the logic itself — not a missing patch but a design that is exploitable as built. Business-logic bypasses, missing rate limits as a design choice, and race conditions (TOCTOU: time-of-check to time-of-use) all live here. The case — Starbucks gift cards, 2015 (Egor Homakov). Homakov bought three $5 gift cards and found that transferring a balance between cards was a check-then-act sequence — check the source balance, credit the destination, debit the source — performed in a multi-threaded environment without a lock . By firing the transfer from two browser sessions at once, both passed the balance check against the same $5 before either debit landed, and the money was duplicated. He turned $15 into $20 of spendable balance and proved it by buying coffee. The flaw wasn't a bug in one line; it was the design — a non-atomic money movement. chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A05 · Security Misconfiguration — Tesla's Open Console
text: Insecure defaults, unnecessary features left on, missing hardening, or — the classic — an administrative interface exposed with no authentication. The infrastructure is fine; it was configured wide open. The case — Tesla, 2018 (RedLock). Tesla's Kubernetes administration console was reachable on the internet with no password . Inside it, attackers found AWS credentials, which opened an S3 bucket holding vehicle telemetry — and, for good measure, they installed cryptomining software (configured against an unlisted pool to dodge IP-based detection) and ran it on Tesla's cloud compute. No exploit, no CVE: a console that should have required authentication required none. The bug-hunter's recon here is a port scan and a browser. The defensive posture is the fail-closed rule from the access-control chapter, applied to infrastructure: an admin surface denies by default and is only reachable by an authenticated, authorized principal — and secrets never live inside the surface they protect. In application terms, your admin endpoints route through the same authorization that everything else does, with no "internal, so skip auth" bypass. Misconfiguration findings come from breadth, not depth:

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A06 · Vulnerable & Outdated Components — Equifax
text: Running a dependency with a known vulnerability — usually because nobody patched, nobody inventoried, or the scanner missed it. You didn't write the bug; you shipped someone else's. The case — Equifax, 2017 ( 147,000,000 people; CVE-2017-5638). A remote-code-execution flaw in Apache Struts 2 (CVE-2017-5638) was disclosed and patched on March 7, 2017 . Equifax's online dispute portal ran the vulnerable version and was not patched ; attackers exploited it from May through July and exfiltrated the personal data of roughly 147 million people. The brutal detail: Equifax did run a scan meant to find vulnerable Struts installs — and the scan failed to detect the vulnerable host. Knowing about a CVE is worthless if your inventory is wrong. For Go, this category is concrete and tractable, because the toolchain ships the defense: govulncheck cross-references your dependencies and the functions you actually call against the Go vulnerability database. govulncheck doesn't just match version numbers — it traces whether your code actually calls the vulnerable function. That cuts the noise that makes teams ignore scanners (the failure mode behind Equifax's missed scan: alerts nobody could act on).

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A07 · Identification & Authentication Failures — Instagram
text: Weak or bypassable proof of identity — credential stuffing, weak session handling, and brute-forceable verification codes. Often the rate limit exists but is keyed wrong. The case — Instagram, 2019 (Laxman Muthiyah, $30,000). Instagram's mobile password reset sent a six-digit code (a million possibilities) and rate-limited guesses. Muthiyah found the limit was effectively per source IP : of 1,000 requests from one IP, 250 went through and the rest were blocked. So he rotated IPs — a race condition plus thousands of source addresses — and showed that with enough IPs an attacker could burn through the entire code space inside the validity window and take over any account. Facebook paid $30,000 . The fix is to rate-limit the action against the target account , not the source IP, so rotating IPs buys the attacker nothing. --

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A08 · Software & Data Integrity Failures — event-stream
text: Trusting code or data whose integrity you never verified — a compromised dependency, an unsigned update, an unprotected CI/CD pipeline. The supply chain becomes the attack. The case — event-stream / flatmap-stream, 2018 (npm; targeted Copay). The maintainer of the popular npm package event-stream — 1,600 dependents — handed ownership to a stranger (right9ctrl) who'd offered to help maintain it. That account added a new dependency, flatmap-stream, carrying an AES-256-encrypted payload whose decryption key was the literal string "A Secure Bitcoin Wallet" — the description field in the package.json of exactly one target: the Copay bitcoin wallet. So the malware only activated inside Copay's build, where it tried to steal wallet keys from balances over 100 BTC. It sat undetected for 2.5 months . No server was hacked; the trust in a dependency was. Go's toolchain has strong integrity primitives — use them deliberately: Every module Go downloads is checked against a hash in go.sum, and GONOSUMCHECK is off by default so the public checksum database (sum.golang.org) verifies first use. That stops a tampered re-publish of an existing version. It does not stop a new malicious version you cho

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A09 · Security Logging & Monitoring Failures — Target
text: Not detecting, alerting on, or responding to an attack in progress — either because the events aren't logged, the alerts don't fire, or (the cruelest) they fire and no one acts. The case — Target, 2013 (40,000,000 cards; 70M PII records). Target had a FireEye detection system, monitored around the clock by a team in Bangalore. When the exfiltration malware was installed, it fired alerts — and the Bangalore team escalated to Target's security team in Minneapolis. No action was taken. The detection worked perfectly; the response did not. The US Senate Commerce Committee's "Kill Chain" analysis laid out every missed off-ramp. A09 is the only category where the tooling can be flawless and you still lose — because a log nobody reads and an alert nobody actions are not controls. This snippet shows the minimum: log security-relevant events and trip a distinct, escalatable alert at a threshold — the line that must page a human or trigger automation. Target proves the expensive lesson: buying the detection tool is the easy 10%. The 90% is the runbook, the on-call rotation, the alert routing that reaches someone awake, and the drills that prove they'll act. Log the security-relevant events (

chTitle: OWASP Top 10: A Bug-Hunter's Field Guide
heading: A10 · Server-Side Request Forgery — Capital One
text: Tricking a server into making a request the attacker controls — typically to reach internal services the attacker can't reach directly, most dangerously the cloud metadata endpoint at 169.254.169.254, which hands out IAM credentials. The case — Capital One, 2019 (106,000,000 applicants; Paige Thompson). A misconfigured WAF was vulnerable to SSRF. The attacker made it request the AWS instance metadata service at http://169.254.169.254/…/iam/security-credentials/, which returned temporary credentials for the WAF's IAM role (ISRM-WAF-Role). Those credentials could list and read S3 buckets — and out came the personal data of 106 million credit-card applicants across the US and Canada. One forged internal request, pointed at the metadata IP, escalated a web-layer bug into a full data breach. The defender's job is to validate the destination of every outbound request and block the metadata IP and all internal ranges. --

Bug 1 is the Capital One shape — an unvalidated outbound fetch that reaches 169.254.169.254. Bug 2 is the First American shape — read any record by naming its ID. desc: Why Go is the language of the recon toolchain (nuclei, httpx, ffuf, subfinder are all Go), and how to build your own for authorized testing: a bounded concurrent HTTP prober with a worker pool, an in-scope guard so you never touch an unauthorized host, a token-bucket rate limiter, response classification, and the authorization-matrix fuzzer that automates the two-user test against your own API — every example hermetic and runnable with httptest.
text: Here's the thing, sport. The field guide showed you ten doors and the Go that bolts each one shut. This chapter flips the workbench around: now you build the tools — the scanners and fuzzers that find the unbolted door before someone less friendly does. And there's a reason every one of those tools you've heard of is written in Go. nuclei, httpx, subfinder, naabu, katana, ffuf, gobuster, amass — the entire modern recon toolchain is Go. Not by accident. Goroutines make ten thousand concurrent probes a dozen lines of code; a single static binary cross-compiles and drops onto any box with no runtime; the standard library ships a production HTTP client and a test server in the box. You're going to build the core of that toolkit yourself: a bounded concurrent prober, a scope guard that makes it impossible to touch a host you're not authorized to test, a rate limiter that keeps you a good citizen, and the authorization-matrix fuzzer that automates the two-user test against your own API. Every example here runs in-process against httptest — hermetic, runnable, no network, nothing out of scope. Build the tools on your own targets first; that's where mastery starts. Everything in this chapt

heading: Why Go for Tooling
text: Three properties make Go the default for security tooling, and you've already met all three elsewhere in this book — here they line up perfectly for a scanner. Ten thousand concurrent HTTP probes is a worker pool over a channel — a pattern you wrote in Background Jobs & Scheduling . No async/await ceremony, no thread-pool tuning. Goroutines are cheap; the runtime schedules them onto cores for you. GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build produces a single file with no runtime dependency. Drop it on a recon VPS, a container, a stranger's box — it just runs. Python needs an interpreter and a venv; Go needs nothing. net/http is a production client and server; net/http/httptest is a real in-process server for tests; net, crypto/tls, encoding/json, regexp are all standard. You build a scanner with zero third-party dependencies. Be honest about the tradeoff: for a quick one-off exploit PoC you'll iterate faster in Python's REPL with requests. Go's edge is tools you keep — fast, concurrent, distributable, the ones that run across thousands of targets in an authorized engagement. Most practitioners use both: Python to prove a single bug, Go to build the scanner that finds the next thousand. This c

heading: The Scope Guard
text: We build this first , on purpose. Before a single probe leaves your tool, it must pass a check that the target is in scope. This is the difference between a security tool and a crime. A scope is the explicit set of hosts, domains, or IP ranges you are authorized to test — defined by an engagement contract, a bug-bounty program's policy, or "it's my own server." An in-scope guard is a function every outbound request routes through that returns the request only if its destination is in scope, and refuses otherwise. Built right, it makes touching an unauthorized host not a matter of discipline but a structural impossibility. The guard is an allow-list , never a block-list — default deny, exactly like the authorization rule from the Broken Access Control chapter. A host is in scope only if it matches an entry; everything else is refused. We match the exact apex domain and any subdomain of it. The suffix trick (acme.test.evil.com) is a real bypass that has burned real scanners and real SSRF filters — strings.HasSuffix(host, "acme.test") is true for it. The fix is matching "."+domain, or parsing to the registrable domain with a public-suffix list (golang.org/x/net/publicsuffix) for produ

heading: A Concurrent Prober
text: Now the engine: hit many paths at once, bounded so you don't melt the target or your own NIC. This is the worker-pool pattern — a fixed number of goroutines pulling jobs off a channel — applied to HTTP probing. Bounded concurrency is the key word: unbounded goroutines is how you DoS the very thing you were asked to test gently. Every probe routes through inScope from the previous section — out-of-scope paths are skipped before any request is made. --

heading: Rate Limiting
text: Bounded concurrency caps how many requests run at once ; a rate limiter caps how many run per second . Both matter: a polite scanner respects the target's capacity (and the program's rules), and a token bucket is the idiomatic way to do it in Go with nothing but the standard library. A token bucket holds up to N tokens. Each action consumes one token; tokens refill at a fixed rate. If the bucket is empty, the action waits for the next refill. It permits short bursts (up to the bucket size) while bounding the long-run average rate — the model behind golang.org/x/time/rate and most API rate limits. You can build a serviceable one from a buffered channel and a time.Ticker. The hand-rolled bucket is here to show the mechanism — buffered channel + ticker is a genuinely useful pattern. For real tools use golang.org/x/time/rate: it gives you a Limiter with Wait(ctx), Allow(), and Reserve(), fractional rates, and context-aware cancellation, all carefully tested. The concept is identical; the library handles the edge cases (clock skew, bursts, cancellation) you'd otherwise reimplement. --

heading: Classifying Responses
text: A scanner that prints ten thousand raw HTTP responses is useless — you'd never read them. The signal comes from classification : mapping each response to a semantic outcome so you can filter to the handful worth a human's attention. This is the exact step the field guide's methodology called out — "don't eyeball responses, classify them." --

heading: The Authz-Matrix Fuzzer
text: The payoff. The whole field guide kept returning to one assertion — the two-user test : a different user, fully authenticated, must be refused your resource. This is the tool that runs it automatically against your own API, for every actor × endpoint combination. Point it at your service in CI and a missing ownership check becomes a failing test instead of a breach. Of everything in this chapter, the authz-matrix fuzzer is the tool to put in your own CI today. It's the offense methodology from the field guide pointed inward: enumerate your endpoints, run each as owner / stranger / unauthenticated, assert the expected allow/deny. The attacker has to find one missing check; this asserts every one of yours on every push. Generate the matrix from your OpenAPI/protobuf spec and a new endpoint without authorization tests fails the build. --

heading: Exercises
text: Build the toolkit. Each of these is a component you'd actually keep. Write InScope(rawURL string, allow []string) bool that parses the URL, lowercases the host, and returns true only if the host equals an allowed domain or is a subdomain ("."+domain). Prove it refuses the suffix trick acme.test.evil.com against scope ["acme.test"]. The leading dot in "."+a is the entire defense against the suffix trick: acme.test.evil.com does not end in .acme.test, so it's refused. Write Classify(status int) string returning "accessible" (2xx), "protected" (401/403), "missing" (404), "errored" (5xx), or "other". Demonstrate it on a spread of status codes. A status-code switch is the cheapest, most reliable first-pass triage. Body-content signatures (panic traces, bucket names) refine it into a "leaks internals" flag. heading: The Lab
text: Time to wire the toolkit together — with the safety gate that makes it a security tool and not a liability. I've written a mini scanner with two defects: its prober doesn't route through the scope guard (so it would happily hit out-of-scope hosts), and its classifier mislabels server errors. Fix both so the self-check passes: every out-of-scope target must be refused before any request, and a 500 must classify as "errored". Fully sandboxed — the only "network" is an in-process httptest server, and the scope list is fixed.
